en: Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
In the year Renzi of the Huangqing era, I sat together with the monk Prajñāśrī of Gaochang in the summer at Mount Lingshi in India.
We read and translated the Tiantai *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) together every day. This was followed by Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu.
The monk Yigong of Duanya occasionally came to visit me.

During our conversations, he often recounted how he had previously received the essential teachings of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from Master Wen, a lecturer in Guansi, and that he had also translated it into the Uyghur script and phonology.
At that time, Dujiang Xuegong possessed a copy of the *Lengyan jizhu* (Collected Commentaries on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) from Cángtóngzhōu.

Because Śrī was summoned to court, he wished to ensure that the Emperor would certainly hear of it and have it carved onto printing blocks for circulation; thus, he took it with him as he returned north. However, he ultimately failed to fulfill this wish. It has come down to the present day.
The Layman Ryō wished to carve and distribute this sutra, yet at first he could not determine which version constituted the superior text.
He recalled that in the past, while at the Scripture-Receiving Chamber in Ling-shi Mountain, Master Xue had recounted the time when Śīlabhadra transmitted the text to him.
Consequently, he specially sent a letter to inquire with the Upādhyāya of the White Lotus Court, Master Yugō. The Master personally traveled to Wu Town in Jiahe to seek it out.
At Mijin Temple, I inquired and learned that the late bhikṣu Yuangu (圓具) had constantly served as an attendant to Master Jǔ of Dǐngshān and studied under Master Zìwénxūn.
Indeed, his mastery of the teachings possessed a profound lineage and tradition; he left behind a handwritten manuscript of the annotated scriptures.
These were identical to the texts brought back to the north by Śrīmitra, which I have now specially dispatched eastward for transmission.
Relying upon these [sources], I have once again organized the treatment [of the subject] and slightly revised it, thereby completing this work.

Thus we know that the circulation of the scriptures in the world is also related to the course of destiny and fortune. Yet, more than one hundred and twenty years have passed since the Master of Tongzhou departed;
his book remains extant in the Three Wu regions and has spread throughout—
In the Imperial Capital, it ultimately could not be carved into printing blocks.

It is only now that it has been successfully published as a woodblock edition in the home of the lay practitioner Master Wang of Siming, so that it may be widely disseminated throughout the realm. How could this be a mere coincidence?
I have carefully recorded its origins so that those who examine it may believe in the existence of the specific conditions of the time.

In the third year, the year of Dingchou, on the day of the winter solstice, at my hermitage where there is originally nothing to be cultivated or maintained, I have respectfully completed the postscript to the *Lengyan Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).

With profound reverence, I pay homage to the World-Honored One, the Tamer of Men: his nature-awareness is wondrously luminous, and his fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous—truly inconceivable. May this merit be as vast as the original vessel.
He was the son of King Śuddhodana, born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; thus he was named Ānanda (Joyful One).

As a kinsman born to attend upon the Buddha and as his youngest brother, he followed the Buddha into the homeless life. Relying on the Buddha’s compassion and affection, he held extensive learning in high regard but was negligent in cultivating the outflows-free path.

Having merely entered the first fruit of realization, when compared to the Mahāyāna perspective, he had cultivated only a provisional cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). He encountered...
King Prasenajit’s father, whose name was Guangying (Extensive Preparation), had prepared exquisite delicacies to welcome the World-Honored One and extend an invitation to the assembly of pure monks.

Because Ānanda had gone to attend to another donor, he went alone to beg for alms. Passing by the home of a master of illusionist arts, the daughter of Mātanga used the "Golden Head and Yellow Hair" faction of the *pūrvavideha* (First Brahma) spell to draw him into her chamber.
Initially, the First Brahma spoke of the practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Śaṃkara discussed the doctrine of *tattva* (ultimate reality) and his false reckoning of throwing ashes upon oneself; furthermore, he mentioned the worldly and heterodox teacher Mātanga, who practiced illusory arts.

He intended to destroy Ānanda’s *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four announcements). [The opponent argued that] the essence of the precepts—neither form nor mind—is maintained by those who are neither fat nor emaciated;
this is but one precept among the eighty thousand practices. The Sūtra states that because Ānanda’s mind was pure, he had not yet fallen [into transgression].

Because they were drowning, the Buddha emitted light from the crown of his head and manifested a transformation body to proclaim the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-samuccaya-sitātapatrā-guhya-gāthā-sūkṣma-mantra-hṛdaya*.
This is the essential core of all mantras. The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī:
He went forth with this mantra to protect [them], extinguishing their evil. He exhorted Ānanda and Mātaṅgī to return to the Buddha’s presence.
This mantra-heart transcends the realm of ten thousand kinds of adornments and is named the King of Śūraṃgama;
through the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits, its great samādhi and majestic virtue crush all delusions and karma. It is also called the Vajra-King Samādhi.
The essence of the Dharma is all-pervasive and vast, without boundaries; it is also called Mahāvaipulya (Great Extensive). It is free from all defilement and is thus called Padmarāja (Lotus King).
It gives birth to wholesome dharmas and is thus called Buddhamātṛ-dhāraṇī (Dhāraṇī of the Mother of Buddhas). Its nature is fundamentally luminous;

the seven locations—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—are themselves the originally awakened Bodhisattvas, the primordial and pure essence of Nirvāṇa. Sentient beings have lost their way regarding this eternal abiding.
This principle [is such that] the continuity of birth and death revolves without end. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"They do not know that birth, cessation, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the eternally abiding and wondrous gate, the immovable and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness. It further says: "The five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
A practitioner of *dhyāna* should take it as their primary task to clarify this essence. This nature of the Sūtra is the body of original enlightenment; how could it be merely pervasive?
It merely completes sentient beings. As for the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the lands, and space—not even a single pebble or a speck of dust is not fully endowed [with it].

Why is this? It is because the subtle, tranquil, and pure essence of *śamatha*—the fruit of the myriad practices perfected through the diligent cultivation of all Buddhas over kalpas—is the entirety of the awakened body manifesting its function.
It manifests infinite bodies to respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust, turning [the wheel of Dharma].
The Great Dharma Wheel subdues and brings into submission all Māras and heretics without exception.

Regarding the cultivation and realization of the causes and effects of the Mahāyāna, there is no possibility that one can sit at the site of enlightenment and achieve wondrous, perfect awakening without upholding this samādhi.
Any teaching that fails to accord with the essential nature of this sutra and its mantras is the speech of Pāpīyas; otherwise, it is a māra-essence possessing a person.
To verbally recite the sutras and Dharma is like boiling sand and stones for a thousand kalpas in hopes of obtaining rice; it can never be achieved.

How much more so regarding the retention of various mantras—all of which are aids to correct cultivation. For one who constantly and diligently maintains this mantra-heart of the sutra, the primary and auxiliary practices will both advance within the perfect contemplation and conduct.
In the realm of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), there is neither Buddha nor birth. Yet, the gates of practice arise, wherein there are precepts and meditative concentration.

Ranks are established according to the teachings so that those who hear and see may emulate one another, thereby avoiding the arising of arrogance or despondency. As for the complete and sufficient sequence of these ranks, none surpasses the *Yingluo* (The Necklace).

These are still but provisional expedients. Only in this sutra is the complete and perfect stage fully prepared; from the initial Stage of Dry Wisdom up to the Stage of Dedication, it opens forth the four roots of goodness.

At the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the consecration is set forth, metaphorically likened to a Wheel-Turning King taking the waters of the four oceans to pour over the crown of the crown prince’s head, signifying his assumption of royal office.
Now, at the stage of partial realization, the water of Buddha-wisdom is poured upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, signifying his assumption of the rank of Dharma-King.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, one attains perfect enlightenment at the very first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); in the *Daśabhūmika*, the assumption of office (*abhiṣeka*) is first explained at the tenth stage.
Although various texts each have their own assertions, their underlying principles converge on a single path. This sutra enumerates fifty-seven stages;

however, whether it refers to the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*), the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, or the stages of the "Noble Ones" (*ārya*) as described in the *Abhidharmakośa*, one must certainly understand the meanings of "subduing and severing," "true and semblance," and the "borrowed names. As for... [text continues]
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* explains that by cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one perceives the Buddha-nature. Jingxi’s precept states:

"Not recognizing the identity or difference between names and their referents is a great affliction for those studying the Buddhist teachings. In the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, the ten wholesome actions are distinguished as transcending the three realms of suffering;

this is identical to the merit described in the present sutra regarding the three transformations, the overlapping of the one, ten, hundred, and thousand, and the expansion or contraction of the six sense faculties. Furthermore, these must be reconciled with the treatises on the Dharma.

Regarding Master Huihua’s doctrine of the "Six Sense Organs Purified" (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*) and the "Perfection of the Source" (*zongyuan*): were it not for a profound investigation of the scriptures and teachings, how could this be easily spoken?
He repeatedly examined the meaning of the mind and the discernment of vision, citing the texts concerning the beating of drums and bells and the tying of a layered flower-towel.

Although these accounts follow a sequential order, they are all uniformly intended to clarify the ultimate, perfect principle of the nature. Furthermore, when the Buddha questioned his great disciples...
They realized the eighteen realms and entered samādhi, each claiming to have attained the Buddha’s empowerment.
Mañjuśrī distinguished and clarified [the true path], excluding all twenty-four practitioners, including Mahāsthāmaprāpta;

he alone singled out Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, who, eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges ago, beheld Avalokiteśvara Buddha and entered samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, uniquely manifesting perfect penetration.
Explanation: Kātyāyana first attained realization upon hearing the Buddha’s voice; Avalokiteśvara likewise entered through hearing.

Were it not for the analytical exposition of the two paths—the *ālayavijñāna* and the *pariniṣpanna*—how could the profound meaning be clarified? Do not assume that the twenty-four sages each cited their past causes merely to be selected [for this assembly], as if they were part of the provisional gate of sequential practice (*pravṛtti*) found in the *Avataṃsaka*.
This is because the present Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic light, stands in contrast [to them].
"O Great Beings, each one has individually demonstrated the perfect principle (*yuanli*).

Furthermore, if a sutra states that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha and serve as the direct cause (*zhengyin*), and the twenty-four masters hear this discernment and immediately understand it to be the perfect teaching (*yuanzong*) as the revealing cause (*liaoyin*), then they shall next, without interruption, abide in this path amidst the three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle details.
Having reached the point of establishing the altar site, they shall rejoice and snap their fingers."
The scattering of flowers is entirely due to the causal seeds. Regarding the long stream of water that flows forth, the world takes it as a source of goodness;

thus, this sutra is judged to properly belong to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), while also clarifying the Sudden and Perfect teachings. To claim otherwise would be a contradiction of one's own words. Someone may ask:

"To which of the five periods and four teachings does this sutra belong? You must answer with precision. (It definitely belongs to the Perfect Teaching and is categorized within the Vaipulya division. As for the bhikṣu of the nature of Ānanda...

For those with capacities such as the bhikṣuṇīs and others, the benefits obtained before and after this sutra differ; ultimately, however, they take the principle of the perfect non-arising nature as the formal conclusion of the benefit.
For subsequent eons as numerous as motes of dust, they shall propagate and disseminate this sutra, and by themselves protect and obtain this Dharma.
Eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *koṭi* Bodhisattvas, retinues of Vajragarbha-rāja, attend him day and night.
If a Māra should come to invade the samādhi of a virtuous person, he shall strike down its head with a precious vajra, reducing it to mere dust.
This sutra has been explained; the many who have recorded the commentary are from the Southern Lake of Siming. I...
The Dharma Master Wufa of An collected the commentaries of various schools and collated them, taking the edition of the *Tongzhou Jijie* as his primary basis.

He privately added some refinements and abridgments. Together with this preface, the lay devotee Yuanming of the Wang clan from Taiyuan, a faithful donor, has with sincere reverence provided pure funds for carving these woodblocks, so that they may be widely circulated.
Within the scripture, it is further stated that one should write [this] upon birch bark, paper, or silk, and place it [in a stupa].

Even for a single person or a single family, one may obtain most profound and wholesome benefit; yet compared to the present effort of transcribing and publishing this work, my two aspirations are exceptionally difficult to place in the same category.
I now follow suit in offering this humble account, which is like a mote of dust added to a mountain or a drop of water joined to the sea.
In the autumn of the *bǐzǐ* year of the Zhìyuán era, the bhikṣu Ziwén of Bǎoyún [Temple] burned incense and prostrated while writing this preface to the *Commentary on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra*.
The Elder of the Yellow Face said: "If there is a person who gives rise to the true mind and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish."

[The Master] passed away. Zen Master Wuzu Yan said: "If there were a single person who gave rise to true realization and returned to the source, the void of the ten directions would be struck and bumped [by them].
These words are all spoken out of compassion; they are talk for those who have descended into the weeds.

Layman Jingliang Wang Yuanming of Siming, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, said of himself regarding the section on the investigation of the mind and the discernment of vision: "I realized that the mind has no locus of origin, and I fully understood vision."
This is not a matter of eloquence. I have re-carved these blocks to circulate this sutra; though it may be like adding flowers to brocade, it is nonetheless like placing grit in one’s eye.
What more could I say amidst the thousand crags? The sutras have their own masters, and the treatises have their own masters—how can they blame this old monk?
Respectfully inscribed by Yuanchang of Fulong Mountain.
Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:

True jade is flawless, yet its beauty cannot be revealed without the diligent effort of grinding and polishing. Fine gold is free of dross, yet its brilliance cannot be manifested without the labor of the furnace and hammer.
The ultimate teaching is without words, yet it cannot be fully elucidated without the breadth of commentary and exposition.
One cannot reach its profound depths. With a single-mindedness free from signs, one cannot exhaust its subtlety without relying on deep investigation.

Once one has obtained the exquisite beauty of precious gems and refined gold, one will surely attain nobility; thereafter, one can relieve the destitute without exhaustion, which constitutes the perfection of virtue.
Likewise, once one has attained the profound subtlety of the teachings that accords with the mind, one will immediately realize sagehood. However...
Later, he opened up the benefits for all ordinary beings without exception; this is what constitutes the perfection of the Way.

Now, the Master Wang of Siming, the Layman Wuyuanming, has internally clarified his single mind and externally disciplined his manifold practices. He joyfully sought the collected transmission of the true teaching of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*.

He then donated his own funds to carve the woodblocks so that it might endure for future generations. His efforts were directed toward making it easy for readers to discern the truth without confusion and allowing seekers to find it with ease;

he hoped that through this, all might equally realize the Perfect Wisdom (Samyak-saṃbodhi), and only then did he cease from his vow. Alas! This is like the dialogue between the Buddha Śākyamuni and Ānanda.

The twenty-five Bodhisattvas have recounted their realization of perfect penetration; the sublime assembly remains as solemn as ever. How could there be even the slightest interval between then and now?
You should therefore increase your faith and remain diligent.
On the ninth day of the ninth month in the third year of the Zhizhen era, the cyclical year being Dingchou,
Śramaṇa Shi Qieliāo, abbot of Jinshan Chan Monastery in Zhenjiang Prefecture,
bows his head and writes this preface to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* on the Great Buddha-Crown.
Composed by the Sōng dynasty monk Beifeng Zongyin;
briefly recorded by Benwu, the fourth-generation descendant of Beifeng.
Regarding the National Teacher Zhiyi of Tiantai: whenever he commented upon any sutra, he invariably began with the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*). This [Lengyan]...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* takes the person and the dharma as its title; the eternally abiding true mind as its essence; the perfect and penetrating wondrous samādhi as its thesis;
the reversal of delusion and return to the truth as its function; and the most sublime *amṛta* (clarified butter) as its doctrinal manifestation.

First, regarding the explanation of the title: the title reads, "The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas," consisting of twenty characters.

Regarding the explanation of the title as stated by the Master of Wuxing: the first nineteen characters constitute the specific name (*biemíng*), while the two characters "Sūtra" (*jīng*) constitute the general name (*tōngmíng*).
Within the explanation of the specific name, there are further two parts; first, the three characters "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (*Dàfódǐng*) are—

The name of the secret mantra consists of sixteen characters, such as "Tathāgata," which are its manifest names. Regarding the first, the name of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Secret Mantra, there are two interpretations.
The first is an interpretation based on what was spoken by the manifested response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is because the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Radiance Mahā-sitātapatra Unsurpassed Divine Mantra; this is the Tathāgata’s Unseen Summit Mark... [and so forth].
It is the Mind-Buddha. From the crown of his head, radiance issues forth as he sits upon a precious lotus flower, and it is from this that the Heart-Mantra is spoken.
By this one may verify that the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Secret Mantra of the True Eye states: "The Tathāgata’s Unseen Crown-Mark is the Unconditioned Mind-Buddha, from whose crown radiance issues forth.

Therefore, we know that the word "Buddha" (佛) refers to the Nirmāṇakāya of Śākyamuni, while the word "Crown" (頂) contains the meaning of the Saṃbhogakāya of Śākyamuni; thus, it is the [Saṃbhogakāya] which is capable of...
Regarding the person who speaks it: because the response-transformation (nirmāṇa) is itself the Dharma, it is called the "unconditioned Buddha of the mind.
To be complete, one should say "Siddhārtha," etc.; the title here is abbreviated. Second, the explanation based on the veneration of all Buddhas:

according to the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, there is a dhāraṇī named "Tathāgatoṣṇīṣa. That mantra was not spoken by a Buddha upon the crown of his head; rather, it proceeds from the fruit [of Buddhahood].

That which people revere is called a "name" (*nāman*). How much more so now, when we repeatedly speak of the Buddha-peak mantra (*buddhoṣṇīṣa-mantra*) and further state that this mantra is also called the "Tathāgata’s Peak.
If this is the case, then "peak" (*uṣṇīṣa*) takes on the meaning of being honored and held in high esteem; it does not take on the characteristic of being invisible.

Upon detailed examination, this single interpretation is appropriate both in its phrasing and its meaning. As stated prior to the title: "It is not a metaphor but the Dharma itself," and it also pertains to the person [the Buddha], because it is revered.
To take "wearing" as the "crown" refers to the Dharma; to take the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) as the "crown" refers to the person. The Sub-commentary by the Abbot of Fajie states:
"The scriptural text does not say 'just like the crown of a Buddha. The Supplement by Yunjian states: "The scriptural text has never used the Buddha’s crown as a metaphor.
Thus, the interpretation of the title by Ren Falü of Wuxing is indeed based on a standard authority. ○ Second, "Tathāgata," etc.

The term "manifesting" (*khyāna*) also has two interpretations. First, regarding the realization and attainment of the person who is the fruit: it manifests the Dharma with which one accords. The Tathāgata is the person who is the fruit;

the "secret cause" (*guhyahetu*) refers to the sublime practice of the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*). This is not different from the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost of all practices.

Since this samādhi has already been realized by the Tathāgata, the four characters "secret cause, cultivation, and realization" (*guhyahetu-xiuzheng*)—of which the first three characters belong to [the preceding category]—are explained as follows.
The "cause" (hetu) and the "realization" (sākṣātkriyā) belong to the category of the fruit (*phala*). Yet, both this cause and fruit are the means by which one accords with [the truth].

Only the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is precisely the object to be accorded with. Second, regarding the person who acts as the cause: the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*) demonstrate the means by which one accords;

these are the bodhisattvas, namely those who are currently practicing and training throughout the ten directions in the present and future. The "myriad practices" are the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) possessed by them; their essence is...

The Middle Way encompasses all phenomena without exception. Thus, a sutra states: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices" (and so forth).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Śūraṅga means 'all matters are completed'; 'sema' (yan) means 'firmness.
Because all things are ultimately completed and one attains firmness, it is named Śūraṅgama. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śūraṅgama..."
This [term] means, in the language of Qin, "skillfully distinguishing characteristics. It refers to knowing the number, depth, and subtlety of the various characteristics of samādhis.
For example, it is like a great general who knows the strength and numbers of his troops. When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, various afflictions and the like cannot destroy it.

It is like the "treasure of the military commander" possessed by a Cakravartin King; wherever he goes, no one dares to cause destruction. Therefore, it is also translated as [the aforementioned term].

This marks the conclusion of the subject matter. ○ Second, the explanation of the general name, which is the character *jīng* (sūtra). While its specific name differs from other sections, its general name is shared by all scriptures.
The Sanskrit term is *sūtra*; here it is translated as "Scripture of Accord" (*qi jīng*). Regarding "scripture" (*jīng*): it is glossed as "dharma" and glossed as "constant."

Based on these verbal expressions, which clarify and manifest the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they cause sentient beings to give rise to understanding; therefore, they are called "Dharma" (*dharma*).

All Buddhas speak in this same way, and thus it is called "constant" (*nitya*). The above is the explanation of the name, which follows entirely the *Wuxing xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Title by Wuxing) and does not adopt the theory of Gushan that the title comprises three elements.
This is fully detailed in the "Explanation of the Title. The explanation of the name is complete.
Second, regarding the definition of its essence: following the interpretation of Gushan, the essence is taken to be the eternally abiding true mind (*nitya-satya-citta*).
At the beginning of the main body of this sutra, the Buddha tells Ānanda:

"You should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have had their births and deaths continue in succession because they do not know the essence of the eternally abiding true mind, which is pure and luminous by nature. They employ various false thoughts; these thoughts..."
It is true. Therefore, there is cyclic existence. The scripture explicitly states that "the eternally abiding true mind is a body of intrinsic purity and luminosity.

How could one not take this as the essence of the scripture? One should know that the primary purport of this sutra, relying on the occasion of Ānanda, is precisely to reveal for all sentient beings the eternally abiding true mind—the body of intrinsic purity and luminosity—that serves as the ground for cultivation. Since the meaning of the text is thus manifest, it may be trusted and accepted.
Furthermore, since the eternally abiding true mind is both eternal and true, it clearly manifests as the essential nature (*dharmatā*).
If Wuxing separately identifies the essence as the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, claiming this is what the sutra emphasizes, the *Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes) states:

"One should know that the sutra text refers to it as a 'store' (*garbha*) because it seeks to trace back to the awakened mind of the causal stage. The primary purport of this sutra is precisely to reveal the eternity of the causal ground."
The essence of the true mind is a nature of pure luminosity, which is fully realized by all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas;
this is the Tathāgata’s unique establishment of the substance of the mind as the primary substance of the sūtra. The exposition of the substance is complete.

Third, regarding the clarification of the primary tenet (*zong*): The *Gushan Shu* states, "This sutra takes the wondrous samādhi of perfect penetration as its primary tenet. A "tenet" (*zong*) refers to that which is essential.

Although the true mind is fundamentally quiescent, those who are deluded do not realize this; therefore, one must cultivate the illusory-like *samādhi* to penetrate the primordial quiescence of all phenomena.
At the beginning of the sutra, Ānanda requests, saying, "I regret that since time immemorial I have been solely devoted to much hearing (*bahuśruta*)."

Because they had not yet fully perfected the power of the Way, they earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means to attain the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that bring about the realization of Bodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, in successive stages, revealed and instructed them, causing them to understand that the true mind is fundamentally such that all phenomena are like illusions.
Although these were explained through various distinct names, they were merely an extensive exposition of the wondrous samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama*. [End of] Cessation.
All deluded thoughts are thus transcended, reaching the state where all phenomena are quiescent; contemplating only the nature of the mind is termed "wondrous concentration" (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the wondrous concentration of universal penetration is taken as the primary tenet. (Text) To examine this wondrous concentration of universal penetration:

it specifically adopts the "ear-faculty's universal penetration" of Avalokiteśvara, while comprehensively encompassing the practices of concentration elucidated throughout the entire sutra. Its meaning is most correct. The *Supplement* (*Buyi*) also states that this is the *Śūraṅgama*.

The wondrous samādhi is the central tenet. Ānanda requested it by means of the three types of cessation. From the beginning to the end of the sutra, what is discussed is not emptiness or the provisional, but rather the teaching of the Middle Way;
this constitutes the essential core. This was also adopted and utilized by the Master of the Dharma-realm Hermitage (Fajie Anzhu), who took the excellence of Mount Gu (Gushan) as his own.
The exposition of the central tenet is hereby concluded.
Regarding the fourth point, the function [of the treatise]: the *Gushan Shu* (Commentary by Gushan) takes "returning from delusion to the truth" as its function. The Sūtra states:

Regarding the phrase "thus it was said": the "Dharma transmitted" refers to the teachings—the expressive words and the expressed meanings—transmitted by the compilers of the canon as having been taught by the Buddha. Because these expressive texts are not different from those of the Buddha, they are called "thus" (*tathā*).

That which is expounded as principle is none other than reality; thus it is called "is. Furthermore, the text accords with the principle, and the principle accords with the text. Since this principle permeates the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), such dharmas differ in being either partial (*prādeśika*) or complete (*paripūrṇa*).

These distinctions are fully detailed in the various sutra commentaries of Tiantai, which analyze their characteristics. Here, we exclude the partial and adopt the complete: the sole *tathāgatagarbha-citta* (Buddha-nature) is the essential body (*dharmatā-śarīra*) of this sutra.

"Thus have I heard. Regarding "fourfold—not-self, not non-self, not heard, not un-heard": the first three types refer to the provisional meanings previously heard; the latter one, "I have heard," refers to the primary meaning of the present [teaching].

"The time when the capacity and the principle meet" means to bring them together. This refers to the present teaching bringing together the capacities of those in the present and future—this is called "meeting the capacity";

Regarding why Pratyekabuddhas do not praise one another's virtues or list their names: they loathe clamor and delight in stillness, mostly dwelling in secluded places and remaining unknown to the masses; this refers to those who practice in groups (*vargacārin*).

As for those who encounter a Buddha and dedicate [their merit], the "Rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) appear in worlds where no Buddha exists; they emerge alone in a trichiliocosm, like the single horn of a rhinoceros. The term "Rhinoceros-like" is explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*. The *Erya* states:

"The *lin* has the body of a deer, the tail of an ox, and a single horn. The *Chunqiu Ganjing Fu* says: "The Rhinoceros has a single horn, signifying that within the seas there is but one sovereign. The Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) are likewise; in a great trichiliocosm...

Because they are solitary, they serve as the metaphor. Guishan says: *Pratyekabuddha* is translated here as "Conditionally Awakened" (*yuanjue*), because they awaken to the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination;

it is also translated as "Solitary Awakened" (*dujue*), because they appear in an age without a Buddha and awaken spontaneously without a teacher. Taixi says: Since the scribe of the sutra states "together with those at the initial stage," this precisely refers to the gathering of teachers and disciples, which is the "group-practice" (*buxing*) type.

This group-practice type also appears in an age without a Buddha; as the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "The group-practicing *pratyekabuddhas*, in an age without a Buddha, provide instruction and transformation to their teachers and disciples. [End of excerpt].

The commentary states: "The Sūtra says 'furthermore there were,' referring to those who were always walking shoulder-to-shoulder with the aforementioned Śrāvakas. Since the subsequent text clearly mentions the ten directions, it is verified that these individuals were high disciples of Śākyamuni.

Otherwise, how could there be no one within Śākyamuni’s own assembly who had received the teachings of the branch schools? However, in the listings found in various sūtras, they are sometimes subsumed within the ranks of the Śrāvaka assembly;

here, they are simply distinguished as two separate assemblies. Regarding the meaning of the relative status of these two assemblies as listed in this sūtra, there are two points. First, since they have already been revealed [as distinct], then...

The previous mention of "Arhat" and the subsequent mention of "One Beyond Learning" (aśaikṣa) are both spoken from the perspective of the Mahāyāna. In the case of "One Beyond Learning," the stage encompasses the various grounds and dwellings; the initial mind, however, lies at or below the level of the Ten Faiths.

Second, names are established based on their original status. Those of the Two Vehicles have already undergone the revelation [of the Buddha-nature] and entered the Perfect Teaching; though they would naturally call themselves Bodhisattvas, they are here named Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas according to their original designations.

It would be appropriate to resolve this by referring back to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings. Regarding the term "One Beyond Training" (*aśaikṣa*): according to the *Xuanji* (Commentary on the Profound), one is called "Beyond Training" because within this stage the four knowledges (*jñāna*) are already perfected, and there is no further dharma to be learned.

As for the four knowledges: first, the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering that "my births have been exhausted"; second, the knowledge of the Truth of Origination that "I shall not undergo further existence"; third, the knowledge of the Truth of the Path that "the holy life has been established."

The fourth is the knowledge of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) once what was to be done has been accomplished. This is the explanation according to the Hīnayāna. If one applies the Mahāyāna standard to the Hīnayāna, it should be said that the three virtues are already perfected and there is no further dharma to be studied.

Therefore, they are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). However, it is the stage of abiding that manifests the state of being beyond training; the ultimate perfection of wondrous awakening is the pinnacle of being beyond training.

This is because, as previously cited from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the title of Arhat actually encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles. Xunwen said: "The reason miscellaneous assemblies are not listed is that the ritual of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for confession) originates from monastic practice and is not attended by laypeople;

therefore, there are only the Sanghas of the Three Vehicles. Guyxiang said: "The assembly of Bodhisattvas is fully detailed in the introductory section; this refers to what the sutra says: 'Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment. This concludes until the end of the fast.

Upon returning, the king, along with the great ministers, elders, and householders, all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma; because the matter was to take place on the following day, there was a lay assembly present.

At that time, as the bhikṣus concluded their summer retreat and held the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, bodhisattvas from the ten directions consulted the Buddha to resolve their doubts. With reverence for his compassionate yet majestic presence, they sought the profound meaning [of the Dharma].

Thereupon, the Tathāgata arranged his seat and sat in tranquil repose, proclaiming the deep and abstruse teachings to the assembly. The pure multitude in the Dharma-hall attained what they had never experienced before. His *kalaviṅka*-like celestial voice resounded throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī serving as their leader.

Gushan says: "Shu" (屬) means "to belong to" or "to fall under. "The summer retreat has ended" (*xiū xià*) refers to the ninety-day period having been completed. According to the Vinaya, three days are permitted for the *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism): the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month. Changshui says:

"One confesses one's own transgressions and allows oneself to be subject to the monks' censure; one should then repent and become pure. Alternatively, it is called *zìzī* (自恣): "self" (*zì*) refers to one's own faults, and "censure" (*zī*) refers to allowing others to raise those faults.

Gushan says: "Bodhisattva" is fully expressed as *bodhisattva*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Bodhi" refers to the Buddha-way; "sattva" refers to accomplishing sentient beings. This is because one uses the Buddha-way to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.

Furthermore, "bodhi" refers to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), while "sattva" refers to transforming others (*para-caryā*). The *Zhuo zhuan* says: "To consult those who are virtuous is called 'asking'.

This expresses reverence for the mind of the Bodhisattva and clarifies the compassionate and majestic virtue of the Tathāgata. Thus, he respectfully requests the secret teachings of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, saying: "I shall seek its profound meaning. The *Shoujian* says: "Whenever entering samādhi..."

Each of these has six intentions: First, because this true samādhi is the very essence of the dharma to be realized, if one wishes to expound this dharma, the mind must first merge with this essence. Second, because it is not expounded unless it is realized. Third, to reveal that this dharma is not within the realm of discursive thought.

Fourth, to observe the faculties of the listeners and examine the dharma accordingly. Fifth, to show that both the teaching and the realization are identical. Sixth, to establish the ritual procedures for practice.

Now, this "seated in quietude" (yanzuo) that is proclaimed here is none other than Great Samādhi and Great Prajñā. Yet, in what follows, Ānanda remains entirely incomplete; this is because he lacks this [realization]. Since the Tathāgata wished to discourse upon Great Samādhi, he therefore...

Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) is the foundation. Concentration (*samādhi*) is able to give rise to wisdom; without wisdom, there is nothing to discuss. The general purport of this sutra has already been manifested herein.

Before explaining the esoteric meaning, he first speaks of other sutras so as not to disperse the assembly before expounding this scripture. This is just as the *Anantamukha-sūtra* was preached prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Samantaprabhāsa-sūtra* was preached prior to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.

However, what is indicated here specifically refers to the future. *Xunwen* says: "The 'esoteric meaning' generally refers to the essential points of the Mahāyāna; it means that beyond resolving doubts through inquiry, one will subsequently seek the Mahāyāna further."

Regarding the subtle and profound meaning: although the preceding text on the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) mentions "bhikṣus," it necessarily includes the Buddha as well. *Pravāraṇā* pertains to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*); "tranquil composure" pertains to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and "proclaiming and instructing" pertains to wisdom (*prajñā*).

When the Sage responds to sentient beings and establishes models for them, the three trainings are thus preserved therein. Question: On what sūtras and vinayas is this based? How do we know that the Buddha performed the *pravāraṇā*? Answer: The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"The Tathāgata sat together with the Saṃgha upon grass mats and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: 'I wish to receive the [end of the] year. Furthermore, the *Navavarṣa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha joined his palms toward the bhikṣus and confessed his transgressions, etc. Guishan says: "Kaling..."

*Piṅgala* is translated here as "wondrous voice. It originally comes from the Snow Mountains; while still within its egg, it can already sing. Its sound is harmonious and elegant, such that listeners never tire of hearing it.

Regarding the phrase "sands of the Ganges," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that among the sands of the Ganges River, no calculation can know their total number; only a Buddha and a Dharma-body Bodhisattva can know that number.
Regarding the name *Mañjuśrī*, Mount Gu says it is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*), because he has partially realized the three virtues of Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation.

At that time, King Prasenajit, observing the fast on behalf of his deceased father, invited the Buddha to the inner palace and went himself to welcome the Tathāgata. He prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and further personally extended invitations to the great Bodhisattvas.

*Si-ni* (彼斯匿) is here translated as "harmonious joy" (*he-yue*). The new translation is *pó-luō-xī-nà-shì-duō* (鉢邏犀那恃多), which is rendered as "Victorious Army" (*sheng-jun*). A "memorial day" (*hui-ri*) is also called a "taboo day" (*ji-ri*). The *Jiyi* (禮記·祭義) states: "On a taboo day, one must feel sorrow;

pronouncing the name is like seeing the parent. "Fasting" (*zhai*) means "to align" (*qi*). One does not eat past midday in order to align the body and mouth, thereby manifesting the Middle Way within. *Xunwen* says:

regarding the palace quarters, Ban Gu’s *Xi-du fu* (西都賦) states, "In the inner court, there are the Yeting and Jiaofang [palaces]. Lü Xiang’s commentary notes: "Yeting is the name of a palace. It is situated at the left and right of the Son of Heaven, like the elbows (*zhi*)."
"Ye" means "to serve. "Xiu" means "cooked," referring here to cooked food.

Within the city, there were also elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously providing meals for the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival to respond to their offerings. The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the bodhisattvas and arhats to attend to these various hosts of donors.

Changshui says: "He is called a '长者' (zhǎngzhě, elder/wealthy man) because he possesses ten virtues and dwells in the three grades of wealth. He is called a '居士' (jūshì, lay practitioner) because he maintains the Way for his own delight, has few desires, and accumulates virtue.

Shoujian says: "Regarding the 'three grades,' it is the custom in India for many to take up commerce as their profession; traveling abroad and traversing dangerous paths, they do not shrink from hardships, accumulating rare treasures over the course of many years."

The superior [type] serves the king; the others, having entered [the community], possess wealth exceeding one hundred million (*koṭi*) and are of lofty virtue, thus they are called *śreṣṭhin* (elders).

The *gṛhapati* (householder) acts as an assistant to the king. In the numerical system of that land, ten million is one hundred million. This is the lower grade. One billion is the middle, and ten billion is the superior. In India, those who accumulate vast wealth are called *śreṣṭhin*, while those who preserve the Way and abide in rectitude are called *gṛhapati*.

Guxiang says: the *Hanzi* states that one who dwells in gravity and substantiality is called an elder (*shèngzhě*). The *Yùzǎo* speaks of the *jūshì*. The commentary to the *Jǐndài* says: "The *gṛhapati* is the Way..."
Yi was a retired scholar (chushi). According to Xunwen, those who "feed the Sangha" mean they invite monks with food to provide them a meal.
However, Ānanda alone had previously accepted a private invitation; having traveled far and not yet returned, he was unable to attend in the order of the assembly.

Zizhong said: "First, one may accept a private invitation (bieqing) due to other matters, even if it is not during the fast-day (zhai). Changshui said: "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Ānanda did not accept private invitations;

this likely means he did not follow the Buddha in accepting such invitations. Xunwen said: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies that there are two types of inviting the Saṃgha: namely, the sequential invitation (sengci) and the private invitation.

Although the Vinaya permits private invitations, many texts condemn them while praising the sequential invitation. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: 'Inviting the Buddha and five hundred arhats privately is not as good as the sequential invitation.'"

Please invite a monk who resembles one who is extremely wicked. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Inviting monks according to the order of the assembly is like drinking seawater; one thereby drinks all its constituent streams.
Since there was neither an elder (*sthavira*) nor a preceptor (*ācārya*), he returned alone on the road. On that day, no offerings were provided.

Because he was not in the regular order of the *saṃgha*, he was not invited by the various *śrāddha*-masters. On the way back, he returned alone to manifest that he had no companions; this serves as the basis for the encounter with the sorcery described in the subsequent text. That day there were no offerings;

it is said that because the Jeta Grove was remote and there were no other donors to provide offerings, he entered the city to beg for food. Guishan says: "Ācārya" is translated here as "Preceptor of Conduct" (*guifanshi*).

The *Shoujian* says: "There are five kinds of Ācāryas according to the Vinaya: first, the one who grants renunciation; second, the one who confers the precepts; third, the one who provides instruction; fourth, the one who transmits the sūtras; and fifth, the one who provides reliance (*niśraya*). Regarding the conferring of precepts and providing reliance, these two are most common."
Those with ten years of seniority were appointed to this task; others were mostly those with more than five years of seniority.

At once, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl and went through the city where he was traveling, begging from house to house in sequence. In his mind, he initially sought out the final donor to serve as the host for the meal, regardless of whether they were pure or impure, of noble Kṣatriya lineage or even a Caṇḍāla.
Thus he practiced equal compassion, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble, resolving to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.

The term for "alms bowl" (應器) is *pātra* in Sanskrit. It is so called because its material, color, and capacity all accord with the Dharma. *Xunwen* states: "The Vinaya clarifies that there are essentially two materials for the body of the bowl: clay and iron.

As for the color, it is blackened, reddened, or made to resemble the color of a peacock’s throat or a pigeon, and so forth. Regarding the capacity: the large bowl holds three *dǒu*, the small holds one and a half *dǒu*, and the medium can be inferred accordingly.
Nanshan says: "This refers to the *dǒu* of the Western Zhou dynasty; according to the Tang *dǒu*, the upper bowl holds one *dǒu* and the lower holds five *shēng*. *Tányuè* means... [text truncated]

Regarding the donor: Xunwen says that the city where he traveled was Śrāvastī. In his mind, he first sought the final patron (*dānapati*), looking forward to the sequence of monks; this was considered the "final" [offering].
Gushan says: "Jing" (Pure) refers to the Kṣatriya royal caste. In full, it is called Kṣatriya; this translates as "Lord of the Fields.

The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) clarifies that this clan has held sovereign power for generations and takes benevolence and forbearance as its guiding principle. "Wei" (Filthy) refers to the Caṇḍāla, the executioners. Guxiang says: "The Sanskrit term Caṇḍāla translates as 'butcher.

The correct pronunciation is Caṇḍāra, which means 'rigid insignia. This refers to those who adorn themselves with evil karma; they carry specific insignia when traveling, such as shaking bells and holding bamboo poles, to mark themselves. 'Kuai' (Leader) means a chief; 'huan' (cutting) means slicing meat."

"Practicing impartial compassion" refers to the great compassion of equality. Because he desires to cause both the pure and the defiled to all proceed toward Bodhi, it is said that he "perfectly accomplishes immeasurable merit.

Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for having minds that were not impartial as Arhats; he now reverently looks up to the Tathāgata to expound this unobstructed teaching and resolve all doubts and slanders.

Changshui says: "Subhūti abandoned the poor for the wealthy, while Yinxiang abandoned the wealthy for the poor; both were rebuked by Vimalakīrti, hence it is said that their minds were not impartial. Zizhong says:
"The present mention of 'Tathāgata' refers to what was sealed by the Buddha, attributing the merit to the World-Honored One."
Passing through that city’s moat, he walked slowly toward the outer gate, maintaining a solemn and dignified demeanor and observing the rites of pure devotion with reverent gravity.
Regarding the term "cheng-huang" (城隍): a city moat (*cheng*) that contains no water is called *huang* (隉).

At that time, as Ānanda was on his almsround, he passed by a brothel. There he encountered the great sorceress Matangi, who, using the *sāvikāra* mantra of the ancient Brahmā, drew him into her bedchamber.
As she physically caressed him, he was on the verge of violating his precepts.

Changshui says: "The meaning of *Mātanga* is translated as 'Original Nature' (*Bǐngxìng*). This woman was named Original Nature in the past; because her present nature is the same as her past, she is also called the Bhikṣuṇī Original Nature. Zizhong says:
"Śāvikāra is the Golden-Headed Rishi, a follower of the *Wàishí Mízǐ* (External Rice-Belly) heretics. He served Brahmā and obtained this mantra. Gushan says: "The *Mātanga Sūtra* states:

'In the past, for five hundred lifetimes, Ānanda was once the husband of the woman Mātanga. Because the habituation of his attachment had not yet been forgotten, this incident occurred. Tiaoxi says: [As cited above].

Regarding the phrase "about to destroy the essence of the precepts" (*jiāng huǐ jiè tǐ*): this refers to the woman’s desire to break the essence of the precepts maintained by Ānanda—namely, the unmanifest essence (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of the precept against sexual misconduct.

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "She merely intends to curse you to violate the Buddha’s code of discipline; among the eighty thousand practices, she destroys but a single precept. Because your mind is pure, you have not yet fallen into ruin. If the two characters "about to destroy" (*jiāng huǐ*) were applied to Ānanda himself, then although he might be said not to have committed an offense, would he not still be subject to reproach?
The Tathāgata knew that he had been subjected to the arts of seduction;
having finished his meal, he turned back and departed. The king, along with the great ministers, elders, and householders, all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.

Zizhong said: "It is the constant practice of the Tathāgata that upon concluding a meal offered by invitation, he invariably preaches the Dharma. Since he has now returned so swiftly, there must be a specific purpose; therefore, the king, his ministers, and the great assembly have followed him here."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness. From within this light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which transformation Buddhas sat cross-legged, proclaiming divine mantras.

Gushan says: "The crown represents the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the light represents the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) represents the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The light emerging from the crown signifies that wisdom arises from principle. Because it universally illumines the hundred realms, it is called 'hundred jewels.

As for the presence of the transformation Buddha preaching the mantra, this signifies that when principle and wisdom are in profound accord, they can give rise to great function to eliminate evil and gather good. Xunwen says: "The lotus represents the Real; the flower represents the Provisional.

The Response-body’s arising of function does not depart from these two wisdoms—the provisional and the real. Therefore, the transformation Buddha sits cross-legged within it. Regarding the universal illumination of the hundred realms: [the first] six are the ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*)."

The four noble truths and the ten realms are mutually inclusive. Regarding "subduing evil and gathering good": this refers to subduing the evil of Ḍaṅga and gathering the goodness of Ānanda. *Xunwen* states: "Sitting in the full lotus posture. *Shenglun* states:
"Placing the two feet' heels upon the two thighs, like the coiled knot of a dragon."
The imperial decree states that Mañjuśrī was sent with a mantra to provide protection, whereby malevolent spells were extinguished.

Xingfu says: "Mañjuśrī secretly expounded a subtle interpretation of the heterodox methods; thus, although Ānanda did not hear it openly, he received its hidden protection. Therefore, the seventh fascicle states:

"Although he received the hidden protection of the Tathāgata’s *Buddhoṣṇīṣa* and *Buddha-mantra*, he had not yet personally heard them. According to the *Dharaṇīkośa-sūtra* (or *Tengjia jing*), this refers only to the World-Honored One himself reciting a single mantra to resolve that [issue of] lust.
The Master [Śāriputra] encouraged Ānanda and Mātanga to return to the Buddha’s presence. Gushan said:

"Mātanga attained the benefit of realizing the stage of Anāgāmin; that the sūtra compiler did not record this is because it will be made manifest later in the text. It says: "Mātanga’s fire of lust was suddenly extinguished."

He attained the fruit of Anāgāmin. This was the attainment of the third fruit following the recitation of the mantra. Upon returning to the Buddha’s presence, he heard the sūtra until the section where Mañjuśrī concludes the selection of the perfect penetration, at which point he became an Arhat.

According to the *Dengqie jing* (Śūramgama Sūtra), it is not stated that he gained benefit at the moment of hearing the mantra; rather, Ānanda sought it out for himself and went to the Buddha’s presence, and it was not Mañjuśrī who escorted him back.

Furthermore, upon hearing the preaching of the Dharma, they also attained the path of Arhatship. Thus, both sūtras demonstrate the realization of the four fruits through the hearing of the sūtra; it is simply that the capacities and perspectives of those of the Great and Small Vehicles differ.

However, regarding actual practice, it is because Ānanda was drawn by the hook of desire that he entered the Buddha’s wisdom later when his faculties had matured and he attained the Way. If we consider him as one of great expedient power (*mahopāya*), then he was like Ānanda in initiating this teaching to benefit the various capacities of sentient beings.
Question: In that sutra, one hears of the Small Vehicle and attains the four fruits; why is it that in this sutra, one hears of the Great Vehicle and yet also realizes the stage of an Arhat?

Answer: In that sutra, the clarification of the Small Vehicle explicitly sets it apart from the Great. In this sutra, which expounds the Perfect [Teaching], what hindrance is there to realizing the Small? Since the capacities of the practitioners differ, there is no contradiction.

Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself in worship, and wept with grief. Regretting that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to much hearing (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting his power of the Way, he earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means by which they attained the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the past, at the place of the Buddha Śūnyarāja, we simultaneously resolved our minds for enlightenment. Ānanda was always fond of much learning, while I was always diligent in energetic effort.

This means that because the Tathāgata cultivated both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) equally through the complete power of the Path, he was able to swiftly realize Bodhi, subdue Māra, and overcome external adversaries. Because I was biasedly attached to limited wisdom and remained at the level of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), I was instead beset by evil arts and forced the Buddha’s compassionate rescue;

my sorrowful weeping and regret lie precisely in this. To be "one who possesses much learning" refers to one who is biasedly practiced in limited wisdom. To be "one who has not perfected the power of the Path" refers to one who does not cultivate Great Samādhi.

However, how could the Hīnayāna possess not only the principle of meditative concentration of the Śūraṅgama, but even the perfectly interfused Buddha-wisdom? For the present Tathāgata’s manifestation of supernatural powers and recitation of the mantra all issue forth from this principle of meditative concentration.

Therefore, Ānanda was made to realize that limited wisdom is insufficient and to specifically request the Great Samādhi. Nevertheless, the essence of perfect interfusion between samādhi and prajñā is fundamentally without distinction. It is only when applied according to the capacities of sentient beings that they are differentiated;

thus, while quiescence and illumination are distinct, they remain non-dual. Consequently, the three subsequent requests encompass both samādhi and prajñā. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "Now, it is said that Ānanda’s role was provisional as an initiator;

he should be understood according to the 'small' [lesser vehicle] interpretation. The phrase 'beginningless' refers merely to a vast duration of time. The *Tiáoxī* commentary says: "Observing Ānanda’s formal request now, he has already entered the Dharma-gate of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which constitutes the entirety of this scripture."

In their discussions, they all responded to this request. Xunwen said: "The Śūraṅgama is the collective name for śamatha and so forth; śamatha and so forth are the specific designations of the Śūraṅgama."

Zizhong said: "According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (here referring to the *Awakening of Faith*), *śamatha* has 'quiescence' as its characteristic; *samādhi* has 'illusory transformation' as its characteristic; and *dhyāna* is that which is free from both characteristics of quiescence and illusion.

This general meaning corresponds to the three contemplations within a single mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). The characteristic of quiescence is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); the characteristic of illusory transformation is the contemplation of the provisional (*pratītyasamutpāda-vipaśyanā*);

and the characteristic of being free from both is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*). Gushan said: "One who attains *bodhi* realizes this perfect fruit through that perfect cause. What is the perfect cause? It is precisely the three types of cessation (*trividha-śamatha*) within a single mind."
The Great Samādhi is the single path by which all Buddhas realize the fruit; therefore, it is called the "initial expedient means" of wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.

Although the names differ in the Tathāgata’s orthodox response to the request for instruction, the essential meaning lies within these three. Now, this shall be explained in two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the reconciliation of differences. Regarding the first, the direct explanation: there are three names for *nirvāṇa*.

First, *śamatha*, translated here as "stopping" (*zhǐ*). Second, *vipaśyanā*, translated here as "contemplation" (*guān*). Third, *yuganaddha* (or *ubhayatobhāga*), translated here as "stopping-and-contemplation-in-equality" (*zhíguān děng*). The essence of stopping is stillness; contemplation is...

"Essence-clarity" (*ti-ming*) refers to the non-duality of clarity and stillness. Although Ānanda specifically requested instruction on *śamatha* (calm abiding), because the one [essence] is identical to the three [aspects], this *śamatha* is simultaneously *vipaśyanā* (insight) and equanimity.

Since the one and the three are mutually integrated, it is termed "wondrous. Because it is wondrous, it is called the "Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. Thus, within this single *śamatha*, there are again three names:

*śamatha*—this means "stopping by means of the true essence," as it stops at the level of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). *Samādhi*—in its full form it is *samāpatti*, also called *samādhi*; this is translated as "equilibrium" (*ting*), which refers to the skillful means (*upāya*).

"Following conditions" (*suiyuan*) means to bring [the mind] to rest within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Dhyāna"—here translated as *jinglü* (calm contemplation)—means to cease the two types of dualistic discrimination and bring [the mind] to rest within the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

In "stopping by realizing the reality" (*tizhen zhi*), one knows that things are a provisional combination of causes and conditions; because their illusory nature is empty, this is called "realizing" (*ti*). When攀缘 (*pányuán*, objectifying thought) and deluded conceptualization attain emptiness, they are extinguished.

Since emptiness is itself the reality, it is called "stopping by realizing the reality. This accords perfectly with the name and meaning of *śamatha*. Regarding "skillful means following conditions" (*fāngbiàn suiyuán zhǐ*): because one knows that emptiness is not [a mere] emptiness, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya*). Because one discriminates between the medicine and the disease, it is called...

"Following conditions": because the mind rests in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). What is now termed "equipoise" (*samādhi*) is precisely this conventional truth samādhi; the names differ, but the meaning is the same. "Stopping the discrimination of the two extremes":

what is now termed "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*)—here, "stillness" (*ching*) means "to cease," and "contemplation" (*lü*) means "discrimination of the two extremes"; the names differ, but the meaning is the same.

These three names and meanings for "stopping" originate from the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), which is the dharma-gate practiced by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai. Second, regarding the reconciliation [of these terms]: these three types of stopping are themselves the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), because they are simultaneously illumination and stillness.

Because it is quiescent yet illuminating: *śamatha* is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), *samādhi* is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*), and *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*).

Nāgārjuna said: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be empty; they are also called provisional designations, and are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. This is precisely what is meant here. Thus, as for the skillful means for accomplishing *bodhi*, how could they exceed these three types of cessation and three types of contemplation?

One knows that from beginning to end, this single sutra does not depart from this principle. Ānanda initially requested instruction on the three dharmas; having received the revelation, he proceeded until his full realization.

He then uses these three [aspects] to praise the Buddha. Thus, the subsequent scripture says: "The Wondrously Profound, the Universal Retainer, the Unmoving Honored One. "Wondrously Profound" refers to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*).

"Universal Retainer" refers to the wisdom of the provisional (*upāya-jñāna*). "Unmoving" refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyama-jñāna*). Furthermore, when the Buddha expounded the Tathāgata-garbha—the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and circular mind—to Pūrṇa, he said: "It is neither mind nor emptiness; it is both mind and emptiness."

"Detachment is itself detachment from non-detachment; the three truths are as vividly clear as pointing at one's own palm. Furthermore, when [the Buddha] spoke to Ānanda regarding the "six dissolutions and the disappearance of the one," he concluded with this praise:

"This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Adamantine King, the Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi. The opening of the flower and the appearance of the lotus is a metaphor for the Middle Way (*madhyama*). The adamantine hardness and sharpness is a metaphor for Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The illusory nature of having form is a metaphor for the Provisional (*prajñapti*).

When Mañjuśrī later selected and demonstrated the Perfect Penetration (*pariṣamantābhigama*), he likewise praised it in this way. Therefore, it is said: "Ānanda, listen attentively! I shall proclaim this by receiving the Buddha’s majestic power."
The *Vajrarāja-māyopama-acintya-buddhamātṛ-bhūta-samādhi* differs from [the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*] only in that it uses the "Buddha-mother" as a metaphor for the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

Throughout its various passages, it repeatedly expounds upon each point to shatter delusion; whether it employs emptiness (*śūnyatā*), discusses the provisional (*prajñapti*), or reveals the Middle, its words may seem partial while its intent is perfect, fully encompassing the three dharmas.

This is indeed in response to Ānanda’s request for the "three cessations. Tiaoxi remarked: "Since the three names in the *Yuanjue jing* are identical to those in the present sutra, Master Yuan’s interpretation follows their meaning accordingly. Although the three [cessations] within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*..."
The second [point] is that while their names differ, their essence is the same. However, *dhyāna* takes dual negation as its "separation," whereas *upāya* takes dual illumination as its "equality.

That Mount Guoshan specifically employs the three *śamatha* of Tiantai to correspond to these three names is yet another instance of grasping the profound meaning of the sutra. Why is this? *Śamatha* belongs to concentration (*samādhi*), while *vipaśyanā* belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since Ānanda had already reproached himself for his excessive learning and limited wisdom, he was precisely requesting the Great Concentration of the *Śūraṅgama*. What else could this Great Concentration be but the three *śamatha*? Furthermore, since *samādhi* and *dhyāna* are clearly names for concentration, even though this...

Concentration (*samādhi*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), though their primary functions differ. If this is so, then it is not only evident that Master Gu shan has attained the profound depths of the Sūtra; it also demonstrates that the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*) of Tiantai are in perfect accord with the sacred words.

Regarding "the initial skillful means": Ānanda’s request contains both a general and a specific aspect. The general refers to *śamatha* and the other [practices], which are the methods by which all Buddhas attain enlightenment.

The specific refers to the "initial skillful means," which is the cause for the practitioner to initiate practice according to their capacity. One should know that from the subsequent section on "breaking through mind and views" onwards, the text responds to his general request, as when the Buddha told Ānanda: [...text continues...]

“There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend [samsara] through a single gate.

Listen attentively now,” and so forth, until the various sages’ fundamental roots of perfect penetration were distinguished in response to their individual requests. As the Buddha told the great assembly: “I now ask you:

when you first resolved to attain enlightenment, regarding the eighteen realms, which did you take as your perfect penetration? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi? To state the essential point: it was only the ear-faculty’s perfect penetration, as observed by Avalokiteśvara, that is truly so.
This is the initial expedient means of this sutra. *Xunwen* (薰聞) states: "With earnestness, [the assembly] requests from those who have attained the fruit the Dharma practiced on the causal ground.

Therefore, it says, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi," and so forth. One should know that "attaining Bodhi" refers to ultimate awakened wisdom (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). "Sublime śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna" refer to the meditative practices cultivated by those from the stage of the provisional and actual [teachings] up to the outer ordinary beings (*bāhya-prthagjana*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Although the Śūraṅgama-samādhi pervades both cause and fruit, here it specifically pertains to the causal stage. Cause and fruit follow one another, forming a single, continuous thread from beginning to end. (Supplement)

It is said that Zizhong used the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to provide an explanation of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) based on the *Awakening of Faith*. Gushan, however, relied on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to translate *śamatha* as "stopping" (*zhi*), thereby opening up the single [contemplation] into three as an explanation of stopping.

Now, observing these two masters, Gushan’s understanding is more extensive. For instance, regarding the three dharmas of the *Awakening of Faith*, they are also referred to in the sutra as "concentration" (*samādhi*).

As that sutra says: "At that time, there were twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of concentration. Furthermore, a verse states: "O Bianyin, you should know that the unimpeded and pure wisdom of all Bodhisattvas is born entirely dependent upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*)."

Regarding what are called *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*: it is known that even those three dharmas of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) can be directly explained as the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*). How much more so, then, in the case of this sutra? Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, *śamatha* is explicitly translated as "concentration" (*ding*).

Moreover, *samādhi* is named "equanimous maintenance" (*samā-dhāraṇa*), and *dhyāna* is named "meditative contemplation" (*dhyāna*); both are names and definitions for states of concentration. Since they are explained through the three cessations (*tri-śamatha*) in accordance with the text, how could there be any doubt?

Question: In the *Zizhong* (資中), *śamatha* and the others are correlated with the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*). What is the meaning of this? Answer: There is no fault in the correlation. However, the names were established at that time [specifically for that context].

What is primarily emphasized here is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, it is simply convenient to eliminate [the three poisons] by means of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*). Question: The term *samā* refers to "equanimity" (*samatā*) and *dhāraṇa* to "holding" (*dhāraṇā*). How can this be seen as a dharma of concentration? Answer: *Samā* is the skillful means of cessation that accords with conditions.

The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*) calls this "contemplating only illusory transformations. This means employing the dharma of cessation to maintain equanimity (*samā*) toward provisional phenomena so that they do not scatter;

thus, it is named "equipoise" (*samādhi*, literally "equal holding"). Question: Master Wuxing directly correlates the three names from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* with the three meanings presented here. For instance, he correlates *vipaśyanā* with the present-day *samā*, and *ubhayatobhāga-vimukta* (or *ubhayapakṣa*)— [The text ends abruptly.]

Regarding the present *dhyāna*, is this interpretation correct? Furthermore, the *Zhiguan* states: "Cessation (*śamatha*) is itself severance; severance universally constitutes liberation (*vimukti*). Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*); wisdom universally constitutes *prajñā*. When cessation and contemplation are equal, it is called the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā-lakṣaṇa*).

This characteristic of equanimity universally pertains to the *dharmakāya*. Cessation is *śamatha*; contemplation is *vipaśyanā*. Because they are equal, they constitute *yuganaddha* (union), which, as previously stated, universally encompasses the three virtues.

Based on this, *śamatha* corresponds to liberation and should correspond to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Now, Wuxing considers [this] to be "cessation that realizes the true" (*tattva-darśana-śamatha*), while *vipaśyanā*...

Śamatha corresponds to *prajñā* and together they correspond to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Now, why is it that Wu-xing considers [this] to be *samādhi*, such that its meaning of correspondence differs from that of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*? The answer is:

Generally speaking, when terms are paired according to their primary meanings, this is merely a provisional approach and cannot exhaustively capture the underlying principle. Furthermore, the name *śamatha* signifies "concentration" (*samādhi*), taking "quiescence" as its practice; since *śamatha* follows this name, it corresponds to liberation (*vimukti*).

Now, Wu-xing follows the practice [itself] and thus calls it "realizing the true nature" (*tattva-bhāvanā*). The name *vipaśyanā* signifies "wisdom" (*prajñā*); since wisdom takes "discernment" as its meaning, and *vipaśyanā* follows this name, it corresponds to *prajñā*. Wu-xing...

Because conceptual discrimination belongs to the conventional (prajñapti), its correspondence with *samādhi* is merely a general reconciliation that cannot be subjected to further scrutiny. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty, states: "Śamatha is called 'that which can extinguish,' because it can extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*).

It is called 'that which can discipline,' because it can discipline the faculties (*indriya*) from their evil and unwholesome states. It is called 'tranquility,' because it can cause the three types of action (*trikarma*) to become tranquil.
It is called 'separation,' because it can cause sentient beings to separate from the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). It is called 'purification,' because it can purify greed, hatred, and delusion."

Because it is the antidote to the three turbidities of delusion (*moha*), for this reason it is called the "characteristic of concentration" (*samādhi-lakṣaṇa*). *Vipaśyanā* is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*);

it is also called clear seeing, seeing with power, universal seeing, sequential seeing, distinct seeing, and seeing distinct characteristics. This is what is called wisdom (*prajñā*). *Upekṣā* is called equanimity; it is also called non-contention (*araṇā*).

It is also called "non-contemplation" and "non-practice"; this is termed "equanimity. Furthermore, when Gushan uses these three types of cessation (*śamatha*) to interpret the text of the present sutra, we know that there is a profound correspondence between them and the three cessations of Tiantai.

Thus, the *Zhiguan* states: "Although the names of these three cessations are not yet seen in the sutras or treatises, they correspond to the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) and are established as names according to their meaning.

The *Śāstra* says: "When a bodhisattva relies on the teachings of the sutras to establish names, it is called 'Dharma-giving. There is no fault in establishing such names. If one can seek out the names within the sutras, they immediately correspond to this principle. Now, I have indeed attained this.
[The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*] is indeed so. Now, it is said that the three names in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* clearly indicate that this is samādhi.

Furthermore, since that [text] is the most closely related to the Chinese translation of the [same] sūtra, we know that the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) correspond precisely to the two sūtras. Moreover, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Good son, for three reasons one cultivates śamatha.

What are the three? First, for the sake of non-negligence; second, for the sake of adorning great wisdom; third, for the sake of attaining mastery. Furthermore, for three reasons one cultivates vipaśyanā. What are the three? First, for the sake of observing arising..."
