When one has not yet realized that objects are mind-only, various kinds of discrimination arise. Once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises. The first two lines refer to being turned by objects; the latter two lines refer to being able to turn objects.

As for "then one is identical to the Tathāgata," Master Zhaolun said: "Is it not only the Sage who unifies the myriad things to constitute himself? The present text precisely clarifies the infinite as the one;

this is essentially subsuming phenomena into principle. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "If one is turned by objects, then one is not identical to the Tathāgata. Why is it that all sentient beings..."

To realize perfect enlightenment is as Jingxi [Zhanran] has said: first, to show that delusion fundamentally arises from the transformation of nature; second, to show the nature itself, so as to cause one to reform their delusion.

Master Nan had a verse that says: "If one can turn things over, one is a Tathāgata; when spring comes, mountain flowers bloom everywhere. One naturally possesses a pair of hands with nothing to do, which have never easily performed the Three Terraces Dance.

This elder not only exhausted the meaning of the sutra, but also wondrously grasped the essence of principle. Zhenji said: "Since the external objects have been extinguished, spatial dimensions are no longer established; all is..."

First, its nature is perfectly accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All dharmas tend toward one dharma. This is precisely what that refers to. In the following text, both principle and phenomena are manifested together, and the complete array of essence, attributes, and functions is presented;
hence there is the expression "one as the infinite" and the meaning of "turning the Dharma within a single mote of dust."

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, then this wondrous nature is now present before me. Since seeing must be my true self, what then are my current body and mind?

Yet, while my current body and mind possess a real capacity for discrimination, that vision does not distinguish itself from my body. If it were truly my mind that enables me to see now, then the nature of vision would be my true self and the body would not be the self.

How would this differ from the objection raised by the Tathāgata earlier—that an object can see me? I pray only that you will bestow great compassion and reveal the truth to one who has not yet awakened."

Gushan said: Previously it was stated that by mistaking oneself for objects, one loses the fundamental mind and is thus turned by objects. If one can turn objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata; consequently, the mountains and rivers one perceives are all one’s own wondrous nature.
Thus it is said: "Now this wondrous nature is present before me. This is the realization of the essential meaning. Regarding the phrase "what is seen must be my true self," etc.:

this arises because Ānanda still maintains the duality of subject and object. Since what is seen is already the true nature, what then is the seeing subject? If one says the body lacks the nature of seeing, yet current discrimination is not false; if one says [it is] manifest...

The former was the perspective of seeing. If those external objects were distinct from the mind and intellect, yet one instead identifies them as one's own body; and if those external objects were truly one's own mind, such that they can now be seen, then it follows that external objects are one's internal body and not the self.
How does this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted? Since the previous refutation has already been resolved, why bring it up again? The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

Within this request for clarification regarding doubt, there are two major points: first, doubt concerning the subject and object; second, doubt concerning the internal and external. Because of the previous inclusion of all phenomena, both objects and their environments are my own true nature; thus, that which is perceived is the Truth.
Because one is able to see that body and mind are not yet the true nature, it is said: "What, then, are my current body and mind?

Since body and mind are capable of discernment, and the true nature exists as a reality within objective phenomena, why can one not turn back and discern that one's own body is likewise the truth? Therefore, it is said: "Now, body and mind, etc.

Furthermore, if the true reality of objective phenomena is my own mind-nature, then that [nature] is my reality; does it follow that the internal body becomes unreal? This is truly because one is mired in the view that objective phenomena are themselves the truth; thus, below—
This passage immediately refutes [the opponent's] reasoning.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have just said—that the seeing is before you—is not true.
If it were truly before you, and you truly saw it, then this essence of seeing would have a specific location and could not be said to be without a point of reference."

Furthermore, we are now sitting together in the Jeta Grove. Surveying the groves, the streams, and the halls, from the sun and moon above down to the Ganges before us—you now point out these various phenomena before my lion throne.
That which is dark is the forest; that which is bright is the sun; that which obstructs is the wall; that which is unobstructed is space.
Thus, even down to the grasses, trees, and the finest hairs, though they differ in size, as long as they possess form, there is nothing you cannot point to.
If this seeing must necessarily be present before you, you should point it out with your hand with certainty: "Which is the seeing?

Ānanda, you should know that if space were the seeing, since it has already become the seeing, what would be space? If matter were the seeing, since it has already become the seeing, what would be matter?

"You may minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena, extracting the essence of the brilliant, pure, and wondrous faculty of vision, and point it out to me so that it may be as clearly understood as those other objects, without any doubt."

Lord Jing said: "The essence, purity, nature, and consciousness; the clarity, subtlety, nature, and awareness—when these two are united and inseparable, this is called the 'source of seeing' which is essential, pure, bright, and wondrous.

Ānanda said: "Now, from this multi-storied lecture hall, reaching as far as the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, pointing with my hand, and surveying with my eyes—all that I point to are merely objects."
"World-Honored One, there is no one who holds such a view.
As the Buddha has taught, how much less could I— a defiled beginner śrāvaka— even a bodhisattva— extract a pure vision from before the myriad phenomena and objects,
such that it exists as a distinct self-nature apart from all things?"

To perceive through characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is coarse; to perceive through essence (*svabhāva*) is refined. Since the perception of characteristics lacks essence, when this mind ceases, it is identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.

Since the perception of essence lacks characteristics, light and darkness, penetration and obstruction may be returned [to their sources], but the seeing itself cannot be returned. That which cannot be returned is because it lacks characteristics. Lacking characteristics, it is not a thing, yet it is not separate from things;
therefore, one cannot extract the refined seeing from before the images of the myriad phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.

The Buddha further addressed Ānanda: "As you have said, if there were no essential seeing apart from all objects and possessing a distinct self-nature, then within those objects you point to, there would be no such thing as seeing."
Now I speak to you again: you and the Tathāgata are seated in the Jeta Grove; observe further the groves and gardens, even down to the sun and moon and their various distinct forms.
There will certainly be no "essence of seeing" that can be pointed out by you. You must then discern which among these various objects is not the seeing itself.
Ānanda said, "I have indeed seen this Jeta Grove everywhere. I do not know what within it is not seen. Why is this? If the trees were not seeing, how could one see the trees?

If the trees were themselves the seeing, how could they be called 'trees'? This applies even to the void: if the void were not seeing, how could one see the void? If the void were itself the seeing, how could it be called 'void'? Furthermore, I reflected:"
"Among these myriad phenomena, this subtle illumination is none other than seeing.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is. Gushan says:

"The two answers regarding 'identity' and 'separateness' were both affirmed by the Buddha because the nature of seeing is neither identical with nor separate from [the phenomena]. If one seeks it through identity or separation, it certainly cannot be found; thus, this..."

The seeing-nature is clearly like a flower in the sky. Master Xunwen said: "First, regarding the sense of 'separation,' one distinguishes that objects are not the seeing. Second, regarding the sense of 'identity,' one distinguishes that objects are not the seeing."

At that time, the great assembly—none of whom were yet those beyond training—upon hearing these words of the Buddha, were utterly bewildered and did not understand the beginning or end of their meaning; for a moment, they were struck with terror and lost their composure.

Zhenji said: "Previously, I held the view that mind and objects are distinct and perceived them as clearly separate. Now, having been subjected to the investigation of 'one' and 'different,' my judgment on right and wrong remains undecided; my mind has no place to rest, and I am left in a state of bewilderment. Tiaoxi said:

"The assembly first heard that the nature of seeing is not a thing, and the Buddha confirmed it, saying, 'So it is. In the end, they heard that the nature of seeing is a thing, and the Buddha again confirmed it, saying, 'So it is.'"

Therefore, he was utterly bewildered, not knowing where the two meanings of "beginning" and "end" were ultimately directed. Consequently, in the following passage, Mañjuśrī recounts the matter once more, saying: "If this were something seen, there should be something pointed out."
If it were not seeing, there would be nothing perceived; yet now we do not know where this principle leads. Thus, we know that from beginning to end, these two meanings are being pointed out.

Since the meaning of "seeing" has already been lost and the principle of "non-seeing" is likewise contravened, it is difficult to clarify the beginning and the end. Adhering to what, then, shall we find our refuge?

The Tathāgata, knowing that their spirits were trembling with fear, gave rise to compassion and comforted Ānanda and the great assembly: "O sons of good family, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth;

he speaks according to reality, neither deluded nor false. This is not the fourfold doctrine of indecisive equivocation regarding immortality held by Maskari Gośālīputra. You should contemplate this carefully; do not fail in your sorrowful longing."

Zizhong said: "Even worldly kings do not speak with duplicity; how much less could that which is spoken by the Dharma King—who has personally realized it—be false? The Tathāgata has five modes of speech: true speech, real speech, suchness-speech, non-deceptive speech, and non-differentiated speech.

That which is without falsehood is called 'true. That which accords with principle is called 'real. That which is unchanging is called 'suchness. That which accords between mind and object is called 'non-deceptive. That which foresees what is yet to come is called 'non-differentiated.
Wuxun said: 'This is explained by citing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. There, it is 'nothing but non-false'; here, it is 'nothing but non-differentiated. To synthesize these: because..."
Because it is not false, it is not different. Lord Jing said: "The Buddha’s 'True Words' are those shared with the Two Vehicles; his 'Real Words' are those shared with Bodhisattvas;

his 'As-it-is Words' are unique [to the Buddha]. There is neither reality nor falsehood. Because there is no falsehood, he does not deceive; because there is no reality, he is not different. Now, regarding what is called "not false," "false" is a name given in contrast to "true. What is meant by "true" is simply straightforwardness and suchness (*tathatā*).

Thus, even that which is real is still false; therefore, speaking in accordance with suchness is what is called "not false. That which is "in accordance with suchness" is what is called "suchness-as-such" (*tathatātathatā*). [This concludes the section on] the four kinds of pretension.

The details are fully provided in the following text. That you still show such compassion for my grief and longing is because I, your disciple, have looked up to and admired our Original Teacher for the sake of hearing the Way.
Now, being unable to engage in contemplation, I fear only that I may bring shame upon the intent with which you have shown me this compassion.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, this great assembly has not yet awakened to the meaning of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the two kinds of refined vision—the seeing of form and the seeing of emptiness, as well as what is and what is not.”

There are two kinds. Zhenji (the Ultimate Reality) refers to the essence of vision perceiving both form and emptiness. Gushan (Mount Gu) interprets this as the meaning of "is" and "is not. Previously, Ānanda analyzed the essence of vision as it relates to the myriad phenomena;

he realized that the phenomena are not the vision itself, yet there are no phenomena apart from the vision. This was the point of his dilemma regarding their identity or difference. Consequently, he was bewildered and did not know their ultimate beginning or end.

Thus, Mañjuśrī recounted how the great assembly had failed to understand the Tathāgata’s elucidation of the two kinds—the essence of vision perceiving form and emptiness—and their relationship as being either identical or distinct, and so he requested further instruction. These "two kinds" refer to the aforementioned essence of vision in relation to form and emptiness, concerning whether they are identical or distinct, and whether they are "is" or "is not."
This is the second point of that meaning.

World-Honored One, if these external objects such as forms, emptiness, and so forth are what see, they should have something to point toward; if they are not what see, there should be nothing perceived. Yet now I do not know where this principle leads, and thus I am struck with fear.

It is not that my past roots of goodness were meager or slight; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, will clarify the relationship between these various objects and this essence of seeing.
"What was its original substance? Within it, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not.

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: 'The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, while abiding in their own samādhi, perceive that both the seer and the conditions of seeing, as well as all imagined appearances, are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent.
This seeing and these conditions were originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within this?'"

Xunwen says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions"—this refers to what is realized by those who have attained the fruit, presented to show that which sentient beings are deluded about. Although there is a difference between delusion and realization, the seeing of nature is one and the same;

this also applies to the Great Bodhisattvas at the stage of Perfect Abiding and above. Changshui says: "They personally abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Shoujian says: "Generally, all samādhis possess three characteristics."

This refers to entering, abiding, and emerging. When the five consciousnesses confront their objects, the mental faculty (manas) issues forth through the gates; when it protects the sense faculties regarding distant objects, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) recedes back within. This [explanation] is common to the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle.

Now, we clarify the three phases through the single mind alone: that which is stillness within illumination is called "entering"; that which is illumination within stillness is called "emerging"; and the state where [illumination] has entered but not yet arisen is called "abiding. Since this is not attainable by those of the provisional or Lesser Vehicles, it is further described as "self-."

Furthermore, this wondrous samādhi melts all phenomena such that they are all solely one’s own samādhi; hence it is said, "The seeing and the conditions for seeing, etc. Here, "seeing" refers to the sense organ (the faculty), "conditions for seeing" refers to the objects, and "the characteristics of what is conceived" refers to consciousness.

These—the organ, the object, and consciousness—constitute the eighteen *dhātus*, which encompass everything without exception. All that belongs to the deluded mind has no true essence from the beginning; it is like flowers in the sky seen because the eyes are clouded by cataracts.

All phenomena exist because of non-awakening (*abodha*); yet non-awakening is itself awakening, and is fundamentally *bodhi*. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "This passage merely merges phenomena back into [reality]."

Regarding the characteristics of the two truths of principle: because the preceding section clarified the meaning of the identity and difference between the nature of seeing and its objects, when phenomena are subsumed into principle, there is nothing further to be inferred. How, then, could there be any marks of right or wrong?

However, since it was previously clarified that the conventional is subsumed into the ultimate—thus being like flowers in the sky—it is subsequently clarified that the ultimate is subsumed into the conventional; hence it is said, "it has always been so."

Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: apart from you, Mañjuśrī, is there another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī? Or is there no such Mañjuśrī? This involves two meanings: that which is relative and that which is absolute.

If it is relative, there is a distinction between the true and the false, and between right and wrong. If it is absolute, there is no differentiation between the true and the false, nor between right and wrong.

The Buddha asks only whether, outside of the true Mañjuśrī, there exists another or not. If there were one, then there would be the distinctions of right and wrong, or true and false; this is the relative sense. If there were none, then there would be only the single Mañjuśrī, free from right and wrong.
"From what does it arise? It is beyond all dependence.

Thus, World-Honored One, I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no such Mañjuśrī. Why is this? If there were such a thing as 'this,' there would then be two Mañjuśrīs. Yet, today I am not without Mañjuśrī."
Within this, there is in reality neither the mark of "is" nor the mark of "is not.

"I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no 'Mañjuśrī who is'"—this is the meaning of being free from dependence (*atyantānapekṣa*). Why is this? If there were such a thing as "is," then there would be two Mañjuśrīs; this is the meaning of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣa*).

However, my departure today again demonstrates the meaning of being free from dependence, for I wish to show within that prior state of non-dependence the absence of the marks of "is" and "is not"; thus, I explain it once more. It is not that today [the truth] is absent.

Mañjuśrī, this is precisely what was said above when it stated, "I am truly Mañjuśrī. Since there is but a single Mañjuśrī existing in the present, how could there ever be the characteristics of right or wrong?

If one transcends all dependence, this accords with the primordial, wondrously pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. If one relies on mutual dependence, this accords with the two paths of the nature of seeing and the non-nature of seeing. Master Jie’s commentary states: "If one establishes two bodies..."

There would then be the marks of "is" and "is not. Since there is but a single essence, it ultimately lacks names of mutual dependence or opposition; this illustrates that the True is fundamentally without the False. The Buddha said:

"This seeing, wondrously luminous, and these various empty objects are likewise thus. Originally, they are the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind. It is through delusion that they become form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing."

"Originally wondrously luminous" corresponds to the preceding "True Mañjuśrī. "Delusively [conceiving] form and emptiness" corresponds to the subsequent "further Mañjuśrī. Once form and emptiness are established, their mutual opposition gives rise to latent conceptualization.
From the true, the delusory arises. If one knows that the fundamental nature is like flowers in the sky, then all dependencies cease at this point of manifestation.

It is like a second moon: who can say which is the real moon, and which is not? Mañjuśrī, there is only the single, true moon; within it, there is inherently neither "this is the moon" nor "this is not the moon."
The sutra mentions only the second moon; by implication, it already treats the true moon as the first. Once the two moons are established, there arises the distinction between the real and the false.

Which one is the true moon? And which one is not the moon—the second moon? The second moon is what is seen by pressing upon the eye; this is the meaning of "relative" (相待), corresponding to the two preceding Mañjuśrīs.

However, within the single true moon, there is inherently neither "this moon" nor "not this moon"; this is the meaning of "absolute" (絕待), corresponding to the single Mañjuśrī mentioned above, who is not non-existent today. As for the true moon—who would say it is?
The second can carry the first.

Therefore, when you now observe the interaction between the self and external objects, the various manifestations that arise are called deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). You are unable to discern within them what is real and what is not.
Because of this essence of true, wondrous, and luminous awareness, it enables you to distinguish between what is a finger and what is not a finger.

Zhaoxi said: "Objects are that which are pointed to; seeing is not something that can be pointed to. Because the true nature is free from both, it is said to 'issue forth. Jing Gong said: 'That which cannot issue forth is not the "is. "
"Because you perceive two dharmas, I have caused you to distinguish between 'the finger' and 'that which is not the finger.

This is because one knows the single nature [of all things]. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma-King has said. That which perceives conditions pervades the ten directions; its profound stillness is eternally abiding, and its nature is neither arising nor ceasing.

How does this differ from the 'Dark Principle' (Tattva) spoken of by the former Brahmin Śāṃkara, and from the 'True Self' that fills the ten directions as taught by the various non-Buddhist schools, such as those who smear themselves with ashes?"

Zhaoxi says: "Awakening" refers to *bodhi*; "conditions" refer to form, emptiness, hearing, seeing, and so forth. As the preceding text states: "This seeing and these conditions are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of *bodhi*."

Zhenji said: "The 'Primal Truth' (Pradhāna) is the first of the twenty-five truths of the Sāṃkhya school. Those who smear themselves with ashes and so forth are non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism. Ānanda raised a doubt, saying:
'They also reckon that the Primal Truth and the True Self pervade the ten directions; how does this differ from this awakened nature?'"

The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others. Those non-Buddhists constantly speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is not their domain.

Now I observe that this awakened nature is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, and far removed from all false delusions; it appears to be neither caused by conditions nor identical to the spontaneity of those outsiders.

The name of Mount Laṅkā means "Inaccessible" in this language; only those who have attained supernatural powers can reach it. In the second fascicle of that sutra, Mahāmati raises the question of how the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha taught by the Buddha in the past differs from the *ātman* (self) postulated by non-Buddhists.

The Buddha explains the true self, stating that he spoke of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature to eliminate the fear of the foolish regarding the phrase "non-self," and thus it is not the same as the *ātman* of the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, in order to refute the naturalism (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it is taught that there are causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Based on worldly characteristics, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is analyzed; now, the following point is cited as a challenge. *Xunwen* (薰聞) states:

"Those who fear the phrase 'no-self' (*anātman*) are the non-Buddhists whose calculations do not exceed four propositions: namely, existence, non-existence, both, and neither. This [fear] belongs to the proposition of non-existence. *Buyi* (補遺) states: The non-Buddhists calculate the existence of a divine self (*ātman*).

Fearing the Buddha’s teaching of the phrase "no-self," the World-Honored One at times also speaks of a "true self" (*tathāgatagarbha*); therefore, it is said that he does not teach "no-self" exclusively. Such is what the non-Buddhists calculate.

The four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are precisely the "existence" proposition; yet one fears speaking of non-self (*anātman*). Why, then, does the Master of the Record state that these four propositions of the non-Buddhists belong to the "non-existence" proposition?

Is it not because the Buddha’s teaching of non-self belongs to the "non-existence" proposition of externalist calculations? Within the four gates of Buddhism, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self are likewise the "non-existence" proposition; thus it is said, "one fears the proposition of non-self.

This seems to be a case where [the fear] is not due to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), for it would otherwise be inconsistent with the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of those [non-Buddhists]. Regarding this, Gushan says: "The word 'with' (*yu*) means 'to categorize' (*lei*)."
"How does one demonstrate how to avoid entering among the heterodox and attain the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind?

Tiaoxi says: This implies that the present enlightened nature is spontaneous (*svabhāva*), as if it were not the same as the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the past; if so, how is this distinguished from the 'spontaneity' of the non-Buddhists?"
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I have now thus revealed these skillful means and truly informed you; yet you still do not realize it, being deluded into thinking it is spontaneous.
Ānanda, if it were necessarily spontaneous, one must clearly discern that it possesses a spontaneous substance."

You should now observe this wondrous, luminous faculty of seeing: what constitutes its self-nature? Does this seeing take light as its self-nature? Does it take darkness as its self-nature? Does it take space as its self-nature? Or does it take obstruction as its self-nature?
Ānanda, if light were your own self, you should not perceive darkness. If, moreover, empty space were your own essence, you should not perceive obstructions.
Likewise, if any such characteristics as darkness were your own self, then at the time of light, your faculty of seeing would be annihilated; how then could you see the light?

Xingfu said: "The doubts of Ānanda concerned only the true essence (*tattva*). Why did the Tathāgata refute this by means of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)? Since the single substance is quiescent and, in principle, lacks both subject and object, the arising of a calculating subject must necessarily involve an object of perception.

Such perception arises only in relation to characteristics; apart from characteristics, there is no principle of perception. Therefore, by using conditions to investigate the self, the self is found to be unestablished. When characteristics cease and the mind perishes, false calculations are forever eliminated. Xunwen asked:

"In the previous doubt, it was suspected that the perceiving consciousness (*vijñāna*) was conflated with the *pradhāna* (the primordial cause) and the True Self (*ātman*). Why did the Tathāgata refute only 'spontaneity' (*svabhāva*)? Answer: "Because spontaneity is the root of those two views. By refuting spontaneity, one simultaneously eliminates the two."

Ānanda said: "I now observe that this nature of awakening is spontaneous. This very nature of the conditions for prior awakening is what is meant by 'pervasive,' and it is spontaneously pervasive as well.

As the preceding text stated: 'The conditions for awakening pervade the ten directions, remaining tranquil and eternally abiding. Thus I know that [the term] is used interchangeably with other characteristics. Although there are three names, what I myself am in doubt about is simply this spontaneity."

If *svabhāva* (nature) were thus refuted, how could there be any confusion regarding the *tattva* (ultimate principle) or the true self (*ātman*)? Lord Jing said: "Generally speaking, that which is called 'self-existent' does not arise without a source; furthermore, it must have something else as its counterpart.
It is merely a single nature, and thus is not truly 'self-existent'."

Ānanda said: "If this wondrous nature of seeing is certainly not spontaneous, I have now discerned that it arises from causes and conditions. Yet my mind is still not clear; I seek counsel from the Tathāgata:
how does this principle accord with the nature of causes and conditions?"

Gushan said: "At first, I suspected that the wondrous nature was identical to external spontaneity (*ziran*). Once I heard it refuted, I took it to mean what the Buddha previously taught regarding the principle of the correct cause and conditions;
I simply did not know how the wondrous nature could be in accord with this."
The Buddha said, "You speak of causes and conditions; I shall question you further. As you now perceive the nature of seeing manifest before you, does this seeing arise because of light?
Does it arise because of darkness? Does it arise because of space? Or does it arise because of obstruction?"

Ānanda, if it exists because of light, one should not perceive darkness; if it exists because of darkness, one should not perceive light. This applies even up to the cases of space and obstruction, which are analogous to light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing arises in dependence upon light; it arises in dependence upon darkness; it arises in dependence upon space; and it arises in dependence upon obstruction.

Ānanda, if it were to exist in dependence upon space, it should not see obstruction; if it were to exist in dependence upon obstruction, it should not see space. This applies even unto light and darkness, which are the same as space and obstruction.

The cause is briefly [defined as] emptiness; the condition is briefly [defined as] light and darkness. The Buddha’s skill in expression allows these analogies to be understood by extension. Zhenji said: "Because the cause is proximate and the condition is remote, two gates are distinguished. Xunwen said:

"If seeing exists because of light, then the object is proximate and the faculty is remote; if seeing exists by conditioning emptiness, then the faculty is proximate and the object is remote. Both cause and condition are refuted in relation to the object."

Regarding the refutation not directed at the sense organs (*indriya*): because objects possess characteristics such as light and darkness, or openness and obstruction, it is easy to investigate them through reasoning; the sense organs lack these characteristics, and therefore they are not discussed here.

Furthermore, Ānanda’s perception of the nature of seeing had not yet been liberated from external objects (*viṣaya*), and he consequently gave rise to conceptual proliferations based on those objects, as stated in the preceding passage: "Now, you rely on seeing to perceive the nature of seeing manifest before you," and so forth. For this reason, all that is refuted is spoken of in terms of the objects.

You should know that this subtle, wondrous, and brilliant awareness is neither caused nor conditioned; it is not spontaneous, yet it is not non-spontaneous. It is neither "not" nor "not-not," and neither "is" nor "is-not.
It is free from all marks and is identical with all phenomena.

Zhaoxi said: "Neither from causes and conditions, nor from external spontaneity, nor from non-spontaneity" means that it is not non-existent. This refers to the spontaneity of the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*) which is not non-existent. As the following text states: "That which is without arising or ceasing is called spontaneity.

The reason he does not say "nor from non-causes and conditions" is that this passage is primarily refuting the doctrine of production through causes and conditions; therefore, that point is set aside for now. Regarding "there is no non-... and so forth:

this reveals that the awakened nature is fundamentally without "non" and "not-non," and likewise without "is" and "not-is. The former phrase refers to causes and conditions, while the latter refers to spontaneity; by departing from these, [the true nature] is revealed.

The True is not the conventional; it is precisely that all encountered objects are but mind. It is both absent and present, such that it cannot be named. The *Supplement* states: At the time Ānanda raised his doubt and request, he inquired generally about the two meanings of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) and "causality" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The Buddha first answered these two meanings separately. From the passage beginning "You should know," he answers the two meanings collectively. Within this collective response, he first refutes the attachment to "nature" (*svabhāva*). From the passage beginning "It is neither non-existent nor not non-existent," he refutes the attachment to "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).

By stating "it is not causality," he refutes the conceptualization of the nature of causality; by stating "it is also not spontaneity," he refutes the conceptualization of the nature of spontaneity. It is not "not-spontaneous"; rather, it is the awakened nature (*bodhi-svabhāva*).

This is because the preceding passage’s discussion of the spontaneous nature of the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*) was similar to the [Buddhist] refutation of the non-Buddhists' notion of spontaneity; now, we shall distinguish between them, refuting that [former view] to establish this [latter one].

According to the underlying principle, there ought to have been the phrase "it is certainly not without causes and conditions. This was intended to refute false causes and conditions and establish true causes and conditions; it is precisely as Ānanda cited above from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* regarding the Buddha’s teaching on true causes and conditions.
Now, it is said that this phrase should indeed have been present, but the redactor of the sutra omitted it in order to introduce the following question from Ānanda. The subsequent question states:

"If the wondrous enlightened nature is necessarily neither cause nor condition, why did the World-Honored One further state that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions? If the principle of causes and conditions had not been established here, how could this question have arisen? It would not have been possible.

The phrase "neither not" (*fei fei*) refutes the attachment to the characteristic of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). The phrase "no 'is' or 'is not'" (*wu shi fei shi*) refutes the attachment to the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The preceding passage refuted the nature (*prakṛti*), stating it is not spontaneous; now it refutes the capacity for negation, hence it says "no non-. Above, the naturalness of the awakened nature was established by saying it is "not not-spontaneous"; now that too is refuted, hence it says "not not. "Not not" (*bukei*) and "not not-is" (*feibukei*) are inversions of phrasing with the same meaning.

As for "no 'is'" (*wushi*), this corresponds to the phrase "there is 'non-' because it is not due to conditions," which refers to the correct principle of dependent origination. Fearing that taking "is" as a fixed point would become a disease, it is now also negated.

"Is not this" refers to that which is neither cause nor condition within the negation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since false causes and conditions are not true causes and conditions, and since we are now negating the capacity [of such conditions], it is said that "there is nothing that is not this.
The subsequent phrase, "detached from all marks," means that attachment to marks has perished.

How can you now apply your mind to this, attempting to make distinctions through the conventional names and signs of worldly conceptual proliferation? It is like trying to grasp and rub the void with the palm of your hand;
it only increases your own fatigue. How could the void ever be grasped by your seizing?

Gushan said: "The palm of the hand symbolizes deluded sentiment; grasping and rubbing it symbolize speculative reasoning; empty space symbolizes the true mind; and merely increasing one's own toil symbolizes the cycle of birth and death."

Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor produced by conditions, why does the World-Honored One constantly proclaim to the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing possesses four kinds of conditions?"
What are called the causes of emptiness, clarity, mind, and the eye—what is the meaning of this?

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains nine conditions, whereas the present sutra and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explain only four; this is merely a difference between the detailed and the abbreviated. As for the "Echo in a Valley" (*Guxiang*), it states that the nine conditions of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* are:

first, emptiness; second, the sense organ (*indriya*); third, clarity; fourth, the object (*viṣaya*); fifth, attention (*manasikāra*); sixth, seeds (*bīja*); seventh, discrimination (*vikalpa*); eighth, defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*); and ninth, the fundamental [consciousness]. If the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*) is added, they become ten.
The present sutra states that "mind" is the causal condition, which refers to the condition of discrimination; "the eye" is the causal condition, which refers to the condition of the sense organ.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When I speak of the various characteristics of worldly causes and conditions, these are not the ultimate truth (paramārtha)."
Conditioned by causes and conditions, these are merely provisional names. They exist in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but they do not exist in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Ānanda, I ask you again: when people of the world say, "I can see," what is called seeing, and what is called not seeing?

Ānanda said: "Ordinary people perceive various forms by means of the light of the sun, the moon, or a lamp; this they call 'seeing. If these three kinds of light were absent, they would be unable to see."

Ānanda, if it were the case that one is said to "not see" when there is no light, then one should not see darkness. If one necessarily sees darkness, this is simply the absence of light; how then can it be called "not seeing"?

Ānanda, if one does not see light when it is dark, it is called "not seeing. Now, when it is bright, one does not see the characteristic of darkness; this too is called "not seeing. Thus, both of these characteristics are equally termed "not seeing."

Furthermore, even if these two forms mutually obstruct and supplant one another, it is not the case that your seeing-nature momentarily ceases to exist within them. Thus, you should know that both are called "seeing"; how could it be that you do not see?

Zhaoxi said: "This is identical to the 'blind man seeing darkness' in the first fascicle regarding the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*); however, what is refuted differs. Previously, it was revealed that the nature of seeing is the mind, and the capacity of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to see was refuted.

Now, it is revealed that the nature of seeing is not light, and the capacity of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to see is extensively refuted. Since the refutation of conditions is so extensive, the revelation of the reality of the nature is profoundly deep. Consequently, the subsequent text discusses how seeing sees and yet is not seeing."

Therefore, Ānanda, you should now know this: when seeing light, the seeing is not the light; when seeing darkness, the seeing is not the darkness; when seeing emptiness, the seeing is not the emptiness;
when seeing obstruction, the seeing is not the obstruction. Thus, these four principles are established.

Gushan says: By examining the four meanings of brightness, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction, one realizes that the nature of seeing is established as being independent of external objects. The phrase "the establishment of these four meanings" serves as a concluding summary of what precedes it.

Furthermore, you should know this: when the seeing sees, that seeing is not [itself] seeing. Seeing is already apart from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. How, then, can one speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, or the characteristics of their conjunction?

The former was not that which is seen; therefore, it is detached from the four objects. The present is not that which can see; therefore, it is detached from the nature of seeing. The preceding text stated: "The clarity and lucidity of seeing is the fundamental source.

Although this seeing is not the wondrous, clear, and lucid mind, it is like a second moon—it is not a reflection of the moon. Now it says that seeing is not seeing. The "seeing" mentioned above is like the clear and lucid mind, like the bright moon. That which is negated below is as follows:

This is precisely the pure essence of the faculty of seeing; it is like a second moon. As Xunwen says: "To consider the Buddha’s intent: since he has already refuted the four conditions as not being the nature of seeing, he now wishes to reveal that the true nature is likewise not the 'seer.

Therefore, he first restates the seer to distance it from the four conditions—saying, for instance, when one sees light, 'the seeing is not the light,' and so forth—and subsequently employs the true nature to distance itself from the seer, saying, 'when one sees the seeing, the seeing is not the seeing.
Seeing cannot reach it. This explains the meaning of the preceding passage: "Why is it that seeing is still separated from seeing? It is truly because of the essence of seeing.
This belongs to the realm of delusion, for it cannot reach the ultimate truth. Furthermore, according to the previous passage, it says: "When seeing light, the seeing is not the light," and so forth;

all of this refers to using the subject that sees to perceive the object that is seen, wherein the subject is not the object. By analogy, when we speak of "the seeing of seeing," the principle is the same: that which was previously the subject that sees now becomes the object that is seen.

This means that when true seeing is manifested within the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*), since the true is devoid of delusion, it is said that "seeing is not seeing. Question: Since the essence of seeing belongs to delusion, how can the true again manifest within the deluded?

Answer: The essence of seeing is the nature that reflects forms; it is like flowers in the sky, which fundamentally do not exist. True seeing is the wisdom of original enlightenment, the *bodhi-dhātu* as the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*).

Once true seeing is revealed, both the seeing and its objects are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. This is merely called "true seeing seeing deluded seeing"; how could it be the same as [deluded] seeing?

That the subtle faculty still takes form as its object—how can subject and object be spoken of as being of the same day? Why is this? Because within the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind, a single thought of non-awakening suddenly causes the division between object and wisdom;

what was not two becomes two, namely, the seeing and the conditions for seeing. When ignorance is completely shattered and true seeing is fully revealed, this seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.

It is merely a change of name; fundamentally, there are not two distinct entities. This is what is called "seeing the seeing. It is not that there is some further essence, like a second moon, which is seen by the true seeing as its object.

Xunwen says: The fourth fascicle states, "Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness (*zhan*) becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision. The essence of vision reflects forms, and by binding with forms, the sense organ is formed.

What is here called "nature" (*xing*) refers precisely to the nature of seeing (*jian-xing*) within the eye faculty that is capable of seeing. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: This refers to the initial delusion regarding true nature.

At the time when it reflects upon objects and grasps at discrimination, it has not yet merged with the various latent afflictions (*anuśaya*); its substance is therefore not entirely subsumed under falsehood. Thus, the sutra below states: "Within the wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision. The *Awakening of Faith* says: [and so forth].

"Arising from non-awakening, it is able to see. The Commentary (*Shu*) states: "Now, the pure mind is perfumed to become the *ālayavijñāna*; this arises based on delusion as something resembling [the original state]. The Editorial Revision (*Bishuo*) explains:

"Arising based on delusion as something resembling [the original state] means that the deluded mind arises based on the fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodha*). This term 'resembling' (*xi*) indicates that because one has newly become deluded regarding true nature (*tathatā*), this deluded thought flows forth subtly, appearing as if it were unmoving."

It appears as if there is no distinction; thus, it appears as one and appears as permanent. This is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* calls "the shadow-illumination of deluded awareness. Although the seeing belongs to the realm of delusion, its nature is fundamentally true.

One should know that at the moment of seeing the seeing, there is nothing else to be seen; it is simply seeing the nature within the seeing. That being so, if one has not yet seen the nature, the nature resides within the seeing and is termed "seeing-essence" (*darśana-sāra*).

If one can see the nature, the nature is liberated from the seeing, and only then is it called "seeing the seeing. Therefore, the text below states: "Awareness is not within the eye-disease; this is truly seeing the seeing. This refers to the "seeing the seeing" herein.

And so forth. Furthermore, it is precisely because Ānanda had not yet escaped the conditions of seeing that [the Buddha] first clarified that the nature of seeing is detached from conditions, and subsequently clarified that true seeing is detached from seeing;

this is the essential purport of this sutra. Although seeing belongs to the realm of delusion, its nature is fundamentally true. If Ānanda were to attain the stage of the Perfect Abiding (yuanzhu), he would partially escape this seeing and partially manifest his original truth.

If he reaches the stage of fruition (guodi), he will then be ultimately detached from it, and his entire being will manifest [this truth]. Xunwen asked: "When one sees the seeing, to what stage does this belong? The answer is: the *Liushu* states that the preceding detachment from conditioned objects belongs to the stage of semblance-correspondence (*xiangsimi*), which corresponds to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

The "Three Worthies" refer to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei shi song) states: "To manifest before oneself a slight object and claim it to be the nature of consciousness-only—because there is still something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.

Now, to be free from the subject that perceives is the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), which corresponds to the stages of "Abiding" (*bhūmi*) and above in the Separate and Perfect Teachings. The verse further states:

"When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended, because it is free from the marks of the two graspings [subject and object], one truly abides in consciousness-only. Now, I say this should also be explained according to the six levels of identity (*liu ji*) of the Perfect Teaching: from the level of "Identity in Name" (*mingzi ji*), one takes understanding as vision.

Up to the ultimate realization, one takes realization as seeing. Lord Jing said: "Only after seeing the seeing can it be called seeing; thus, seeing is not seeing. Therefore, one knows that seeing is non-seeing.
This is the true purity and non-outflow (anāsrava) of nirvāṇa. The seeing that sees [this] is free from the seeing of signs; thus, it is beyond the reach of the seeing of signs.
For the seeing of signs merely perceives signs and cannot perceive the nature (dharmatā).

"You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in wisdom; you are unable to penetrate the pure true reality. I now instruct you: you should contemplate this well and must not grow weary on the sublime path to bodhi."

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed for us the nature of causes and conditions as well as spontaneity, and the characteristics of both conjunction and non-conjunction."

My mind was still not yet awakened; now, hearing further that "seeing seeing is not seeing," my confusion and distress have increased all the more. I prostrate myself, entreating your vast compassion to bestow upon me the eye of great wisdom, so that you may reveal to us the clarity and purity of the enlightened mind.
Having spoken these words, he wept with grief, prostrated himself, and received the Sage’s instruction.

Changshui says: "The proclamation of causes and conditions as well as spontaneity" refers to what was already heard previously; "all those that are compounded" and so forth describe what has not yet been realized. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

This passage requests that what was previously heard be pointed out and what has not yet been realized be described. This is because in the subsequent sutra text, the Buddha himself points it out, saying:

"Ānanda, although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of fundamental enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, you have still not clarified that this source of awakening is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination. However, in this context, he requests [clarification] from afar.

The characteristics of conjunction and non-conjunction; the invitation to observe what is seen and what is not seen. For this reason, he first answers regarding "seeing what is seen," and subsequently answers regarding conjunction and so forth.

Furthermore, it must be understood that conjunction is the characteristic of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), while non-conjunction is the characteristic of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Although I have heard of causes and conditions, I do not yet understand conjunction;

although I have heard of spontaneity, I do not yet know the characteristic of non-conjunction. Therefore, the preceding text asks: "Why, then, do you speak of the characteristics of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and conjunction? Moreover, Ānanda initially asked about causes and conditions and spontaneity...

However, he did not previously inquire about "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*). This passage offers a reprimand because conjunction is itself the characteristic of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). That the term "causes and conditions" is mentioned concurrently within the subsequent refutation of conjunction also carries this same meaning.
The reason conjunction is not explicitly mentioned in the reprimand is simply that the text is abbreviated.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, and wishing to expound upon the path of sublime practice consisting of the various *samādhis* and great *dhāraṇīs*, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Although you possess a powerful memory, it merely increases your learning; yet regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, your mind has not yet fully realized it.
Listen attentively now, and I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all those with outflows in the future may also attain the fruit of Bodhi."

Gushan said: *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*); it is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). *Samādhi* is translated here as "right reception" (*samyak-pratigraha*); it is the nature of concentration (*samādhi*). Because concentration and wisdom are balanced and equal, it is called "wondrous cultivation.

As this is the essential path for attaining the fruit, it is likened to a road. *Śamatha* refers to the three types of cessation; "subtle and secret contemplation" refers to the three types of observation.

In the preceding narrative by the scribe, wisdom is mentioned first and concentration later; in the subsequent direct instruction by the Buddha, concentration is mentioned first and wisdom later. This is used to manifest that the essence of sudden and perfect *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is non-dual. —Tiaoxi.

[The Buddha] said: "What Ānanda is confused about is that his mind and objects have become increasingly subtle; what the Tathāgata has shown is that his contemplative insight has become ever more profound. Therefore, it is called 'subtle and secret.
Ānanda, all sentient beings revolve in the world due to two inverted, discriminative, and deluded views. These arise from their respective locations and revolve according to their respective karmas.
What are these two views? First, the deluded view of the individual karma of sentient beings; second, the deluded view of the common lot of sentient beings."

To mistake oneself for external objects is called perversion (*viparyāsa*). To establish a cognition based on seeing is called discrimination (*vikalpa*). Since this discrimination has no intrinsic nature apart from its objects, it is called "seeing the delusion.

Delusion is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*); its arising is seeing, and seeing constitutes karma. Karma results in suffering, which is why one revolves in saṃsāra. To reveal that the three stages of delusive karma and suffering are not distinct moments, it is said:

"Arising in that very place, revolving in that very karma. The *Shoujian* says: "Place" refers to the True. This means that the entirety of the True becomes delusion; hence, it is called "arising. Because causes evoke effects, [it is said...].

It is said that while revolving through the karmic wheel, a single thought-moment of delusion regarding the Truth results in the simultaneous presence of all three realms, like a cluster of akṣa fruits.

Changshui says: "Because the deluded consciousnesses of sentient beings perceive objects differently, they are called 'distinctive karma' (bieye). Since non-seeing is the Truth and seeing is entirely delusion, it is called 'deluded seeing' (wangjian). This deluded seeing is so for each and every being within the realm of sentient beings; therefore, it is called 'commonality' (tongfen).

One should know that deluded seeing is one, yet it is differentiated by name according to the individuals. The Supplement states: "The sequential analysis and separate explanation has two parts. First, citing a metaphor. Second... [End of fragment]
The Analogy of the Circular Shadow of Lamp Light.

What is meant by "deluded vision resulting from distinct karmic actions"? Ānanda, it is like a person in the world who has a red film over their eyes; at night, they see a circular shadow appear beside the light of a lamp, with five colors layered one upon another.

Gushan says: "The 'people of the world' metaphorically represent the sentient beings of the nine realms. The 'eyes' metaphorically represent the true wisdom inherently possessed; the 'lamp' represents the true principle inherently possessed. The 'red cataract' represents the deluded mind; the 'circular shadow' represents the deluded environment.

'Environment' refers to the five aggregates (skandhas); hence it is said that 'the five colors are layered. Chaoci says: 'Although this [metaphor] within the context of individual karma (bipartite karma) generally points to people of the world, its intent is merely to take one person as an illustration.
It is only when reaching the context of collective karma (shared karma) that one speaks of many people.'"

"What do you think? Is this circular light manifested by the lamp’s flame the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the vision? Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, why would those who do not have the cataract not see it as well?

Yet this circular shadow is seen only by the one with the cataract. If it were the color of the vision, then since the vision itself has become a color, what would you call that person with the cataract who sees the circular shadow?"
Gushan said: "The person with cataracts is a metaphor for the Buddha-realm.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular reflection existed separately from the lamp, then when one looks at a screen, a curtain, or a table from the side, a circular reflection should likewise appear. If it existed separately from the vision, it should not be visible to the eye.
Why then does the person with cataracts see this circular reflection?"

Therefore, you should know this: the form actually resides in the lamp; the visual disorder is perceived as a shadow. Both the shadow and the perception are defects of vision; the perception of the defect is not itself a disorder. Ultimately, one should not say that "this is the lamp" or "this is the vision," nor that within these there exists something that is neither lamp nor vision.

The substance of form truly resides in the lamp; its principle and essence are fundamentally authentic. To perceive it as a disease is to mistake it for a shadow; the deluded mind thus creates an objective realm. Both the shadow and the perception are defects (*śuṅga*); both mind and object are illusory.

A person with wisdom who recognizes that [the shadow] is caused by a defect in the eye will never insist that the circular shadow truly exists. Therefore, although the defect is present, it does not constitute a disease of vision. This is analogous to the fact that although ignorance remains within the initial stage of the Bodhisattva path, it is like the presence of a defect.

When one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, then no delusive objects can be found. Thus, the Great Sutra says: "One who knows nirvana, though possessing afflictions, is as if without afflictions."

Zhaoxi said: "One should know that when the Tathāgata raised this [analogy] to refute the attachment to intrinsic nature, he was precisely intending to cite the example that Ānanda’s visual perception of mountains, rivers, and so forth is entirely false vision.
Changshui said: "'Color' refers to the light of a lamp. A lamp truly possesses light; it has never possessed a shadow. Buyi said: "'Seeing' (jian) is a term for cognitive discernment."

It is like a second moon: it is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why? Because the perception of a second moon is produced by the pressure of the fingers. No wise person should say that this source of the pressed organ is a shape or not a shape, or that it is distinct from seeing or not distinct from seeing.
*Nie* (pronounced *nie*) means "to grasp" (*nai*). Changshui says: "It is simply a matter of grasping; because the faculties and consciousnesses are discordant, two aspects are perceived."

This case is also like that; it is produced by a cataract in the eye. Now, whom do you wish to name as being the lamp or the seeing? How much more so regarding the distinction between what is not the lamp and what is not the seeing? Tiāoxī said:

"To say 'it is the lamp' or 'it is the seeing' means that the circular reflection exists because of the lamp and the seeing; this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). To say 'it is not the lamp' or 'it is not the seeing' means that the circular reflection exists apart from the lamp and the seeing;

this is the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). The former passage has already refuted these views; here they are again challenged. Chángshuǐ said: "It is not the form that sees, nor is it the seeing of the form. A person of wisdom...

To say that "the place where this moon arises is form and seeing, yet it is apart from form and seeing" is merely a stylistic variation by the translator. Next is the analogy for the retribution induced by karma.
What is meant by "common delusory vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level lands in between.

The central great island, measured from east to west, contains two thousand three hundred large nations; as for the other small islands scattered among the seas, they contain between two or three hundred nations each, or perhaps only one or two.

"Ānanda, as for those who live for thirty, forty, fifty, or even sixty years: suppose among these there is a small continent containing only two countries, where the people of only one nation have collectively experienced adverse conditions.

Then the sentient beings of that specific land on the small continent will behold all manner of inauspicious phenomena—such as seeing two suns or two moons, or even various evil omens such as halos, solar spots, rings, crescents, comets, meteors, falling stars, 'burdened ears,' and rainbows.
These will be seen only by the people of that country; the sentient beings of the other country will neither see nor hear of them."

Gushan says: *Yun* (halo) and *shi* (aura) are both vapors surrounding the sun. *Shi* refers to the transformation of black vapors that appears before the sun is about to be eclipsed (*yun-shi* should be read as *yun-shi*;

if read as *yun-da*, it is taken as the character *da*). *Pei* should be written as *bei*; its shape is like the character *bei*. *Jue* (ring) refers to a shape like a jade ring. *Sui* (comet) is so called because it sweeps away the old to spread the new. *Bo* (meteoric vapor) resembles a *sui*; the *Shiming* says it is called *bo* because the vapor is *bo-bo* (swirling), resembling a broom; the form of the *yao-xing* (falling star) resembles this [broom].

*Fei-liu* (flying streamer) refers to a flying star. A *liu-xing* (shooting star) flies away, leaving no trace; a *liu-guang* (flowing light) has traces that connect one another. *Er* should be written as *ri* (ear-ornament); the pearl is located... [in the ear].

The character for "ear" (*ěr*) is written as *rì*. Its form resembles that [of the sun]. The *Tongzhàn* states: "The 'bearing' (*fù*) and 'warring' (*zhàn*) qi; the circular qi is an aberration (*shěng*) that is red like a half-halo. When it appears upon the halo, it is called 'circular' (*yuán*); when it appears above the sun, it is called 'bearing' (*fù*)."

"Fu" (負) means "to lean against. The *Wuxing zhi* (Treatise on the Five Phases) reads "bào'ěr" (抱珥). Meng Kang says: "Bào" refers to the vapor leaning toward the sun; "ěr" refers to black spots [appearing around the sun]. (These black spots resemble pearls worn behind the ear. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: [as above].

Chun said: "Generally, when vapors are above the sun, they form a 'crown' (guàn) or a 'pair' (duì). When they are on the sides directly opposite, they are 'ears' (ěr). When they are on the sides like half-rings facing the sun, they are 'embraces' (bào);

facing away from it, they are 'backs' (bèi). When vapors pierce the sun, they are 'claws' (jié); *jié* means to wound or damage. Jing Gong said: "A halo (*yùn*) is a type of vapor. What was previously called 'sudden appearance' (*shì*) refers to calamities involving the sun and moon.

The shapes of the vapors known as 'pendants' (*pèi*) and 'rings' (*jué*) are like those of comets (*huì*). What is called a 'sweeping star' (*sǎoxīng*)—a comet—has its tip pointing in one direction; when its radiant vapors spread out in all directions, it is called a *bò*. A flying star that rises from below is a meteor (*liúxīng*)."

Regarding those that descend from above: the "burdened" (*fu*) appear with their vapors facing away from the sun like those carrying a load; the "ear-shaped" (*er*) have their vapors flanking the sun like ears. Changshui says: "The *peijue* are jade ornaments.

The baleful vapors approach the sun and moon in the shape of *peijue*. Xunwen says: "A *jue* is like a ring but has a gap. Gushan says: "As for rainbows and halos (*hongni*), the male is the rainbow and the female is the halo.

They mostly appear as a pair beside the sun; the bright and vibrant is the rainbow, while the dark is the halo. (The *Tongzhan* states: "When the vapors of yin and yang harmonize, they form harmony; when they are enraged, they form wind and thunder; when struck by baleful vapors, they disperse to form rainbows and halos.")

The Supplement states: The *Erya* says, "The *didian* is called the rainbow. There are two further points for the method of correlation. First is the general heading. The previous citations used metaphors to provide an exposition that appeared to be quite different;
now, wishing to correlate and clarify them, we shall speak of their commonality.
Ānanda, I shall now clarify these two matters for you by advancing and retreating between them.

As the *Zhengji* says: "Now, taking the same as different and using the different to illustrate the same, it is called 'advancing and retreating' (because the individual karma was first elucidated and the common lot was explained afterward, it receives the name 'advancing and retreating').

There are two parts to the separate explanation; first, the application of the analogy, which has two sections. First, the application of the individual karma, which also has two sections. First, the formal application, which also has two sections. First, citing the preceding metaphor."

Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to the deluded vision of their individual karma, perceive the circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light. Although it appears to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the visual impairment of the observer;
this impairment is simply the fatigue of seeing and is not created by the color-form itself.
Lord Jing said: "To take movement as movement is called 'seeing toil.
However, one who sees their own optical aberration (sheng) ultimately incurs no fault in seeing.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The 'superior seeing' refers to the name for liberation and understanding; the 'inferior seeing' refers to the seeing of deluded perception. As the lower scripture says, 'All are immediately the seeing of an aberration, not the seeing of one who possesses the aberration,' this principle may be applied accordingly."
This concludes the explanation. Next, regarding the correct application of the analogy, there are two parts. First, applying it to the cataract in the eye:
take, for example, your own present observation of mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings; these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.

Zhaoxi said: Ānanda’s visual observation is like a deluded perception arising from a separate karmic activity; the mountains, rivers, lands, and so forth are like the circular reflections in a lamp’s light; and his perception of illness is like a cataract in the eye.

Speaking in terms of the Dharma, it is the *ālaya-vijñāna* that is able to perceive the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). Speaking in terms of afflictions, it properly belongs to ignorance (*avidyā*). Next, we combine these with the case of "not being afflicted by cataracts.

In the preceding analogy, one who possesses vision is not a person afflicted by cataracts; now, the person of perfect realization understands that the faculties and objects are awakening-clarity, and thus is free from the disease of cataracts.
The seeing and the conditions for seeing appear as if they were present objects; yet fundamentally, they are my own enlightened awareness. As stated above:

"Although they appear as external objects, they are ultimately produced by the cataracts of that seer," which is a metaphor for how ignorance produces phenomena. Now it is said: "That which appears as a present object is fundamentally my own enlightened awareness."

This demonstrates that True Suchness is unchanging. The *Zhuānzhù* (Explanatory Notes) states: "These three phrases constitute the general heading. Next, [the text] responds to the request [of Ānanda]. Previously, Ānanda was still confused regarding the meaning of 'seeing-seeing' not being 'seeing.
After the Tathāgata had set forth the inverted false seeing, he further elucidates 'seeing-seeing' in detail to respond to that request."

To perceive an object is a cataract; to perceive that perception is itself a cataract. When the originally enlightened, luminous mind perceives objects, it is not a cataract. To perceive that which is perceived is a cataract; when one perceives that there is no cataract within the cataract, this is truly the seeing of seeing.
How can this further be called perceiving, hearing, knowing, or seeing?

This means that once one perceives the arising of the object of focus, both are equally a cataract (*taimira*). If one gives rise to awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) to realize that these two are empty, this very wisdom capable of awakening is also a cataract.

As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To rely on illusion to speak of awakening is also called illusion" (these two lines explain the preceding "seeing" and the following two lines). Tiaoxi says: "The next two lines explain why awakening is itself the seeing of a cataract. This is because within the nature of original awakening, awakening and its conditions merge into a single essence;

it is not like a person with a cataract who perceives a distinction between subject and object" (these two lines explain the preceding "originally I" and the following line). Changshui says: "The next two lines [explain] both..."

[This] concludes [the discussion on] the true and the delusory. If one gives rise to a subject that perceives and perceives an object, both are illnesses of the cataract (*taimira*). The essence of true awakening (*tathatā-jñāna*) is neither subject nor object; therefore, it is not within the cataract.

(The first phrase concludes the "seeing-as-an-object," while the following two phrases conclude the "fundamental awakening. Regarding the phrase "this is truly seeing-seeing": this fundamental awakening, the luminous mind, which is devoid of subject and object, is called "seeing-seeing.

Because it is eternally illuminating while quiescent, and eternally quiescent while illuminating, how could it be designated by such terms as "seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing"? Tiaoxi says: "Awakening is not within the cataract," etc., refers to the aforementioned point that "awakening-seeing is precisely the cataract. If one departs from...

Regarding the cataract: this awareness is precisely the true seeing of seeing. The previous passage stated, "At the time of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [the] seeing. This statement was still somewhat general and abbreviated; therefore, it is discussed in detail here. The section beginning with "How so?
reveals its freedom from delusion and also rebukes his lack of realization. Now, as for the two kinds of inverted, discriminative false views spoken of by the Buddha:

because Ānanda had previously said, "World-Honored One, you have expounded for me the doctrines of causality and spontaneity, yet my mind is still not enlightened," [the Buddha] has thus extensively shown the characteristics of what is seen within the individual karma and the common lot.

All of these are false and illusory. This constitutes a further refutation of the two types of attachment to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, Ānanda said: "Now I hear again that 'the seeing of seeing is not seeing,' which increases my confusion and distress.

Therefore, it is now stated once more: "Apart from the awareness that [the eye] is not a disease, this is truly the seeing of seeing. Regarding the phrase "this is truly the seeing of seeing," there should be two meanings. First, with respect to true seeing, it distinguishes it from false seeing;

this generally includes both understanding (*parijñā*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), both of which are termed "seeing of seeing. Second, specifically with respect to true realization as opposed to seeing, it distinguishes it from seeing through what is merely a semblance of understanding.

The Supplement states: "Regarding 'seeing the object of perception as a cataract': 'seeing' refers to the faculty (the sense organ), and 'the object of perception' refers to the sensory field; these constitute the disease of the cataract. To 'realize that seeing is itself the cataract' means to be able to realize and be able to see [this truth]."

The preceding faculties and objects are that which is perceived and seen. If one maintains the characteristics of subject and object, not only is the perception of conditions a cataract, but the very act of perceiving and seeing is also a cataract.

This refers to Ānanda’s attained "seeing-essence" (jīng) which has not yet escaped from seeing. The two phrases, "The originally awakened luminous mind perceives conditions; this is not a cataract," explain the meaning above. The intent is: why are both subject and object equally cataracts?

It is precisely because within the originally awakened luminous mind, the awakening and the conditions are of one essence, devoid of the characteristics of subject and object; only then is it "not a cataract. The character "awakened" (jué) refers to—

The phrase "the superior [mind] can take the seeing as its object" refers to the "eye-disease" (*taimira*) of the seeing that is being taken as an object; the character "object" (*yuan*) points to the aforementioned object of perception, which is the "eye-disease" of the perceived. The four preceding phrases clarify the essence of seeing.

They explain the previous statement, "seeing is still apart from seeing," referring to the very seeing that is to be transcended. The three subsequent phrases—beginning with "awakening to the eye-disease of what is awakened to"—clarify true seeing. They explain the previous statement regarding the time of "seeing the seeing. As for "awakening to the eye-disease of what is awakened to":

this one phrase provisionally distinguishes between the object and the contemplation, taking deluded seeing as the "eye-disease" that is the object of awakening, and awakening itself as the subject that awakens. It is like the sky.

Tiantai initially takes the realm of darkness as the object of contemplation and the ten vehicles as the means of contemplation. [The text states: "To realize that this is not a defect within the vision, but is truly the seeing of seeing—since the substance of the preceding defects and illnesses is entirely the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance, fundamentally free from any defect, then subject and object are of one essence;
this is truly the seeing of seeing. This resembles the Tiantai "inconceivable realm," wherein there is no distinction between subject and object or separate entities.

Lord Jing said: That which is called "the luminous essence of seeing" (jiansheng mingyuan) is the essence but not the source; it is the self but not an object; it is the seeing but not the mind. This is precisely what is meant by "the luminous essence of seeing.

As for what is called "the fundamentally enlightened luminous mind" (benjue mingxin), it is the source but not the essence; it is the mind but not the seeing. It is neither the possession of a self nor the absence of a self. Why is this? Because sentient beings mistake objects for themselves.

Thus, to regard what is non-self as self is to mistake oneself for an external object; to regard what is self as non-self is to mistake an external object for oneself. Consequently, that which is non-self is the object, and that which possesses self is the self.

The nature of seeing is the clarity of awareness; it is "I" and not a thing—this is what is meant by "nature. If this is the originally awakened, luminous mind, then it is the One Mind manifested from the very beginning, and that One Mind is simply one.

Who is there to oppose it? How could there be an "I"? Since the nature of all things has never ceased to exist, how could there be no "I"? Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "I and non-I are non-dual"—this is the meaning of non-self. Because the mind is thus, the term "I" is insufficient to describe it.

As for the phrase "the vision of objects is an optical illusion, and the awareness of seeing is itself the illusion": when the clarity of awareness gives rise to seeing, one sees the objects of perception.

"An optical aberration. That which is perceived and seen by him is precisely the aberration. As for 'the originally awakened luminous mind perceiving conditions is not the aberration,' this means that while this originally awakened luminous mind perceives that seeing and the capacity to perceive as well as the perceived object, this originally awakened luminous mind itself is not the aberration.
