When it is said 'perceiving the aberration of what is perceived, the perception is not within the aberration,' it means that when the luminous mind gives rise to seeing and perceives there is something external, this is called 'what is perceived.

This originally awakened luminous mind perceives that 'what is perceived' is the aberration, yet this originally awakened luminous mind is not within the aberration. To say 'perception is not within the aberration' is precisely to see the seeing."

Furthermore, the subsequent section on "Unifying" is divided into two parts. First, unifying so that all people of the nation see the same thing: those who perceive the optical defect immediately behold inauspicious omens and calamitous anomalies; they truly see them only because of their own visual impairment.

Therefore, when you now see me, yourself, and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, you are seeing only a visual distortion; it is not that you are seeing the one who perceives the distortion.

Zhaoxi says: "This rebukes Ānanda for not being one who sees the distortion rather than the person with the ailment. Next, it is appropriate that those in that land do not see [this], referring to those from the stage of the 'Ground' (bhūmi) onwards among the Perfect Ones.
That which perceives the true essence has a nature that is not afflicted by cataracts; therefore, it is not called "seeing.

If that perceiving nature belongs to one who is free from cataracts, they do not perceive the marks of the phenomenal world. That which perceives the true essence with a nature free from cataracts is precisely the true moon.
Because it is free from cataracts, there follows a further section on the combined clarification of advancing and retreating, which is divided into two parts. First, the general heading.

Ānanda, just as those sentient beings share a commonality of deluded vision, so too may one person with a distinct karmic condition be compared to that deluded vision; and one person with diseased eyes may be compared to that single country.

The preceding passage states: "I shall now, for your sake, clarify these two matters by advancing and retreating them for comparison. The meaning is seen here as follows: "Those sentient beings" and so forth advances the general case to illustrate the particular;

"one person with diseased eyes" and so forth retreats the particular to illustrate the general. Because the metaphor of the eye's cataract (*taimira*) is drawn from individual karma (*pratyeka-karman*), it is easy to reveal the nature of delusion;

since everyone knows that the shadow-person seen due to the cataract is unreal. However, because the metaphor of the miasma is drawn from the common lot (*sabhāga*), it is difficult to reveal the nature of delusion; since all phenomena perceived due to the miasma appear as if they were real. Therefore, the Buddha’s intention was to manifest the common lot.

These delusions are entirely like the delusions of individual karma; thus, there is the teaching of "advancing and retreating" for the sake of clear illumination. The subsequent detailed explanation has two parts. First, "retreating" to align with the example of the individual.

The Sūtra says, "That vision of a circular reflection is produced by the delusion of an eye disease (*taimira*)," which cites the previous case of individual karma as the illustrative example. From the phrase "this shared portion (*sabhāgatā*)" onwards, it formally uses the shared portion to illustrate that individual karma.

It then takes the delusion seen within the shared portion and "retreats" it to the deluded vision of a single person in the previous case of individual karma, showing that both are fundamentally the beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).

That vision of a circular shadow arises from the delusion of a cataract; this manifestation of ill omen within the commonality of the group arises from the corrupting evils of shared karma; both are produced by the beginningless delusion of seeing.

Gushan said: "The 'sickness of the eyes' and 'miasmic evil,' though used as metaphors, actually illustrate that the very capacity for seeing is delusion, for all worldly distinctions between the real and the unreal are nothing but delusion.
For one who understands it thus, how could they seek the dharma being illustrated apart from the illustrative event itself? Tiaoxi said:

"Although the illustrations are all delusive, the dharma being illustrated must clarify that the deluded vision of Ānanda alone, as well as the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa and even the ten directions, is all likewise so; furthermore, within the context of shared karma, this refers to the delusion of miasmic evil."
This is still easy to understand. However, the various realms of outflows (*sāsrava*) and the illusory conditions for the sicknesses of sentient beings are in fact difficult to believe.

Therefore, the scriptural text proceeds from the narrow to the broad, using what is easy to illustrate what is difficult, elucidating them in sequence so that they mutually support one another in this manner. The *Xunwen* (Explanatory Notes on Hearing) states: "Without beginning" refers to the fact that the deluded perceptions currently manifest before us have no initial cause. Next, it advances a specific analogy:

taking the deluded vision of a single person and advancing it to be the same as the delusions of calamity and auspiciousness perceived by all beings in the subsequent text; both are equally delusions regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*).

O Wondrous Mind, there is indeed seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Since it is already stated that this refers to Jambudvīpa, there must necessarily be a corresponding instance; the scriptural text merely alludes to it by implication.
Furthermore, the preceding passage explicitly states that "one person with diseased eyes is like that one country," and within this context, such an implication may be abbreviated.

For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans and the Sahā world, as well as all the realms with outflows throughout the ten directions and all sentient beings therein, they are all alike the pure, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind;
yet through the conditions of the delusory afflictions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they falsely conjoin to give rise to birth and falsely conjoin to undergo death.
Zhaoxi says: "Because the true and the false are in union, there is birth and death. To speak of the false alone is because the True Suchness is in a state of delusion. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says:

"To examine the establishment of these two kinds of false views—the collective and the individual karmic—whether taken together or separately, it is clear that all sentient beings, due to their beginningless false views, cause objective realms to manifest before them. This is like a person with red eyes seeing circular halos;

if the false view were absent, the realm would likewise vanish, as is the case for one without such eye-disease. This is how the individual karma of one person is; since this is so for one person, it is so for all."

It is the same for all sentient beings. To demonstrate that every sentient being possesses this delusion, the analogy of a lamp casting a circular shadow can only illustrate the case of a single person;

it cannot be applied to the multitude. Therefore, the analogy of perceiving calamities and auspicious signs is further cited to show that such false perceptions exist in all sentient beings alike. Although the shared perception of miasmic evils is common to all, the meaning of "delusion" is not yet fully clarified.

Thus, this is set aside and equated with the analogy of the lamp in its sense of falsity: since both have existed from beginningless time, they are both equally false. Indeed, it is because of these miasmic evils that [the analogy is introduced].

How does the appearance of calamitous portents differ from seeing a circular halo due to the delusion of a visual impairment? Furthermore, if one person with a visual impairment sees a circular halo around a lamp and advances [to observe] alongside the others, would they not likewise see the external omens of disaster or fortune?
This is truly because they equally share the delusion regarding the enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind; thus, all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known is no different.

Therefore, by advancing and retreating to clarify this, we ensure that these two types of karma are equalized, as they both ultimately return to a single deluded vision. Question: Are these two deluded visions caused by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), or are they caused by ignorance (*avidyā*)? Now, let us address these two...

I shall clarify this point. First, the inauspicious sights seen within this shared environment (*sabhāgatā*) are merely illustrative metaphors. In the Sūtras, citing a metaphor to illustrate a principle refers here to beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikāvidyā*).

Furthermore, it can be directly observed that malignant miasmas (*dustavāyu*) likewise arise from beginningless ignorance. Now, by using those malignant miasmas as an analogy for what people perceive, [it is shown that] these too flow forth from ignorance alone.

If one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction and disjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death, perfects the nature of bodhi which is neither born nor extinguished, and realizes that the pure fundamental mind—
the original enlightenment— is eternally abiding.
Lord Jing said: "The Dharma of sentient beings is characterized by combination; the Dharma of the Two Vehicles is characterized by non-combination.

Ānanda, although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous, you have not yet clarified that this source of enlightenment is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination."

Changshui says: "In the previous passage, Ānanda stated, 'The mind has not yet opened regarding all phenomena of conjunction and non-conjunction. Therefore, he now restates them. *Bu-yi* (Supplementary Notes) states: "Conjunction refers to the characteristic of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);

non-conjunction refers to the characteristic of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). To calculate based on causes and conditions is coarse; to calculate conjunction as the subtle. To calculate spontaneity as coarse; to calculate non-conjunction as the subtle.

Thus, although the preceding text mentions hearing about causes and conditions and spontaneity, one has still not yet awakened to conjunction and non-conjunction. Furthermore, the preceding text was based on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

Question: Regarding the discussion on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), why does a doubt suddenly arise later in the text concerning what is "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*) and what is "not conjoined"?

This is truly because that which is conjoined is precisely cause and condition, while that which is not conjoined is spontaneity. Furthermore, within the section refuting conjunction, the Sūtra states: "You still harbor doubts of your own by means of the nature of all worldly false conceptualizations and their various causes and conditions.

Based on this, it is clearly shown that causes and conditions are themselves conjunction. Question: By what is the meaning of "coarse" and "subtle" expressed? One must understand that regarding cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya*), as well as calculation (*kalpanā*) and...

The refutations each consist of four propositions. If one considers "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), there are eight propositions comprising both "conjoining" (*saṃ*) and "uniting" (*yoga*). Thus, if one calculates that the cause conjoins with the objective field (*viṣaya*), then the cause has eight propositions;

the conditions (*pratyaya*) are likewise. If one considers "neither conjoining nor uniting," there are likewise eight propositions. By examining these characteristics, is it not the case that in refuting the dharma of characteristics, there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle?

Lord Jing said: "The wondrously luminous nature arising from original enlightenment is not a nature produced by causes and conditions; thus it can be known that it is not a composite. It is not a spontaneous nature;
thus it can be known that it is not non-composite. Yet Ānanda did not understand this clearly, so the Buddha explained it in detail for him."

Ānanda, I now ask you again about the objects before you. You still harbor doubts based on the nature of all worldly delusions and their combined causes and conditions, questioning whether the mind of Bodhi arises from a combination of factors.

Zhaoxi said: "The bodhicitta is the very nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*). The preceding passage states: 'Yet it is not yet clear that such an origin of awakening is not produced through combination,' and so forth."
Thus, as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing that you now possess: does it blend with light? Does it blend with darkness? Does it blend with openness? Does it blend with obstruction?

If it blends with light, then when you observe light and it appears before you, where does the seeing intermingle with it? The characteristics of the seeing and the light can be distinguished; what kind of form would their intermingling take?

Zizhong said: "Luminosity belongs to the preceding characteristic; seeing belongs to the internal mind. At what point can one discuss their intermingling? Seeing and characteristics can be distinguished at a glance;
as for luminosity and seeing being intermingled, what form would they take?"
If it is not the seeing that sees, how can it see clarity? If it is the seeing itself that sees, how can it see the seeing? Guishan says:
"If one claims that clarity is not the seeing, and therefore its mixed form and appearance cannot be described, he refutes this by asking: 'How can it see clarity?
If one claims that clarity is identical to the seeing, which is called their mutual intermingling, he refutes this by asking: 'How can it see the seeing?'"
If seeing is complete, how can it be conjoined with clarity? If clarity is complete, it cannot be conjoined with seeing.
"Complete" means all-pervasive. If seeing itself were pervasive, there would be no room for clarity to intermingle; if clarity itself were pervasive, there would be no room for seeing to intermingle.

Seeing must be distinct from illumination. If they are mixed, one loses the names and natures of both; if they are mixed, the nature of seeing is lost. To conflate seeing with illumination is not correct. "Nature" refers to the nature of seeing.

If seeing is mixed with illumination, how can it still be called "seeing"? If illumination is mixed with seeing, how can it still be called "illumination"? Since the two names—nature and illumination—are lost through such conflation, we know that the claim that seeing is conjoined with illumination does not accord with principle.
Therefore, it is said that "conjoining seeing with illumination is not correct."
It is the same with darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for this wondrously pure essence of seeing within you now: is it joined with light? Is it joined with darkness? Is it joined with openness? Or is it joined with obstruction?
Zizhong said: "The preceding explained the meaning of 'harmony,' like water mixing with soil; now it explains the meaning of 'union,' like a lid fitting onto a box.
If one speaks of union, then when darkness arrives and the characteristic of light has already ceased, this seeing does not unite with the various forms of darkness. How, then, can it see darkness?"

Changshui said: "If seeing conjoins with light, then when the characteristic of darkness appears, the characteristic of light must necessarily cease. Since it has conjoined with light, it should perish along with the light; how then can one see darkness?"

If, when seeing darkness, the faculty of sight does not conjoin with darkness but conjoins with light, it should not be seeing light. Since it does not see light, how can it be said that by conjoining with light, it perceives light and not darkness?

If he should attempt to rescue his position by saying, "This nature of my seeing does not conjoin with darkness, yet it does not hinder the seeing of darkness; what fault is there in this? you should immediately refute him by saying: "If it were to conjoin with light, it should not be the case that it sees light, and so forth."
It is the same with darkness, light, and all various obstructions.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I reflect upon it, is this wondrous, fundamental awareness not in harmony with the various sense objects and the mind’s thoughts?"

Zhenji said: "If a combination does not achieve [reality], it is not a combination, for form and its counterpart must necessarily exist in relation to one another. This calculation holds that the two dharmas of reality and delusion do not touch at all; this is called 'non-combination. Tiaoxi said:

"The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes all calculations without exceeding the four natures—namely, self, other, both, and no cause. First, the refutation of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is precisely the refutation of no cause. Second, the refutation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) covers self, other, and both.

For example, when examining dependent origination through the lens of light, darkness, space, and obstruction, it specifically concerns the nature of the other (*parabhāva*). Furthermore, there is the emptiness, clarity, and mind grasped by Ānanda."

The eye has four kinds of causal conditions: space and light are "other," while the mind and the eye are "self. Furthermore, the Buddha spoke of two kinds of objects of vision—the common and the distinct; in both cases, the seeing is "self" and the object is "other."

Since there are both self and other, they must necessarily accord with their nature. However, because the common nature (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) is difficult to refute, I have further employed the teaching of "harmonious union" (*saṃyoga*).

Nevertheless, even the meaning of non-union is derived from the analysis of self and other; this is done merely to thoroughly investigate and clarify [the truth] in order to prevent the lingering habits of delusion. Question: How does this differ from the previous seven locations and the four natures used to examine the mind?

Answer: The seven locations and the four natures do not yet touch upon the ultimate reality (*tattva*); they merely refute the conceptualization and calculation of the sixth consciousness-mind (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*). Now, in the case of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) and the others, all are based on the awakened nature (*bodhi-svabhāva*) to refute the false and reveal the true. This is a subtle and profound contemplative observation.
This can be seen here.
The Buddha said, "You have now further stated that this awakening is not a composite. I ask you again:

as for this wondrous essence of seeing which is not a composite—is it because it does not combine with light? Is it because it does not combine with darkness? Is it because it does not combine with openness? Or is it because it does not combine with obstruction?"

If seeing and light were not harmonious, then there would necessarily be a boundary between them. You should observe closely: where is the light, and where is the seeing? Within the seeing and within the light, from what point do they demarcate their boundaries?
Xunwen said: "Pàn means 'boundary' or 'limit.

Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were necessarily no seer, then [the seer] would not reach it; one would not know where the characteristics of light are located. How, then, could a boundary be established?"
It is the same with darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.

Furthermore, this wondrous seeing-essence is not something that comes into combination; does it not combine with light? Does it not combine with darkness? Does it not combine with openness? Does it not combine with obstruction?

It is not that harmony lacks substance because they do not interpenetrate; therefore, one examines it through its boundaries. It is not that harmony lacks a nature because it is inherently differentiated; therefore, one refutes it through its discordant aspects.
Thus, harmony brings the intimate together with the distant.

If there were no union with light, then the nature of seeing and the nature of light would be mutually opposed; they would be as distinct from one another as the ear and light, which clearly do not touch. If seeing itself does not even know the location of the characteristics of light, how can it discern the principles of union and non-union?

Gushan says: "Divergent corners" (*guǐjiǎo*). "Corner" (*jiǎo*) refers to an angle. When an object is at an angle, it does not face [the observer] directly. Since their natures are already divergent in this way, how is this different from taking that faculty of hearing and confronting this objective realm of light?
Therefore, it is said to be "like the ear and the light," and so forth.
The same applies to darkness, penetration, and all various obstructions.
The above has been an analysis of the mind and vision to shatter the false and reveal the true. Guishan says: "The second major section generally refutes all dharmas.

As for the previous specific refutation of the mind and vision, it was truly because Ānanda, observing the sublime marks of the Tathāgata with his own eyes, felt joy and delight in his heart; thereupon he resolved to renounce birth and death, yet he constantly craved further explanations regarding the Buddha-dharma. For this reason, [the third...]"

Illnesses do not converge upon a single principle; therefore, the preceding text refuted attachments through successive stages, finding that they did not transcend the mind’s perceptions and the auditory object. Although other dharmas were involved, these were not the primary intent. Now, for the first time, we shall examine the three categories and the seven elements in detail, scrutinizing and refuting them until nothing remains obstructed. By searching through both the general and the specific, not a single dharma can be found; thus, the eternally abiding true mind is revealed herein, and the wondrous *śamatha* is distinguished herein. This is precisely why one may attain the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of cultivation and realization—it lies right here. There are two [categories]: first, the refutation of the four dharmas; second, the refutation of the seven greats. By adding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to the three aggregates (*skandha*), they constitute the four dharmas. Question: Why are the seven greats categorized separately? Answer:
The preceding four proceed from the few to the many—namely, five, six, ten, and twenty-eight. The seven greats deviate from that sequence; therefore, they must be categorized separately.
Furthermore, while the four dharmas are presented individually as they manifest before one, the seven greats are explained collectively due to the presence of doubt.

Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these floating, superficial, illusory, and transformative appearances arise at the very place they appear and perish at the very place they are; they are called "appearances" because they are illusory and false, yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.

Previously, I have extensively refuted the view that the mind perceives objects; yet you have still not traversed the three categories [of body, sensation, and mind]. Therefore, it is said: "You have not yet clearly understood that all these floating, mundane, illusory, and transformative phenomena are empty and devoid of substance."

It obscures the true nature; therefore, it is called "floating dust. All phenomena are unreal, like illusions and transformations; therefore, they are called "the marks of various illusions and transformations. "Place" refers to the true substance.

Being born as illusions and ceasing as illusions, they do not depart from the truth, just as waves arise and subside without departing from the water. Therefore, it is said: "They are produced in this very place and extinguished in that very place.

Coming and going are false views of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said: "Illusory falsehoods are called marks. Because illusion is false, it is termed "illusory falsehood. As for "their nature is equal": waves are the marks of water, and water is the nature of the waves. Waves and water are one and the same; so too are nature and marks.

It is called "loss" (śī). To provide clarification, it is referred to as "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) and "nature" (svabhāva); yet these characteristics and natures are themselves neither characteristic nor nature. The three truths are the one truth, and the one truth is the three truths—this can be understood through reflection.

Xunwen says: "Regarding all illusory manifestations," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For example, like illusory elephants, horses, and various other objects, although one knows they have no reality, they can still be heard and seen."

In this way, it extends even to the five aggregates, the six sense bases, from the twelve entrances to the eighteen realms. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is illusory birth; through the separation of causes and conditions, there is what is called illusory extinction.

Yet one is utterly unable to know that birth, extinction, coming, and going are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, unmoving, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this true and eternal nature, if one seeks coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.

Gushan says: "All sutras enumerate three categories—namely, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—because there are three [categories] each corresponding to the delusions, faculties, and inclinations [of sentient beings]. Guxiang says: "The *Abhidharmakośa* states: 'Aggregation, gateways for arising, and lineage are the meanings of aggregate, base, and element.

Because there are three types of delusion, faculty, and inclination, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught. As for the three types of delusion: first, for those deluded regarding the mind, the five aggregates are taught."

Thus, for those who are deluded regarding the mind as fourfold and form as a single unity, the twelve *āyatanas* (bases) are taught; this opens up form into ten and a half bases—namely, the five sense organs, the five objects, and a small portion of the *dharmāyatana* (mental object)—while consolidating the mind into one and a half bases—namely, the mental organ (*manas*) and a small portion of the *dharmāyatana*.

For those who are deluded regarding both mind and form, the eighteen *dhātus* (elements) are taught; this further opens up the mind into seven and a half elements—namely, the six consciousnesses, the mental organ, and a small portion of the *dharmadhātu*.

All these terms refer to being "deluded" or "confused. Regarding the three types of faculties, they are superior, middling, and inferior. Regarding the three types of inclinations, they are... [text ends]... happiness.

The "abbreviated" and "intermediate" [explanations] are all, respectively, correlated with the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements]. Yet here there are four; the addition of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is merely a breaking down of the internal six bases within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

These are increased or decreased according to the capacity of the recipient; why must they necessarily be three? These are all variations in the opening and closing of matter and mind, and are the vast floating dust and various illusory transformations mentioned above. The section beginning with "Because of conditions" expands upon the phrase "arising in their respective places" and so forth from above.

The section beginning with "By no means" expands upon the phrase "its nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity" from above. First, it clarifies that the nine realms are in fact the Buddha-realm; because of delusion, they are not [realized as such].

Know that within each and every realm, the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth are fully present. This very deluded thought is itself the ultimate truth; therefore, it is devoid of such characteristics as arising and ceasing, or coming and going.

Regarding the title of the Tathāgata’s fruition, there are three bodies (trikāya). Because the causal principle contains and encompasses these, it is called a "Treasury" (garbha). It is termed "eternally abiding" because it does not belong to the past, future, or present. It is called "wondrously luminous" because it is quiescent yet illuminating; it is called "immovable" because it is illuminating yet quiescent;

it is called "all-pervasive and perfect" because the three and the one mutually encompass one another; and it is called "Suchness" (tathatā) because its essence is neither false nor deceptive. To remain unchanging while following conditions is what is named...

Nature. Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha encompasses the three truths (*trisatya*) in general; the subsequent passage specifically reveals these three truths. "Eternally abiding, wondrously luminous" refers to the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārthasatya*).

"Immovable and all-pervading" refers to the Truth of Conventional Reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*). "The wondrous nature of True Suchness" refers to the Truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā satyā*). This accords perfectly with the Fourth Fascicle, where the World-Honored One explicitly explains the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha by means of the three truths.

The section beginning with "The nature is true, eternal, and central" clarifies that the perfect principle of the Buddha-realm is free from the characteristics of the two extremes. To speak of it in a general sense, the three pairs such as coming and going are both extremes. However, if one investigates its ultimate significance deeply, then even these...

Because the ultimate is the conventional, it does not depart; because the conventional is the ultimate, it does not arrive. Because the extremes are the middle, there is no delusion; because the middle is the extremes, there is no awakening.

Because cessation is wisdom, there is no death; because wisdom is cessation, there is no birth. Since these six characteristics do not apply, it is said that "ultimately nothing is attained. Furthermore, this is not the same as the three preceding provisional teachings of skillful means.

Therefore, it is said that there is ultimately nothing to be attained. Why is this? According to what is taught in the Tripitaka (Āgama) and Shared (Sādhāraṇa) teachings regarding the analysis of the body (*dharma-dhātu*), ordinary beings depart from nirvāṇa and come to saṃsāra, while sages depart from saṃsāra and come to nirvāṇa.

According to what is discussed in the Gradual (Krama) teaching of the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha-yāna), the nine realms depart from the Middle Way and come to the two extremes, while the Buddha-realm departs from the two extremes and comes to the Middle Way.

Thus, the three teachings possess the characteristics of coming and going. In the Tripitaka and Shared teachings, one abandons delusion regarding the six realms to achieve the awakening of the Two Vehicles. In the Distinct teaching, one abandons delusion regarding the eight realms to achieve the awakening of the Bodhisattva. Therefore, we know that the three teachings involve delusion.

This is the realization of their characteristics. In the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, one transcends the birth-and-death of limited segments (*duanfen shengsi*), yet there remains the birth-and-death of transformation (*bianyi shengsi*). In the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching, one transcends both types of birth-and-death, vowing to enter the Middle Way, which is neither of these two types of birth-and-death.

Thus we know that the three teachings possess the characteristics of birth and death. Even within the specific doctrines taught in those respective schools, they do not transcend coming and going; viewed from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), they have not escaped the six aspects (*liu xiang*).

How could this be called conforming to the fundamental nature? Now, the teaching of perfect interfusion conforming to the nature refers neither to the coming and going of birth and death, nor to delusion and awakening;

therefore, it is said that "ultimately nothing is attained. One who realizes this is termed "perfectly awakened. Changshui said: "These various illusory appearances originally have no basis; they merely arise suddenly through delusion regarding the Truth.

Therefore, it is said they 'arise in their own place. Since arising is non-arising, they are fundamentally quiescent; therefore, it is said they 'perish everywhere. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "All dharmas are unarisen; I speak of the meaning of the moment (*kṣaṇa*). First..."

That which arises is immediately subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both, nor without a cause;

therefore, one knows there is no arising. This non-arising is precisely what is meant by cessation. Because it is grasped through deluded vision, it appears to have floating characteristics, yet ultimately it has no substance, being like a magical illusion.

Thus it is said: "Illusory and false, they are called characteristics. In the place where there is no substance, there is originally the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature of Bodhi. Therefore it is said: "Its nature is truly the essence of wondrously enlightened luminosity. Question: If illusory appearances are unreal...

"Ultimately they have no substance. How can you further say that their nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity? The answer is: "It is like flowers in the sky (*ākāśa-puṣpa*). Because of the eye disease of *timira*, one perceives flowers in the empty sky.

Thus, in truth, apart from the emptiness there is no separate appearance of flowers. Although these sky-flowers lack self-nature, they nevertheless take empty space as their substratum. If the eye disease is cured, although the appearance of the flowers ceases, the nature of the emptiness does not cease.

The nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so. Although illusory appearances cease, the true nature remains unmoved. Question: "If this is so, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) is identical to the myriad phenomena."

All phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*). How can one establish a distinction between reality and delusion within a single essence? Answer: It is like the illusory vision of flowers in the sky by one with cataracts. If there were no cataracts in the eyes, one would see only the clear sky and no flowers.

Thus, we know that although all phenomena are true, they are known only through realization; they cannot be seen by the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*). Because the minds and consciousnesses of ordinary beings are coarse and restless, they perceive only the coarse and restless characteristics of the world.

Clinging to these coarse appearances, they are obstructed by those very marks and fail to see the true nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the preceding text says: "Deluded regarding oneself, one takes it for an object. For this reason, in this [passage]:

In the Madhyamaka, the great view subsumes the small; therefore, it is now refuted at length. When attachment is lost, emptiness becomes clear. Through this, one awakens to and enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "All phenomena are unborn."

All dharmas are without extinction. If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas will always manifest before one. As the preceding text also states: "If one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata.

Both of these express this same meaning. The Supplement (*Buyi*) states: When the sutra reaches this point, it proclaims the name "Tathāgatagarbha" because the preceding text has shown that the essence of the eternally abiding true mind pervades all dharmas;

it now intends to extensively explain all dharmas to reveal that the eternally abiding true mind contains all and encompasses all, for there is nothing that is not the principle-nature of the three truths. By proclaiming this single name, its meaning is comprehensive.

Regarding emptiness and non-emptiness: why is this so? Because the rational nature (li-xing) is endowed with the three truths; because all phenomena are both identical to and separate from themselves; and because the *tathāgatagarbha* is used to extend the principle of the true mind (*zhenshin*).

If one were to take the names and categories of the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*" from the subsequent scriptural passages as referring exclusively to the stage of fruition (*guo-wei*), that would not be correct here, for this section precisely clarifies the causal mind (*yin-xin*). Thus, they cannot be directly cited as being identical.
"Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally such as they are, being by nature the wondrous, true *tathatā* (Suchness)?

Changshui says: 'In Sanskrit, this is called *skandha*; here it is translated as "aggregates" (*yin*). "Aggregate" means accumulation; "aggregate" [as *yin*] means covering. It refers to the accumulation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which covers the true nature.

There are five such aggregates, which exhaustively encompass all conditioned things; what is there that they do not include? Shoujian says: 'Regarding "accumulation" and so forth, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "The burden of the fruit of the storehouse."'"
Regarding the meaning: "heap" (*skandha*) has the sense of a cause; "burden" (*bhāra*) has the sense of a collection. As for "comprehending all conditioned phenomena":

although the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) also pertain to the uncontaminated and supramundane sense—as in the five aggregates of the Buddhas who, through the cessation of impermanent form, attain permanent form, and so forth—and thus also pertain to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), here we take only the contaminated and conditioned aggregates and do not include the unconditioned, because their meanings are not compatible.

Nevertheless, one should know that the five aggregates possess three meanings: first, knowing their characteristics. That is to say, form has the characteristic of change and obstruction; feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception... [is] the one that...

Grasping at images; "formative activity" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the process of flux; and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to discernment. Second, one knows their arising and ceasing, meaning that arising has no source and ceasing has no destination. Third, one knows their non-arising and non-ceasing, meaning that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and thus have no cessation.

Therefore, a sutra says: "When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent; because they are empty, they cannot cease—this is the meaning of non-arising. However, if one can understand this, one transforms the five aggregates into the fivefold Dharma-body:
the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is transformed into the body of ethical discipline (*śīla-kāya*). The manifest and unmanifest precepts are all the aggregate of form.

Therefore, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is transformed into the body of meditative concentration (*samādhi-kāya*). Concentration is termed "right reception" (*samyag-upabhoga*). Perception (*saṃjñā*) is transformed into wisdom (*prajñā*); for all that possesses marks (*nimitta*) is entirely false and illusory, and by seeing that marks are not marks, one realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are transformed into liberation (*vimukti*). The absence of craving and other such formations is called "liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimukti*); the permanent severance of ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "liberation through wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukti*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is transformed into the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

Since this is conjoined with right reception and wisdom, it constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of reality as it is. As the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* says: "By contemplating form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, one attains the patience of the precepts."

This refers to the patience of vision (*darśana-kṣānti*), the patience of meditative concentration (*samādhi-kṣānti*), the patience of wisdom (*prajñā-kṣānti*), and the patience of liberation (*vimukti-kṣānti*). Furthermore, these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*); this may be seen by comparison. The *Śìyào lùn* (Essentials of Explanation) asks: "What is not encompassed?

It states that because the five aggregates subsume the hundred dharmas—excluding only the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena—all others are fully included. Thus, a verse says: "The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) subsumes eleven [dharmas] in their entirety; Sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) each account for one;

Eight [of the ten great earth-dharmas] are gathered within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); Seventy-three are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); The unconditioned is not an accumulation; It is not included within the category of aggregates. Therefore, it is said that the five aggregates subsume all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.

[The section on] "Exhaustion" concludes. Guxiang said: "Among these five [aggregates], one is matter (rūpa) and four are mind (citta). Regarding whether three [mental factors] and one [the mind-king] arise together or separately, each follows their respective school's tenets;

this is not essential for our present purpose, so I shall not discuss them in detail. If you wish to understand briefly the characteristics of the simultaneous arising of the mind-king and mental factors: the mind-king apprehends the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), while the mental factors apprehend the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).

When consciousness first arises, it merely takes the general characteristic of blue and so forth as its object. Next, the grasping of the image of the object is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā). Next, the experiencing of the preceding object is the aggregate of feeling (vedanā). Next, the arising of craving and other afflictions..."

The affliction of volitional activity is precisely the mind of formation (*saṃskāra*). Ordinary people, through false conceptualization, reckon it to be truly existent; now this sutra reveals and refutes it, showing that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty.
Ānanda, it is like a person with clear vision who gazes at the bright, pure sky. There is only a vast, clear void, utterly devoid of anything.

For no reason, that person does not move his eyes but stares fixedly until they become fatigued, whereupon he perceives illusory flowers (*keśoṇḍuka*) in the empty space, as well as all manner of other delusory, non-existent forms. You should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exactly like this.

Gushan says: "The 'pure eyes' (jingmu) symbolize the true wisdom inherently possessed; the 'clear sky' (qingkong) symbolizes the true principle inherently possessed. This single, clear void is the oneness of principle and wisdom.

That it is 'far removed and nothing exists' signifies the severance of the deluded forms of the nine realms. The 'person' is a metaphor for sentient beings. Because they turn their backs on the truth and unite with delusion, it is said they are 'without [foundation]' (wu). Not moving the eyes represents the grasping and attachment of the deluded mind;

'staring' (deng)—as the *Picao* glosses, 'to gaze straight ahead'—represents the moisture of delusive afflictions that nourishes karma. Thus, within the wondrous nature, the forms of the nine realms manifest; hence it is said, 'in the void one sees wild flowers and the like.'"

Changshui says: "The eye is a metaphor for wisdom; emptiness is a metaphor for principle (*tattva*). Since the ocean of fruition has no distinct forms or sounds, only the principle of suchness and the wisdom of suchness remain.

Because that person does not [stabilize the mind], it is not due to any external object, but simply because their own unmoving eye gazes directly at empty space. When the eyes become fatigued, they then perceive the appearance of flowers, or see hair-whirls, a second moon, and so forth. Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is likewise:

because one does not know True Suchness as it truly is, one fails to realize that the movement of thought manifests the objects of the six sense-fields; this is precisely the arising of the aggregate of form."

Xunwen said: "This must be understood by correlating it with the preceding and following textual contexts; only then will its meaning become clear. Since the preceding text has already used 'wild flowers' as a metaphor for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the subsequent text says:"

The passage beginning with "These various delusive flowers do not come from space" is a direct metaphor for the fact that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) does not arise from causes and conditions. Since the illustrative text is already exhaustive, the phenomenon illustrated is treated very briefly;
it is explained in between [the two], which is a skillful and true mode of expression. The subsequent four aggregates may be understood by analogy with this. Master Jing said:
"Because space is inert, it is not the case that there is a 'present existence' which constitutes the emptiness of form."
Ānanda, these various delusory flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes.

[The phrase] "pervading the hearing" means that "not coming from space" refutes the nature of the other (the external), and "not emerging from the eyes" refutes the nature of the self (the internal). Speaking in terms of dharmas, one should distinguish between self and other by way of the mind and its objects.

Within the remaining four aggregates (*skandhas*), both the meanings of self and other exist; thus, among the four natures, some are omitted while others are refuted. Only within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is there the meaning of departing from both self and other, which seems to refute non-existence.

Regarding the nature of causality: Question—The sutra refutes the two attachments to self and dharmas; why, then, must one refute the four natures? Furthermore, among the four natures, why is there such an emphasis on refuting the natures of self-origination and other-origination? Answer—Jingxi says:

The four natures are the root of all views; self, other, and both together are likewise without a root. This is why it is so. Thus, the Venerable Nāgārjuna [taught] because the faculties of people in later generations had become dull.

He extensively composed the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* as a method of contemplation, taking the analytical investigation of the four modes of existence (*catuskoṭi*) as its foundation; this is precisely in accord with the final instructions of the present sutra.
Thus, Ānanda, if these flowers come from emptiness, since they come from emptiness, they must return to emptiness. If there were actual coming and going, they would not be empty space.

If emptiness were not empty, it could not accommodate the arising and ceasing of these illusory forms, just as the body of Ānanda cannot accommodate another Ānanda. If they emerged from the eyes, since they emerge from the eyes, they must return to the eyes; thus, the nature of these flowers would follow the eyes.

Because it emerges, there ought to be seeing. If there were seeing, then as the flower departed into the void, upon returning it should see the eye. If there were no seeing, then as the flower emerged and obscured the void, upon returning it should obscure the eye.
Furthermore, when seeing the flower, the eyes should be free of obscuration; why then is the clear sky called "clear and bright eyes"?

Changshui said: "Empty space originally has no flowers; they arise from deluded perception. Who could have brought them forth? True emptiness originally has no form; it is through delusion that one distinguishes obstructive substance.

From where, then, could they emerge by breaking through emptiness? Since you see the flowers as emerging from emptiness, you should see them as entering back into emptiness. Emptiness has neither interior nor exterior; how can there be such things as entering or exiting? If there were indeed such entering and exiting, they would be substantial forms."

It is not appropriate to call this "emptiness. Since it is not empty space, how could flowers emerge from it? For when one sees a solid object, no flowers emerge. Therefore, Ānanda’s body is its actual substance; when you see his body, how could there be another Ānanda emerging from it?

If [the flowers] were to emerge from the eyes, I shall now refute the idea that they emerge from the eyes. Just as when a person emerges from a house, they must necessarily enter somewhere else, if the eyes possess the power of vision such that they can emit flowers, then the flowers should likewise possess vision.
Emerging from the eyes to go out into the void, they would then return from the void to the eyes to be seen by them. If these flowers, by their very nature, emerge from the eyes...

That which emerges yet is not seen is merely an optical aberration (*timira*). Once it has departed from the eye into the empty space, when it returns to the eye, it should necessarily obscure the eye.

If you insist that it does not actually form an aberration and thus does not hinder the seeing of flowers, then since one can see flowers even without an obscured eye, the clear and bright sky that is seen must itself be an aberrated eye. How can seeing the sky be called having "clear and bright eyes"?

Since the flowers have no source of emergence and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is not produced, how could the fundamentally wondrous, true, and eternal ever arise or cease? To claim that they exist through causes and conditions or arise spontaneously is truly false and delusory.

The *Shiyao* says: "Because it emerges from the eyes, there must be a seer; because the mother exists, the child also exists. [The text asks: "Why is the clear sky called the 'clear and bright eye'? It should be answered:
"Why is seeing the clear and bright sky called having a pure and bright eye? The meaning is: if seeing flowers is a good eye, then seeing the clear sky should instead be called a blind eye.

Furthermore, why do people of the world call it a pure and bright eye when they gaze upon the clear sky? Gushan says: If, as Ānanda suggests below, the sky had a substantial reality, then it could not accommodate the flowers of the sky.

Regarding the passage "This very nature of the flower... and below: since the eye already possesses the capacity for seeing, the flower should likewise be seen. Furthermore, regarding the passage "When seeing the flower... and below, this again refutes [the opponent's view] by means of the flower emerging from the eye.
If one sees empty flowers due to the absence of an obstruction, then what kind of eye is it that sees the absence of empty flowers?

Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor is it of a spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*). Zizhong says:

"If one knows that the appearance of the flower is itself emptiness, then the aggregate of form is revealed to be fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. The *Shiyao* states: "Fundamentally not produced by causes and conditions, etc.," refers to the analytical investigation through the four natures (*catur-svabhāva*), which leads one to perceive non-arising.

"Cause" refers to the attachment to self-nature (*svabhāva*); "condition" refers to the attachment to other-nature (*parabhāva*); the combination of cause and condition refers to the attachment to common nature (*ubhaya-svabhāva*); and "spontaneous" refers to the attachment to causelessness (*ahetu-svabhāva*).

Consider this: now, when we examine all phenomena, if they were produced from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could they be produced in the absence of conditions? It would be like water without wind—how could it produce waves of its own accord?

If you say they are produced by other conditions, how can "the other" itself produce a phenomenon? It would be like wind without water—how could it give rise to waves? If you say they are produced by both [self and other], this is untenable; since each lacks the capacity individually, how could they possess it when combined?

Furthermore, [the self] would share in both extremes; to whom, then, would its substance belong? Since arising from both together is not possible, how could it exist without a cause? Once these four [extremes] are empty, names are also extinguished. When attachment to essence and characteristics is removed, the three emptinesses manifest of themselves.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose hundred limbs are in harmony; suddenly, as if forgetting their very life, they experience no sense of opposition or compliance.

For no apparent reason, this person rubs their two palms together in the air, and within those hands, various illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat arise. You should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this.

Xunwen says: "To 'forget birth' means to 'forget the form. This refers to the hundred members of the body being harmoniously adjusted, such that one does not correspond with any sensations of suffering or pleasure, grief or joy;

dwelling in tranquil stillness as if devoid of form and life. Zizhong says: "Nature has neither opposition nor compliance, serving as a metaphor for the quiescence of true nature. Because delusion fundamentally lacks a cause, it is said to be 'non-existent. The union of the true and the delusory is like two hands rubbing together;

the experiencing of opposition and compliance is like the arising of roughness or smoothness through delusion. Jing Gong says: "Because awakening is deluded, there is nothing produced or perceived, yet it functions as a sensation."
"Ānanda, these illusory touches do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm.

In this way, Ānanda, if they came from space, since they can touch the palm, why do they not touch the body? Space should not be able to choose where to touch. If they emerged from the palm, they should not depend [on anything else]."

[Objection: It is joined. Furthermore, because it emerges from the palm, when joined the palm perceives it; when separated, the contact enters [the body]. The arm, the wrist, and the marrow should likewise perceive the traces of its entry. There must certainly be a perceiving mind that knows the exit and the entry, such that there is a distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. Why wait for the perception upon joining to call it "contact"? [Response: No. Because it is not perceived. If there were a distinct entity within the body that came and went, one would surely perceive it. Since it is not perceived, there is no such thing. Furthermore, if this entity were to enter through the pores, it would have to pass through the skin. If it passed through the skin, it would be like wind passing through a wall—what need would there be for it to emerge from the palm? If it did not pass through the skin, then even when the hand is joined with the body, it would not be able to reach the marrow. Moreover, if it emerged from the palm, it would be like a bird emerging from a cage; how could it then be called "contact"? Therefore, the coming and going of a distinct entity within the body does not exist. It is merely the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. Furthermore, if there were a distinct entity within the body that came and went, it would have to be either material or immaterial. If it were material, it would be subject to obstruction. If it were immaterial, it would be like space and could not be perceived. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. Furthermore, if there were a distinct entity within the body that came and went, it would have to be either permanent or impermanent. If it were permanent, it would be like space and could not be perceived. If it were impermanent, it would be subject to arising and ceasing and could not be said to come and go. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. Furthermore, if there were a distinct entity within the body that came and went, it would have to be either internal or external. If it were internal, it would be like the internal organs and could not be perceived. If it were external, it would be like external objects and could not be said to enter the body. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. If it were coarse, it would be subject to obstruction and could not pass through the pores. If it were subtle, it would be like the wind and could not be perceived. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. If it were the same as the body, it would be like the body and could not be said to come and go. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. If it were produced by causes, it would be subject to arising and ceasing and could not be said to come and go. If it were unproduced, it would be like space and could not be perceived. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. If it were eternal, it would be like space and could not be perceived. If it were non-eternal, it would be subject to arising and ceasing and could not be said to come and go. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Thus, there is no separate substance that comes and goes within the body. This is established. Furthermore, if there were a distinct entity within the body that came and went, it would have to be either the self or something belonging to the self. If it were the self, it would be like the self and could not be said to come and go. If it were something belonging to the self, it would be like the aggregates and could not be said to enter the body. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. It is simply the coming together of various conditions that gives rise to the sensation of contact. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, it is established that there is no distinct entity within the body that comes and goes. If it were the cause of contact, it would be like the sense organs and could not be said to enter the body. If it were the agent of contact, it would be like the mind and could not be said to come and go. If it were the object of contact, it would be like the tangible and could not be said to enter the body. Since neither is possible, there is no such entity. Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who, upon speaking of sour plums, has saliva flow from their mouth, or who, thinking of treading on a precipice, has their feet turn numb and sour; you should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise so.

Zizhong said: "The term 'conception' (xiang) takes the grasping of images as its meaning. Such mental imagery is unreal because it arises from the void; thus, the tasting of sourness when thinking of a cliff is used as a metaphor. Master Jinggong said: "When one speaks of the sourness of a plum, there are only words and names;

when one thinks of treading upon a precipice, there is initially no actual event. Yet, it can cause the mind to truly experience a bitter and astringent sensation. This is sufficient to know that it is the wondrous nature of True Suchness."

Xunwen says: Regarding the saying that talking about sour plums causes water to flow from the mouth, the *Shishuo xinyu* records that when the Wei Emperor lost his way while on campaign and all three armies were parched with thirst, he issued an order:
"Ahead there is a large plum tree laden with fruit; its sweet and sour taste can quench our thirst. When the soldiers heard this, water flowed from their mouths.
Ānanda, this sourness you speak of does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth.

It is just so, Ānanda. If it arose from the plum, the plum should speak of it itself; why wait for someone else to say it? If it entered through the mouth, the mouth itself should hear it; why need there be the ear?
If it were heard by the ear alone, why would this water not emerge from within the ear? This imagining of treading on a precipice is similar to what has been said.

Zhendi said: One should say that such thinking does not come from the precipice, nor does it enter through the soles of the feet. If it came from the precipice, the precipice itself would have to perceive it;

why wait for human thought? If it entered through the feet, the feet themselves would have to think; why wait for mental conception? If it were thought by the mind alone, why do the soles of the feet feel a sensation of aching bitterness?
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a torrential stream where waves succeed one another, such that the preceding limit and the succeeding limit do not overlap; you should know that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is likewise.

Gushan said: "Movement takes 'transmigration' as its meaning; therefore, it is likened to a torrential flow. The preceding thought ceases and the succeeding thought arises, yet the latter does not reach the former; hence it is said that they do not overstep one another."
The *Shiyao* says: "The preceding wave just ceases, and the subsequent wave arises in succession; this continuous sequence has no error, as it does not leap over its order.
Ānanda, such a nature of flow is not produced because of space, nor does it exist because of water; it is neither the nature of water, nor is it separate from space and water.

Thus it is, Ānanda. If it were produced from space, then the inexhaustible space of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible torrent, and the worlds would naturally all be submerged and drowned within it. If it existed because of water, then the nature of this torrent should not be water;

the characteristics of something else existing there should now be manifest. If it were identical to the substance of water, then when the water is clear and still, it should no longer be the essence of water.
If it were separate from both space and water, space would not exist outside [of the torrent], and there would be no torrent outside of water.

Zizhong said: "If one were to claim that the water possesses a distinct nature of flowing such that cause and effect are of different natures, then the nature of the torrent should not be the water itself.

That which *has* the water would be the water, while that which *is* the flow would be the flow; if these two characteristics were distinct, both should be simultaneously present. Changshui said: "The flow arises from the water; thus, the substance of the water and the torrent must be different. The water is the producer and the flow is the produced.

It is like a tree producing fruit—the fruit is not the tree, yet both are present at once. However, this is not the case here. The characteristic of the flow is drifting and moving, whereas the characteristic of the water is clarity and stillness. If this drifting..."

Regarding the statement that "movement is the characteristic of water": when it reaches a state of perfect clarity, it should no longer be water; yet, because the surging torrent and the drifting movement are already water, Lord Jing said: "The essence of consciousness is water."

Their nature is emptiness; their activity is like the flow of water. Relying upon this emptiness-water, if there were no emptiness-water, the flow would have nowhere to arise. If there were no nature of consciousness, then activity would have nowhere to originate.
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar, plugs its two openings, fills it with space, and carries it for a journey of a thousand li to present as a gift to another country. You should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is likewise.

Xie Li says: The *piṅgala* is a bird with a beautiful voice; it is modeled after the shape of a bottle. Zhenji says: "Stopping its two holes" is a metaphor for the two types of grasping—the grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*)—of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses obstructing the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).
Taoci says: The *Dharmapada* states, "The spirit dwells within the body, like a sparrow hidden in a bottle; when the bottle breaks, the sparrow flies away.

Here, the person is used as a metaphor for karma, the bottle for the body, and the empty space for consciousness. The *Buyi* (Supplementary Notes) says: Since the *Dharmapada* belongs to the *Hīnayāna*, it uses the sparrow to metaphorize the conscious mind. This sutra, however, seeks to reveal the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Therefore, emptiness is used as a metaphor for the mind. Emptiness cannot be carried; this illustrates that the substance of consciousness pervades all. When a person carries a vase of empty space while walking, it is like consciousness, sustained by karma, carrying the body as it departs.

Xunwen says: Both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth possess both form and mind, and both are sustained by the power of karma. "Other lands" refers to the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) of the six realms of existence.

Changshui says: The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is formless; its presence within the body of a sentient being is like empty space contained within a jar. *Shiyao* says: Alternatively, one may use the jar as a metaphor for karma; karma is able to bind consciousness so that it receives a physical body.

"A jar can contain space" means that the person carrying the jar is used as a metaphor for the afflictions of craving, which moisten karma and lead to rebirth. "Sending provisions to another country from afar" refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna* being driven by karma to undergo rebirth in various places;

when this set of aggregates (*skandha*) ceases, another set of aggregates arises in succession, like a person carrying space on their head to travel thousands of miles away. Regarding the "echo in a valley," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 27, states: "For example, it is like a wax seal pressed into clay.

As the seal and the clay meet, the seal disappears and the impression is formed. This serves as a metaphor for the cessation of the present aggregates of an ordinary person and the arising of the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). — *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

It is clear that those who commit extreme good or extreme evil do not pass through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) but immediately receive the birth-state (*upapattibhava*), like a spear leaving the hand and immediately reaching the ground. Master Jing said: "The nature of true awakening is emptiness."

Space pervades the entire dharma-realm. Once that which is falsely established comes into being, the principle of clarity does not exceed it; thus, this consciousness arises. It is like the space contained within a jar being separated from the external space, yet in reality there is no separation—it is merely a false discrimination.

Xunwen says: "Regarding the fact that the initial sections on the five aggregates all begin with 'For example' (pí-rú) and so forth, one should know that although these employ concrete phenomena in their explanation, the intent lies in using them as analogies.
From the section on the six sense bases onwards, although the word 'example' (pì) appears, they primarily refute [the delusion] by means of the characteristics of phenomena themselves."
"Ānanda, in this way, empty space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter this direction.
Guishan says: "It does not come from that direction to enter this direction. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "'That direction' refers to the direction from which one carries the vase;
'not entering this direction' means that one does not bring that space from there to enter here."

Thus it is, Ānanda. If that space were to come from that direction, then since the original bottle was already filled with space before it departed, there should be a deficiency of space on the spot where the bottle originally stood. If it were to enter from this direction, one should see space emerging as the bottle is opened and overturned.

If the space contained in a jar were to enter here from there, why is it that the space in that place is not seen to decrease, nor is the space seen to depart from this place? If it had come from there, the space in that place would necessarily have diminished;
if it had entered here, one would certainly perceive the phenomenon of its exiting the jar.

Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. Gushan says: Question:

The previous explanation of the five aggregates was entirely based on the nine realms (*navadhātu*). Are the noble ones of the Three Vehicles also said to possess aggregates? Answer: According to Zhan’an’s *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is clarified that all ten realms are discussed in terms of the five aggregates.

The aggregates of the six paths of existence carry the meaning of "covering" (*āvṛti*). They cover the wholesome states of humans and devas, as well as untainted wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*). Covering the wholesome states of humans and devas leads to sinking into the three miserable realms (*durgati*).

The outflow-free wholesome [factors] cover the various realms of saṃsāra; the aggregates (skandhas) of the two vehicles cover the [four] immeasurables (apramāṇa). If one covers the four immeasurables, one cannot deliver sentient beings;

if one covers the four virtues, one cannot reach the place of treasure. The aggregates of the bodhisattva cover both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: by covering saṃsāra, great compassion extracts them from suffering; by covering nirvāṇa, great kindness bestows happiness upon them.

The Buddha’s “shadows” (āvaraṇa) cover both the phenomena and the principle of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Covering phenomena means that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) universally responds to all capacities and faculties. Covering principles means that the dharma-realm body pervades all places.

However, although the phrasing of the following three sections of the sutra appears to overlap, their intended meanings differ in terms of what is secondary and what is primary. First, in the refutation of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), although the objects and consciousnesses are examined through mutual comparison, the primary intent lies solely in the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).

Second, in the refutation of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), although the faculties and objects are mutually refuted, the focus is on the objects, because the faculties had already been refuted in the preceding section. Third, regarding the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*)...

Although the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are analyzed through their mutual opposition, the primary intent of this treatise lies solely in the six consciousnesses, because the two— the faculties and the objects— have already been refuted previously.

Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?

Changshui says: The Sanskrit term is *praveśa*, which here means "entry" (*ru*) or "locus" (*chu*). It refers to the locus where objects enter. The *Shiyao* states: "The six sense-faculties cannot disregard their objects and reflect back; they are entered by objects.

From this, the mind is led to give rise to delusions and create karma, resulting in endless saṃsāra. Furthermore, it is the place where consciousness arises. However, both the faculty and the object are places where consciousness arises.

Since we now analyze and refute them separately by distinguishing the six faculties, we designate only the faculty as the "entry. Xunwen says: "The faculty is able to receive the object and absorb the sensory fields (*qianchen*). Therefore...
This is specifically called "entry.
Ānanda, that very act of the eyes staring fixedly until they become fatigued—both the eyes and the fatigue—are equally the signs of the fatigue produced by staring, which arise within Bodhi.

Zhaoxi said: In the previous section on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it was stated that "it is like the eyeball staring fixedly until fatigue arises, whereby one perceives distinct signs such as floating flowers in empty space.
Here, the eye is used as a metaphor for the True [Self], fatigue for delusion, and the flowers for form. Now, referring back to that previous explanation, he says "that very eyeball," etc.

By taking both the eye and the fatigue from the preceding text, these are employed as the phenomena being illustrated here. This is because that fatigued eye is precisely the illusory characteristic of the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*); thus, he takes the illustrative metaphors from the previous text.

As for the root of this, that which serves as the metaphor within this context: Question: If this is so, what serves as the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) here? Answer: That which is identical to Bodhi—the appearance of fatigue from staring—is precisely the analogy.

However, this analogy is expressed in terms of the phenomenon (*dharma*). "Bodhi" means awakening (*bodha*). From awakening, delusion arises, just like the appearance of fatigue from staring. The intent of the Sūtra is this:

the eye and the fatigue mentioned within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are also the appearance of fatigue from the staring of awakened clarity. This appearance of fatigue is itself a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*). One should understand that the "flower in the sky" mentioned in the preceding text serves as a universal analogy.
The forms of the nine realms and the five sense organs—among these, the "empty flowers" serve only as a metaphor for the characteristics of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within those nine realms.

The former is broad and this is narrow; they must not be conflated. One should know that from the eye-base up to the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*), all are like empty flowers. Thus it is said in the six texts that they are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by staring into *bodhi*. Question:

Why not directly investigate and dismantle the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) with respect to the faculties and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*), rather than pointing to the matter of the fatigued eyes mentioned previously? Answer: Since the faculties and objects pervade both delusion and awakening, one must proceed from what is essential. Pointing to this [example] makes it easy for ordinary people to understand.

These are delusive matters used to resolve Ānanda’s lingering attachments. The subsequent passages—such as hearing sounds while the ears are plugged, or the sense of touch perceived by the nose—are to be understood by analogy in the same way.

These examples are like the "fatigued eye" and are all easily understood. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The texts concerning the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) all say 'the appearance of fatigue arises from staring. This is a general metaphor indicating that both the faculties and objects of the six entrances are appearances of fatigue."
