The fixed gaze is used as a metaphor for the deluded eye, and emptiness is a metaphor for bodhi. Although the phrase "as if there were a person" occurs within the discussion of the six sense bases, it is merely a provisional designation employed to clarify and instruct regarding their meaning.

If one were to speak directly in terms of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and their objects, the meaning of "delusion" would not be manifest; therefore, the metaphor of "staring with fixed eyes" and "plugging the ears" is employed to reveal the nature of the false and illusory.

Master Wuxing explains this in two sections, a literal and a metaphorical, noting that because the six sense bases share the same analogy as "staring," the former must be the actual phenomenon (*dharma*). Thus, one understands that both "staring" and "plugging" serve to clarify the delusory meaning of the six sense bases.

However, the word "staring" (*ding*) found within the phrase "the appearance of fatigue arising from staring at Bodhi" is a simile; it serves as a metaphor for the initial movement of delusion, specifically the "staring eyes" and "plugged ears" among the six sense bases.

These are, in fact, the analogies for the signs of movement and delusion. Only by observing the characteristics of the two individuals—the body and the mind—below can one understand that although the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) contain words of comparison, they are merely phenomena (dharma).
Master Jing said: "Bodhi is entirely suchness (tathatā). When it accords with emptiness, it is tranquil; when it accords with sensory objects, it is weary."

Based on the two kinds of false objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective phenomena, which is called the nature of seeing. This seeing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.

Because seeing is triggered by objects, it is called the "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*). Apart from objects, it has no inherent nature; this is what is meant by "false and illusory. The others are all to be understood in this same way.

Regarding the phrase "the two kinds of false objects": the former refers to the fatigued eye. For now, we rely on the condition of light to demonstrate its false appearance. Light must exist in relation to darkness to be established.

Since this seeing lacks any real nature when separated from its objects, then all instances of the eye-base are equally false and illusory. This principle applies to the ear-base and all other sense-bases as well.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced in space.

It does not emerge from the organ—this refutes the notion that consciousness is pushed out by the organ. What was referred to above as the "nature of seeing" and below as the "nature of hearing," and even the faculty of mind called the "nature of cognition"—this nature is precisely consciousness.

If it were not consciousness (*vijñāna*), how could there be the meaning of seeing and hearing when the various sense-faculties (*indriya*) have not yet produced consciousness? One should know that the refutation of the faculties by means of consciousness is because the arising and ceasing of the six present faculties are difficult to perceive;
therefore, one refutes them by tracing back through the various consciousnesses. If consciousness does not arise, how can the faculties be established? It is like the roots of grass and trees:

they are only called "roots" because they can produce branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves die, one knows the roots have already withered. By using this analogy to contemplate the Dharma, the general meaning becomes clear. Question: If that is so, then you are merely refuting the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

If that were sufficient for your understanding, why would it be necessary to refute the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the twelve sense fields (*dvādaśāyatana*) in their entirety? The answer is: because there are differences in the "real dharmas" (*bhūta-dharma*) as they are conceptually constructed, the treatise divides them into three categories;
yet when it comes to the actual refutation, these three must necessarily be explained in combination.

Why is this? If it comes from light, then darkness would cease along with it, and one should not perceive darkness. If it comes from darkness, then light would cease along with it, and there should be no perception of light. If it were produced from the sense organ itself...

There must be either light or darkness. Thus, this essence of vision originally has no self-nature. If it were to emerge from space and gaze upon external objects before you, it would have to return to see its own organ; furthermore, if space were to observe itself, what would that have to do with your faculty of entry?

"Does not arise from emptiness": by this phrase, the realization of truth refutes arising without cause. Previously, "not emerging from the sense organs" refuted self-arising; "not coming from light or darkness" refuted other-arising. Thus, three propositions are established.

If one were to combine self and other to form a common nature (sādhāraṇa), that would be the intent of the four propositions. Question: Since within the previous discussion of the five aggregates, emptiness was taken as "other-arising," why is emptiness now considered "arising without cause" upon realizing truth?

Answer: Generally, the meaning of the four natures is distinguished according to the specific context of the text and cannot be fixed rigidly. In the preceding text, there was no separate "other-nature" apart from emptiness.

This is the meaning [of the term]. Therefore, emptiness (ākāśa) can be taken as the "other. For emptiness is also an object perceived by the visual faculty; since the present text mentions both light and darkness, it can be contrasted with them.
Taking emptiness as the causeless opposite is highly convenient for the argument.
Therefore, you should know that the eye-base is illusory; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who plugs both ears tightly with their fingers; because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head. Both the ear and the strain are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

Zhaoxi said: "Regarding the term 'for example' (譬如下文亦爾): this is used to establish a hypothetical situation in order to instruct and lead one to awakening; therefore it is called 'for example. It does not carry the sense of a mere comparison.
The same applies to the subsequent passages.

Based on the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within them and absorbs these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of hearing. Apart from those two objects of movement and stillness, this hearing ultimately has no substance.

Gushan said: "The ears perceive movement and stillness, just as the eyes perceive light and darkness. What is taught in the various sutras is that hearing exists in response to sound, and seeing arises conditioned by light. However, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the present text is that stillness is also called 'hearing,' and darkness is also called 'seeing.

This applies analogously to the nose perceiving permeability and obstruction, and the mind cognizing arising and ceasing. Xunwen said: "The statement that stillness is also called 'hearing' and so forth is intended to reveal the permanence of the nature [of consciousness].

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: 'Sound itself undergoes arising and ceasing within hearing; it is not that your hearing-nature is sometimes existent and sometimes non-existent. Thus, the definitive meaning is established."
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this hearing does not come from stillness or motion; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If it came from stillness, it would cease as soon as motion occurs, and one should not hear motion. If it came from motion, it would cease as soon as stillness occurs, and there should be no perception of stillness.

If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither motion nor stillness. Thus, the essence of hearing fundamentally lacks self-nature. If it emerged from space, then the existence of hearing would constitute the nature of space itself, and it would no longer be empty space. Furthermore, if space itself were to hear, what concern would that have with you?
[It] enters. Therefore, you should know that the ear-entrance is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who pinches their nose tightly; after pinching for a long time, fatigue arises, and they perceive a sensation of cold within the nose. Based on that sensation, they distinguish between permeability and obstruction, emptiness and solidity. Just as...
This extends even to all fragrant and foul odors; together with the nose and its fatigue, these are likewise the signs of the delusive labor arising from the fixed gaze of Bodhi.

To "forcefully hold" the nose means to contract the breath—*chū* (畜) meaning to contract or withdraw. As it says in the *Xunwen*: "Permeation and obstruction correspond to the objects (*viṣaya*); emptiness and solidity correspond to the faculties (*indriya*). When the faculty is empty, the object is permeable; when the faculty is solid, the object is obstructed."

Based on the two kinds of delusory objects—openness and obstruction—the faculty of hearing arises in their midst and absorbs these objective phenomena; this is called the nature of smelling-hearing. Apart from those two objects of openness and obstruction, this hearing ultimately has no essence.
You should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If hearing came from openness, then when there is obstruction, hearing would cease; how then could one know of the obstruction? If it were due to obstruction existing, then when there is openness, there would be no hearing; how then could it manifest the perception of fragrances, odors, and tactile objects?

If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no alternation between being open and obstructed. Thus, the faculty of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature. If it emerged from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose;
since space itself would possess the power of hearing, what connection would it have with your sensory faculty?
Zhaoxi said: "The term 'trigger' (*ji*) carries the meaning of being drawn back and then released; thus it is used as a metaphor.
Therefore, one should know that the olfactory faculty is empty and false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature."

Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until they become weary, if that person is ill, there is a bitter taste, whereas for one who is not ill, there is a slight sensation of sweetness.

Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, it is revealed that when the faculty of the tongue is at rest, its nature of neutrality is ever-present. Furthermore, both the tongue and its weariness are but manifestations of the fatigue produced by the staring of *bodhi*.

Due to the two kinds of false objects—sweet, bitter, and bland—a consciousness arises within them that absorbs these sensory images; this is called the nature of the sense of taste. This nature of tasting, when separated from those three objects of sweet, bitter, and bland, ultimately has no substance.

Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that when one tastes bitterness and perceives it as not sweet, this bitterness does not arise because of the sweetness; nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.

Why is this? If sweetness or bitterness arises, then one knows that the blandness has ceased. How does one know the blandness? If one emerges from the blandness, then one knows that the sweetness has perished. Furthermore, how does one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness?

If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no objects of sweetness, blandness, or bitterness; thus one knows that the root of tasting has no self-nature. If it were produced from space, then space itself would have the taste, which would be known upon leaving your mouth;
furthermore, if space knew it for itself, what would it have to do with your faculty of sensation?

Changshui says: "Taste (rasa) is like 'tasting'. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "From 'the flavor of space itself' to 'what concern does it have with your faculty of entry'? However, these four phrases appear to be somewhat confused;
one should know that the first two phrases clarify the object-field of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*), while the latter two phrases clarify the sense-faculty of the tongue (*jihvā-āyatana*).
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one hand with another—one cold and one hot. If the power of the cold is greater, the hot becomes cold; if the efficacy of the heat prevails, the cold becomes hot.

In this way, the sensation of contact through their union makes known the awareness of their separation. When these forces interact and form a causal condition through their mutual touch, the body and its fatigue are both the appearance of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.

By means of this tactile sensation of conjunction, it is revealed that [the capacity] exists apart from the knower.孤山 (Gushan) says: "The simultaneous perception of separation and conjunction is like the simultaneous hearing of movement and stillness, or the simultaneous seeing of light and darkness."

Based on the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—the faculty of awareness arises from within; it draws in these objective images and is called the nature of cognition. This essence of cognition is independent of those two objects of separation and union, as well as opposition and compliance;
ultimately, it has no inherent substance.
Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this perception does not come from the union or separation [of sense objects], nor does it exist through opposition or conformity.

It does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space. As Xunwen says: "It does not come from union or separation" refutes co-arising, because even "separation" is in relation to an object. "Not through opposition or conformity" refutes arising from another.
"Does not emerge from the sense organs" refutes self-arising. Furthermore, "nor is it born from space" means it is without cause.

Why is this? If [the sense-organ] comes together when in union, it must have already ceased when separated; how, then, could one perceive separation? The two characteristics of opposition and compliance are likewise so. If [consciousness] emerged from the sense-faculties, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of separation, union, opposition, or compliance;

thus, the cognition of your body would fundamentally lack self-nature. If it necessarily emerged from space, then space itself would possess cognition and awareness; what connection would that have with your sense-faculties?
Therefore, you should know that the body-faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, it is like a person who sleeps when weary and awakens from deep sleep; upon encountering sensory objects, there is recollection, and the loss of such recollection is forgetfulness. These are the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within this state of inversion.

As they are inhaled and cultivated, they return to their source without exceeding one another; this is called the faculty of mental cognition. Together with the mind and its weariness, these are all the signs of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

Zhaoxi said: "When awake, one perceives sensory objects and thus recollects them; when asleep, one loses this recollection and it becomes delusion. Furthermore, there are dreams within saliva and forgetfulness within waking;

these are all manifestations of perceiving sensory objects and losing their recollection. When recollected, they arise; when forgotten, they perish. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: 'Due to the two kinds of deluded sensory objects—arising and ceasing. To oppose the deluded to the True is itself an inversion.

These two deluded sensory objects further constitute the four subtle characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, which flow and shift from moment to moment. One inhales and habituates these characteristics, returning them to the mental faculty (*manas*). (Supplement)

Yun says: "Gushan takes 'forgetting the record' (*jìwàng*) as the habituation (*xí*). Wuxing’s intention is that the mental faculty (*manas*) perceives and inhales this phenomenon of forgetting the record, much like the process of learning. Changshui says:

"'Inhaling into the midst of habituation' means that these arising and ceasing phenomena are entirely taken in by the mental faculty, such that the perfuming habituation (*vāsanā*) remains uninterrupted. Tiāoxī says: "The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) occur in each moment without preceding or succeeding moments being intermingled; therefore, it is said they do not 'mutually transgress.'"

Based upon the two kinds of delusory objects—arising and ceasing—the aggregate of cognition abides in the center. It draws inward and seizes internal objects; its seeing and hearing flow against the current, reaching a ground that the current cannot attain. This is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This nature of cognitive awareness, when separated from those two objects of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, ultimately has no substance.

Gushan says: "The four characteristics were previously cited; now there are only two because 'abiding' is subsumed under 'arising,' and 'alteration' is included within 'cessation. Furthermore, that which is remembered is taken as arising, and that which is forgotten is taken as cessation."

The "internal objects" (*viṣaya*) refer to mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*). Regarding "reversing the flow of seeing and hearing": because of memory (*smṛti*), one is able to take as an object those five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that have already fallen away.

This means that by perceiving the objects, one then recalls them. *Xunwen* states: "The five sensory objects that have fallen away are called 'non-informative matter' (*avijñaptirūpa*) in the Abhidharma; they are also called 'invisible and non-resistant matter' (*anidarśanāpratigha-rūpa*). *Buyi* adds:

"Now it may also be said that 'reversing the flow' means the mind takes the present quantity (*pratyakṣa*) as its object. The mind constantly seeks out the realms of what has been seen and heard; this is called 'following the flow. Now, because the fallen-away objective realms return and enter the mind, it is termed 'reversing the flow.'"

This is the definition of their names. When the mind follows the objects, it is called "conforming" (*anuloma*); this refers to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the present. When the objects follow the mind, it is called "contrary" (*pratiloma*); this refers to the five sensory objects of the past.

Regarding "the flow does not reach the ground": because of forgetfulness, it becomes a condition for thought that reaches a place beyond its capacity; thus, the loss of memory constitutes forgetfulness. Zizhong said: "When the eyes and ears seize external sensory objects, they flow instantaneously into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

To move from the external into the internal is called 'flowing against the current. By the second moment of thought, one is unable to perceive them as conditions; hence it is said that 'the flow does not reach the ground.'"

Thus it is, Ānanda. You should know that this faculty of cognition does not come from waking or sleeping; it does not exist through arising or ceasing; it does not emerge from the sense-faculties, nor is it born from space.

Xunwen says: It is not from waking or sleeping that [arising] is refuted as co-arising; it is not through the existence of birth and extinction that other-arising is refuted; it is not by emerging from the sense organs that self-arising is refuted. Arising from emptiness is as explained previously.

Why is this? If [the dream] comes from the waking state, then upon falling asleep it would immediately cease; with what, then, would one dream? If it must exist during the time of birth [of the dream], then upon its cessation it would become non-existent; who, then, would undergo that cessation? If it exists from the moment of cessation...

If birth were simultaneous with cessation, who would know the one that is born? If it arises from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would open and close along with the body;

yet apart from these two forms, this cognizer is like a flower in the sky, ultimately lacking any inherent nature. If it arises from space, then it is simply the knowing of space itself—what concern does it have with your sense faculties?

Zizhong said: The *Liezi* states, "In waking, the form opens; in sleeping, the form joins. "Joins" means to unite. Thus, the two states of waking and sleeping are themselves the opening and closing of the form.
The nature of your faculty of cognition has no separate substance; therefore, it is said to be identical to a flower in the sky.
For this reason, you should know that the mental sense-field (*manāyatana*) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The *Śìyào* states: "The faculty of mind (*manas*) is the seventh consciousness. In Sanskrit it is called *kliṣṭa-manas*, which translates as 'defiled mind. As for 'mind' (*manas*), that which constantly and deliberatively cogitates is termed 'mind.

According to the teachings of the Abhidharma school (Xiangzong), it can only take the internal as its object, reckoning the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the internal self.

As for the Hīnayāna, they only speak of all phenomena being established from the six consciousnesses and do not speak of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. However, the 'mind' (*citta*) is also of many kinds; the Abhidharma school speaks of the seven consciousnesses as the root of the mind, which is an invisible phenomenon and is not the same [as the physical heart]."

Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are visible; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If one considers them with the physical mind, they appear like a lotus flower with seven petals; this is the ephemeral sense-organ (*āśraya-mūla*). However, the present sutra does not distinguish between the material and the non-material;

all are but the wearying manifestations of ignorance within the nature of bodhi. They are all identical to flowers in the sky, having no essence that can be apprehended, because they are precisely the *tathatā-garbha* (storehouse nature).
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think? Do these forms arise and are seen by the eye, or does the eye arise and manifest the characteristics of form?

Zizhong said: "The six sense organs and the six sense objects serve as the locus for the arising of consciousness; therefore, one investigates them through the meaning of 'arising'. Changshui said: "Previously, the sense organs were refuted; now, the sense objects are being refuted.

However, since they are refuted in relation to one another, both are questioned. Tiexi said: "In the initial section on the five aggregates (*skandha*), the analogy was used to refute clinging attachments.

Next, in the section on the six entrances (*āyatana*), provisional phenomena were pointed out to reveal their illusory nature. Now, from the twelve loci (*āyatana*) up to the seven elements (*dhātu*), [the teaching] demonstrates [the truth] within the very objects currently seen and heard, and those directly perceived before one's eyes."
Regarding this nature of the treasury: one can clearly discern the intention behind the sutra’s skillful unfolding—from the remote to the proximate, and from the provisional to the real.

Ānanda, if it were the eye-faculty that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve. If it dissolved, then everything would manifest as utterly non-existent.

Since the appearance of form would no longer exist, who would perceive the substance of emptiness? It is the same with emptiness. Furthermore, if it were the visual object (form-dust) that produced the seeing of the eye, then when observing empty space—which is not form—that seeing would perish. If it perished, then everything would be non-existent; who then would perceive both emptiness and form?

Initially, the sense organ is taken as the producer and form as the produced. When emptiness is perceived, since the produced form has dissolved, the producing organ also ceases; therefore it is said that "when they dissolve, everything is non-existent.

This refers back to the previous point regarding the absence of the characteristics of form. Who would clarify the nature of emptiness to challenge this error? If one claims that when form dissolves the organ perishes, who then clarifies the essential nature of the perception of emptiness? Emptiness is likewise so; one should say:
"If the eye-organ again produces the appearance of emptiness, then upon seeing form, emptiness is not [perceived], and the nature of emptiness should dissolve," and so forth. Next, if...

Again, it continues below: taking form as that which gives rise [to seeing] and seeing as that which is produced. When one contemplates emptiness, the form that gives rise [to seeing] has already dissolved, and the seeing that is produced also ceases;

therefore, it is said that when they perish, they are entirely non-existent. Following the previous example, one should say: "Since the nature of seeing is non-existent, who clarifies the substance of emptiness? Emptiness is likewise so. This meaning is thus understood; hence the Buddha spoke with omissions, or perhaps the translator abridged it.

As for the phrase "who clarifies empty-form," if one were refuting the arising of emptiness from the eye's seeing, one ought to demand: "Who clarifies the characteristics of form? Now, this contains both meanings simultaneously; therefore, it says:

Regarding "emptiness-form," Xunwen said: "Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? This statement is used to investigate the person, while its underlying intent lies in the deconstruction of phenomena; that is, the eye-faculty. Now, as for the deconstruction of the locus within this context, it further deconstructs the faculty itself:

because the faculty is like pressing on the eyes, and form is like flowers in the sky. If the pressing ceases, the flowers vanish accordingly. One should understand that the same principle applies to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and so forth.

Therefore, you should know that seeing and the emptiness of form both have no location; thus, the two locations of form and seeing are illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.

Ānanda, listen further to this: when the meal is prepared in this Jeta Grove, the drum is struck and the assembly gathers, and the bells are tolled. The sounds of the bells and drums continue one after another. What do you think?
Do these sounds come to the side of the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sounds are?
The drum is struck to assemble the multitude, and the bell is tolled to dismiss them.
Ānanda, if this sound comes from the vicinity of the ear—just as when I went to Śrāvastī for alms, I was not present in the Jeta Grove—then this sound must necessarily come to Ānanda’s ears.

If that were so, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it simultaneously; how much less so the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the sound of the bell, all came together to the place of the meal?

Furthermore, if your ear were to travel to the location of the sound—just as I am currently staying in the Jeta Grove and there is no "me" in the city of Śrāvastī—then when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear would have already gone to the place where it is being struck.

In that case, when the sounds of bells arise simultaneously, they should not be heard together; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them? If there were no coming and going, there would likewise be no hearing.

Gushan said: "In the first case, 'self' is used as a metaphor for sound, the city for Ānanda’s ear, and the forest for the ears of others. When the self enters the city, there is no self in the forest; this is like sound entering your ear—how could the ears of others hear it?
Next, 'self' is used as a metaphor for the ear, the forest for the sound of the drum, and the city for the sound of the bell. When the self returns to the forest, there is no self within the city;

likewise, when the ear goes to the place of the drum or the place of the bell, it is not there. If there is no coming or going, then there is also no hearer. Sound does not come to the ear, nor does the ear go to the sound; thus, the meaning of 'hearing' cannot be established."

Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound both have no location; thus, these two locations—hearing and sound—are both illusory. Originally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner. If even one *zhu* of this incense were burned, its fragrance would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* of Śrāvastī.
What do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree, does it arise from your nose, or does it arise from space?

*Xunwen* says: Regarding *candana* (sandalwood), one explanation is that it is not translated because it does not exist in this land; another says it is translated by its meaning as "bestowing joy. The *Śāstra* states: "Among all fragrant woods, *candana* is the foremost. *Guying* says:

Regarding "one *zhu*," the *Lilishi* (Annals of Music and Calendar) states that twenty-four *zhu* make one *liang*. The present mention of "one *zhu*" is intended to indicate its smallness. *Xunwen* says:

According to Zhang Hua’s *Bowuzhi*, there was an envoy from a Western country who presented incense. Under the Han regulations, anything weighing less than one *jin* could not be accepted. The envoy then secretly departed and applied the incense as follows...
A portion the size of a soybean was placed atop the palace gate; its fragrance wafted for ten *li* in all four directions throughout Chang’an, only subsiding after a month.
Furthermore, Ren Fang’s *Shuyiji* states that the fragrance of the "thousand-li pine" is sensed for ten *li*, and it is thus also called "ten-li fragrance."

Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced in your nose, and is thus said to be produced by the nose, it should emerge from the nose. Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose? If you say that you smell the fragrance, it should enter through the nose;

to say that fragrance emerges from within the nose while claiming it is "smelled" is illogical. If it were produced in space, since the nature of space is eternal and constant, the fragrance should be eternally present.

Why then would one rely on burning this dried wood in an incense burner? If it were produced in the wood, then the substance of the wood, having been burned, becomes smoke. If the nose were to perceive it, it should be enveloped by the scent of that smoke. Yet that smoke rises into the air and has not yet reached far.
[The opponent objects: "It is forty *li* away; how could it have been heard already?

The *Shiyao* states: "It is sufficient to cite Ānanda’s reasoning to naturally refute [the opponent], for it possesses great force. This is because Ānanda assumes that the fragrance arises from within the wood, and thus the refutation says:"
When wood burns and becomes smoke, how can there be fragrance? If the smoke were itself the fragrance, then when the nose perceives it, that smoke ought to envelop your nose.
The smoke has not yet traveled far, having merely circled about; why, then, is it already smelled within forty *li*?

Therefore, one should know that the nose’s smelling and the act of hearing have no location. Thus, both the smelling and the fragrance are empty and false; they originally lack causes and conditions and do not possess an inherent nature.

Ānanda, you regularly carry the alms bowl among the assembly during the two times of the day. In that interval, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called the finest flavors. What do you think?
Does this flavor arise from space, does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise within the food?

Ānanda, if this flavor were produced in your tongue—since you have but one tongue within your mouth—and that tongue at that time had already become the flavor of ghee, it should not change upon encountering black rock honey.

If it did not change, it could not be called "knowing flavors. If it did change, then since the tongue is not a plurality of entities, how could a single tongue perceive many flavors? If [the flavor] were produced in the food...

If food does not possess consciousness, how can it know itself? Furthermore, if food knows itself, it would be the same as another person’s food; what concern would that have with your own perception of name and flavor? If it were produced in space, what flavor would you experience when eating empty space?

If that empty space were to have a salty taste, once your tongue was salted by it, your face would also be salted; then the people of this world would be like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness and never knowing what fresh water is.
If they do not recognize the fresh, they cannot perceive the salty; if there were nothing known at all, how could there be such things as name and flavor?
Zhaoxi said: Regarding "black rock honey," the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states it is the dregs of sugarcane; it is as hard as stone.

Therefore, one should know that the sense of taste and the tongue have no location. Thus, both tasting and flavor are equally illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, you habitually rub your head with your hand every morning. What do you think? Regarding that which is known through this rubbing, who is it that performs the touching? Does the capacity to touch reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head?

The *Shiyao* states: "The method of massage is generally consistent with this standard practice. In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus that they should rub their own heads. This is to cultivate introspection regarding the internal body so as to advance upon the Path.

Introspection of the internal consists in shaving off the beard and hair; introspection of the external consists in the earthen bowl and tattered robes. These serve to eliminate greed so that one may swiftly realize the goal."

If [the faculty of touch] resides in the hand, the head would be without sensation; how then could contact be established? If it resides in the head, the hand would be useless; how then can it be called contact? If it were present in both simultaneously, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.

If the single contact produced by the head and hand implies that the hand and head are one entity, then contact cannot be established. If they were two distinct entities, with which one would the contact reside?
That which is the agent (the subject) is not the locus (the object), and that which is the locus is not the agent. It is not possible for empty space to enter into contact with you.

Therefore, you should know that the perception of touch and the body both have no location; thus, both the body and touch are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.

Ānanda, regarding the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—which you constantly take as objects of your mind, these constitute the laws that give rise to phenomena. Do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately from the mind in some other location?

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "This text is sufficient to serve as a divining stalk for scholars of the Shanjia school to resolve questions regarding the discernment of objects (*jǐnjìng*) in *zhǐguān* (cessation and contemplation).

Master Tiantai’s primary aim here is to discern the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) as the subjective cognition capable of creating the objective realm of mind. Zhengji says: "The objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), namely the *dharmas*, differ according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and vary between the provisional and the real. The *Buyi* states:

"As it is said, the 'evil' [objects] refer to the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while 'evil sentient beings' refers to provisional designations (*prajñapti*). The same applies to the 'good' and 'neutral' [objects]. "Because these [designations] produce understanding by following specific rules, they do not overlap with one another; therefore—"

It is said that they constitute the "generated dharmas" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The three natures (*trisvabhāva*) that serve as the objects of focus herein are the dharma-objects (*dharmālambana*). The mental concomitants (*caitta*) also pervade all three natures; this does not mean that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) itself pervades the three natures.

If one is discerning the object for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and observes only the mind-king within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), this refers to observing the essence of the mind—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—as a whole.

This is as stated in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning): 'First, all minds do not transcend consciousness. As for the term 'generated dharmas,' these mental concomitants arise from the mind-king, and are thus called 'generated. For example, the wholesome mental factors (*kuśalacaitta*).

When a virtuous king establishes the Dharma through proper regulations, then that which is practiced will be wholesome. By this analogy, the unwholesome and the indeterminate may be understood. Ānanda, if the Dharma were identical to the mind, then the Dharma would not be an object;

since it is not an object of the mind's perception, how could it constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? If it exists apart from the mind in a distinct location, then is the self-nature of the Dharma conscious or unconscious? If it is conscious, it is called the mind;

being different from you yet not an object like other external things, it would be of the same measure as another’s mind. If it were identical to you, it would be identical to your mind; how then could your mind be dual with respect to you? If, on the other hand, it is unconscious...

Since this dust is neither form, sound, fragrance, nor flavor, and is distinct from conjunction, disjunction, cold, heat, and the element of space, where could it possibly reside? Now, within both form and emptiness, there is no indication of its presence.
It cannot exist elsewhere outside of emptiness in the human realm. Since the mind is not its object of perception, from what basis could its location be established?

Gushan says: "If knowing is called 'mind,' then there must be a dharma apart from the mind. Since that dharma possesses knowing, it too is called 'mind. 'That which differs from you is not your dust' means:

if it differs from you, it is not your mind; if it has knowing, it is not your sensory dust. Being both different and not [yourself], it would then be the mind of another person. 'It is you, it is the mind' is intended to prevent a shift in conceptualization. The phrase 'How can... is a challenge: your mind is one; how can there be two?
If both the faculty and the object have knowing, these constitute two minds. 'If it were not... implies that this mental object (dharmadhātu) is not among the five sensory objects. Five.

The sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and empty space (*ākāśa*) encompass all phenomena (*dharma*). Xunwen asked: "There are two kinds of phenomena: first, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), which refers to the various mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the mind;

second, non-mental phenomena (*acitta-dharma*), which refers to form (*rūpa*) and so forth in the past and future. Thus, there are mental phenomena external to the five sensory objects and so on. Why, then, do you say they encompass all? Answer:

"In this context, it is for the purpose of refuting the notion that if a phenomenon is not cognition, it must belong to the five sensory objects or to empty space. Therefore, it is said that they 'encompass' them. As for those that are mental phenomena, they were already subsumed under the previous refutation."

All objects of direct perception (pratyakṣa) belong to their respective five sense faculties. Since mental objects (dharmas) do not belong to these five, one asks: where would they reside? Cold and heat, whether separate or combined, are simply the object of touch (spraṣṭavya).

There is nothing that can be indicated, because the mental object (*dharmadhātu*) is formless; it arises only by taking as its condition the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that have already passed away.

Since the appearance of a mental object is not perceived within the realm of form and emptiness, how could it exist as a separate entity outside of emptiness? If the mind has no object of perception, where does the meaning of its "abiding place" lie? Master Jing said: "The self-nature of phenomena is empty; they are not sensory objects.

If there is something here that you perceive, it is simply your own mind—what then would constitute a 'phenomenon'? If this were different from your mind and yet not a sensory object, it would be identical to the mental capacity of another person—what then would constitute a 'phenomenon'?"

Therefore, you should know that dharmas and the mind both have no location; thus, both the mental faculty and dharmas are equally false and illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the eighteen *dhātus* fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

Changshui says: "The Sanskrit term is *dhātu*, which here means 'element' (*jie*). An element has the sense of a cause, because the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—are mutually causal. It also has the sense of a lineage (*gotra*), as the three—organ, object, and consciousness—each constitute a single lineage.

Furthermore, from the six organs to the six consciousnesses, each acts as its own lineage. Gushan says: "Although these eighteen elements are analyzed by being paired and deconstructed, yet [the essence remains]..."

Regarding the six consciousnesses: since their faculties and objects have already been refuted previously, when the false attachments to the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha are destroyed, the nature of the Garbha is established. Thus, this single sutra, from beginning to end, consistently involves both refutation and establishment.

Although it may at times emphasize refutation, it never fails to establish; although it may at times emphasize establishment, it never fails to refute. Consequently, there is an appearance and disappearance of these elements throughout the text.

The essential meaning is eternally perfect and complete. "Dismantling" (po) refers to emptiness (kong); "establishing" (li) refers to the provisional (jia). The mutual identity of dismantling and establishing is precisely the middle (zhong). In which text are the three truths and three contemplations not thus?
Let readers and practitioners diligently illuminate this.

Ānanda, as you understand it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye such that the eye constitutes its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of visible forms such that visible forms constitute its constituent element?

Zhaoxi said: "As you have explained, those of the Lesser Vehicle understand that all phenomena produced by causes and conditions are substantially real, failing to realize they are empty from the very beginning. It was based on their own assertions that he interrogated them, in order to refute their attachments.
All other cases should be understood in this manner."

Ānanda, if [consciousness] arises because of the eye, then since there is neither form nor emptiness with which to make distinctions, even if your consciousness were present, what would it have to function upon? Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white;

having nothing to represent it, from where could its boundaries be established? If it arises because of form, then when there is no form in emptiness, your consciousness should cease; how then could you cognize the nature of empty space? And if form undergoes change...

You also perceive the shifting and changing of the characteristics of form; yet your consciousness does not shift. From what, then, could the sensory realm (dhātu) be established? If it arises from change, then as it changes, the characteristic of the realm would naturally cease to exist.

If it does not change, then it is constant; since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of empty space. If it were produced by both together, such that eye and form arise in conjunction, then where they join they would be separated, and where they separate they would be joined—thus their essential natures would be confused and disordered.
How, then, could a realm be formed?

Zhengji said: "You see the tip of the finger. Because it is an invisible, resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*), and because it is not a color such as blue and so forth, it is invisible; yet it can illuminate the object and give rise to consciousness."

Therefore, it can be answered: this refers to the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ), not the *ābhāsa-indriya* (manifested sense organ). Since it is invisible, it has no manifest representation. Guishan says: "The subsequent section beginning with 'If [the consciousness] follows [the form]' contains three points of refutation:

first, that consciousness perishes along with form; second, that the meaning of 'dhātu' (element/constituent) cannot be established; and third, if form perishes but consciousness does not perish, then one would migrate while the other does not—these two categories being dissimilar, how could they be called a 'lineage' (*gotra*)?

Thus he says: 'If your consciousness does not migrate, from what would the dhātu be established? If it perishes along with consciousness, both phenomena have already ceased; how then could the characteristic of a 'dhātu' remain? Therefore he says: 'If it follows the transformation, then it transforms.'"

The characteristics of the realms (*dhātu*) are inherently non-existent. The three [perceptions] constantly fail to know emptiness. Since the mind itself is unchanging, and since it arises from form (*rūpa*), it serves only to cognize form; it should not cognize emptiness. Changshui said:

If it is combined with the lower [realms], and if this consciousness arises from the middle realm through the conjunction of sense organ and object, then there must be a distinction between knowing and not-knowing within this middle realm of consciousness;

therefore, it is said to be "separated. If such a distinction were established, then this middle realm of consciousness would have one half conjoined with the sense organ and one half conjoined with the object; therefore, it is said to be "conjoined with both. If it were conjoined with both, there would be the fault of confusion, because knowing and not-knowing would belong to the same realm, and thus the definition of a "realm" (dhātu) would be invalid.

The *Shiyao* states: "Separated means distinct. If one says that this consciousness arises from both the sense organ and the object together, then this intermediate consciousness must necessarily possess the distinction between knowing and not-knowing. If...

If one grants that there are two distinct entities, then it is known that they combine with the sense organ themselves, yet it is not known that they combine with the object; therefore, it is said that "if separated, the two combine. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if separated, the two combine":
if they were truly distinct, then the two factors—knowledge and non-knowledge—would combine to form a single consciousness; hence, it is said that "if separated, the two combine."

Therefore, you should know that when the eye and forms serve as conditions for the arising of the visual consciousness-element, these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the eye, forms, and the form-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The Supplement states: "Gushan categorized this as the conclusion of the 'no-separation' view (*mukta-vāda*). If the three locations—root, object, and consciousness—are all absent, that constitutes 'no [separation]'; thus, 'the eye and form' and below refer to the 'separation' view.

However, in that case, for the triad of "eye, form, and the realm of form," it would be more appropriate to say "the consciousness-realm and the triad. This pattern persists throughout the subsequent text, making the underlying intent difficult to discern.

It is likely that "eye" refers to self-arising above the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), "form" refers to other-arising above the conjunction, and "the realm of form and the triad" refers to co-arising above the conjunction. If one were to use the term "consciousness," the meaning of "co-" (*saha*) would not be made manifest; this is why [the text proceeds in this manner].

The commentary on the section concerning the mind-element (*manodhātu*) concludes by stating: "Thus, the mind, mental objects (*dharma*), and the mind-element—these three—are designated together based on the sense faculty (*indriya*). The same applies to the tongue and body [elements]. According to principle, the faculty and its object should be paired together.

This indicates the shared meaning. The first three and the latter three mutually manifest this significance. Fundamentally, they are not [arisen from] causes and conditions; they collectively refer to the three natures (trisvabhāva) as being produced by self, other, or both. The meaning of the five subsequent passages is likewise the same.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood— that the ear and sound act as conditions to produce ear-consciousness— does this consciousness arise because of the ear, taking the ear as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of sound, taking sound as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if [the ear-consciousness] were produced because of the ear, then when the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to constitute cognition; there would necessarily be nothing known. Since even cognition itself cannot be established, what form or appearance could consciousness have?

If one takes "hearing" to be the ear, then in the absence of motion and stillness, hearing itself cannot be established. How then can the ear-faculty, being a mixture of visible forms and tactile objects, be called the "element of consciousness"? If so, from whom would the element of ear-consciousness be established?

If consciousness arises from sound, and consciousness exists because of sound, then it has no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish. If you claim that consciousness arises from sound and that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing, then hearing should hear the consciousness itself;

yet if it does not hear [itself], it is not a sensory element (*dhātu*). If hearing were to hear the consciousness, then who would know that hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass or wood. Sound and hearing should not be conflated to form a middle element (*madhyadhātu*);
since an element has no middle position, how could the characteristics of "inner" and "outer" be established?

Changshui says: "The first 'if' [referring to] 'if there is no cause' below, refutes the *paramārtha-indriya* (the ultimate sense organ). If there is no external object, the organ itself has no cognition; if it truly lacks cognition, what further consciousness could there be?

The second 'if' [referring to] 'if one takes' below, refutes the *sāṃvṛti-indriya* (the conventional sense organ). Even if one were to take the conventional ear and suppose there were hearing, if there is neither movement nor stillness, hearing is not established.

How can this visible conventional organ be mixed with color, touch, and dharmas to constitute the element of consciousness? Thus, 'then the ear' below doubly interrogates both organs. Since sound is able to produce consciousness, why rely on hearing? If there is no..."

[The ear] hears; yet sound itself does not exist [as a separate entity]. Even if one claims that consciousness arises because of sound, and further grants that it exists because of the sense organ, then at the time of hearing sound, it would be the hearing-consciousness [itself] being heard.

If one does not hear the consciousness, then it does not fulfill the definition of a "sphere" (*dhātu*). If one hears the consciousness, then the consciousness becomes identical to the sound. Since the consciousness that is capable of discerning [the object] has become the perceived object (*ālambana*), who then acts as the knower that knows this hearing-consciousness?

From "If [the object] were non-existent... below, there is a general refutation of [consciousness] arising from an object. From "It should not... below, there is a refutation of [consciousness] arising from both [object and organ] together.孤山 (Gushan) says: "If consciousness were formed through a mixture, then half would belong to the sound and half would belong to the hearing."

Therefore, it is said that within the elements (*dhātu*) there is no middle position. Since the middle consciousness does not exist, the meanings of "internal sense-faculties" and "external objects" are both unestablished.

Thus, one should know that with respect to the ear, sounds, and the auditory consciousness-element arising from these conditions, all three positions are entirely non-existent; consequently, the ear, sounds, and the auditory element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand— that the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to give rise to nose-consciousness— does this consciousness arise because of the nose and take the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of fragrance and take fragrance as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if [the sense of smell] arises from the nose, then within your mind, what constitutes the "nose"? Is it the physical form of the two nostrils, or is it the nature of olfactory cognition and its movement?

If you take it to be the physical form, then that fleshly substance is the body; the cognition of the body is contact (*spraṣṭavya*). To call it the "body" is not to call it the "nose," and to call it "contact" is to designate it as an object (*viṣaya*). Since the nose itself would have no name, how could a sensory field (*dhātu*) be established? If, on the other hand, you take it to be olfactory cognition...

Furthermore, within your mind, what constitutes "knowing"? If you take the flesh as that which knows, then the knowing of the flesh is fundamentally a matter of touch and not the nose. If you take space as that which knows, then space would know itself; the flesh, in that case, would not be the faculty of sensation.

If this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would have no capacity for cognition; today, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence. If you take fragrance as that which knows, then the knowing belongs to the fragrance itself—what concern is it to you?

If the scents of perfume and stench must arise from your nose, then those two types of flowing air—the fragrant and the foul—would not exist in the *eranda* plant or in sandalwood. If these two substances do not come [to your nose], you [would not perceive them].

When you smell your own nose, it is either fragrant or foul. If it is foul, it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, it should not be foul. If both fragrance and foulness could be smelled simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.

He asked me: "Ānanda, there are two [factors] here. Which one is your essence? If the nose were a single entity, then fragrance and stench would not be two distinct things. If what is stench becomes fragrance, and what is fragrance again becomes stench, then these two natures do not exist;

from what, then, could the boundaries be established? If it arises because of fragrance, then consciousness exists because of fragrance. Just as the eye has the faculty of seeing but cannot see itself, so too, because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it should not know that fragrance.

If it knows it, it is not 'arisen'; if it does not know it, it is not 'consciousness. Since fragrance is not known by consciousness, the fragrance-element is not established. If consciousness does not know fragrance, then the element is not established from fragrance. Since there is no middle ground..."
This establishes the internal and external. That nature of hearing is ultimately illusory. The physical form is the superficial dust;

the act of smelling and knowing is the ultimate reality. Tiāoxī said: "If it is called 'contact,' it is the object perceived by the body-faculty; therefore it is said that what is named contact is precisely the sensory dust.
Gūshān said: "To say 'emptiness is you' means you do not see the form; to say 'the body is you' means you cannot know [it]. Seeking both, it is not to be found; thus it has no location. Iti.

The orchid is a fragrant tree. Ruanxi says: From the phrase "the two things do not come [to the nose]" downward, he refutes [the notion of] the sense organ by means of the object. Since the objects are two, the sense organ should likewise become two. First, he establishes the point by asking whether it is fragrance or stench;

next, he challenges it by saying that if it is stench it cannot be fragrance, and if it is fragrance it cannot be stench. His intent is to show that if both were perceived, one would fall into the error of having two noses. If the nose is one, then from this point downward he refutes [the notion of] the object by means of the sense organ.

Since the sense organ is singular, how can the objects be two? When the dual nature is not established, where does the realm of consciousness exist? All of the above constitutes the refutation of the sense organ as the source [of perception].

Question: It was stated above that "knowledge arises by means of fragrance. Since knowledge itself belongs to the fragrance, does this not constitute a refutation of the object? Answer: This was spoken in response to the sense organ; it primarily refutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The subsequent passage does not address the sense organ, but rather refutes the arising [of knowledge] from the object. If one refutes the arising from the object based on the following example—just as the eye has the faculty of seeing yet cannot look back at the eye itself—then by analogy, although fragrance possesses consciousness, how could that consciousness look back and know the fragrance?

Even if you were to grant that consciousness can know the fragrance, it would be inconsistent to say that it arises from the fragrance. Therefore, it is said that "knowledge is precisely not arising. Suppose, however, that...

If one who can perceive this fragrance is not called "consciousness" (vijñāna) or "discernment" (vijñapti), then it is said that what is not known is not consciousness. Fragrance does not depend on consciousness, and consciousness does not arise from fragrance;
thus, the meaning of the "elements" (dhātu) is not established for either.孤山 (Gushan) says: "The middle is consciousness; the internal and external are the faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya)."

Therefore, you should know that with the nose and fragrance as conditions for the arising of the nose-consciousness element, none of these three locations exist. Thus, the nose, the fragrance, and the fragrance element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that tongue-consciousness arises with the tongue and flavors as conditions— does this consciousness arise because of the tongue and thus take the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of flavors and thus take flavors as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if [taste] were produced because of the tongue, then all things in the world—sugarcane, *ume* plums, *hānglián* (Coptis), rock salt, *xīxīn* (Zingiber officinale), ginger, and cassia—would have no taste at all. You yourself should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter?

If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? The tongue does not taste itself; what, then, would be the cognizer? If the nature of the tongue were not bitter, taste would not arise of its own accord. How, then, could the sense-sphere be established?

If consciousness arises because of flavor, and consciousness itself constitutes the flavor, then it would be identical to the tongue-organ and thus should not be able to taste for itself; how then could it discern whether something is a flavor or not a flavor? Furthermore, all flavors do not arise from a single substance.

Since flavors arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise have multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were a single unity, then whenever a flavor arose—whether salty, bland, sweet, or pungent—and various transformations occurred together, they would all become a single flavor based on their common characteristics;

there would then be no differentiation. If there is no differentiation, it cannot be called "consciousness. How, then, can it be called the "element of tongue-flavor-consciousness"? It is not the case that empty space gives rise to your mind-consciousness. [The same applies to] the tongue...
The blending of flavors: within this very state, there is fundamentally no intrinsic nature.

How, then, could the elements (dhātus) arise? Tiaoxi says: "Salty, bland, sweet, and pungent"—these four flavors are mentioned briefly; in detail, there are six, adding bitter and sour. The *Buryi* (Supplement) states: According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the inferior three types of cultivation are used to refute the deviant three types of cultivation.

Using these six flavors, I fear that the purport of the present text merely mentions them in a general sense regarding the tongue; it does not necessarily require one to speak of all six. As for the term "blending," it refers to the collective formation of various flavors.

Furthermore, that which is "co-nascent" (*sahaja*) has an innate nature that is not subject to change, whereas that which is "transformed" (*vikāra*) differs from its original state through processes such as burning or boiling.

If these various types of seeds were to produce a single entity of consciousness, then since the produced consciousness is one, how could the producing tastes be distinct? In that case, all taste-objects (*rasa-viṣaya*) would be conflated without distinction. If there were no distinct consciousnesses, the meaning of the "realms" (*dhātu*) would not be established.

Xunwen says: Furthermore, from "all flavors" downward, the consciousness is refuted by following it from the sense organ (*indriya*) to the object (*viṣaya*). From "if the essence of consciousness were one" downward, the consciousness is refuted by following it from the object to the sense organ.

Gushan says: The first, based on the tongue, refutes self-arising; the second, based on flavor, refutes other-arising; the third, based on space, refutes causeless arising; and the fourth, based on the conjunction of tongue and flavor, refutes co-arising.
This pattern applies to all preceding and subsequent passages, though it is most clearly manifest here.

Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness element arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the tongue, flavors, and the tongue-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that body-contact serves as a condition for the arising of body-consciousness— does this consciousness arise because of the body and thus take the body as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of contact and thus take contact as its constituent element?

Ānanda, if [the perception of contact] arises because of the body, there would necessarily be no conditions for the two types of mental observation—conjunction and separation. What, then, would the body perceive? If it arises because of touch, there would necessarily be no such thing as your body;

who, then, being non-embodied, could know conjunction and separation? Ānanda, objects do not know through touching; it is the body that knows there is touch. To know the body is itself touch; to know touch is itself the body. Thus, what is touch is not the body, and what is the body is not touch.

The two characteristics of body and touch fundamentally have no location. When conjoined with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself; when separated from the body, they are merely the characteristics of empty space. Since neither "internal" nor "external" can be established, how could a "middle" be posited? As for this middle...
One no longer establishes the emptiness of internal and external natures. From whom, then, could your consciousness arise to establish the realms?孤山 (Gushan) says:

"Coarse investigation is called *vitarka* (覺), and subtle discernment is called *vicāra* (觀). The union or separation of sensory objects is the condition for bodily *vitarka* and *vicāra*. Since the condition of contact is absent, there is no *vitarka* or *vicāra*."

It is not that objects do not touch the cognition; rather, it is simply that objects do not know the touch. Since the body knows there is touch, one knows that at the very moment the body exists, it receives the touch;

and at the moment one knows the reception of the touch, that is precisely the body. If it were merely the touch alone, then there would be no characteristic of the body; if it were merely the body alone, then there would be no characteristic of the touch. Tiaoxi says:

"The section from 'Next, Ānanda' onwards is a detailed refutation of the initial argument that the body and the touch arise separately. First, it distinguishes that objects do not touch the cognition; next, it clarifies that the body knows there is touch. Once it is understood that the body knows there is touch, then..."

The body and touch are simultaneous. Since they are simultaneous, one knows that the body and touch arise separately; there is no basis for their being two [as a single entity]. By joining the body and pushing downward, one joins and then separates—this refutes the intermediate element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).

The subsequent passage concerning the "internal and external" not being established concludes by refuting the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). How can the "middle" be established? This concludes the refutation of the intermediate [element].

Therefore, one should know that when body-contact as a condition gives rise to the body-consciousness element, these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the body, contact, and the body-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that the mental consciousness arises with the mind and mental objects as conditions— does this consciousness arise because it takes the mind as its cause and the mind as its realm, or does it arise because it takes mental objects as its cause and mental objects as its realm?

Ānanda, if consciousness arises because of the mind, then within your mind there must be something thought of that brings forth your consciousness. If there were no preceding object, the mind would have nothing from which to arise. Being devoid of conditions, it would have no form; what then would consciousness be used for?

Furthermore, is this consciousness of yours identical to or different from the nature of the deliberating mind and the faculty of discernment? If they are identical, how can the mind give rise to itself? If they are different, being distinct from the mind, it should have no capacity for cognition.

If there is no cognition, how can the mind give rise to it? If there is cognition, how can consciousness be the mind? Thus, neither identity nor difference can be established as two natures; how then can the element [of consciousness] exist?

[Ananda] stood up. "If consciousness arises because of dharmas (objects), then all worldly phenomena do not exist apart from the five sense objects. Observe these dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch;

their characteristics are distinct and correspond to the five faculties, yet they are not subsumed under the mind-faculty. Your consciousness must certainly arise dependent upon these dharmas. Now, examine closely: what is the actual nature of these dharmas?

If one is separated from form, emptiness, motion, stillness, penetration, obstruction, conjunction, separation, arising, and ceasing—if one transcends all such characteristics—ultimately nothing can be found. When they arise, form, emptiness, and all other dharmas arise together; when they cease, form, emptiness, and all other dharmas cease together."
Since the cause is absent, what form or characteristic could the consciousness produced by that cause possess?

If its marks do not exist, how can the realms arise? Tiāoxī says: Furthermore, regarding "your consciousness-mind" (*rìshíxīn*), the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "That which accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena] is called 'mind' (*citta*); that which deliberates is called 'thought' (*manas*); that which discriminates is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*).

Here, "consciousness-mind" corresponds to the seventh [consciousness], the deliberating [thought] (which is the thought-faculty), as well as the nature of discrimination, which corresponds to the second and third [consciousnesses]. These are the consciousnesses produced by the thought-faculty. Xūnwén says: Regarding the scriptural text...

The preceding and following passages both refer to Ānanda’s present sixth consciousness-mind (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) to refute his emotional attachments. One may simply adopt the minor tenets of the *Abhidharmakośa* to explain these three meanings. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"Deliberation (*manana*) is that which calculates and measures, thus it is called 'mind' (*manas*); the nature of discernment (*vijñapti*) is that which distinguishes objects, thus it is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). The intent of the Sūtra is that those two [the seventh and eighth] and the third [the sixth] are all consciousnesses produced by the mind."

Therefore, it is said that they are "concurrent" (*sāṃyukta*). However, as for the statement in that second [text] regarding "mind" (*manas*), it is merely another name for consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is explained that there is no difference between the three—mind, intellect, and consciousness.
It is like fire, which is called a flame, a blaze, and also that which burns wood. The *Xunwen* states: That treatise asks, "What is the distinction between these three:

mind, intellect, and consciousness? The answer is: they may be distinct or not distinct. Regarding their non-distinction: mind is itself intellect; just as fire is called a blaze and so forth, it is simply one mind that has three differentiated aspects. Regarding their distinction: it is a matter of names...

This is precisely their distinction. Some say that what is past is called *manas* (mind), the future is called *citta* (thought), and the present is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Others say that what resides in the *dhātus* (elements) is called *citta*, what resides in the *āyatanas* (bases) is called *manas*, and what resides in the *skandhas* (aggregates) is called *vijñāna*, and so forth.

The above citations are from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. Now, the meaning of this sutra also distinguishes these three names based on a non-distinction that is itself distinguished. Therefore, while the names for consciousness and mind are identical, they are divided into two meanings based on priority and sequence.

Changshui says: "If [the text] states 'arising from the mind' (*manas*), it refutes the view that consciousness arises from the sense organs; since phenomena arise, the mind arises, and because they are non-existent, it does not arise. Below, 'separate from conditions' serves as an analogy."

This refutes that which is produced. Since even the sense organs (*indriya*) lack [independent] roots, how much more so consciousness? Furthermore, in the passage "Moreover, as for your consciousness," there is a general inquiry into identity and difference. "Consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*) refers to the eight consciousnesses; "deliberation" (*manana*) refers to the seventh consciousness; and "discrimination" (*vijñapti*) refers to the sixth consciousness.

Because both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses share the sixth organ as their basis and are likewise named "mind" (*manas*), this general inquiry shows that both positions are flawed. In the section beginning with "If [the cause is] dharmas," the text refutes the production of consciousness from objects.

The five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not immediately subsumed under the mind (*manas*), because each has its own specific object (*pratigocara*). If one were to separate them from form (*rūpa*) and below, it would clearly demonstrate that apart from these objects there is no substance.

Regarding the phrase "arising," this refutes alternative views concerning form and below. The *Śāstraviniścaya* states: "The sixth and seventh consciousnesses both take the sixth faculty as their basis. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "The fifth, fourth, and sixth have two [bases]; the seventh and eighth rely on one.

This means that the sixth consciousness takes the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as its supporting faculties; hence it is said that "the sixth has two. Furthermore, they are all equally named "mind" (*manas*). Since the *Awakening of Faith* speaks of five consciousnesses, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both included.

It is called "intention" (*manas*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: Changshui says that the eight consciousnesses are called "mind" (*citta*), the seventh is called "intention" (*manas*), and the sixth is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

That they are collectively termed the "intention-faculty" (*manas-indriya*) when residing in the sixth [consciousness] is solely because Ānanda and the great assembly were about to break through ignorance; thus, this interpretation was provided. In the *Siming Guangming Ji*, it is stated that the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] both reside in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), precisely because the seventh and eighth depend exclusively upon the sixth for their abiding.

The *Shiyao* states: "That which is contemplated" refers to the object of contemplation; "that which brings forth illumination" arises from the object of contemplation inducing clarity and manifestation.

This is because of the mental faculty (*manas*). Since cognition arises based on objects, this passage now specifically refutes the sixth consciousness while simultaneously refuting the seventh and eighth. Tiāoxī says: "If it were identical to the mind," meaning: if consciousness were identical to the mind, how could there be that which produces and that which is produced?

If consciousness were different from the mind, then what is produced would be equivalent to insentient matter. Furthermore, even if one were to argue that what is produced lacks consciousness, its essential nature would not be of the same category as that which produces it.

Moreover, if one were to defend the position by saying that what is produced does possess consciousness, since this consciousness would lack any preceding dharma to take as an object, it would necessarily have to turn back and cognize itself.

[Question: If the mind (*manas*) were to take objects as its domain, the definition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) would not be established. *Xunwen* says: "All worldly phenomena do not depart from the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). [Objection:

Previously, when investigating the objects of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) within the mind, it was stated that these objects are not form, fragrance, taste, or the like. Why, then, are the five sense-objects now taken as "phenomena" (*dharma*)? [Answer: In the preceding passage, the text was specifically investigating the sphere of mental objects;

therefore, it spoke in reference to the five sense-objects that have already passed away. Here, however, since the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is being refuted, it must be explained in relation to the five present sense-objects, because the five sensory consciousnesses arise from present objects and are not subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*).
