This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) and its objects (*dharma-āyatana*) to refute [the claim]. It states that the phenomena of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are themselves subsumed under the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), and do not belong to the category of the mental faculty’s sphere of phenomena (*mano-dharmāyatana*). Zizhong said:

The five objects (*viṣaya*) are each assigned to the five sense organs (*indriya*). Apart from these five objects, there is no separate dharma for the mental faculty (*manas*). Changshui says: "Because it is the dharma of the object-field of dharmas (*dharmadhātu*), it is called 'dharma-dharma. That which serves as its cause is precisely the object-field of dharmas. Xielin says:

"Color and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction—these are the three objects of form, sound, and fragrance. Conjunction and separation are the two objects of taste and touch. Arising and ceasing is the object-field of dharmas.

However, arising and ceasing merely apply universally across the five objects; apart from the five, it has no independent substance. Therefore, it is said that when [the objects] arise, all dharmas arise, and when they cease, all dharmas cease."

Zhaoxi says: First, the arising from the sense organs is refuted; next, the arising from the objects is refuted. The case of arising from both [organ and object] together can be understood by analogy with what precedes. Xunwen says:

One should say that if the mind and dharmas arise together, if they were to combine, they would be separated in the middle; if they were to separate, they would be joined as two. Their essential natures would be confused and disordered; how then could they constitute a "dhātu" (element)? Buyi says: Here, "arising and ceasing" also refers to the six mentioned above.

Among the six [sense bases], the mental base (manāyatana) involves the two objects of arising and ceasing. These should be described in terms of recollection and forgetfulness to explain arising and ceasing. When it is said that they "arise," it means that all phenomena, such as form and emptiness, arise together;

this is the mind-ground apprehending the object and thus recollecting it. When they "cease," it means that all phenomena, such as form and emptiness, cease together; this is the mind-ground losing its recollection and thus forgetting it.

Therefore, one should know that when the mental faculty (*manas*) and phenomena (*dharma*) serve as conditions for the arising of the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the mental faculty, phenomena, and the mental-consciousness element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the principle of the conjunction of causes and conditions. All the various transformations in the world are manifested through the conjunction of the four great elements."

How is it that the Tathāgata simultaneously sets aside both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity? I do not now understand to what this meaning belongs. I only pray that you will compassionately reveal to sentient beings the definitive teaching of the Middle Way, free from conceptual proliferation.
Gushan says: Since Ānanda clings to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) previously discussed, he doubts the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) now being expounded.

He fears that if sentient beings hear of the former "harmony," they will be obstructed by existence; if they hear of the latter "rejection," they will drown in emptiness. Failing to realize the Middle Way, they will inevitably fall into frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, he requests an elucidation. Xunwen says:

Regarding the statement that all things are manifested through the harmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one should know that these four elements exist both internally and externally. "Internal" refers to the primary retribution (*upapatti-vipāka*); "external" refers to the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). Within the first five aggregates (*skandha*), form (*rūpa*) must necessarily possess all four elements.

The "Great" [elements] are twofold: first, they generally encompass both the internal and external; second, they pertain exclusively to the internal. Regarding the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind within the lower section: first, they generally encompass both the environment (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*); second, they pertain exclusively to the environment.

As for the element of space, it belongs entirely to the objective realm (*viṣaya*) when contrasted with the other four; thus, together with the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), these constitute the repeated refutation of the three categories of phenomena.

The sacred teachings benefit sentient beings according to their respective needs, resulting in different gains; therefore, these differing explanations exist. The *Shiyao* states: "Furthermore, these seven great elements are identical to the previous three categories. The five great elements, such as earth, are identical to the previous twelve bases (*āyatana*). The organ-element..."

These are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). They are merely restated because their gates of entry differ and their inclinations vary. Regarding the "echo in a valley" (*guǔxiǎng*):
frivolous discourse (*prapañca*) refers to talk that is like children’s play—discourse that lacks substantial principle.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Previously, you were weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and you resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, I now reveal the Ultimate Truth for you. Why do you again entangle yourself with worldly frivolous arguments and delusive conceptualizations?

Although you have heard much, you are like a man who knows about medicine but cannot distinguish the actual medicine when it appears before him. The Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied. Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal it for you. Furthermore—
This is intended to enable those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future to penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Gu-shan says: "Regretting that from time immemorial one has been solely devoted to much hearing" refers to the weariness with the Lesser Vehicle. "Earnestly entreating the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth through which they realize Bodhi" refers to the seeking of the Great Vehicle.
This may also be pointed to within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s holy instruction.

“Ānanda, it is as you have said: the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world. Ānanda, if the essence of those great elements were not itself a combination, they could not give rise to the various mixtures of the elements;

they would be like empty space, which does not combine with material forms. If they were indeed combined, they would be identical to transformations—beginning and end mutually forming one another, arising and ceasing continuing in succession, [the cycle of] birth and death.”
Birth and death; birth within death and death within birth, like a whirling firebrand, never having a moment’s rest. Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water.

Next, Ānanda, below this it clarifies that the great nature is fundamentally true and thus not a product of combination; therefore, the analogy of empty space is cited. This is identical to what follows later: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form.

To die and then be born again, and having died to return to life—hence it is called "birth-death and death-birth," which refers to the mutual completion of end and beginning. Now, from this life to the next life, from this death to the next...

Death. Therefore it is said, "life and death, life and death," which refers to the continuous succession of arising and ceasing. Next, two metaphors are presented: continuity is like a whirling firebrand, and mutual formation is like ice and water.

Lord Jing said: "It is like water turning into ice, which remains obstructed and does not flow; when the ice turns back into water, it flows freely without obstruction. This ice and this water are but a single nature. When the four great elements combine, it is like water turning into ice;

when the true nature is perfectly interfused, the ice turns back into water. The *Buyi* (Supplementary Notes) states: "The meaning of the sutra is that the nature of the seven elements is fundamentally true and eternal."

The essence is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; it is not that they do not harmonize. Furthermore, if they were to harmonize, they would lose their true nature, and there would consequently be the fault of birth and death. This is the general meaning of the passage, though the specific wording is not provided here. The overall purport is as stated above.

Xunwen said: "Ānanda, you have only grasped at conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is based on the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). The Tathāgata now refutes both the ultimate and the conventional;

this is according to the Great Meaning (*Mahāyāna*). Observe the nature of earth: grossly it is the great earth, subtly it is minute particles, down to the *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal particle). If one analyzes that extremely subtle limit of form until it is composed of seven parts, and further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is simply the nature of true emptiness.
Ānanda, if these *paramāṇus* are analyzed away to become empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the characteristics of form."

Gushan says: "The Tripitaka masters and those of the Two Vehicles contemplate emptiness through the analytical method (*pravicaya-dharma*). Therefore, [the text] refutes their attachments by relying on their own understanding. Xunwen says:

"'You contemplate the nature of earth' refers here to the differentiated nature resulting from analytical deconstruction; water, fire, wind, and so forth are all merely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) nature. What was previously called 'that great nature' refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) nature within the four great elements.

One must not conflate these when interpreting the meaning according to the text. For instance, within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there are two kinds of dharma-nature: first, the phenomenal dharma-nature, because its natures are differentiated; second, the real..."

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because its nature is true reality, Mount Gu said: "As for the term 'neighboring atom' (*paramāṇu*), this particle is extremely subtle and neighbors upon empty space.

Thus, seven neighboring atoms constitute one *tōkinjin* (gold-penetrating dust); seven *tōkinjin* constitute one *tōsuijin* (water-penetrating dust); seven *tōsuijin* constitute one rabbit-hair dust; and seven rabbit-hair dusts constitute one sheep-hair dust."

Seven wool-dust particles (*ūrṇā-rajas*) constitute one cow-hair dust (*go-rajas*). Seven cow-hair dust particles constitute one mote floating in a sunbeam (*vātāyanacchidra-rajas*). There is an interpretation which states:

when the various practitioners of yoga perform the meditation on the analysis of form to clarify emptiness, they use the power of their conceptual wisdom to divide coarse matter into its constituent parts. Even a single atom (*paramāṇu*) still possesses spatial divisions in the ten directions; it is merely called an "atom" and not yet a "subtle atom" (*aṇu*).

If this atom is further divided into seven parts, it no longer has spatial divisions in the ten directions, and is thus termed a "subtle atom. It is also called "extremely condensed matter" (*atyanta-saṃkṣipta-rūpa*), "proximate void" (*paramāṇu*), or "the limit of form" (*rūpa-paryanta*).
Because they cannot be further analyzed; if one were to analyze them, they would become empty space. Changshui says: "The 'minute' (wei) refers to the directional parts of a subtle atom (paramāṇu).

The 'neighboring atom' (aṇu) has no directional parts and is the ultimate minute particle (paramāṇu), the limit of form. Now, the term "limit of form" is used to refer to that which possesses directional parts. There is no need to reconcile this with what appears in the sutras. Xunwen says:

"When the sutras speak of analyzing those ultimate minute particles, they are generally referring to subtle atoms as 'ultimate minute particles. Buyi says: "If we rely on the neighboring atom, it is precisely..."

Only at the level of the *paramāṇu* (extreme atom) can one speak of the limit of form (*rūpa*). Now, this sutra analyzes the extreme atom until it becomes the "neighboring" [atom], thereby designating the mote of dust as the *paramāṇu* and also calling it the limit of form.

Thus, the *Xunwen ji* (Record of Arousing Hearing) states: "This refers to the general convention of calling a mote of dust a *paramāṇu*. This is truly because, in comparison to those motes of dust found in a crevice, does not this [subtlest mote] qualify as the limit of form and thus receive the general name *paramāṇu*?
Guishan says: "From 'Ānanda' onwards, it means that since one can already analyze form into emptiness, one can likewise combine emptiness to form form."

Now, as for your question regarding how the various manifested forms of the world arise through combination: consider this single *paramāṇu* (subtle atom). By how many spaces (*ākāśa*) must it combine to exist?

It cannot be that *paramāṇus* combine to form a *paramāṇu*. Furthermore, if a *paramāṇu* is analyzed and enters into space, by how many material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is that space itself composed? If it were composed of matter when combining, it would be matter and not space;
if it were composed of space when combining, it would be space and not matter. Matter may still be analyzed, but how can space be combined?

If atoms were to combine, they would necessarily possess spatial dimensions; since things of the same kind combine with their own kind, they do not mutually constitute one another. Zizhong said: "If space cannot be combined, from what could form arise?
Thus we know that this form has no inherent nature from the very beginning."

You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha there is essential form which is true emptiness, and essential emptiness which is true form— pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know,
and manifesting in accordance with their karma.

Gushan says: This passage is a specific refutation; the following passage is a general refutation. Specifically, it concerns Ānanda’s failure to understand the nature of the *ālaya*; generally, it concerns the worldly arising of false attachments and calculations.

However, because one fails to understand the true mind, false calculations arise; and because false calculations arise, one fails to understand the true mind. Although the texts point to these individually, their meaning ultimately converges. While this principle has been fundamentally present from the beginningless past, Ānanda has likewise been fundamentally deluded from the beginningless past;

hence it is said, "You originally did not know. The *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely the Middle Way within the nature of the mind. It is true while being conventional; hence it is called "the nature of form" (*xing-se*).

True emptiness is itself the conventional; thus it is said that "emptiness-nature is true form. Because the conventional and the true are themselves the Middle Way, they are both termed "nature. These three truths are perfectly interfused—neither identical nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal—and are called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Nirvāṇa is also referred to as the "Secret Treasury. The *Guxiang* says: "Because it encompasses and integrates the three truths, it receives the name 'Treasury.

It is what the Buddha has realized, hence it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Sentient beings, though lost in delusion, are equal to the Buddha in principle; therefore, the nature of the treasury is such that ordinary people and sages are of one essence. This is not the knowledge of the partial or the small vehicles; thus it is further called..."

It is secret because, being mundane, the ten realms are perfectly distinct; thus it is said that "the true color is the emptiness of nature. It is true because both sentient beings and Buddhas are quiescent; thus it is said that "true color is the emptiness of nature.

These words refer to the inherent possession of principle (*li-jù*), not to the actual production of phenomena (*shi-zào*); therefore, it is called "nature" (*xing*). The inherent possession of principle is like a *maṇi* jewel possessing all treasures; the actual production of phenomena is like the *maṇi* jewel raining down treasures. The inherent possession of principle is like water possessing the nature of waves.

The manifestation of phenomena is like waves arising from the wind. If the nature of the jewel were not complete, other pearls would have to rain down jewels; if the nature of the wave were not complete, the great earth would have to give rise to waves.

Therefore, this school clarifies that the perfect must necessarily be explained as being inherently complete (*li-jù*). This deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent and wonderfully captures the true nature (*svabhāva*). Whether in theory or in practice, one must understand this completeness. Jingxi said: "Question:

Since the single mind is already complete, why is it necessary to contemplate 'completeness' rather than simply contemplating the mind? Answer: The contemplation-gate of this school is forever distinct from all other teachings. It encompasses all things throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, whether mundane or..."

The Sage’s realization of all causes and effects arises precisely from the contemplation of the "endowment. This endowment is provisional; the provisional is emptiness. Although the rational nature is inherently endowed, if one does not contemplate it, then to speak merely of "contemplating the mind" is insufficient.

This would not accord with principle. How could it be that the Hīnayāna has never contemplated the mind? It is simply that they are deluded regarding the fact that the One Mind contains all dharmas. If this were not so, how could it be said that "the initial aspiration and ultimate realization are ultimately no different"?

Once perfect enlightenment is attained, how could one manifest bodies and lands across the ten realms? Furthermore, principle must necessarily integrate with phenomena; how could phenomena ever be separate from principle? When both principle and phenomena are simultaneously transcended, it is called "pure and fundamental.

Just as water must necessarily integrate with waves and waves cannot exist apart from water—if wave and water are already one, who can distinguish between principle and phenomenon? Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three things without difference.

Each and every thing mutually encompasses one another, and each and every characteristic is interfused; therefore, it is said that they pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Since my own mind already possesses this nature, living beings and Buddhas are identical. Now, for the sake of direct instruction, we speak only of "mind."

Ultimately, it is that my own mind and the Buddha-mind arise from the mind and mutually pervade one another; this is termed "non-differentiation. When following sentient beings, it is termed the "storehouse nature conforming to conditions to produce the phenomena of the ten realms.
This means that in accordance with defiled or pure minds and following differentiated karma, the fruits of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are manifested.

The nine realms, with their various heights and depths, are collectively termed "deluded defilement," while the fifth [the Buddha realm] is generally designated as "true purity," because the perfect teaching holds that the five [realms] are identical and universally constitute the Buddha-realm. Because the mind is either defiled or pure, karma is differentiated; however...

Thus, within the Buddha-realm, there is fundamentally no distinction or opposition; it is only the nine realms that are termed "differentiated. When following the deluded, defiled mind and accordant black, evil karma, the environments and beings of the three miserable paths manifest.

When following the deluded, defiled mind and accordant white, pure karma, the environments and beings of the three good realms manifest. When following the deluded, defiled mind and accordant untainted (anāsrava) karma, the environments and beings of the two vehicles manifest.

When following the deluded, defiled mind and accordant karma that is both tainted and untainted, the environments and beings of the Bodhisattvas manifest. If one distinguishes these through the six stages of identity (*liu ji*), then the nine realms are all in accord [with the Buddha-nature].

The deluded and defiled mind is the state of "principle-as-such" (*liri*). It refers to that which is inherently endowed with principle yet remains deluded in its emotional afflictions. It is like being in the west and mistakenly perceiving it as the east; the Buddha-realm follows the true and pure mind.

These five are precisely those who awaken in accordance with principle. Because there are degrees of depth in awakening, there are five stages of high and low. Changshui said: "Being in accord with non-delusion and possessing untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, it is called 'pure.

Because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called 'primordial' (*prakṛti*). Because it is omnipresent, it is called 'pervasive. This means that the essence, qualities, and magnitude of the lineage (*gotra*) are all fully complete.

If one recognizes this dharma, one accomplishes the three sublime contemplations; only then will one know that within a single mote of dust are contained all Buddha-dharmas, all mental dharmas, and all sentient-being dharmas, without exception.

It is not that they all reside within a single minute atom; rather, one sees Vairocana therein, one sees oneself therein, and one sees all dharmas therein. As it is with one minute atom, so it is with all dharmas.

The *Shiyao* (Essentials of Explanation) states: Regarding the accomplishment of the three sublime contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*): if one can realize that the dharma-nature of both the dependent and the primary [realms] is true emptiness within form, this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

This is what is meant by "when one is empty, all are empty; there is nothing of the provisional or the middle that is not empty. To realize that the true nature of emptiness is true form is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

This is what is meant by "when one is provisional, all are provisional; there is nothing of the empty or the middle that is not provisional. That form and emptiness are non-dual is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*). This is what is meant by "when one is the Middle, all are the Middle; there is nothing of the empty or the provisional that is not the Middle. Thus, these three contemplations are a single mind; they are not sequential.

They are horizontally aligned yet distinct. Therefore, according to the Contemplation of Truth in the Tiantai School, while their names are distinct, their substance is identical. Thus, the two—the subject (the capacity) and the object—are not two. The *Zhuanyi* states: The *Contemplation Sutra* says, "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Tiantai’s commentary says:

Regarding "this mind creates the Buddha," the Buddha is originally non-existent; it exists because the mind is pure. It is also because of this samādhi-mind that one ultimately succeeds in becoming a Buddha.

Regarding "this mind is the Buddha," having previously heard that the Buddha is originally non-existent and exists only because the mind is pure, one might think they are entirely different. Therefore, it is said that they are "identical" (*ji*). Outside of the mind...

There is no Buddha, nor is there any cause for a Buddha. The *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "The two phrases in the explanation are divided into two parts. First, 'making' (*zuo*) is explained separately. This first part explains 'making' in terms of that which can evoke and that which can accomplish.

There are two meanings to 'making': first, the pure mind can evoke the responsive Buddhas of other directions; therefore, it is said that 'this mind makes the Buddha. As for the statement that 'the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent,' it means that the Dharma-body is wondrously transcendent and has no form or appearance to be seen.

As for the statement that 'it exists because the mind is pure,' it means that the pure mind of sentient beings, relying upon the *ālayavijñāna* (karmic consciousness), perfumes the Buddha-dharmakāya, and thus perceives the sublime form and appearance of the excellent response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)."
Furthermore, these two samādhis can bring about one’s own fruition as a Buddha; thus it is said that they are also the causes, and so forth. They are also called "becoming a Buddha":

first one becomes a Buddha for others, and subsequently one becomes a Buddha for oneself. This is explained according to the principle of the identity of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the fruition-body (*dharmakāya*). This also has two meanings: first, because the mind is itself the responsive Buddha, it is said that "this mind is the Buddha. Regarding what was heard previously, the essence of the Buddha is without marks, yet it exists because of the majesty of the mind.

Thus, the mind, the Buddha, and existence or non-existence are fundamentally and eternally distinct. The Sūtra eliminates this view, stating that the mind is the responsive Buddha and that there is no Buddha outside of the mind. Second...

The mind is itself the resultant Buddha; therefore, it is said that "this mind is the Buddha. This is precisely the phrase meaning there is no cause for the Buddha. Since the mind is already the resultant Buddha, there is no cause capable of producing a samādhi.

Within the minds of sentient beings, the Tathāgata is already seated in the full lotus posture; how could one wait for a future time to finally become a resultant Buddha? The first [of the two Buddhas] is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body Buddha), and the second is the resultant Buddha. This is the explanation of the text of the sutra and its commentary.
As for the meaning of the phrase "to act as this" (*zuòshì*), it refers to the non-contemplative protection of the three contemplations. Why? Because it clarifies that the mind acts as the Buddha.

Therefore, it is revealed that there is no Buddha who exists naturally as an inherent quality (*dharmatā-guṇa*); this is to clarify that the mind itself is the Buddha. It is also revealed that there is no attainment of Buddhahood through the causes and conditions of cultivated qualities (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).

One should know that all conceptualizations within the various propositions of non-Buddhists and the four gates of the three teachings do not transcend the categories of "causes and conditions" and "natural nature. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies that the seven elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma.

Each conclusion states: "The ignorant of the world delude themselves by taking these to be causes and conditions or natural nature; these are all merely the discriminations and calculations of the conscious mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and have no reality."

There is no substantial reality. That which is called "the world" encompasses the nine realms. Now, through wondrous contemplation in a single thought-moment, one is able to dissolve the defects of nature by means of this very activity;

thus, activity itself constitutes practice, whereby all natural natures are dissolved. Because activity is itself suchness, all practice is identical to nature, whereby all causal natures are dissolved.

If it is so, how could thought not cease? How could deliberation not be forgotten? Since the view of activity has already severed the bounds of thought and deliberation, and since this very activity further manifests the three contemplations—whether through negation or affirmation—then [all is resolved].

All are termed "action" (*zuò*); this refers to the two contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*). That which neither destroys nor establishes is termed "correctness"; this refers to the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

When one fully realizes [the truth] through action, then all three truths are simultaneously destroyed and all three truths are simultaneously established; this is termed "one emptiness, all emptiness" and "one provisionality, all provisionality. When one fully realizes correctness through action, then regarding the three truths, there is neither destruction nor establishment; this is termed "one middle, all middle.

Thus, the emptiness and provisionality within the middle are termed "action," for they can destroy the three delusions and establish the three dharmas, thereby evoking the perfect response of the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the other Buddhas. It can...

The fulfillment of my mind’s three bodies as the ultimate fruit is precisely what is meant by "the Middle within Emptiness and Provisionality. Thus, delusions are entirely wisdom and hindrances are entirely virtue. Therefore, this mind is the Responsive Buddha and this mind is the Fruitional Buddha.

Know that those who practice this single mind cultivation are engaged in the inconceivable three contemplations; it is the general essence of the Sixteen Contemplations and the sublime core of this sutra.
The text emerges from within this, while its meaning pervades from beginning to end.

The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [conditions] to be causes and conditions or inherent natures; all these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning whatsoever.

Zhaoxi says: "The 'world' generally refers to the nine realms. Xunwen says: "Speaking specifically, it mostly refers to humans and devas, up to and including those from the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) downwards.

This is because their conscious minds engage in discrimination and calculation regarding causes and conditions, spontaneity, and so forth. This is as stated in the first fascicle: 'Various practitioners are unable to achieve supreme Bodhi;

at best they separately become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or they become non-Buddhists, various devas, Māras, or the retinues of Māra. The Supplement states: "Within the section on the Seven Great Elements, the mundane world is refuted."

It is known that although "pervasive" (*sāmānya*) applies to the nine realms, it does not apply specifically to the four *durgati* (evil destinies). First, there is textual evidence, as cited in the first fascicle of the record you quoted. Second, there is a logical argument: because the four *durgati* are base and inferior, it is feared they would not reach this [level of understanding].

Those who receive the provisional teachings are all said to be "ignorant," for they do not comprehend the true meaning; thus, they are called "deluded. Because they cling to established names and forms, they are said to "act" (*wei*). The meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) encompasses the three natures—self, other, and common.
"Spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) refers to the nature of causelessness. All other cases should be understood by analogy with these.
"Ānanda, the nature of fire is without self; it relies upon various conditions.
The Supplement states: "Without self" means without substance. As is the case below with the nature of water being without fixedness and the nature of wind being without substance.
Observe the households within the city that have not yet eaten. When they wish to cook their food, they hold a magnifying glass (*ādityakānta*) in their hands and seek fire from the sun.

Ānanda, that which is called a "combination" is like myself and you, these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now constitute a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, if one examines its basis, each individual possesses a body; all have their own ancestral lineages and names.
Regarding Śāriputra, who was of the Brahmin caste; Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who was of the Kāśyapa caste; and even Ānanda, who was of the Gautama clan—[the text] says, "Xieli.

As for the *yangsui* (sun-stone lens), the *Xunwen* states that in ancient texts it was written as *feng*. Master Ying stated that it is the refined essence of the five metals. Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states: [text follows].

It is made of copper and shaped like a mirror. When it reflects objects, the image appears inverted; when directed toward the sun, fire is produced by applying a moxa stick (*ārdra-puṭa*). Furthermore, the *Huainanzi* states that the *yángsuǐ* (sun-crystal) is the source of fire, while the *Lúnhéng* says:
"On the day of the *bǐngwǔ* hexagram at noon on the fifth month, one smelts and refines stones from the five directions to form a circle like a mirror with a concave center;

when the sky is clear and facing the sun, it produces fire. As for my following example, it does not accord with the principle of combination (*saṃghāta*). Question: In the refutation of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), why is only this example of the fire element used to illustrate combination? Answer: [As previously stated regarding] the earth element...

The meaning of the combination of fuel and fire is remote; its attachment is easily refuted. From fire up to consciousness, the meaning of their combination is intimate; what is thus conceived is difficult to refute. For instance, regarding the nature of fire, if viewed from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it clearly arises due to the combination of the three factors:
the mirror, the sun, and the tinder. Now, by interrogating the root of these various combinations of people, one finds that each is distinct.

This serves to demonstrate that the combination of all phenomena (*dharma*) is entirely false and lacks any reality whatsoever. Since this is the case for the element of fire (*tejas-mahābhūta*), this principle must be applied to the remaining five great elements (*mahābhūta*); they are likewise so. As for the Śāriputra mentioned:

The three individuals, such as Śāriputra and the others, are not identical [to the examples], yet they follow the same principle as the mirror, the sun, and the tinder. The triads of water, wind, and so forth can be understood according to their respective meanings. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"The intention of the Master of the Record (*Juzhu*) is to take the three individuals, Śāriputra and the others, as examples following the principle of the conjunction of the mirror, the sun, and the tinder. The triad of the jewel, the space, and the moon within the water; and the triad of the garment, the space, and the face within the wind—these may likewise be taken as examples following the principle of the conjunction of the three persons.

Therefore it says: 'the triads of water, wind, and so forth. The Sanskrit term for this is *saṃgha*; here it is translated as 'assembly' (*zhòng*). 'Assembly' is precisely the meaning of conjunction. Conjunction, however, is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*); apart from..."

That "real person" (pudgala) has no distinct substantial nature. Xunwen says: "Brahman" is a corruption and abbreviation; the Master Yingshi says it should be called *brāhmaṇa*, which means "to inherit and practice.

Regarding the "Dharma of Brahmā": that class of people claims for themselves that they were born from the mouth of Brahmā, that they are superior among the four castes, and that they exist only in the five regions of India and not in other countries.

The term "Brahmacārin" mentioned in various sutras is also this same name. Gushan says: *Uruvilvā* means "Pawpaw Forest" (*kapittha-vana*); *Kāśyapa* means "Turtle Clan"; *Gautama*... [text continues].
The name of the clan was derived from the star; in later generations, they changed their surname to Śākya.

Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, when that person holds a mirror toward the sun seeking fire, does this fire emerge from within the mirror, or does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun?

Ānanda, if the fire comes from the sun, it should naturally burn the moxa in your hand; the forests through which it passed on its way here should all have been consumed by flames. If it emerges from within the mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and ignite the moxa;

why then does the mirror not melt? Since your hand holds it and yet shows no sign of heat, how could it ever be melted away? If the fire were produced within the moxa itself, why would it depend on the meeting of the light of the sun and the mirror before it could arise?

You should observe this carefully: the mirror is held by your hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the moxa grows from the earth. From what direction has the fire traveled to reach this place? What is the relationship between the sun and the mirror?
It is neither conjoined with nor separated from [the fire]. It should not be that the light of the fire arises spontaneously from nowhere.
Gushan says: *yu* means to bend, to wind, or to curve; it may also be glossed as "toiling. Zizhong says: the sun and the mirror are far apart;
the sun is forty thousand *yojanas* away from the human realm. Xunwen says: one *yojana* is twenty *li*.

You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition.

Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place; if they hold it throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire world. Since it arises throughout the world, how could it have a fixed location?
They manifest according to karma.

The world is ignorant of this and deludedly regards them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of words and lacking any real meaning.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.

For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the mahāsiddhas Kapila, Jāṅgulī, Padma, Mahasattva, and others—great masters of illusion—who sought the essence of the moon to mix with their illusory elixirs.
These masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, would hold a *fangzhu* (a concave crystal lens) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.
Changshui says: *Kapila* means yellowish-red; *cakravāṭa* means wheel; *padma* means red lotus; *hasada* is not clearly explained (alternatively translated as "water-matter");

*soma* refers to the moon. Gushan says: when the moon is at its zenith, it is called "day"; *fangzhu* is the water-extracting pearl. The *Huainanzi* states: "When the *fangzhu* sees the moon, it exudes moisture that becomes water. The *Lunheng* states:

"On the night of the *renzi* day of the eleventh month, at the hour of midnight, one refines stones from the five directions in the north to create it; its shape is like a cup or basin, and it faces the moon."

"Obtaining the ford. Gao You’s commentary states: "Fangzhu and yinsui refer to the large clam (*mahāśukti*). By rubbing it until it is hot and holding it toward the moon, water will be produced. Xu Shen further comments:

[These are] various beads and square stones. The translator likely adopted the later explanation of Xu Shen. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The character for *suì* (fire-drill) was originally written as *diàn*; it is also interchangeably written as *fèn*. *Diàn* refers to a mirror of water and fire.

If one uses this [character], it originally refers to the beacon fires maintained by watchtowers on the northern frontier, and it also refers to the 'drill' in the act of drilling for fire. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) asks: "What is the difference between *héng* (constancy) and *cháng* (permanence)?
It answers: "That which does not arise from causes and conditions is *cháng*; that which remains unchanged from beginning to end is *héng*."

Does this water emerge from within the pearl? Does it exist spontaneously in the air? Or does it come from the moon? Ānanda, if it came from the moon, being able to cause the pearl to emit water from such a great distance, then all the trees and forests it passes by should likewise discharge streams.
If they were to flow, why wait for the water to be produced by the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror)? If they do not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon.

If it emerged from the pearl, then water should constantly flow from within this pearl; why wait for the middle of the night under the bright full moon? If it were born from space, the nature of space is boundless, and the water should likewise be limitless, so that from humans up to the heavens, all would be submerged in a single flood.

"Submerged! How, moreover, can there be movement upon water, on land, and in the air? You should observe this more closely: the moon traverses the sky; the pearl is held in the hand; the basin for receiving the pearl's reflection was originally set out by a person.

From what direction does the water flow here? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the water-crystal [reflection] exists of its own accord without a source."

Since the forest trees neither emit nor flow [water], it is clear that this water does not descend from the moon. *Xunwen* says: "All likewise sink and drown" (*yǐ xián yǐ xiàn*). The two characters *xián* and *xiàn* both mean to be submerged by water.
*Gushan* says: "Essence (*jīng*)" is synonymous with "nature" (*xìng*).

You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know:

if one person grasps the pearl in one place, water appears in that place; if it is grasped throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire Dharma-realm. Since its arising fills the entire world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature; all of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robe upon entering the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and touches those beside you, whereby a subtle breeze brushes against their faces.

Zhenji says: "Sanghāṭī" refers to the great outer robe (*mahākāṣāya*). Xunwen says: "Sanghāṭī" has no direct translation; its meaning is 'a robe of many pieces' (*zàsuì yī*), because it consists of a great number of strips."

If named according to its function, it is called the "robe for entering royal palaces" or the "robe for entering villages. The *Huishang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Wisdom Superior) refers to it as the "Great Robe" (*mahākāṣāya*).

The *kāṣāya* derives its name from its color; this is an improper color, also known as a "discolored" (*rañjita*) color. The *Nanshan yeshu* states: "Originally it was written as *jiasha*. When Ge Hong compiled the *Ziyuan* during the Liang dynasty, he added the radical for 'clothing' below it, naming it the 'Daoist robe' (*daofu*).
The *Yijiao jing* (Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "Wear discolored robes. This is the general designation for the three robes (*tricīvara*).

Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, arise from empty space, or is it produced within that person’s face? Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind;

thus, as the robe flutters, it should be separated from your body. Now, as I preach the Dharma in this assembly, my robe hangs down; look at my robe—where is the wind? There can be no place within the robe where the wind is hidden.
If wind were produced from empty space, why would your robe not move when it is not being brushed? Since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, the wind should be constantly produced.

If there were no wind, then empty space itself would perish. If the wind could be seen to perish, what would the state of perished emptiness look like? If there were arising and ceasing, it could not be called "empty space. If it is called "empty space," how can wind emerge from it? If the wind arises spontaneously on the side of your face that is being brushed, then it should brush you instead.

When you adjust your own robe, why does it brush the Buddha’s face? Examine this carefully: the adjustment of the robe is yours; the face belongs to that other person. Empty space is tranquil and motionless.

"Venerable One, this movement arises from the wind. From which direction does the wind stir and come here? Since the nature of wind and space are distinct, they neither blend nor unite; yet it is not possible that the wind and mind exist spontaneously without a source."
Changshui said: "Because movement and stillness are different, they are said to be separated by nature. The mind is also 'nature.

You, however, do not know at all that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know.

Ānanda, it is like when you alone slightly move your robe, a slight breeze arises; it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm, fills the lands, and is produced everywhere in the world—how could it have a fixed location?"
They manifest according to karma.

The world is ignorant and deludedly regards them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature; these are all merely conceptual calculations of the discriminating consciousness. They are nothing but words and have no real meaning whatsoever.
"Ānanda, the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is formless; it is manifested through form (*rūpa*). Zizhong said:

'Both space and form are equally provisional and exist in mutual dependence. Their essence is not separate from form. Therefore, the Hīnayāna takes light and darkness as its essence, while the Mahāyāna takes the single manifest color of space (*ekavarṇa-śūnya-rūpa*) and the color of extreme distance (*atyanta-pratibhāsa-rūpa*) as its essence.

Looking upward, one sees the manifest color of the clarity of space; looking downward, one sees the distant color of the clarity of space. Now, regarding this sūtra, the element of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) comes first."

First establishing [the position] and then refuting it: Nirvāṇa and space are also like this. How is this clarified? In that sutra, the Buddha says that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space; this is the establishment.
Kāśyapa then contrasts space with the four great elements, asserting that space is an existent thing. Therefore, the Buddha uses ten successive arguments to negate this error.

His intention was to prevent sentient beings from identifying the nature illustrated by the analogy with the space that serves as the illustration. This is the refutation. When it is now said that the nature of space is formless, it simply means that it lacks the forms of the supported (the body) and the supporting (the environment).

Furthermore, it is by depending upon the colors of the "correct" (the environment) and the "substantive" (the beings) that the characteristics of the great element of space (*ākāśa*) are manifested; thus it is said that "space is manifested through form. This refers specifically to the space used as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, and is not the absence of form.

Therefore, the passage in the following text about "digging a well and finding space" refers to the category of "distant color" (*pratyag-rūpa*). Moreover, the preceding text states, "Even though empty space has names and appearances," and the subsequent text says, "seeing the perception of inert space," and so forth.

Thus, how could inert space be without form? One should understand that when this sutra speaks of space as a "great" element, it is to clarify that deluded ignorance gives rise to the existence of space as a basis.

The world is established upon emptiness. Furthermore, it is said that when one awakens to truth and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions completely vanishes. For this reason, the element of space must be explained immediately after the four great elements; this is its preliminary establishment.
It is only when one proceeds to the later section and subjects it to a threefold analysis that it is then deconstructed. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"I now say that the 'emptiness' clarified within the deconstruction of the false in this sutra refers to the single manifest color of emptiness, similar to the passage in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* which uses a metaphor to show that the Buddha-nature is all-pervasive. The 'emptiness' clarified within the manifestation of truth here refers to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, similar to [the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*]."

This emptiness of the Buddha-nature refutes the deluded sentiments of ordinary people. Zizhong follows the sutra in refuting delusion; by means of form, he reveals and elucidates it to clarify the essence of emptiness.

For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, various Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Pāraśavas and Caṇḍālas, have newly established a dwelling and dug a well seeking water.

When they have excavated the earth to a depth of one foot, there is one foot of empty space within; likewise, when they have excavated the earth to a depth of ten feet, they obtain ten feet of empty space.
The depth of the empty space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth that has been removed.
Gushan says: *Kṣatriya* refers to the royal caste; for generations, their lords and subjects have made benevolence and forbearance their primary aim. *Brāhmaṇa* refers to those of pure conduct;

they preserve the Way, abide in rectitude, and maintain the purity of their character. *Vaiśya* refers to merchants; they trade goods for one another, pursuing profit both near and far. *Śūdra* refers to farmers; they exert themselves in the fields and labor diligently at sowing and reaping. These four castes differ in their clarity or turbidity like separate streams;
they do not intermarry, and their paths of flight and concealment are distinct. *Pīluode* (Bhāradvāja); Zhen Di translates this as "swift" or "sharp-witted. Cien says: *Brāhmaṇa*.

There are eighteen clans in total; this [caste] is one among them. *Caṇḍāla* means "rigid insignia" (*yan-zhi*); they adorn themselves with evil karma and carry distinctive emblems, namely, shaking bells and holding bamboo poles.

Does this space arise because of the earth? Does it exist because of the excavation? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause? Ānanda, if this space arose spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth was excavated?

Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration? If it arises because of the earth, then when the earth is excavated, one should see the space entering. If the earth were excavated first and the space did not enter, [how could it exist now?]

"How can empty space emerge because of the earth? If there is no coming forth or entering, then space and earth must fundamentally have no different cause. If they are not different, they are the same; if they are the same, then when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?

If it emerges because of digging, then the digging should produce space rather than producing earth. If it does not emerge because of digging, then the digging itself produces the earth—how then do you perceive space? You should examine this more carefully; examine it with true scrutiny.

The digging proceeds from the human hand and moves according to direction, while the earth shifts according to the ground. Thus, from what source does this empty space emerge? The act of digging and the voidness of space are real and unreal; they do not function for one another."
It is neither identical with nor separate from it. It should not be that empty space emerges from nowhere on its own. Regarding the supplementary note:

"If [the earth] emerges because of the soil, why does it not emerge when reaching space? This is because there are two parts to the argument concerning the soil: first, refuting space by showing that the earth emerges from the soil and enters the well;

second, if there were no [earth], refuting the alternative view that space [emerges]. Since space is what enters, and having already been refuted, one might fear the opponent would shift their position and claim that space has no entering or exiting. The refutation states: "Space..."

If there were no coming forth or entering, then emptiness would not possess the characteristic of appearing through the emergence of earth. Since they do not depend upon one another, it would follow that they are distinct entities. If so, when the earth emerges, why does emptiness not emerge as well?

Since space and earth are identical, how could it be that the earth departs while space remains? You have further proposed the refutation of co-arising; the Buddha’s intention is even more consistent with the aspect of thorough investigation, which appears in the following text.

As it says, "The digging follows the hand" is the thorough investigation, and "the earth shifts according to the ground" is the thorough observation. Although there are three instances of the word *di* (thorough) in the text, the first phrase serves as the general heading.

In the following passage concerning the great element of the sense-organ (*indriya-mahābhūta*), there are four instances of the character "shen" (to examine). The first line provides a general heading; the subsequent three "shen" characters examine how the triad of light, darkness, and space cannot produce the great element of the sense-organ.

In the subsequent section on the great element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*), there are only two instances of the character "xiang" (to detail), which correspond to the two meanings of the "seeing" (*darśana*) and "phenomenal" (*nimitta*) aspects. Regarding the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), [the text notes that] it arises from the earth by itself, or it arises from digging by another;

these two meanings combined constitute "co-arising. The scriptural text proceeds from the point where the digging creates the voidness of space, merely reiterating the absence of a cause. The intent is to say: the digging produces the solidity and the voidness; the essential natures of these two are...

They are discordant; therefore, they do not function for one another. This is equivalent to saying they do not act as causes for one another. Furthermore, regarding the refutation that "if [the world] arises from earth," there are two meanings. First, the refutation based on the difference between the characteristics of space and earth.
Second, if there were no entering or exiting, it would refute the established characteristics of the earth element based on this principle.

If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the five great elements. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious;
they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Zhaoxī says: The reason why "space" (*ākāśa*) is added after the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and collectively termed the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) is that the various sūtras usually speak only of the four.

Since this case differs from those, it is specifically mentioned. The same principle applies below in the section on the faculties and consciousnesses. As for the general designation "great," it is established provisionally based on phenomena. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha taught that the four great elements are nowhere not present; therefore, they are called 'great'. This speaks of the pervasive nature of the "great";
one must point to phenomena as being identical with principle, subsuming the derivative back into the fundamental. That which cannot be named yet is named is the Tathāgatagarbha.

Furthermore, Ānanda, your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate whether space comes out or goes in, or whether it neither comes nor goes.

You do not at all know that within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, awakened awareness is true emptiness, and true emptiness is awakened awareness—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know. Ānanda, it is like one...

Just as empty space arises within a well, so it is with the empty space of the ten directions. Being perfectly pervasive throughout the ten directions, how could it have a specific location? It manifests according to karma;

yet the world is ignorant and deludedly regards it as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature. All of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind; they are nothing but words and lack any real meaning.
Ānanda, seeing and awareness are devoid of cognition; they exist because of form and emptiness.

Seeing-awareness is the essence of vision (*darśana-śuddhi*), which, like a mirror reflecting an image, attains the realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is not like consciousness (*vijñāna*) which discriminates between blue and yellow; therefore, it is said to be "without cognition.

Previously, in the refutation of consciousness and the refutation of seeing, there were originally two layers, both of which were refutations manifested in contrast to emptiness. Therefore, following the discussion of the four great elements, [the text] again cites emptiness, seeing, and the essence of consciousness as the Tathāgatagarbha. Due to delusive confusion, this single essence is divided.

This clarifies that "seeing" refers to the conjunction of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing with the six [senses]. There are those who fail to comprehend this principle and insist on taking "seeing" and "cognizing" as the primary sense organs (*indriya*); this is a great error.

That the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is composed of pure material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) is the terminology of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang). This is clearly evident from the text below, which states: "The nature is seeing; the cognitive clarity is awareness; the essence of awareness is the clarity of seeing. It is manifest.

As you are now in the Jeta Grove, it is bright in the morning and dark at night; even if it were midnight, it would be light during the waxing moon and dark during the waning moon. Thus, light and darkness are distinguished through the act of seeing.

Furthermore, does this vision share the same substance as light and darkness, and with the great void of space? Or is it not of one substance? Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different?

Xie Li said: "This question consists of four propositions: first, identity; second, difference; third, both identical and different; and fourth, neither identical nor different. However, in the scriptural text, two instances of 'identity' and 'difference' are each treated as a single proposition."

Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally one with light, darkness, and empty space, then the two entities of light and darkness would mutually negate each other. When it is dark, there would be no light; when it is light, it would not be dark.

If it were identical to darkness, then seeing would cease when there is light. If it were necessarily identical to light, then seeing would perish when it is dark. If it perished, how could it see light or see darkness? If light and darkness were distinct...

Seeing is without arising or ceasing. How can it be established as one? If this essence of seeing were not of the same substance as darkness and light, then when you separate yourself from light, darkness, and empty space to analyze the source of seeing, what form or appearance would it have?

Apart from light, apart from darkness, and apart from empty space, this source of seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established?

Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they be the same? Apart from these three, seeing does not exist at all; how could it be different? To distinguish between space and seeing, there is originally no boundary; how could they not be the same? Thus, seeing...
The nature of clarity seen in darkness does not undergo change. Why is it not different?

Analyzing the source of seeing, one finds it to be the very essence of the clarity of seeing; the subsequent text refers to this as the "seeing-root" (*mūla*). Although it is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), it is called a "root" because these six [faculties] act as the root for the wheel of birth and death, and serve as the foundation for realizing wondrous permanence, being derived from the single, original, pure clarity.
Master Jing said: "The perceived and the perceiver have no inherent nature; apart from the three [elements], they do not exist. The nature of seeing has no form; fundamentally, it is non-existent."

Arising and ceasing. You should examine this more minutely, scrutinizing it with extreme care and precision: light comes from the sun; darkness follows the dark moon; openness belongs to empty space; and obstruction returns to the great earth.

From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise? The faculty of seeing is aware, while emptiness is inert; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the essence of seeing arises of itself from nowhere.
Xie Li said: "The preceding four lines refute birth from causes and conditions; these refute birth from causeless spontaneity.

If one perceives that the nature of seeing, hearing, knowing, and cognizing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that the boundless, unmoving void, together with the moving earth, water, fire, and wind, are collectively termed the six great elements.
Their nature is truly interfused and perfectly harmonious; they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing."

Gushan says: Previously, in the extensive refutation of "seeing with the eyes" among the six sense faculties, the other faculties were treated briefly. Now, by way of analogy, their nature is shown to be universally pervasive. "Hearing" refers to the ear faculty; "perceiving" (*jue*) refers to the nose, tongue, and body faculties;

and "knowing" (*zhi*) refers to the mind faculty. The reason "perceiving" is not mentioned [in the verse] is for the sake of brevity. Changshui says: However, in the Lesser Vehicle, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are frequently discussed, whereas in the Great Teaching, the term "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) first appears.

As for the roots and consciousnesses being given the same name as "great," I have not yet seen this appear in the sūtras. In the various Perfect and Real Teachings, one performs a perfect contemplation of all phenomena; the triad of root, object, and consciousness is universally pervasive and immovable. Although...

There is a reason why the Great Name was not established previously, yet it is specifically brought forth here; this truly serves as the final, ultimate model for posterity. The *Shiyao* states: "Regarding the fact that the name 'Space' first appears in the Great Teaching:
within the Mahāyāna, the five wheels are taught—namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Because the nature of space is all-pervasive and exists throughout time and place, it is called 'Great.

As for the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness having the quality of pervasiveness, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: 'The nature of enlightenment is omnipresent and perfectly boundless. One should know that the six sense faculties pervade the Dharma-realm. Because the faculties are pervasive, one should know that the six sense-objects [are likewise so]."

It pervades the entire dharma-realm and so forth. Furthermore, the light also possesses six elements, all of which are not manifest; by comparison, these seven great elements are most clearly evident.

Alternatively, it may be stated as a single faculty, "seeing," meaning that the nature of seeing is fundamentally non-existent and no such nature can be apprehended. One awakens to and realizes this nature.

Ānanda, your nature is mired in delusion; you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should examine this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they born or do they perish? Are they the same or are they different?

Are they neither born nor perishing? Are they neither the same nor different? You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness are one—the clarity of awareness is itself the essence of seeing—and that they are pure and fundamental from the very beginning.

It pervades the entire Dharma-realm, corresponding to the minds of sentient beings and the capacity of what they know. Just as with the faculty of sight, where seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of touch and feeling pervade the Dharma-realm.
Their wondrous virtues are brilliantly pure and pervade the Dharma-realm, filling the ten voids; how could they have any fixed location? They manifest according to karma.

Changshui says: "Zeng" means "formerly. The two faculties of nose and tongue perceive their objects only when they come into contact; therefore, they are called "tasting" and "touching. To perceive touch is the body; to perceive and know is the mind. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says:

As stated in the preceding section on the six sense organs, the Buddha’s refutation regarding the nose-root’s perception of fragrance was analogous to his refutation regarding the body-root’s perception of touch. Thus, we know that the nose and other organs also receive the designation "touch.

This is because the nose distinguishes fragrances and stenches, and the tongue discriminates sweetness and pungency; these are instances of "tasting touch. "Taste" (甞) implies testing. The body cannot test fragrances and stenches; it merely perceives touch.

However, according to the present text, "tasting touch" still pertains to the tongue, for when flavor reaches the tongue, the principle of "touch" is most evident. When smoke or vapor reaches the nose, the principle of "touch" is still somewhat remote. Therefore, in this text, "tasting touch" resides in the tongue. —Jing.

The Master said: "The six faculties all receive their nature from awakening; therefore, regarding the faculty of sight, it is called 'seeing-nature' (xing-jian), 'awakened clarity' (jue-ming), and 'awakened essence' (jue-jing) seeing.

As for the faculties of hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and mental cognition, they are likewise identical to sight in that they all receive the nature of awakening. To speak of 'awakened touching' refers to the nature of the body-faculty as awakening;

to speak of 'awakened knowing' refers to the nature of the mind and tongue faculties as awakening. The two faculties of ear and nose may be inferred by analogy. What is meant by 'seeing-nature, awakened clarity, awakened essence, and clear seeing' is that awakened clarity arises from awakening, and the essence of awakening unites with spirit to possess awareness."

It is also of the same substance as cognition (*jñāna*). Because seeing is not cognition, it may be called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*), but it cannot be called "cognition. Since it was stated above that seeing and awareness are devoid of cognition, it is clear that it cannot be called cognition.
The nature of seeing belongs to awareness; because clarity unites with subtlety, it first speaks of "awareness-clarity" and subsequently speaks of "awareness-subtlety."

The world is ignorant; it is deluded by taking causes and conditions, as well as inherent nature, as real. These are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind; they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no actual reality whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and their objects.
Now, as you survey this assembly of noble ones, let your eyes move through them one by one. As your eyes look around, they are like reflections in a mirror, without further analysis.
Yet your consciousness within them sequentially identifies and points out: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," "This is Maudgalyāyana," and "This is Subhūti."
Zhendi said: "The faculties together illuminate objects; thus it is like a mirror. Consciousness possesses discernment; thus it can point them out.
This consciousness that cognizes—does it arise from the seeing-faculty? Does it arise from the objective-sign? Does it arise from empty space? Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?"

Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—there would necessarily be no fundamental basis for your seeing. If the nature of seeing itself does not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If the nature of your consciousness were produced within the objective phenomena (nimitta) and did not arise from seeing, then you would neither see light nor see darkness. If light and darkness do not impinge upon it, then there would be no form or emptiness.

If those signs themselves lack consciousness, from what could cognition arise? If it were to arise in emptiness, it would be neither sign nor vision. Without vision, there is no discernment; one could not, of oneself, know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

It is not that the signs are extinguished, for the conditions for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have nowhere to be established. Abiding in this state of neither-sign-nor-vision, emptiness is the same as non-existence, and existence is not identical to material objects. Even if you were to give rise to consciousness, what would you intend to differentiate?

Gushan says: To abide in these two "non-s" means that there is neither form nor seeing. "Empty" implies being identical to the ineffable and the non-cognitive; one should rather say "non-existent" to imply being identical to emptiness—it is merely a matter of alternating the terminology.

"Existence" does not mean being the same as things, for it refers to the presence of cognition. Since [cognition] arises within emptiness, there are already no objects of form or seeing. Therefore, he challenges [the opponent]: "Even if you were to activate your cognition, how could you differentiate?"
If it were to emerge suddenly without any cause, why would you not perceive the bright moon at midday?

You should examine this more closely; scrutinize it with great care. Seeing relies upon your essence and extends toward external objects; thus, it can be characterized as existing, yet it cannot be characterized as non-existent. From what source, then, does this consciousness arise as its condition?

When consciousness moves, seeing remains clear; they are neither blended nor joined. The same applies to hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. It is not reasonable that consciousness should emerge from nowhere on its own.

The Supplement states: "You should further minutely examine the general heading; you must scrutinize it with great subtlety regarding the specific illustrations. To examine and scrutinize refers to the confrontation between the seer and the seen. Changshui says: "Harmony" means discernment (*vijñapti*); "clarity" means illuminating the object. Xunwen says:

"Consciousness is active while the seer is clear; they are neither harmonious nor conjoined. This refers to the contradiction between the activity of the sense-faculties and consciousness, which is termed "non-harmonization.

If viewed in relation to external objects, it still refutes the notion of self-arising. As for the passage in the section on the wind element stating, "Wind and space are separated by their natures; they are neither harmonious nor conjoined," since this is discussed in relation to objects, it serves to refute [self-arising].

It is also produced from others. If it were as stated regarding the element of fire: "The sun and the mirror are far apart; they neither blend nor combine. This refers to the mutual relationship between self and other, which precisely refutes the nature of combination.
It is explained according to its specific meaning, and thus is not a single, uniform approach.

If this consciousness-mind originally has no source from which it arises, you should know that its capacity for discerning, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and profound. Its nature does not originate from any external locus;

furthermore, space, earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their natures are truly interfused and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.

Lord Jing said: "Although consciousness resides within the six sense organs, its nature does not derive from them. Since its nature does not derive from them, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous."

Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless; you have not realized that what is seen, heard, perceived, and known is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should examine these six consciousnesses of the sense bases: are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent?

Are they neither the same nor different, or neither empty nor existent? From the beginning, you have not known that within the Tathāgata-garbha there is the nature of consciousness, the clear and knowing awareness, the truly cognizing consciousness, and the wondrously enlightened, profoundly still state.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm and encompassing the ten voids, how could it have a fixed location?

It manifests according to karma. Master Jing said: "Regarding space, you say your mind is deluded; yet the nature of space is enlightened. Regarding seeing, you say your nature is submerged; yet the nature of seeing is externally manifest. Regarding consciousness, you say your mind is coarse and floating; yet the conscious mind is hidden within.

To be "floating" means one merely recognizes the superficial sense organs; to be "coarse" means one does not penetrate the essence of consciousness. This is what is called the "nature-consciousness of clear knowing"—the true consciousness of enlightened clarity.

This means that sensation clearly knows through awareness; the clarity of awareness arises from awareness. The essence of consciousness is knowing. Because sensation clearly knows through awareness, it first mentions "clearly knowing" and subsequently mentions "the clarity of awareness."

To speak of "wondrous enlightenment" means that enlightenment is wondrously realized herein. To speak of the "ten voids" (daśa-ākāśa): the spheres of activity arising from consciousness and the six sense organs exist yet are not real;

hence they are called the ten voids. Wind has no substantial entity and manifests in dependence upon earth; hence it is called the "land" (deśa). Water and fire serve as the utilities of the world; hence they are called the "world" (loka). As for why form (*rūpa*) is not explicitly called the world or the land:

apart from form there is no world or land, and apart from the world or land there is no form. They are perfected by space (*ākāśa*); they are not merely the world or the land, nor are they existent yet unreal. Hence it is said:

The ten directions do not undergo transition or flow; empty space is likewise. The Supplement states: "Containing and exhaling" is like "rolling up and unfolding. The empty space of the ten directions is small when situated within the true mind.
Therefore, one is able to roll it up and unroll it.

Those in the world are ignorant; they are deluded by [the notions of] causes and conditions or spontaneous nature. All of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind; they consist only of verbal expressions and lack any real meaning whatsoever.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

Changshui said: "The three aggregates and the seven elements are both appearance and nature; they are fundamentally unborn and now non-extinguished. Birth, extinction, coming, and going are all the Tathāgatagarbha—perfectly pervasive and immovable, pure and inherently so.

This is the true ultimate nature within the Tathāgata’s proclamation of the ultimate meaning; therefore, it is called 'subtle and wondrous instruction. Because body and mind are perfectly luminous, it is called 'completely cleared away.'"
However, there are no further phenomena regarding which one might have doubts; therefore, there is no obstruction.
