The mind is particular; one should know that while it is pervasive, its locations are always particular. For example, if another land takes sound as its benefit, then Dignāga becomes the particular object of apprehension therein. While particularity is constant, its locations are always pervasive.

As for the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara, if one considers other lands, it likewise falls within the examples already presented; it is not distinct [from them] but is universal. From this it may be said: although the Buddha wished to reveal that all eighteen realms are equally perfectly penetrating (*yuan-tong*), they are distinct according to their respective lands.

Thus, he had to manifest that each gate is distinct—this is the meaning of "conforming to the land" (*shun-tu*). That each gate is universally penetrating—this is the meaning of "universal penetration. How could the ultimate essence fail to recognize this intent? Gushan says:

"The initial contemplation of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) to awaken to the Way... and so forth. This is because from time immemorial we have employed various deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*); since these thoughts are not true, there are the six objects.
[The cycle of] saṃsāra. Now, knowing that the eternally abiding true mind is of one essence and non-dual, one attains awakening to the Way by contemplating even a single mote of dust.

Kātyāyana and the other five bhikṣus then rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the Deer Park and at the Kukkuṭārāma, we witnessed the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of the Way.

Through the Buddha’s voice, we awakened to and clarified the Four Noble Truths. When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus if they understood, I was the first to declare my understanding; the Tathāgata certified me with the name Ajñāta."

Zhaoxi said: *Kauṇḍinya* is his clan name; it translates as "Fire-Vessel" because his ancestors served the fire deity. *Ajñāta* is his personal name; this means "One Without Knowledge," referring to his realization of the principle of non-arising.

It is also translated as "Understanding," which is why it is said, "I was first called Understanding," and so forth. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states in full that he "understood the original limit. Xielin says:

When the Prince first left the city to dwell in seclusion among the mountain valleys, his father, King Śuddhodana, commanded three members of the royal family—first, Aśvajit; second, Bhadrika; and third, Mahānāman Kauṣṭhila—as well as [members of] his maternal clan.

There were two: first, Kauṇḍinya; second, Vappa-Kāśyapa. They had departed for that military encampment at that time. When the Prince attained the Way, the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths three times for these five men.

The Buddha asked, "Do you understand? Kauṇḍinya was the first to answer that he understood. The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens also declared that he understood; therefore, this became his name. *Xunwen* says:

The *Madhyama Āgama* states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the eminent bhikṣus resided at Kukkuṭārāma. The *Sǒngshū* (Collection of Commentaries) cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, saying: "In the past, there was a forest fire that consumed a grove.

Within the grove was a pheasant that entered the water to soak its feathers in order to extinguish the flames. The *Zuanyao* (Essentials of Compilation) identifies this as the Kukkuṭamukha Monastery (*Jītóumó sì*). It remains uncertain which of these two accounts is correct.
"Subtle sound is secretly perfect. I attained Arhatship through sound. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is supreme.

Gushan says: "Subtle sound is secretly perfect" means that he secretly awakened to the principle of perfection. Some say: In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, those who speak of the causes of the body are all Lesser Sages;

in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, those who enter non-duality are all Great Beings. Yet, among these twenty-five sages, both Great and Lesser ones are intermingled. Nevertheless, it is said that while the gates of skillful means are many, their return to the source is non-dual. Furthermore, Śrughna and Śāriputra attained awakening relatively recently.

"Partial emptiness versus universal [emptiness]. Samantabhadra and Maitreya have long since realized the perfect principle; thus, there is a distinction between the distant and the near, and a difference between the partial and the perfect.

How could their ultimate convergence be reduced to a single negation? He replied: "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when describing the past, it is said that the Small Vehicle has no portion of the Great. In the *Vimalakīrti* and the Vaipulya sutras, the Great is separated from the Small Vehicle. How then could what they discuss regarding realization be mixed?

As for this present sutra, the fact that those of the Two Vehicles attain Buddhahood shares the same path as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; that icchantikas possess Buddha-nature follows the same track as the *Nirvāṇa*. Because the teaching reveals and clarifies how the partial is itself the perfect fusion, it causes that which was taught at the Deer Park..."
To realize the sudden principle of the single vehicle (ekayāna) together with others is, in truth, a matter of profound shamelessness for one who claims to be Samantabhadra.

This refers to those śrāvakas of actual practice. As for those who secretly harbor the Great Way while outwardly manifesting the Lesser Vehicle, how could they not have been practicing the Great since the Deer Park? Since their true origins have already been revealed as being of one principle, what doubt can there be? This refers to those śrāvakas of expedient practice.

Since the realization of the principle is identical, who can be bound by distinctions of distance or proximity? Viewed in this light, the teaching that the Small and the Great intermingle becomes naturally harmonious and logical; the delusions regarding distance versus proximity, or partiality versus perfection, will dissolve like ice melting away.

The Supplement states: The following section enumerates the Perfect Penetrations (*yuan-tong*) of the twenty-five sages. It is difficult to determine whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna. For instance, when [the Buddha] tested Cienapa (Candrakīrti) and others, he categorized them as Hīnayāna;

yet now, in questioning the Perfect Penetration, he says it belongs to the Mahāyāna. This describes the meaning of the past—how could it be otherwise than great? Thus, the two accounts differ from one another. By examining the explanation of Gushan, much is gained.

However, taking the "subtle sound and secret perfection" as the point of awakening, the doctrinal positions established by Wuxing contain many contradictions. First, this sutra clarifies that all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are gates of perfect penetration, citing the various sages who...

This is entered as proof. If there were distinctions between the small and the true within that which is entered, how could one clarify that the meaning of universal penetration (*yuantong*) is uniform? Regarding the previous method for untying the knots: pulling to the left or right in a biased manner is not the method for untying.

How could there be universal penetration while a small-scale understanding still persists? Moreover, the name "universal penetration" is established based on the Great [Vehicle]; it is certainly impossible to define this term by means of a partial truth.

Second, because this sutra has already heard the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and clarification, all sages—whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—enter into perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). The opening of the provisional (*kai-quan*) is not singular;

as it says, "You śrāvakas of the various vehicles shall enter the Bodhisattva vehicle," and again, "Śrāvakas of fixed nature shall all attain the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle. Therefore, regarding the sages, Wuxing’s counter-accusation against Gushan—that the Bodhisattvas and the two vehicles [only] open the provisional through their own giving—is what kind of statement is that?

Third, because the *Lotus Sūtra* has already heard the fundamental and manifested aspects of master and disciple, there is no hindrance to the simultaneous inclusion of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in this sutra.

Regarding the meaning of the "local ground" (mūla-bhūmi) as clarified through perfect penetration: in the cases of Śāriputra and others, they directly describe their local ground, stating, "From the beginningless kalpas... and so forth. Yet, Wuxing still wished to provide an indirect explanation from the perspective of their traces (*vyañjana*).

Now, the *Buyi* (Supplement) states: Among the chapters on the twenty-five sages, each must contain several sections. First, there is the narration of what was realized in the past, whether it be great or small. Second, there is the narration of the perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-abhisamaya*), which, because it proceeds from the revelation [of the truth], is uniformly treated as great.

For example, in the chapter on Ghoṣaka (Cenna), the initial narration of his past realization refers to the small [vehicle]; the subsequent passage, "Miaoyin [Guanyin] is secretly perfect," and so on, narrates the perfect penetration. Although in the past he was... [text ends].
"Small. Now that it has been revealed and clarified, I have realized that my former faculty of sound was indeed a gate of perfect penetration. Thus it is said, "The subtle sound is secretly perfect.

As for my attainment of Arhatship through sound, if one treats this as a small fruit, then one takes only a small portion of that secret perfection; therefore, my former realization was of a small fruit. Herein, in describing perfect penetration, the mention of my former realization still carries over, merely to demonstrate that within the secret perfection there is room to contain the small fruit.

This is explained from the perspective of the Small Vehicle. If explained according to the Great Vehicle, then following my awakening to perfect penetration today, I am an Aśaikṣa who has entered and dwells in the stages.

The above points are all discussed from the perspective of actual practice (*samyak-pratipatti*). If one considers the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) attained through long-term awakening to perfect penetration at the fundamental stage (*mūla-bhūmi*), it is by no means comparable to what is found today.

Regarding the three chapters concerning Śāriputra, Subhūti, and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, they directly recount events spanning vast eons; one must not attempt to evaluate them using the limited scope of this minor mundane realm. The *Śìyào* states:
"To realize that all is the dharma-gate of sound means that apart from sound there is not a single dharma; all dharmas converge in sound. All other cases should be understood accordingly.

Upāniṣada immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I too observed the Buddha when he first attained enlightenment. Observing the signs of impurity, I gave rise to great revulsion and detachment, and realized the nature of all forms.
As they proceeded from impurity to white bones and then to subtle dust, they returned to empty space; with both emptiness and form being non-existent, I attained the path of no-more-learning.
The Tathāgata confirmed my name as Upāniṣada."

Since it is stated that one contemplates the Buddha’s initial attainment of enlightenment, we know that contemplating impure characteristics is precisely the untainted (*anāsrava*) practice of the Hīnayāna. As for the phrase "awakening to the nature of all forms," this refers to the Śrāvaka’s awakening to the *smṛtyupasthāna* of nature.
Master Nanyue said: "It is the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the rational nature of the five aggregates. Xunwen said: "This means contemplating the impurity of form and contemplating sensation as suffering."

One contemplates consciousness as impermanent and perceives volitional formations and perceptions as non-self. Thus, a verse in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says: "This body has the characteristic of impurity; its true nature is eternally fixed. So too are all feelings and mental factors."

It is explained in this same way: because [the body] proceeds from impure white bones and subtle particles back into empty space, one cultivates the remedial dharmas due to excessive greed, thereby accomplishing the nine meditations on repulsiveness.

1. The perception of bloating; 2. The perception of livid discoloration; 3. The perception of decay; 4. The perception of being smeared with blood; 5. The perception of putrefaction; 6. The perception of being devoured; 7. The perception of scattering; 8. The perception of bones; 9. The perception of burning.

One who gives rise to these true perceptions and shatters delusions is a *bhikṣu* Arhat who has destroyed the dharmas. These details are fully explained in the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Stages of Meditation).

"When the defiled forms have been exhausted, the wondrous forms become subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through these physical characteristics. When the Buddha asks about the most direct path to perfect penetration, according to my realization, the cause of form is supreme."

The Supplement states: This chapter first recounts the former realization that established the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*); this pertains to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). From the passage "Since the dust of form has been exhausted," it recounts the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).

Furthermore, the mention of "attaining Arhatship" indicates that one should know there is a different path from the previously established path of no-more-learning. Now, the Perfect Penetration is recounted through the "wondrous form, subtle and perfect," wherein I attained partial realization in the past.

This reveals that within the "Perfect Penetration" (yuan-tong), there is the inclusion of both the small and the great. Below, in the section on Xiangyan, he attains arhatship; since this constitutes the subtle fragrance of profound perfection, it likewise carries the meaning of the great containing the small.
Thus, the principle of first indicating the small and subsequently the great is indeed so.

The youth Incense Reverence immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena.

At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting. I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent:

it was neither wood, nor space, nor smoke, nor fire. As it departed, it left no trace; as it came, it had no source. Through this, my conceptual mind dissolved and the untainted state (*anāsrava*) was revealed. The Tathāgata confirmed me with the title 'Incense Reverence'."

Xīlì says: "Yàn" (宴) means "to rest in peace" (*an-śì*); "huì" (晦) means "to rest in stillness" (*yàn-jì*). A chamber of purity and tranquility is called a "pure fast" (*qīng-zāi*). Zīzhōng says: "That which is not wood, etc., is the contemplation of the emptiness of nature.

Whenever one speaks of the emptiness of nature, one must necessarily examine the four natures. Here, we shall take the wood as "self," the smoke and fire as "other," their conjunction as "common," and emptiness as "without cause.

This resembles the Mahāyāna method of contemplating that illusory existence is itself emptiness. The various Śrāvakas mentioned below also mostly follow the Hīnayāna meaning of contemplating that real existence ceases into emptiness.

Dusty vapors suddenly vanished and wondrous fragrances became subtle and pervasive. Through the "Array of Fragrance," I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect method of penetration, that which I have realized—namely, the Array of Fragrance—is supreme.

Zhaoxi said: "The previous mention of 'Incense-Rigorous Boy' (Xiangyan Tongzi) indicates he received his title from a Bodhisattva; the present mention of him attaining Arhatship is merely a record of what he realized in the past.

This is like the case of Moonlight Boy (Yueguang Tongzi) in the text below, who initially attained the Lesser Fruit (śrāmaṇaphala) but later received the name 'Childlike Purity' (Kumārabhūta) from the Buddha and was included in the assembly of Bodhisattvas."

The two Dharma princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, together with five hundred Brahmās in the assembly, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Throughout kalpas without beginning, we have served as skilled physicians for the world. We have tasted every herb, wood, metal, and stone within this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand.

Thus we know fully their tastes—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their combinations, natural properties, and transformations. Whether they are cold or hot, toxic or non-toxic, we are able to know them all thoroughly. Having attended upon the Tathāgata, we have [attained] realization..."

I know that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor is it separate from the body and mind. By discerning the causes of taste, I have attained awakening.
The Buddha-Tathāgata has conferred upon me and my brother the titles of the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. Now, within this assembly, we serve as Dharma princes.

Gushan said: "Bitter, sour, and so forth are the six tastes. When these various tastes combine, they are called 'harmonized taste' (*saṃyukta-rasa*). To take them directly as they are is called 'innate taste' (*sahaja-rasa*). To refine, roast, or process them is called 'transformed taste' (*vikāra-rasa*).

Tiaoxi said: "Because one serves the Buddha, one will inevitably hear the True Dharma; thus, regarding the nature of taste, one realizes both arising and non-arising. 'Emptiness and existence' refers to the sense-object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*); 'body and mind' refers to the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*).

Since taste is known through their conjunction, they are mentioned in relation to one another. Taste is not empty, therefore it is not separate from body and mind; taste is not existent, therefore it is not..."

This refers to body and mind; the nature of the Middle Way is manifested therein. The Supplement states: "Gold has five colors, all of which are gold. Stone, white *ying*, purple *ying*, gypsum, stalactite, and stone fat—these five minerals are all 'metal-stone' (*jinshi*).
All medicinal substances produced through smelting and refinement are metal-stone."

"By means of the clarity of the sense of taste, I attained the stage of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, I replied that, according to my realization, the cause of taste is supreme.

Bhadrapāla and his sixteen companions, the Bodhisattvas, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying: "In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), we heard the Dharma and left the household life.

Once, while entering the bathhouse according to custom during the time of bathing the Sangha, we suddenly awakened to the cause of water. It neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the interval between these two, one attains a state of tranquil non-existence."

All my past habitual practices have been preserved without forgetfulness, even until this present time when I have gone forth from home under the Buddha and attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla.

Gushan says: *Bhadrapāla* is translated here as "Worthy Protector" (*Xiánshǒu*). He protects his own virtuous qualities and further protects sentient beings; alternatively, he is called "Worthy Head" (*Xiánshǒu*), because his rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), making him the head among all worthy ones.

Xunwen says: In ancient times, *bodhisattva* was translated as "Opening Hero" (*Kāishì*). "Opening Hero" refers to the "beginning hero. "Opening" means the mind has first opened, and "beginning" means having first resolved to attain enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

Zizhong says: According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, twenty-two trillion *Vibhūṣaṇarāja* Buddhas appeared in succession. During the period of the True Dharma (*śāsana*) of the very first Buddha’s image, this *Bhadra-*...

Because [Devadatta] and others harbored overweening pride and slandered Nityaprakāśa (Never-Disparaging), they fell into the Avīci Hell for a thousand kalpas. Once their retribution was exhausted, they encountered a Buddha and subsequently left the household life.

Tiaoxi says: "Water" refers to the cause of that which is touched; "dust" (the object) is the substance, which is the condition of that which touches. Dust is fundamentally without defilement, and its substance is also eternally pure. Subject and object are like illusions; both extremes are empty.
Therefore, the mind that perceives contact within this intermediate state is peacefully in accord with its true nature.孤山 (Gushan) says: "This is the attainment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

When wondrous contact is proclaimed and clarified, one dwells as a child of the Buddha. Regarding the inquiry into perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the faculty of touch is the supreme cause.

Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.

I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its study. After that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics, lit lamps to maintain the light, and applied purple-gold paint to the Buddha’s images.
From that time forth, in life after life and birth after birth, my body has always been perfectly full and a mass of purple-gold light. Thus spoke the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light and the others.

My followers awakened their resolve at the same time as I. Observing that the six sense-objects of the world are subject to decay and transformation, I cultivated the extinction of body and mind through emptiness and stillness; thus, I was able to pass hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if they were a mere snap of the fingers.
By means of the dharma of emptiness, I became an Arhat. The World-Honored One declared me to be the foremost among those who practice dhūta austerities.
Changshui says: Mahākāśyapa is translated as "Great Drinker of Light" (Dà Yǐnguāng Shì). He was the wife of Zǐjīn Guāngní during her time as a laywoman. Gushan says:

This refers to the ninth of the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), namely the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti). Now, Kāśyapa is still able to enter meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya. Dhūta is newly translated as *duo-duo* (抖擻), which means "to shake off. Xunwen says:
The nine successive attainments refer to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), and the cessation of perception and feeling.

The wondrous Dharma was revealed and clarified, extinguishing all outflows (*āsrava*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), I replied that, according to my realization, the cause of the Dharma (*dharmahetu*) is supreme.

The Supplement states: "This describes perfect penetration; following the previous pattern, it should have said 'the wondrous Dharma is subtle and perfect. I attained Arhatship through the sense-object of dharmas (*dharmadhātu*); yet here it simply says 'the wondrous Dharma was revealed and clarified.'"
The words are concise, yet the meaning is complete.

Aniruddha then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the home life, I was constantly fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, calling me the sort of creature that belongs among the beasts.

Hearing the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself; for seven days I did not sleep, and consequently lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination. I—"
"By means of the eye, one perceives the ten directions; its essential purity is so transparently clear that it is like looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand.

The Tathāgata has certified me as having attained Arhatship. Guishan says: "The two types of observation and the five faculties lead to the realization of the Way," and so forth. This is because from time immemorial one has employed various false thoughts; since these thoughts are not true, the six sense-faculties have been subject to transmigration.

Now, knowing that the eternally abiding true mind is of one essence and non-dual, one attains realization of the Way through the observation of any single faculty. Guishan says: "Aniruddha [is translated here] as 'As One Wishes,' or..."
It is said that because this person gave a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha in a past life, he has enjoyed pleasures as he wished in both the heavens and the human realm;

thus he is named "Yìrúì" (如意, *Yathā-vadita*). Since then, he has lacked for nothing; thus he is named "Wúpín" (無貧, *Aparihīna*). He rebuked me, calling me a beast. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park preaching the Dharma to the assembly, Aniruddha fell asleep therein.

The Buddha spoke a verse to rebuke him, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are of the same kind as snails, shells, and clams. Thereupon, Aniruddha remained awake until dawn, and his faculty of sight was consequently lost. Because of this—

This refers to the cultivation of dhyāna, whereby one attains the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the four great elements and sees with half the head, perceiving the trichiliocosm as clearly as a fruit in the palm of one's hand.

As for the present mention of the "Vajra-samādhi," which perceives the subtle reality of the ten directions and thus differs from the former, it is because this sutra reveals and clarifies [the truth]. Therefore, in order to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, it speaks of the past by means of what was kept secret internally, whereas it speaks of the present smallness [of the body] to guide them. Tiaoxi said:

The *Āgamas* speak of "cultivating dhyāna," which is a general and abbreviated indication. What is now called the "Vajra-samādhi" specifically reveals its name. This does not mean that "vajra" is used solely as a metaphor for the Great Samādhi (for instance, the *Dilun* states that the Two Vehicles attain the "Vajra-like Samādhi").

It is like Ānanda entering the "Lightning-Fire Samādhi," which is merely a metaphor for the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the Hīnayāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The divine eye of Nārada consists of the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), purified over half the head;

the Buddha’s divine eye consists of the four great elements and derived matter, purified throughout the entire head. Tiantai Zhiyi says: "In the Tripiṭaka [Hīnayāna], the Buddha’s divine eye is entirely clear through the whole head."
Because their vision is unimpeded, we know that the designations "whole" and "half" merely refer to the contrast between partial and complete realization; they do not differ in terms of magnitude.

As the text below states, even those in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven are said to have "refined vision manifest before them," casting and molding things without obstruction. How much more so for an Arhat who has manifested true outflow-free wisdom—could it not be said that his true essence is transparently radiant?

Changshui says: [The Buddha] rebuked those who were fond of sleep, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like snails, shells, and clams; sleeping for a thousand years, you do not hear the name of the Buddha. Therefore, he rebuked them as "beasts."
O living beings!
The Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way. As I have realized it, to revolve the faculty of sight and return to its source is the foremost method.

By revolving one's deluded vision and cultivating that true source, when the perception of external objects has dissolved, the essential reality shines forth with clarity. When all things are unimpeded, how could this be limited merely to subtle forms beyond physical obstructions? [End of Supplement]

The Master left this instruction: "To turn back the deluded vision of the fundamental source and to follow the true origin of the storehouse nature—this is the essential point of perfect penetration. As for the accounts of the past related previously, although they contain words of refined truth, they are merely matters of the Deer Park."

Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: "I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and possessed no great aptitude. At first, when I encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I sought to remember and hold a single verse of the Tathāgata;

yet for a hundred days, I would forget what came before when trying to grasp what followed, and forget what came after when trying to grasp what preceded. The Buddha, pitying my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat and regulate my inhalation and exhalation.

As I then observed the breath, I scrutinized the subtle details of the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. My mind suddenly opened wide and attained great non-obstruction, until finally I reached the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)."
He attained arhatship and, sitting beneath the Buddha’s seat, was sealed as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Changshui said: "Cūḍapanthaka is translated as 'Snake Slave' because he was born by the roadside; alternatively, he is called 'Successor of the Path. Zizhong said:

"In the past, Panthaka was a great Dharma master who was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras and had five hundred disciples. He was stingy with the Buddha-dharma and refused to teach others. Consequently, in his subsequent birth, he was dull-witted. Shoujian said: "The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states..."

There are five kinds of stinginess (*mātsarya*): first, regarding one’s dwelling; second, regarding the property of others; third, regarding praise; fourth, regarding material wealth; and fifth, regarding the Dharma. There are seven retributions for stinginess regarding the Dharma: first, being blind from birth in every life; second, being foolish from birth in every life; third, being born into a lowly family; fourth, dying while in the womb;
fifth, committing offenses against the Buddhas; sixth, being shunned by virtuous people; and seventh, performing no evil deed that one does not commit.

Furthermore, being dull-witted and dark-minded in subsequent births is the residual retribution of stinginess regarding the Dharma. Because of the roots of goodness cultivated in past lives, he encountered a Buddha and left the household life. There were five hundred bhikṣus who were taught the same single verse; after ninety days had passed, he had forgotten everything preceding it.

Later, the Buddha, knowing his faculties, taught him the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Through this, he attained the Way. *Xunwen* says: "At that time, I contemplated the breath," and so forth; this appears to be the cultivation of the Six Sublime Gates of Contemplation (*liu miaomen guan*) within the practice of counting the breath.

What are called the six are: counting, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purification. The first three are concentration (*samādhi*), and the latter three are wisdom (*prajñā*). Through the support of concentration and the encouragement of wisdom, one is able to give rise to true illumination;

thus, he attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and became an Arhat. *Shiyao* says: Regarding the "one sentence for a hundred days," when the elder brother saw that his younger brother could not recite it, he said to his brother...

He said, "If you cannot recite it, why not return to being a layman? Having heard this as he was about to leave, he went to the gate of the Jetavana and wept. The Buddha asked him, and he fully related the preceding events. The Buddha said, "The attainment of Bodhi depends upon your elder brother.
The Buddha then took him by the hand and led him into a quiet chamber, instructing him: "Recite: 'Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let the body commit no transgression;

one who practices thus shall transcend the world. He recited it until it was mastered. The Buddha said, "You are now old; merely reciting a single verse is not remarkable. You must understand its meaning. That which is called the ten [paths of action] of body, speech, and mind—observe their arising."

He examined that which leads to extinction: through it one is born in heaven; through it one enters the abyss; by extending it, one attains the Way. Bodhi is spontaneous; because of this, his mind opened and he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "As I have realized it," he said, "the reversal of the breath to follow emptiness is the foremost.

Then Kātyāyanīputra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "In past kalpas, I committed verbal karma by mocking śramaṇas. Consequently, in life after life, birth after birth, I suffered from the ailment of ruminating like an ox.

The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-door of the single-flavor pure mind-ground. By this, I attained the cessation of the mind and entered samādhi. I observed that the cognition of taste is not the substance [of the mind]."

He was no longer a worldly being. By means of mindfulness, he transcended all worldly outflows (*āsrava*); internally, he was liberated from body and mind, and externally, he cast off the world. He distanced himself from the three realms of existence as a bird escapes its cage.

Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, his Dharma-eye became pure, and he attained Arhatship. The Tathāgata personally certified him, establishing him on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the mention of Nandika: Kuvamtriputra is translated here as "Ox-King" (*go-rāja*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he is translated as "Ruminator. The causal origin (*nidāna*) of his name differs from that in the present sutra.

The *Xunwen* (Record of Perfuming the Hearing) states that he suffered from the disease of rumination; having eaten for a long time, he would again bring it out and chew it. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) says that when an ox has finished eating, it habitually makes a hollow sound with its throat, and his ailment resembled this.

Guishan says that to realize flavor as being without flavor is called "one-flavor" (*ekarasa*). Although the sense-object of taste is mentioned, it is intended to reveal the faculty of the tongue; therefore, the text below immediately speaks of "observing the cognition of taste," for that which is able to know is the tongue itself. This is the Dharma-gate.

As for how flavor manifests as the tongue, one must understand that since it is said, "The Tathāgata has shown me the single flavor of purity," this refers to the Buddha explaining that the flavors of what is consumed are entirely devoid of the characteristics of flavor;

furthermore, it is necessary to rely on the flavor within phenomena to cause the essence to become a Dharma-gate. This is not the essence of the tongue, nor is it the substance of flavor. Internally casting off body and mind is liberation of the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*);
externally discarding the world is liberation of the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*).
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties]. According to what I have realized, returning the taste and revolving the cognition is the foremost.

The Supplement states: "Returning the taste refers to the object (*viṣaya*); revolving the cognition refers to the faculty (*indriya*). Since the tongue is a cognition that arises through contact, the faculty of the tongue cannot be manifested without reference to the object of taste;

therefore, the scriptural text speaks of them together. In describing perfect penetration now, I likewise mention both. Since it speaks of 'returning' and 'revolving,' this means that taste and the tongue revert to and merge within the fundamental nature, which is neither a substance nor a thing."

Pilingavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha to enter the Path. I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the many things in the world that are not to be relished.
While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gates; unaware of it, a poisonous thorn pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache.

I reflected that while there is consciousness that knows this deep pain, although the awareness perceives the pain, within the pure mind of awareness, there is no pain within the perception of pain. I further contemplated whether such a single body could possibly possess two simultaneous perceptions. Before I had long finished this reflection..."

His body and mind suddenly became empty. Within twenty-one days, all his outflows were exhausted, and he attained the state of an Arhat, receiving the personal seal of approval and realizing the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Guishan said: "Pilindavatsa means 'Residual Habit. Because he was formerly a Brahmin, he had many traces of arrogance as a residual habit; for example, when he cursed the river goddess, calling her a slave-girl, this was not his true heart, but merely a habit-energy (*vāsanā*).

Guyxiang said: "When he crossed the Ganges River, shouting, 'Hey, little slave! Stop your flow! the river goddess split the current into two branches for him. The goddess went to complain to the Buddha. The Buddha—

He was made to offer an apology, whereupon he joined his palms and said, "Little servant, do not be angry. The great assembly laughed at him; though he apologized, they continued to revile him. The Buddha said, "His former habits are such as this; truly, there is no pride in his heart."

The *Shiyao* states: "Although it is awakening that awakens to pain" means that although it is awakening, it is capable of contemplation (*guan*). "Although it contemplates, it is capable of awakening" means knowing the pain that is being awakened to. "Awakening to the pure mind" means that awakening is also contemplation.

"There is no awakening to pain where there is no pain" means there is neither the pain that is awakened to nor the awakening that awakens to pain. "Double awakening" refers to two types of contemplation; it is the wisdom of contemplation that is capable of observing.

The Supplement states: "However, this preceding passage describing his former practice of 'small' [attainment]—though it speaks of 'casting off the two types of awakening' such that the false is removed and the true remains—is merely the emptiness of true reality (*zhēn-kōng*).

If one refers to the subsequent description within the section on perfect penetration regarding 'pure awakening and casting off the body,' then it must be understood that the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha is such that the false is itself the true; hence it is called 'pure awakening. Because one realizes that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are themselves the Dharma, it is called 'casting off the body.
Thus, the expressions 'pure awakening' and 'casting off the body' are still attached to the description of the 'small' [vehicle]."
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of dhyāna. "As I have realized it," [Ānanda] said, "pure awakening that leaves no trace of the body—this is the foremost.

Changshui remarked: "The subject of observation and the object of observation, the capacity for pain and the sensation of pain—all are quiescently non-existent as even a single dharma; therefore, it is called 'pure awakening that leaves no trace of the body.'"

Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas of the past, my mind has attained unimpededness. I recall my own births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

From the very beginning in the mother’s womb, he knew emptiness and stillness. Thus it continued until the ten directions became empty; he also caused sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness.

Having received the Tathāgata’s awakening to the true emptiness of their own nature, their emptiness became perfectly luminous, and they attained arhatship. Suddenly entering the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, they shared the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and thus became those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Through liberation in the emptiness of nature, I am supreme.

The Supplement states: Regarding the fact that from this point onward, Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra all describe their original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), it is because the Tathāgata has already revealed the matters concerning their fundamental and manifested traces (*honji-kempon*).

Since these meanings have been made manifest and are known by the fourfold assembly, they now directly recount their original ground in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. Their minds have attained unimpededness, having long realized emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

It also causes sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness and manifest the faculties of a Bodhisattva, so that they may suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness and attain the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha. How could there be any doubt regarding their original ground? Now, as for the chapters of these three venerable ones:

Since both accounts describe the original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*), the description of the past as "small" therein is actually the manifestation of a small trace (*chui-ji*). Though small, it is great; it is the provisional [expedient] of the same essence (*tongti-quan*).

This is not the same as the previous accounts of Śāriputra and others, which describe the past as being directly and merely small. If one considers the "small" within the perfect penetration (*yuantong*) described in the chapters on Śāriputra and others, although it appears different from the smallness of the manifested trace, they are equally the provisional of the same essence.

Furthermore, one should know that Śāriputra and the others are not without the smallness of the manifested trace of their original ground; Subhūti and the others likewise equally possess this smallness of inclusive containment.

The text relies on two perspectives to mutually manifest its essential meaning. Furthermore, as the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "I have attained the samādhi of non-contention. Were it not for the emptiness of all phenomena, one could not be free from obstruction.

The Buddha asked about the penetration of perfect enlightenment. "As I have realized it," [Vimalakīrti] said, "all phenomena enter into non-existence; that which is not non-existence is itself exhausted, and one turns the dharmas back to the state of nothingness.
This is the foremost. Zizhong remarked: "First, one uses single emptiness to empty all phenomena; next, one uses double emptiness to empty the very mark of emptiness."

Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Since the distant past, my mind and vision have been pure; thus have I undergone births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”

Regarding the various transformations of the mundane and supramundane worlds, upon seeing them once, I attained unimpeded penetration. On the way, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa, who were traveling together and expounding upon causes and conditions;

through this, I awakened to the boundlessness of the mind. Following the Buddha’s household, I beheld the perfection of enlightened clarity and attained great fearlessness, becoming an Arhat. I am the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, born of the Dharma through transformation.

Zhaoxi said: "The four truths are the realm of both the mundane and the supramundane. Their various transformations are the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Because visual consciousness is clear and sharp, it is said that 'one seeing [it] penetrates [it],' and so forth.

This is spoken of in terms of understanding (*jñāna*). Changshui said: 'The mind’s vision is pure' means that visual consciousness gives rise to wisdom, seeing all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms without fail to penetrate their fundamental origins.
This is the attainment of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*); the discernment of all phenomena is called the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*). Gushan said: "The three contemplations and the six..."

"Awakening to the Way through consciousness," and so forth. This arises from the use of various false thoughts since beginningless time; because these thoughts are not true, the six consciousnesses flow and circulate.

Now, knowing that the eternally abiding true mind is of one essence and non-dual, one attains awakening to the Way by observing even a single consciousness. Kāśyapa and his brothers refer to the three Kāśyapas.

Other sutras all state that Śāriputra encountered Aśvajit on the road, heard that "all phenomena arise from conditions," and thereby attained awakening to the Way. That this [text] now says he encountered Kāśyapa and others is because for those of lesser capacity, he merely heard the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; whereas here, for those of [greater capacity],...

One of great capacity hears the Great Way. Since the questions posed differ, the persons from whom they are heard also vary. Tiāoxī says: "Observe that when Śāriputra was still a layman, this was prior to the twelve years [of the Buddha’s teaching]. Therefore, one cannot differentiate the Dharma based on the person.

Furthermore, the present text states that he 'heard the explanation of the meaning of causes and conditions,' which is identical to Aśvajit’s words on dependent origination. One should know that his realization of the boundless mind is precisely the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Thus, the *Āgamas* clarify that upon first hearing Aśvajit’s preaching, he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and subsequently, having gone to the Buddha’s presence, he thoroughly mastered the Buddha-dharma within seven days."

It is further stated that one attains Arhatship on the fifteenth day. Judging by this, the phrase "the clarity of insight becomes perfect" (*jì jué míng yuán*) is also spoken from the perspective of the initial stage. Even if one were to provide a grand interpretation, the aforementioned awakening of the mind must encompass all four fruits of the path;

only when one subsequently attains Arhatship does one truly receive the authentic name. Changshui [Zhixu] says: "The clarity of insight becoming perfect" refers to the true awakening—the wondrous clarity and perfection—being fully accomplished and manifested through the visual consciousness.
This arises because the Tathāgata revealed the sublime Dharma, enabling me to realize it. Therefore, it is said that the mouth follows the Dharma.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "As I have realized it," I said, "the mind and vision emit light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing.

This is the foremost. From the eye-consciousness, the light of wisdom is manifested; when the light of wisdom reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is the simultaneous perfection of the three knowledges and five eyes; therefore, it is called 'ultimate.'"

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have already served as a Dharma Prince to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct those bodhisattvas of superior faculties who are their disciples to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra; they derive their names from me. World-Honored One, I employ the hearing of the mind to discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings."

If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a sentient being who brings forth the realization of the practice of Samantabhadra within their mind, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of emanations, all arriving at that place.
Even if that person’s obstacles are so deep they cannot see me, I will secretly stroke their crown with my hand, embracing and comforting them to bring their accomplishment to fruition.

Xie Li said: "To traverse throughout the entire Dharma-realm is called 'Universal' (Pu). To stand in a position adjacent to the ultimate Sage is called 'Worthy' (Xian). This is not the 'Worthy' prior to the [ten] stages; rather, it refers to one who abides in the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi at the summit of all ranks, and is thus named 'Worthy.

Changshui said: 'The hearing of the mind' refers to the manifestation of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). From this ear-consciousness, one attains true perfect penetration and enters the principle of the Dharma-realm."

When birth-and-death and consciousness cease, quiescent extinction manifests before one. The object and wisdom merge in mutual obscurity, becoming a single entity without duality. Returning to the "hearing within the mind," it gives rise to function;

for those among sentient beings whose knowledge and vision are capable of being enlightened, it immediately manifests its body. Handian says: This means that without relying on the faculty of the ear, the auditory consciousness is produced directly from the faculty of the mind;

hence it is called "hearing within the mind. This is precisely one faculty giving rise to the six consciousnesses, which is termed "sovereign mastery of mutual function. However, this is no different from Guanyin, provided one does not discuss the initial cause in the same manner as other sages. If this is so, why...

Could it not be that this is not the appropriate capacity for those within this realm? That is to say, if the object is not the sense organ, there is no discernment; if consciousness is not the sense organ, it does not arise. If one does not rely upon the sense organ, how can consciousness be produced?

The sense organ is proximate while consciousness is remote; therefore, Mañjuśrī uses this to make a distinction. Furthermore, the meaning of "hearing with the mind" (*citta-śravaṇa*) is precisely the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*), which is entirely beyond the reach of those at the initial stage of the path;

thus, he excludes them. By taking "hearing with the mind" as identical to the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, subject and object are non-dual. Therefore, within the *dharmadhātu*, all sentient beings who manifest the practice of Samantabhadra within their own minds—[there is none... (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be incomplete in the source text.)

If one does not understand this, there is no non-arising of the response; both the hidden and manifest capacities (*mīng* and *xiǎn jī*) obtain their benefit. If, in the lower [case], it is a manifest capacity meeting a manifest response;

or even if, in the lower [case], it is a hidden capacity meeting a hidden response—furthermore, when a capacity summons a response and a response accords with a capacity, there are four permutations: namely, a hidden capacity and a hidden response; a hidden capacity and a manifest response; a manifest capacity and a manifest response;

and a manifest capacity and a hidden response. These four constitute the fundamental [set]. Each of these four contains four further permutations, which expand into many more as explained elsewhere. The Supplement states: "According to this, [the Buddha] rubbed his head with his hand."

Because it provides consolation and encourages progress, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I declared that my fundamental cause was the illumination of the mind’s hearing, which brings mastery in discernment; this is the foremost.
Gushan said: "The 'hearing of the mind' (*cittāśravaṇa*) is the internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*);

'discriminating with mastery' is the external function. Then Sundarananda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the household life, I followed the Buddha to enter the Way.

Although I observed the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated within *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). World-Honored One, you instructed me and Kūṭadanta to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. I began this earnest contemplation and practiced it for twenty-one days, until I beheld..."

The breath entering and exiting through the nostrils is like smoke. Internally, the body and mind become luminous and clear; the world becomes a vast, hollow void, universally pure and transparent like lapis lazuli. As the appearance of smoke gradually fades away, the nasal breath becomes white.

My mind was opened and my outflows were exhausted. All my inhalations and exhalations were transformed into radiance that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions. I attained arhatship, and the World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain bodhi.

Sundarī means "beautiful and beloved"; it is the name of his wife. Nanda means "joyful"; it is his own name. In the Ci'en [Commentary], both names are translated as "Glorious Joy" (Yanyi). To distinguish him from Nanda the Cowherd, his wife is specified.

Regarding the instruction for the Tathāgata’s own younger brother to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose: because he was prone to great distraction, this method of calming the mind through a physical object (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) served as a skillful means for entering the Path.

According to the *Dhyāna-pāramitā-śāstra*, focusing the mind on five locations is called "stopping by binding the object" (*ālambana-bandhana-sthiti*): first, the crown of the head; second, the hairline; third, the bridge of the nose; fourth, the space between the navel; and fifth, the earth-element wheel (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*).

The Tripitaka Master Jinchi of the Western Regions explained these five gates of dhyāna to Xie Li, saying: "Previously, when Śāriputra’s disciple Cūḍapanthaka contemplated the inhalation and exhalation of breath, he did so by means of the sense organ of the nose (*ghrāṇendriya*).

Now, however, it concerns the contemplation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); thus, there is a distinct difference between the two. Changshui said: "In the previous practice of counting the breaths, one spoke in terms of the sense organ. Now, it concerns the contemplation of consciousness. One uses the white [light] at the tip of the nose as an object to stabilize the mind so that it does not scatter.

First, one contemplates the mark of whiteness. After three weeks have passed, one sees the vital breath (*prāṇa*) appearing like smoke. When this contemplation is perfected, it manifests internally within the body and mind. If the body..."

If the vessel suddenly becomes empty and pure, with its interior and exterior reflecting each other with transparency like lapis lazuli, this arises from contemplating the cessation of the signs of arising and ceasing; the mind of contemplation becomes fused and luminous, on the verge of giving rise to the wisdom of emptiness.

He then penetrates the boundaries of his own body; yet, as he still relies on skillful means, he has not yet forgotten objective conditions. Thus, he sees the smoke transform into a white sign (*śukla-nimitta*).

Once the wisdom of non-arising and emptiness (*anutpāda-śūnyatā-prajñā*) appears before him, the various breaths no longer arise, being entirely pure wisdom. The light of this wisdom illuminates all things as they truly are: the worlds and sentient beings are nothing other than perfectly wondrous. Through this, his outflows are exhausted, and he shall attain Bodhi.

Zhaoxi said: "By observing the nose-consciousness, it appears as if one is developing the sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*) in meditation. Xunwen said: "The sixteen stages of special excellence differ from the six gates of wondrous dharma (*ṣaṇ-mukha-praṇidhāna*) only in their horizontal and vertical, shallow and deep variations.

This meditation begins with knowing the inhalation and exhalation of the breath and extends to the observation of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*). It encompasses the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and enables one to perceive the realized realms of the three worlds and nine stages;

hence it is said that 'one thoroughly penetrates the world,' and so forth. Furthermore, by means of contemplative illumination within each stage, one breaks through the four inversions and gives rise to true non-arising."

Because the outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, it is said that "the mind opens and the outflows are ended," and so forth. This may also be considered the characteristic of universal clarity (*sāmānyābhijñā*), which is fully present in the Chan gate. "Universal clarity" refers to the simultaneous contemplation of three things. When contemplating the breath, one simultaneously illuminates both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);

when contemplating form and mind, it is likewise. Therefore, it is called "universal clarity. Furthermore, by practicing this dhyāna, one can give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the three insights (*trividyā*).

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "When the World-Honored One gave us our predictions... This previously recounted his experiences during his time as a novice; now, wishing to recount his realization of universal penetration (*yuan-tong*), he points to the prediction in the *Lotus Sūtra*, indicating that he has already awakened to universal penetration.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I replied: "By means of the extinction of the breath, after a long time illumination was revealed; through this perfect illumination, outflows were extinguished. This is the foremost.

Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "For kalpas as vast as the ocean, my eloquence has been unimpeded. I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness and have deeply penetrated the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am able to provide subtle and wondrous explanations among the assembly, attaining fearlessness. World-Honored One..."

Knowing that I possess great eloquence, he used the wheel of sound to instruct me to proclaim it. In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma; through this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship.
The World-Honored One has certified my unsurpassed preaching of the Dharma.

Zhaoxi says: "Expounding" refers below to the teachings of the Hīnayāna; "thus" indicates below the meaning of the Mahāyāna. Since it begins with the Āgamas and ends with the Prajñāpāramitā, he says "up to and including. Changshui says: "Lion’s Roar" means fearless preaching.

Internally, one subdues and severs views and attachments through meditative concentration and wisdom; externally, one subdues and restrains Māras and non-Buddhists by manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma.

Thus, the city of Nirvāṇa is preserved and the Three Jewels remain uninterrupted. Xunwen says: "By means of the wheel of sound" refers to the wheel of body manifesting supernatural powers, the wheel of speech preaching the Dharma, and the wheel of mind discerning.

"Ji. This is the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*). That which assists the turning of the Buddha-wheel is the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*). The Wheel of Speech is that which turns; the Dharma-wheel is that which is turned.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of the sound of the Dharma, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows (*āsrava*); this is the foremost."

The Supplement states: "Pūrṇa’s consciousness of the tongue; therefore, it is spoken of in terms of the Dharma-sound. The Dharma-sound of the Middle Way subdues the demons and enemies of ignorance. Since preaching the Dharma can restrain external influences, it is spoken of in terms of demons and enemies."

Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity."

I personally witnessed the Tathāgata subduing all Māras, restraining all non-Buddhists, and liberating the world from the outflows of greed and desire. Having received the Buddha’s teachings and precepts, I have thus purified even the three thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle natures of both positive and prohibitive actions.
With body and mind in tranquil extinction, I have become an Arhat. Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, I am a pillar of leadership;
the Buddha himself has personally sealed my heart regarding my observance of the precepts and cultivation of the person, and the assembly has acclaimed me as supreme.

Gushan says: Upāli is here translated as "Foremost" (*śreṣṭha*), because he upheld the Vinaya and served as the guiding framework for the assembly. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "Framework" (*gangji*) is synonymous with "comprehensive governance.

Alternatively, it is translated as "Attendant" (*upasthāyaka*), because when the Buddha was a prince, he served as his close attendant. Zizhong says: This refers to his following the Buddha into homelessness. The Vinaya states that among all the Śākyas who were ordained, Upāli was ordained first;
this is slightly different [from the former account], as it implies that although he initially left the city, he only later entered the Path. Regarding the two hundred and fifty precepts, each...

There are four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), which together constitute one thousand. When these are applied across the three periods of time, they become three thousand. Allocating these three thousand modes of deportment to the seven branches of body and speech results in twenty-one thousand.

Furthermore, when categorized according to the antidotes for the three poisons and the equal portion (*sāmya*), they total eighty-four thousand; this present figure cites the full number. Guishan said: "Intrinsic offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are not established by the Buddha's decree;

maintaining them is inherently virtuous, while violating them is inherently sinful, such as killing, stealing, and so forth. Prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are established by the Buddha’s prohibition; violating them incurs sin, such as tilling the soil."

[The text continues with: "The *Shoujian* (Hand Mirror) says: For instance, within a single Vinaya collection, although there are many precepts for the two groups—the monks and the nuns—established in relation to various objects, they do not depart from the two categories of *prakṛti-avadya* (inherent offenses) and *pratikṣepaṇīya-avadya* (prohibited offenses).

Generally, those established in relation to sentient beings are called *prakṛti*; those established in relation to non-sentient things are called *pratikṣepaṇīya*. All *prakṛti* offenses are subsumed under the single character 'inherent' (*xing*), and all *pratikṣepaṇīya* offenses are subsumed under the single character 'prohibited' (*zhe*).

Regarding 'the inherent being equal by nature': before the Buddha had established the precepts, the Wheel-Turning King transformed people through the ten wholesome precepts. When the Buddha appeared in the world, there were bhikṣus who committed offenses, and these were [deemed] grave."

Because of this, Nanshan says: "Inherent evil (prakṛti-sāvadya) extends to both the transformative (vinaya) and the prohibitive (prajñapti) precepts. Furthermore, it is only with the appearance of a Buddha in the world that the remaining precepts (avaśeṣa-śīla) exist, much like cultivated land that has been broken up for cultivation.

When non-Buddhists (tīrthika) criticized [the Buddha's followers], saying, "They lack a heart of compassion, as they take the lives of others," the Buddha accordingly established prohibitions to ward off such slander.

Thus Nanshan says: "Prohibitive precepts arise due to specific transgressions. One should know that inherent and prohibitive precepts refer to the offenses committed, while karma refers to the retribution attracted. Moreover, by violating an inherent precept, one incurs two types of grave offenses: first, the path of action (karmapatha); second, the violation of the established rule. Violating a prohibitive offense involves only the breach of the rule.

Therefore, the Nanshan [Vinaya] cites a sutra as saying: "The transgression of one who receives the precepts is heavy; the transgression of one who does not receive them is light. This is precisely what that means.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), I replied: "By fixing upon the body, the body attained mastery; by successively fixing upon the mind, the mind attained penetration. Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely unimpeded and functional. This is the foremost."

Gushan says: "Regarding 'successively grasping the mind,' because the precepts are pure, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are brought forth. Concentration sustains the mind and thereby stops its distraction; wisdom sustains the mind and thereby illuminates its obscurity.

Thus it is said that the mind attains thorough penetration. Tiaoxi says: "If we examine the subsequent text, it states: 'First, one maintains the four parājikas and eight śaikṣa-dharmas of the Śrāvaka, grasping the body so that it does not move;

later, one practices the pure discipline of the Bodhisattva, grasping the mind so that it does not arise. This clearly shows that 'grasping the mind' is not necessarily restricted to concentration and wisdom. Nevertheless, the assignment of body and mind to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is based on their coarse [manifestations]."

If we briefly divide them into two categories: it is not that Bodhisattvas do not examine their physical conduct, nor do Śrāvakas fail to guard the mental ground. For instance, in the various sections of the Vinaya (*piṇḍavastu*), the establishment of prohibitions against preliminary actions (*pūrvaprayoga*)—are these not matters of the mental ground?

What is being described here refers precisely to the "small" [vehicle], which involves grasping at both body and mind. From the coarse to the subtle, this is intended to prevent the subtleties of bodily consciousness. Once bodily consciousness has ceased, true wisdom manifests before one;

this is what is meant by "purity of precepts and the presence of wisdom," whereby one attains the foremost path. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "This opening chapter describes the text on perfect penetration.

According to the subsequent text, one first observes the four parājikas of the Śrāvakas and later practices the pure discipline of a Bodhisattva so that no thoughts arise. The present mention of "successively grasping the mind" points directly to Mahāyāna precepts.

The *Zhìxīndì* (Stopping the Mind Ground) is taken as the model for perfect penetration (*yuántōng*). Taking this very chapter as the standard, one can verify that the preceding sections describe the "Small" [Vehicle] while the subsequent sections describe the "Great" [Vehicle], and thus it may be trusted.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first went on the road to beg for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—as they were proclaiming the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions.

Instantly, my mind was awakened and I attained great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe; as it touched my body, my beard and hair fell away of their own accord. As I traveled through the ten directions, I attained unimpeded mastery.

My supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) became manifest, and I was acclaimed as supreme, attaining the state of an Arhat. Not only does the World-Honored One praise me, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also extol me."
"My supernatural powers are perfect, clear, pure, sovereign, and fearless.
Gu Shan (孤山) says: *Uruvilvā* means "papaya" (*mōguā*); it is so called because the protuberance on his chest resembles a papaya.

*Gayā* is the name of a mountain; it is also called a "city" because the city is near this mountain. *Nadī* is the name of a river. [He had] one elder brother and two younger brothers; thus Śāriputra said, "I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers," referring to these very individuals. [The character] *tiáo* (苕).

Xiyun said: "The spirit is named 'Heavenly Mind' (Tiānxīn), and its penetration is named 'Wisdom-Nature' (Huìxìng). This mind-nature is precisely the manifestation of the conscious intellect (*manovijñāna*). In the Mahayana, it manifests as the *tathāgatagarbha*; in the Hinayana, it manifests as the fundamental dhyāna. Xunwen said:

"The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are collectively termed the 'Twelve Gates of Dhyāna. However, most of its supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are manifested based upon the fourth dhyāna. Gushan said:

"Among the six supernatural powers, only the power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is an internal realization; the other five supernatural powers all belong to external applications. Question: When Śāriputra and Cāṣa both encountered [the Buddha],...

Kāśyapa heard the same causal conditions [as Śāriputra]. Why, then, did Śāriputra realize the truth through visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), while Cūḍapanthaka attained the Way through mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

Answer: Because the innate capacities (*indriya*) of people were planted differently in past lives, the benefits they derive from hearing the Dharma vary accordingly. It is like various species of medicinal herbs; though moistened by the same rain, each flourishes according to its own nature. The *Bùyì* (Supplementary Notes) states:

From the beginning up to "attaining arhatship," the text narrates his former realization; from "Is it only the World-Honored One... onwards, it narrates his perfect penetration (*yuantong*). *Kāṣāya* is translated here as "improper color" (*fēngzhèngsè*); it does not refer to the five primary colors.
This is the correct form; the original Sanskrit manuscript simply read "xuán" (to revolve). Later generations each added the character "yī" (clothing).

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "I attained it by revolving the tranquil mind-light until it was manifested, like clearing a turbid stream until it becomes permanently pure and crystalline. This is the foremost method.
Turning back from ignorance to return to the tranquil nature: this is the Dharma-gate of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).

Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I constantly recall that in the distant past, during many kalpas, my nature was largely characterized by lust.
At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), who taught that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire.”

Zizhong said: "Avalokiteśvara [here] is called Huatou (Fire-Head). He attained the Way by contemplating the nature of fire; thus he was named accordingly. Gushan said: "The four contemplations and the seven elements for awakening to the Way are divided into seven parts, and so forth.

This arises from the use of various deluded appearances since beginningless time. Because these perceptions are not true, the seven elements circulate. Now, knowing that the eternally abiding true mind is of one essence and non-dual, one attains awakening to the Way by contemplating any single dharma.
Changshui said: "Those in whom lust is predominant see the causes of ghosts and hells. The cause is being inflamed by the fire of desire; the fruit..."

Burning with the fires of karma, cause and effect correspond; both are termed "masses of fire. Tiaoxi said: "For those in whom lust is rampant, both present actions and future retributions will summon masses of fire."

He instructed me to observe thoroughly the hundred bones, the four limbs, and all sensations of cold and warmth. As spiritual light coalesced within, he transformed my many lustful thoughts into the fire of wisdom. Tiāoxī says:

"Instructing me to observe below, I saw that the four elements are all objects of the sense-field of touch. The hundred bones and four limbs are the element of earth; the various sensations of cold and warmth are water, fire, and wind.

Once samādhi was established, it is said that 'spiritual light coalesces within. Because those with excessive desire have the fire-element predominating, his lust-fire was thus transformed into the fire of wisdom. (Supplement)

It is said: "From beginning to end, he universally contemplates the four great elements and knows that the fire element is predominant; for this reason, he contemplates them separately. First he attains a small fruit, and later he gives rise to the Great Mind.
Is it not the case that he is the Universal Manifestation of Form (Prabhūtaratna), with the Vajradhara spirit assisting the Buddha to propagate the transformation?"
All these Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship and made a great vow:
