hence it is called 'wondrous wondrous. 'The essence of the mind leaves behind hearing' refers to the single faculty detaching from its adhesive [objects]. 'Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be separated' refers to the five faculties being perfectly uprooted."

Thus it is said. Gu-shan (Gushan Zhiyuan) states: "The head symbolizes the *dharmakāya*, transcending the two extremes. The arms symbolize liberation, uprooting all sufferings. The eyes symbolize *prajñā*, illuminating and comprehending the myriad objects.

Whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, they form the head. Whether manifesting as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), they form the arms and eyes. Because its countenance is compassionate, it gathers the goodness of the Middle Way;

because its countenance is majestic, it subdues the evils of the two extremes—the *dharmakāya* is thus made clear. When there is concentration, the hands stop distraction, and liberation is attained. When there is wisdom, the eyes observe the obscured, and *prajñā* is revealed. (3)

When virtue is perfectly integrated, there is no internal obstruction; thus, one benefits sentient beings externally and attains mastery. Since a human head is singular, the numbers increase from this unitary basis.
Since arms are two, they are distinguished by their pairing. Human eyes are two, while those of devas may be three; thus, both the even and the odd are employed for clarification. Zhenji says:
*śakrāloka-vajra* is the *vajra*, that is, the diamond-thunderbolt. Xielin says: *mudrā* is also called "seal" (*yin*).

Second, because I have been liberated from the six sense objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am able to manifest every single form and recite every single mantra with supreme skill.

These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; therefore, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, I am known as the One Who Bestows Fearlessness.

Third, because I have cultivated this fundamentally wondrous, perfectly penetrating, and pure root, in all the worlds where I travel, I cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures so that they may seek my compassion.

Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, one is able to offer various precious treasures as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.

If they seek a wife, they obtain a wife; if they seek a son, they obtain a son; if they seek samādhi, they obtain samādhi; if they seek long life, they obtain long life; and so on, even unto seeking great nirvāṇa, they obtain great nirvāṇa.

Zhaoxi said: "These four inconceivabilities consist of two that pertain to the response [of the Buddha] and two that correspond to the capacity of the sentient beings. Within the response, both benefits of form and voice are fully manifested. Although the initial passage mentions the 'recitation of mantras,' [it refers to the benefit of voice]."

The first section correctly demonstrates the benefit of form; this is the functional activity of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Although the subsequent passage also manifests form, it correctly demonstrates the benefit of sound;

this is the universal renown of one's name. Within the capacity of the sentient beings, both cause and fruit are clearly elucidated: the light represents the cultivation of causes, wherein among the six perfections, giving is briefly cited to enable the seeking of merit.

The latter clarifies the realization of the fruit, wherein all mundane and supramundane vows are fulfilled to bring about the attainment of happiness. These four sections of the sutra text thus clarify the manifestation of the body and the preaching of the Dharma, following the sequence of extracting suffering and bestowing happiness.

[The preceding] thirty-two marks correspond to the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Although they also clarify manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma, the "extracting from suffering and bestowing joy" was presented as a general characteristic.

Now, the specific manifestations according to the capacities of beings are explained in detail, such that there is nothing that does not appear; therefore, all four are called "inconceivable. From the first [mark] up to the eighty-four thousand [pores], and even including the bestowing of joy, it is likewise this many.

Could anything other than the inconceivable be capable of such a thing? Since the third [mark] says, "Seek my compassion," this is precisely the extraction from suffering. [This includes] the relinquishing of one's body and precious treasures.

This is to clarify that one who seeks to extricate others from suffering employs [the Buddha] for the purpose of prayerful invocation. However, the reason the text on "Extricating from Suffering" is so extremely brief is because it manifests through the teaching of the Dharma in this very body.

The manifestation of eighty-four thousand heads and arms as various distinct forms is for the sake of extricating [beings] from suffering. Since the manifestation of the body and the teaching of the Dharma can save in such a manner, the suffering to be saved is likewise of such a nature;
therefore, the text may be abbreviated.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "I," [Ānanda] said, "attained the Samādhi of Universal Illumination through the gateway of the ear. By bringing the conditioned mind under control, I entered the state of the 'flowing-in' and thereby attained Samāpatti. This is how I achieved Bodhi; it is the foremost method."

The Supplement states: "The ear-consciousness first takes sound as its object; hence it is called 'taking the mind as its object. It does not follow after external objects; hence it is called 'sovereign. By turning the hearing inward to contemplate the nature, it is called 'entering the stream.'"

The Samādhi of Perfect Illumination is identical to the Samādhi of a Single Practice. This means that when one first takes the true reality as the object, the very creation of an objective realm is itself the Middle Way, wherein nothing is not true. One binds the conditions to the Dharma-realm; in a single thought-moment, one is the Dharma-realm.

Therefore, it is said that the mind conditioned by objects attains mastery. This is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the primary tenet of this sutra. It is the true, perfect penetration praised by Mañjuśrī, for which all Buddhas intermingle their light rays to celebrate this teaching together.

World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. In the midst of the great assembly, he conferred upon me the prophecy of the name Avalokiteśvara.
Because I contemplate and listen to the perfect luminosity of the ten directions, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Tiaoxi says: According to the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*, it is stated that this Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood long ago, with the name *Saddharmaprabhāsa*.
Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that in the past, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed a prediction upon Prince Animiṣa, naming him Avalokiteśvara. Xunwen says:

It is said that in the past, beyond incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha-world named Saṃtāraṇa and a kalpa named Sukhadhara. There was a wheel-turning king named Araṇemin, and a great minister named...

He was named Ratnasāgara. He was of the Brahmin caste and fathered a son who possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Upon leaving the household life, he attained Buddhahood and was named Ratnagarbha.

The wheel-turning monarch had a thousand sons, the eldest of whom was named Animiṣa. He invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha and offered various provisions for three full months. The prince made this vow: "May all my roots of goodness be dedicated entirely toward the path of the Buddha.
May it be that when I practice the bodhisattva path, there may be sentient beings who undergo various sufferings, afflictions, and fears, who fall away from the True Dharma, and who [fall into]..."

In places of great darkness, filled with sorrow, isolation, and destitution, where there is no rescue or relief—if any sentient beings can mindfully call upon me and recite my name, and yet they are not freed from suffering within the range of what I hear with my divine ear and see with my divine eye, may I never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagarbha immediately bestowed a prediction upon him: "Observe all sentient beings among devas, humans, and those in the three evil realms;

give rise to a heart of great compassion because you wish to sever all sufferings and cause them to abide in peace and happiness. From now on, your name shall be Avalokiteśvara," and so forth, up to "Immeasurable."

After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, during the latter part of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, at the first watch of the night, the True Dharma will be completely extinguished.

During the latter watch of the night, that land will change its name to the World Consisting of All Precious Jewels; all its various adornments will be such that even the world Sukhāvatī cannot equal them.

At the final watch of the night, you shall attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, receiving the title Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth, named Meru King of Mountains of Virtues Emitting All Light Universally. Thus, both the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* and the present sutra conceal the root and display the branches.

The name of his trace has now attained perfect penetration; he is the very incarnation of the Prince [Sudhana]. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Now, this is precisely the explanation of the name 'Guanyin' (Avalokiteśvara). Within the act of hearing, one employs contemplation (*guan*) to observe the nature of hearing;

only then does it become perfectly luminous. The name is established based on this virtue; therefore, it is not called 'hearing' (*wen*) but 'contemplation' (*guan*). Thus, by saying 'contemplation,' its aspect of 'hearing' is already included.

Because I take contemplation as my hearing, I am able to achieve perfect luminosity. What was said previously regarding 'the revolving back of contemplation and hearing' also carries this same meaning."

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light, which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the various Bodhisattvas who are Dharma-Princes.

Those Tathāgatas likewise simultaneously emitted precious light from their five limbs; from those motes of dust in the ten directions, it came to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head, and also to moisten the crowns of the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats within the assembly.

The trees, forests, ponds, and marshes all proclaimed the sounds of the Dharma. The intermingling lights entwined with one another like a net of precious threads. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, and all universally obtained the golden... [light].

Regarding the *vajrasamādhi*, Gushan says: "The mutual illumination of precious lights symbolizes the reciprocal fusion of the principles of self and other; the sounding of voices from the forest trees manifests the non-duality of the nature of the environment and its inhabitants.

This seals what was previously realized, fully accords with the Buddha-mind, and—beginning from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward—is able to shatter stubborn delusions; all such states are termed *vajrasamādhi*. This should be understood as a general designation for the perfect concentration (*pariniṣpanna-samādhi*), which is also called 'Vajra'. It is also the foremost...
This is another name for the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. As stated in the section on the "Grades" (*bhūmi*) below: "These various stages all employ the diamond-like observation," and so forth.

Guishan specifically pointed out that this refers to those from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) upward who are able to shatter stubborn delusions; this is said by way of the majority case. Changshui said: "The perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing subsumes all five faculties.

It accords with the Buddhas, and their accounts of its realization are identical. As for the 'great bodhisattvas and arhats,' these are the twenty-five sages who spoke of perfect penetration. The seals of approval they gave were all of the nature of perfect penetration. Therefore, he [the Buddha] released...

The precious light flows and灌 (pours) over his crown. As for the groves, trees, ponds, and marshes that proclaim the sound of the Dharma—since they are called "Perfect Sound" (Sambhinnabhadra)—self and other sing it together. His wisdom pervades the myriad things; what dharma would he not proclaim?

"The intersecting lights are like a net" refers to the complete unfolding of the Great Teaching (*mahāśāsana*). The *Shiyao* (Essentials of Explanation) states: "First, the lights of all Buddhas intersect, and the forest trees expound the Dharma.

This means that every phenomenon (*dharma*) and every particle of dust (*rajas*) is none other than the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-dhātu*); therefore, wherever the light of wisdom reaches, it does not fail to expound the wondrous. "The five bodies emit light" signifies the simultaneous liberation of the remaining five sense organs.

"The Great Teaching is completely unfolded as a net" means that the net of the Great Teaching is fully spread out to filter the fish of the ten realms, leading them from the river of birth and death to the shore of Bodhi. Hearing this with the ears and touching this wisdom-light with the crown of the head—this is the third [aspect] of Avalokiteśvara.

They are attained simultaneously and together; thus, these twenty-four sages assemble within the single gate of Avalokiteśvara, and all may be designated as attaining the Vajrasamādhi. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

The fact that both [the Buddha and Mañjuśrī] specifically mention the emission of light from their five limbs serves as proof that the eighteen realms previously discussed are all perfectly interfused. Mañjuśrī’s preaching of the Dharma at the forest pond symbolizes the passage below concerning how all lands are transformations of the single mind.

Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—intermingled and variegated in blue, yellow, red, and white. The voids of the ten directions took on the color of the seven treasures.

The great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world simultaneously vanished from view; only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions were seen merged into a single realm. Chanting and hymns of praise resounded spontaneously.

Zhaoxi says: "This signifies that the Great Assembly, within the Heaven of the Ultimate Principle (paramārtha-dhātu), adorns the merit of the fruition with the flowers of the forty stages of true cause.

Furthermore, it signifies that when one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the realm of emptiness shatters, leaving only the land of Sole Silence and Light (ekānta-prabhāsvara). This matter is rare and marvelous; therefore, it is celebrated in song. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "The hundred precious flowers raining from heaven signify that the thousand dharmas of the hundred realms are all equal in their single principle.

The four colors represent the four stages. Their intermingling and blending signify that a single stage is fully endowed with the merits of all stages. That empty space becomes the color of the seven treasures signifies..."

The principle of the seven factors of enlightenment pervades all phenomena; yet in this Sahā world, it does not manifest as a single Buddha-land. It may be said that Wuxing’s expression "the empty realm shatters" implies that only the Single Radiance of Quiescence remains.

Alternatively, it may be said that having already shattered the distinctions of the eighteen realms above, the single principle of perfect penetration manifests before one. Changshui says: "The Dharma-body is primordially pure; it is something that devas and dragons overlook and disparage."

Now, it will manifest as being like space. Because the myriad practices are integrated and adorned with jewels, flowers are interspersed therein. As the sense organs and their objects dissolve and return [to their source], the Dharma-realm is perfected;

mountains and rivers no longer appear, merging into a single realm. The *Shiyao* states: "The flowers of a hundred jewels" refers to the causal flowers of the myriad practices adorning the primordially existing Dharmakāya, thereby manifesting the wondrous fruit. Thus, mountains and rivers do not appear.

The nine realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are entirely empty in a single thought-moment and merge into one realm; this is the perfect manifestation of the Buddha-realm. Regarding the "valley resonance" (guxiang), it is said that those who chant *bān bèi* (Sanskrit: *bhāṇaka*) should use the full term *bān nì* (*bhāṇaka*).

Some call it *vāśī*; this is translated as "praise. It refers to praising and chanting the Three Jewels with the voice of Brahmā. The *Shoujian* states: The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* says, "I permit you all to perform *bhāṣya*.

*Bhāṣya* refers to words of discourse. Although the Buddha spoke, it was not yet known what kind of Dharma he was teaching. The bhikṣus questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to speak according to their own inclination, from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*.

This current [Chinese] *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice) is based on the *Xuanyan ji* (Record of Manifestation and Verification). During the Wei dynasty, Prince Chen resided at Mount Yushan; one night, he heard...

The resonance of the sounds at the gate of the rocky grotto remains etched in my memory. Because of the *gāthās* within the scriptures, he instructed the monks to perform *fanbai* (Brahmanic chanting). Prince Caisi (Cao Zijing), the fourth son of Emperor Wu of Wei, composed literary works by the age of ten;

his pen would flow with such ease that he never once had to revise his writing. Whenever he read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them in deep admiration, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way.

While traveling at Mount Youyu, he suddenly heard the sound of Brahma-voices from the air, pure, elegant, and plaintive. He listened alone for a long time until his attendants all heard it as well. He then imitated those sounds and immediately transcribed them into *brahmaghoṣa* chants.

He composed texts and established melodic patterns to praise the Triple Gem, establishing a model for future generations. This was like the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, who sat beneath a tree and sang praises aloud.
Upon hearing this, the assembly of immortals realized the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Furthermore, all the devas heard it and were filled with joy.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and Arhats, each of whom has described the skillful means by which they first attained the Way.
They have all declared that they practiced the cultivation of true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*)."
Changshui said: "If one specializes exclusively in the three categories or the seven elements, each according to their respective faculties, these are all merely provisional means (*upāya*).

If, within this world, one were to establish a teaching that is universally applicable for the present and future, such that those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities may all attain awakening and entry, and which serves as a permanent provisional means for sentient beings to achieve the Way—among the twenty-five [methods], which gate would be the most excellent?

Because the initial provisional means for attaining the wondrous *samādhi* of Bodhi by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions was previously requested, I shall now cause you to select a universal Dharma-gate so that you may achieve success."

The Supplement states: "Regarding the 'expedient means for attaining enlightenment,' expedient means (*upāya*) is a term for skillful mastery. Furthermore, concerning the twenty-five who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*):

according to their accounts of past realization, there are those who are no-more-learners of the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle and those who are no-more-learners of the bodhisattva stages. However, according to their accounts of their perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), since they have already revealed and manifested [the truth], they are all indeed no-more-learners of the bodhisattvas."
In their cultivation, there is truly no distinction of superior or inferior, nor of priority or sequence.
Now I wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening; among these twenty-five practices, which one corresponds to his faculties?

The Supplement states: "In this regard, there is truly no superiority or inferiority; it is because they have realized the same principle as all the sages that their paths are equal. As for 'who corresponds to which faculty,' this is a distinct teaching manifested according to the specific dispositions of beings within their respective lands."

One must understand that within the framework of the eighteen *dhātus*, while the faculties (*indriya*) are mutually pervasive, they are also individually distinct. In terms of entering the Path, all are pervasive; in terms of conforming to their respective lands (*bhūmi*), all are distinct.

In the following text, the ear-faculty is treated as the specific faculty for the spiritual capacity of this land; this is merely the structural outline of the principle of distinction. One must know that the Buddha’s intention was to reveal that each and every faculty is distinct—only then does one exhaust the full logic of the matter.

For instance, in the Land of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavatī*), the object-field of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*) would necessarily serve as the distinct gateway to perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-mukha*). Had Mañjuśrī been there, then the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara would certainly have been excluded. Now, looking up to discern the Buddha’s intention, he first lists the twenty-five sages.

It further states that one enters the "Gate of Perfect Penetration" (*yuantongmen*). The Buddha’s seal of approval confirms that there is truly no superiority or inferiority among them, revealing that all eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) are gates of perfect penetration; this is the general meaning.

Furthermore, by instructing [Śāriputra] to select the faculty most suited to his own capacity for easy attainment—specifically choosing the ear-faculty—it reveals that each of the eighteen faculties is distinct according to its respective realm; this accords with the principle of the lands (*dhātu*).

Thus, we know that the selection of the ear-faculty as the "Perfect Penetration" is intended to manifest the principle that each of the eighteen realms and faculties is distinct according to its corresponding land, not merely to highlight the excellence of Avalokiteśvara alone. One must understand that where there is universal penetration, there is always distinction; where there is distinction...
This is eternally universal.

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for those sentient beings in this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle to seek the unsurpassed path, by what gateway of skillful means can they most easily achieve success?

Zhaoxi said: "The preceding section traced the realization of nature to its ultimate unity with perfect penetration. Now, for the sake of accommodating individual faculties, we shall distinguish the various skillful means. Nature is like a magnificent mansion; the faculties are like the doors through which one enters.

Only by finding the door can one receive its bounty. Yet worldly people take intellectual understanding to be realization. I ask you to consider: as for the initial skillful means for entering the Path, how does it compare to those of the twenty-five sages?"

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:

Below this, in order to distinguish the perfect penetration (*yuantong*), the text first clarifies the nature of awakening, next discriminates delusion and falsehood, and finally demonstrates the return to the source. Within the demonstration of returning to the source, the faculty of hearing is selected as the easiest path;
since Mañjuśrī has already attained realization alongside Avalokiteśvara, his offering of this compassionate instruction from the Buddha has a long-standing precedent.
The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this perfect limpidity of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. The nature of true awakening is like the great ocean:

its limpid stillness and perfect fusion both serve as metaphors for being eternally illumined while remaining in quiescence. Furthermore, by restating the awakening illustrated by "perfect limpidity," it shows that this awakening is fundamentally illumined while eternally quiescent;

hence it is called "fundamentally subtle and wondrous. This is similar to the previous passage’s "the nature of awakening is subtly luminous" and "original awakening is luminously subtle"; they differ only in the intermingling of the dharma (the reality) and the metaphor. Limpid and perfect.

Both characters serve as metaphors; one must understand that "stillness" (澄) takes up the meaning of constancy, while "roundness" (圓) takes up the meaning of movement. As for the nature of water, it conforms to the size of its vessel and follows the current or encounters obstacles without anything being impossible.

The meaning of perfect interfusion and non-restriction is such that, in relation to illumination, there is the sense of responding to phenomena. "Perfectly clear" (*yuánchéng*) is the metaphor; "awakened to the primordial wondrousness" (*juéyuánmiàofǎ*) is the reality. It is awakened and yet primordially wondrous; it illuminates and yet remains quiescent.

The two characters "nature of awakening" (*juéxìng*) in the preceding phrase also clarify quiescence and illumination by way of these two dharmas; however, they are placed out of order here because they are intended to correspond with the metaphor to form a complete syntactical unit.

Originally, luminous clarity gave rise to the object; once the object was established, the nature of the illuminating subject vanished. Through delusion and confusion, empty space came into being; based upon this space, worlds were established. As thought became clarified, the physical lands were formed; as perception arose, sentient beings appeared.

Zhendi says: "The phrase 'perfect brightness gives rise to the perceived' means that upon that original nature of brightness, false illumination and function arise, thereby forming the characteristics of the perceived. Xunwen says: "Illumination" refers to the characteristic of the perceiver; "the perceived" refers to the characteristic of the objective realm. When there are characteristics, they manifest before the mind;

when there are no characteristics, they remain hidden. Therefore, the nature of illumination perishes. Tiaoxi says: The meaning of the character "illumination" (zhào) extends to both the true and the false, just as the two meanings of "clarity" (míng) and "awareness" (jué).

Thus, the preceding text states: "The nature of awareness is necessarily clear, yet it falsely becomes clarity-awareness. Awareness is not that which is made clear; rather, because of clarity, the perceived is established. Since the perceived is already false..."

Establishing the capacity for your deluded faculties, through confusion there arises space and so forth. This is the intense manifestation of difference within that which is neither identical nor different. Based on what is different from it, one establishes identity;

based on the manifestation of identity and difference, one further establishes that which is neither identical nor different. Thus, one knows that space is identity and the world-systems and lands are difference, while sentient beings—conditioned phenomena—are neither identical nor different.

As Vasubandhu says: "The clarity of thought forms the land; cognition constitutes sentient beings. This means that both the animate and the inanimate are produced by false imagination. It is as [Vasubandhu] stated.

It is taught that both the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized are termed *vijñāna*. That which is conceptualized is called *vijñāna*; that which is non-conceptualized is termed the "consciousness resembling objects" (*viṣayābhāsa-vijñāna*). Now, when thought (*saṃjñā*) clarifies and forms the land, this is precisely the consciousness resembling objects.

When awareness perceives sentient beings, this is the consciousness of consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*). Those who take Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*) as their tenet merely claim that this consciousness is not identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Since they hold the One Mind to be the source, they assert that True Suchness is without awareness or cognition, remaining quiescent and unchanging, and do not allow for its functioning in accordance with conditions. They speak only of the eight consciousnesses arising and producing all phenomena; it is for this reason that [they differ from the teaching here].

The doctrinal principles of the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong) are as incompatible as water and fire; yet once one understands how our own school has already refuted the four natures (*catur-svabhāva*), then whatever is taught according to the needs of the occasion will accord with the subtle truth, and all contentious calculations will fall away.

The *Zhuanyi* states: "Because ignorance deludes the enlightened nature (*jue-xing*), it consequently transforms into stubborn emptiness (*wang-kan*). All worlds are established in dependence upon this emptiness.

Furthermore, when deluded thoughts (*wangxiang*) coalesce and solidify, they form the three lands of defiled obstruction; when deluded thoughts manifest as cognitive awareness, they form the nine realms of turmoil."

"Empty space arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The lands of conditioned outflows (*sāsrava*), as numerous as motes of dust, are all produced depending upon empty space.

Tiaoxi says: "Conditioned outflows include sentient beings. Xunwen says: "'Outflow' (*āsrava*) means leaking away; it belongs to the afflictions (*kleśa*). As the Vinaya states: 'When a deluded person creates karma, they open the gates of the various outflows.'"
When bubbles vanish, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, are the various realms of the three worlds?

These three worlds encompass both sentient beings and their environments, possessing causes and effects. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* takes the two truths of suffering and its origin as the substance of the three worlds. Delusion is originally without root and ultimately does not arise;
therefore, empty space is like a bubble—extinguished though it is not extinguished. The three worlds are like an illusion—non-existent though they are not non-existent.
"The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; the skillful means have many gates.

The Supplement states: "The former phrase refers to the perfect penetration of the entry [into the Way]; the latter phrase points to the eighteen realms and the seven elements. It is easy to attain the mind of nirvana, but it is difficult to clarify the wisdom that discerns distinctions."
The nature of the sages is such that there is nothing they do not penetrate; both following and reversing are skillful means (*upāya*).

The first phrase indicates that among the twenty-five sages, there is nothing they cannot accomplish through giving; the second phrase refers to the faculties of beings (*indriya*) in accordance with their respective lands. Thus, the meaning of "following" and "reversing" arises.

For example, in this land, it is "following" when the faculty of the ear enters the Path, whereas it is "reversing" when other faculties enter the Path. This may be illustrated by other lands as well; though there are instances of following and reversing, all are gates of skillful means. Likewise, in this land, there are also cases where other faculties enter the Path.

To be slow rather than swift is also a skillful means. Tiāoxī says: "One should also regard what is cultivated by the Śrāvakas as 'contrary' and what is cultivated by the Bodhisattvas as 'conformable.

Furthermore, among the Bodhisattvas, the gradual approach is 'contrary' while the perfect and sudden approach is called 'conformable. As the following text states, 'The shallow and the deep preach the Dharma in the same way'; the principle of this meaning is likewise so."
"Beginners entering samādhi differ in their speed;

they are not of the same class. Tiāoxī said: "If one’s faculties are appropriate, it is swift; if the faculties are mismatched, it is slow. Days and kalpas multiply by tens of millions; thus they are of different kinds. Bùyì says:

"For ordinary people in this land who enter the Way, those wishing to enter samādhi find that within the eighteen realms and seven elements there is a principle of swiftness and slowness. Entering the Way through the faculty of hearing is swift; for this reason, it is selected below, while the other faculties are not."

Entering the Way would then be slow; that is why [the Buddha] set it aside. In the preceding passage, the Tathāgata stated that among the practices of the various sages there is truly no superiority or inferiority. He further asked which of the twenty-five modes of practice would suit their faculties;

this was merely a selection based on the eighteen realms and seven great dharmas in accordance with the spiritual capacities of those in this land, not a selection among the perfect penetrations (*yuan-tong*) of the various sages. This can be seen by examining the subsequent text.

Furthermore, regarding the eighteen realms and the seven great dharmas in relation to the faculties and objects of ordinary beings in this land, [the text] distinguishes between what is suitable and what is unsuitable;

it does not contain a single word that disparages the perfect penetration of the various sages as being erroneous. For instance, concerning the first realm, visible form (*rūpa*), it says: "The dust of form is defiled and lacks clarity; how could one attain perfect penetration through it?

Yet, when Upānanda analyzed form until it reached emptiness, he spoke of "wondrous form, subtle and pervasive"—is this not a clear and thorough understanding of the essence of form? Regarding the realm of sound, it says: "Sounds are mixed with speech; one does not contain all. And yet, as for Dharmatrāta...

One attains awakening through the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), and it is also said that "wondrous sound is subtle and perfect. How can one then say that it is a mixture of worldly speech and does not encompass all things?

Thus we know that although the various sages have attained perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), if their voices and forms are contrasted with the present beginner's state, they merely constitute obstructive and mixed phenomena (*dustāvaraṇa-viśeṣa*) and cannot enter perfect penetration.

The aggregate of form and perception binds together into dust; the essence of clarity cannot penetrate it. Why is it that one does not attain clear penetration? It is through this that one attains perfect penetration.

Tiaoxi said: "First, regarding the dust of form: form is formed into various dusts by deluded thought. Because the substance of the dust is obstructive, it cannot allow the nature of the essence of clarity and discernment to pass through."
Sounds are intermingled with speech; they consist merely of names, phrases, and syllables. Since one does not contain all, how can one attain perfect penetration? Gushan says:

"Intermingled within the object of sound refers to various kinds of speech, yet this speech consists only of names, phrases, and syllables. In the new translations, these are all termed *nāma*, *pada*, and *vyañjana*.

The *Śāstravyākhyā* states: "Names (nāman) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for example, the word 'fire' expresses only fire and does not include water, wind, or what kind of fire it is. Phrases (*pada*) express distinctions; that is, they speak of charcoal fire, mugwort fire, and so forth.

Syllables (*vyañjana*) are the individual letters, serving as the basis for the former two. The ancients referred to syllables as 'flavor' (*rasa*), because syllables can manifest these two [names and phrases], just as flavor manifests the saltiness or blandness within food.

Question: Dignāga’s realization of the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) is similar to Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Why is it now distinguished as being non-identical? Answer: This is because sound is the Buddha’s speech, whereas the faculty...

Regarding one's own self: if you recognize sensory objects (*viṣaya*), you become attached to the words of others; if you contemplate the sense organs (*indriya*), you realize the nature of your own mind. This mind takes both sound and sensory objects as its objects of discernment.

Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since it does not persist as an object of perception, how can it attain perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-abhijñā*)?
The nature of taste is not fundamental; it exists only when there is tasting. Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?

Tactile sensation is clarified by that which is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly perceive. Yet, the nature of contact and separation is not fixed. How can one attain perfect penetration through it?
Xunwen said: "The objects of fragrance, flavor, and touch are all known when in combination; when separated, they are not perceived. This general meaning is largely the same [as for sound].

The object of dharmas is called an 'internal' object. Since the perception of an object must have a corresponding subject, the relationship between subject and object does not involve universal penetration. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

Zhenji said: "It scatters and universally conditions alone; not being grasped by the five sense organs, it is termed 'internal dust' (adhyātma-rasa). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The dharma-dust is the object-conditioned (ālambana), and the mind (manas) is the subject-conditioning (ālambaka)."

However, the mind does not entertain multiple considerations simultaneously; just as when it takes a wholesome mental factor as its object, it cannot take an unwholesome one. Therefore, it is said that it does not pervade all objects.

Since it does not pervade all, how could it possibly attain perfect penetration regarding the sensory objects of ordinary beings? If, in Kāśyapa’s case, perfect penetration refers to the illumination of the wondrous Dharma, how can you dismiss it by saying that the subject and object do not pervade all?

"Although the nature of seeing is transparently clear, it illuminates what is before one but not what is behind; half of the four directions are thus deficient. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Xie Li said:

"At first, when the faculty of the eye is relaxed, its nature of seeing is indeed transparently clear; however, because its characteristic of seeing is stripped away, it does not illuminate what is behind. Changshui said: "What is in front is fully illuminated."
The rear is entirely dark, while one observes two-thirds on the left and right; thus it is said that "the four intermediate directions (caturvidiś) lack half. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"This merely refers to the fact that when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) perceive objects with their sense organs, there are instances where they see clearly and without obscuration. [The author] wishes to deny the clarity of the rear, and therefore allows for 'pervasive clarity' (dōngrán) in this context.

The preceding text itself uses the four corners to clarify that what is perceived by ordinary beings constitutes only one half. If the four intermediate directions were identical to the four cardinal directions, they would not constitute "half. Here, wishing to deny that "half," he specifically points to [the rear].
The four corners are the ears;

the inhalation and exhalation of the breath are pervasive, yet when manifest before one, there is no mingling of the airs. They are fragmented and do not interpenetrate—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration through them?
The tongue is not an entry point without cause; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavors cease, the cognition vanishes—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration through it?

Zhaoxi said: "The tongue-faculty (jihvā-indriya) serves as the basis for consciousness and is also termed the tongue-sphere (jihvā-āyatana). The wording in the present text is inverted; it simply means that this is the tongue-sphere and not something without cause."
The body and its objects of touch are each distinct from Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue). Since their boundaries do not merge, how can one attain perfect penetration?

When the internal body and external objects interact as subject and object, there is then perception and observation; without such contact, there is none. Therefore, it is said that "each is not [Perfect Enlightenment]," and so forth. If one were to claim that perception exists within the state of conjunction, this would be like asserting that an object possesses the nature of cognition itself;
thus, they would stand as two opposing entities. Hence, it is said that "their boundaries do not merge," and so forth.

If one’s faculty of knowledge is muddled by discursive thoughts, then despite profound clarity, one will ultimately have no vision. If one cannot escape such conceptualization, how can one attain perfect penetration?

"Despite profound clarity, one will ultimately have no vision" means that as before, even with refined clarity, one cannot reach through to the ultimate. Because of muddled and discursive thoughts, one can never perceive the nature of profound clarity.

The Supplement states: "This also distinguishes the sage from the ordinary person based on their faculties and objects. To clarify the former while not clarifying the latter is the way of the ordinary person. Nalakūvara’s half-head celestial eye perceives clearly in all ten directions; only then is it [the state of the sage]."

This is merely the mark of supernormal power (*abhijñā*). As I have previously stated: "I do not perceive the ten directions by means of the eye; how could there be supernormal power if it were limited only to what is before one?

The faculty of the nose is sharp and clear, and only then do inhalation and exhalation occur. When these inhalations and exhalations are divided into parts, there is a gap in their intersection. It is when the two phases interpenetrate that this constitutes their intersection.

Among the six sense faculties, only the three—nose, tongue, and body—possess cognition through conjunction. Of these three, the nose faculty perceives odors as if it did not wait for the fragrance to enter [the nostrils]. The body encounters cold, heat, coolness, and warmth as if it did not [wait for contact].

Regarding the entry of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*): if it were only the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) and not the taste-entry (*rasāyatana*), then the tongue would have no cognition. To say that the tongue is not the taste-entry is to lack a basis for knowing it as the tongue-faculty; therefore, the subsequent line states, "Cognition arises because of taste.

Within the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), each speaks of the body and touch as being separate from one another; this is not incorrect, for they are fully established as such. If the body and touch were separate from one another, then sensation and discernment (*vitarka-vicāra*) would not be established.

Although the two entities—the body and touch—are conjoined, each has its own boundaries; "boundaries" (*pārśva*) refers here to the limits of their extent, meaning they do not merge into an indistinguishable unity. The mental faculty (*manas*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is frequently subject to distracted thoughts.

If one cannot perceive principle, how can one enter perfect penetration? If, however, one dwells in emptiness, having attained unimpeded mind since the beginningless kalpas, one may suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of space.
Why do you rebuke me by saying that my scattered thoughts prevent me from seeing profound clarity?

Consciousness and perception are a mixture of the three harmonies; when one interrogates their source, they are called "non-characteristics. Since their own essence has no fixed nature from the outset, how can you claim to have attained perfect penetration?

Regarding the mention of "two": the *Śāstra* states that consciousness arises from the conjunction of two, meaning that consciousness arises within the union of the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*). What is now called the "conjunction of three" is a combined statement of both the agent and the object.
When the sense faculty and the object are disjoined, consciousness itself lacks an intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said to be "without fixed existence."
"The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, arising from the power of the great cause. Since the initial mind cannot enter this, how can one attain perfect penetration? Mount Gu said:

"Within the ear-consciousness, hearing occurs solely through the mind and not by means of the auditory faculty. This is what is attained upon the stage of partial realization; therefore, it is not something the initial mind can enter. Longshui said:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva fundamentally employs the hearing of the mind to discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings, thereby attaining great mastery. Now, [the previous method] was rejected as being too exalted because it would fail to encompass all capacities.

Since the Dharma-realm constitutes his essence and the hearing of the mind constitutes his function, he penetrates the ten directions. This is the result of Samantabhadra’s cultivation of the Great Practice during his causal stage; therefore, those of middling and inferior capacities have no share in this. Thus it is said that they "cannot enter.

This is because the body of Samantabhadra manifests only when one illuminates the practice of Samantabhadra within the mind of a sentient being; it is not like Avalokiteśvara, who manifests according to whatever object is encountered.

"Contemplation of the nose is fundamentally a provisional expedient (*upāya*), intended only to cause the mind to settle. Once it has settled, the mind comes to abide [in that state]. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? Foxue Shan said:

"Counting the breath is a skillful means for harmonizing the mind; therefore, it is called a 'provisional expedient. 'Expedient' (*ji*) refers to a stratagem; it is merely another name for a skillful means. Zizhong said:

"If the mind has an abiding, then it is not truly abiding; there is something upon which it dwells and clings. This is not true contemplation. In truth, there is no abiding. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "This is also spoken from the perspective of the ordinary person of this land."

If one were to cause an ordinary person at the initial stage of practice to rely on this counting of breaths and fix the mind upon the tip of the nose, it would merely result in a method for binding the mind with signs (*nimitta*). Wherein lies perfect penetration (*pariśuddha*)?

It would be like the foolish meditation of worldly practitioners who sit in a daze; how could they enter the Way? If, however, as in the case of Nanda, one perceives the breath transforming into radiance, and even as it is said: "After a long time, the breath gives rise to luminosity, which is perfectly round and extinguishes outflows. Only then is there true progress.
How can you dismiss this by saying it merely requires one to collect the mind and abide therein?

To say that "preaching the Dharma with its sounds and texts brings enlightenment first" is incorrect; since names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*), how could one attain perfect penetration through them?

Regarding the practice of preaching by playing with sounds and texts, this serves to censure those contemporary lecturers who do not strive to discuss the underlying principles but instead flaunt their vocal delivery, embellishing it with extraneous secular classics as mere literary ornamentation.

This is like mere dallying and play. If one wishes to preach the Dharma here and seek awakening from within the faculty of the tongue, one must necessarily rely on prior instruction from a teacher to achieve understanding, or else have previously cultivated seeds of goodness;

otherwise, such awakening will not occur. This is truly because one who can preach the Dharma must first undergo study, and these seeds of goodness must have been established in the past. The merit of awakening today does not reside solely in the tongue.
This is already the case for the sense faculties; how much more so for the names and phrases that are spoken? They are not vessels capable of entering the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, they are now excluded. Observing and violating the precepts merely constrain the body; yet there is nothing to constrain apart from the body itself. Since these [precepts] do not originally pervade all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?
At first, one restrains the body by means of the Hīnayāna; next, one restrains the mind by means of the Mahāyāna; only then do both body and mind attain universal penetration.

Now, to say that one who begins the path today intends to restrain the body through the observance of precepts and enter the Way via body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) is impossible. Why? Because while they may be able to restrain the body, they cannot restrain the mind. To say it is not the body is to mean the mind;

yet fundamentally, this does not pervade all, meaning it cannot universally restrain both body and mind. If that is so, then what is currently called "body-consciousness" is it not, in fact, the mind? One must understand that this is the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.

The precepts you observe involve only the mind alone. In the Lesser Vehicle, that which is to be remedied involves both body and speech as well as the mind; yet if one looks only at the single mind, it merely accomplishes [the restraint of] body and speech.

Since supernatural powers are fundamentally the result of past causes, what connection do they have with the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness takes objects as its condition and is not detached from things, how can you attain perfect penetration?

Xunwen says: Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is an internal realization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), while the first five powers are external functions of the mental consciousness.

These arose because Maudgalyāyana’s past causes had matured through hearing the Dharma from the three Kāśyapas; they were not the standard method for entering the Path at the initial stage. Therefore, he is excluded [from this category]. Tiexi says: Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were obtained through past habituation.

Although it is said that his "mind-light" was proclaimed as he returned to the stillness, these did not manifest through the discrimination of dharmas. Furthermore, all supernormal powers of the Hīnayāna involve deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*).

Xunwen said: This means that a single mind can only produce one thing; it is not like the Mahāyāna teaching where the unconditioned (avyākṛta) transformation-body has universal penetration. When conditioned by objects, it exists; when separated from objects, it perishes.

Tangxiang said: "In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), when one cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye, it takes as its object forms beyond obstructions; when one cultivates the divine ear, it takes as its object sounds beyond obstructions; and the same applies to all other supernormal powers."

Now, regarding the supernormal power of mastery over the body (*kāya-ṛddhi*), transforming the bodies of others and exercising sovereign control over all worldly things according to one's will, these too are objects of mindfulness; they do not exist apart from the characteristics of material phenomena (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).

The Supplement states: Maudgalyāyana attained supernatural powers because he first heard the Dharma and realized the Way; only thereafter did he manifest these powers through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It was not solely by means of the mental consciousness alone.

"Dharma" refers to the discrimination of mental objects (dharmas), which is to say, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is merely citing the manifested in order to indicate the manifestor. Now, for the sake of beginners in this land who enter the Path solely through the mental consciousness, [this teaching is intended].
The mental consciousness must necessarily have objects of perception and thoughts; it cannot be separated from its objective referents. How, then, can it attain perfect penetration?

If one contemplates the nature of earth, its solidity and obstruction prevent thorough penetration; as it is conditioned and not the nature of the sages, how could one obtain perfect penetration through it?
In the first stage, the Bodhisattva Mahādhara contemplates that the atoms of his own body and the atoms of the world are equal and without distinction; even weapons cannot touch him.

How could he be dismissed as being obstructed rather than having attained penetration? It should be understood that within this context, the "Great Earth" (Mahāpṛthivī) is used entirely as a relative term to distinguish it from the initial mind.
If one contemplates through the nature of water, mental conceptions are not real; if it is the Suchness (tathatā) that is beyond both thought and observation, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Xunwen says: "In the element of water, Suchness is beyond thought and observation," meaning that the principle of Suchness cannot be realized through the thought and observation associated with water. The Supplement states:

If a beginner intends to employ the mind of vitarka and vicāra to contemplate the nature of water, how could they possibly accord with the perfect penetration of suchness? "Investigation" (覺) and "observation" (觀) are precisely vitarka and vicāra; it is said that the subject and object do not coincide.
Therefore it is said that this is not suchness.

If one contemplates by means of the nature of fire, one will come to loathe existence as non-real and seek detachment; this is not the skillful means of the initial mind. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration?

The Fire-Head (Agnimukha) loathes existence; Ucchuṣma loathes desire and contemplates fire. These are not true liberation. Those at the initial stage who wish to study the Fire-Head’s loathing of the fire of desire merely accomplish acts of grasping and rejecting;

they cannot realize that lust itself is the true fire of detachment from desire. Furthermore, if one relies on the Fire-Head to universally contemplate the fire-element and transform the lustful mind into the fire of wisdom, this is likewise unsuitable for a beginner.
For a beginner to treat desire, there are natural expedients, such as the meditation on impurity within the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastuka*). Thus begins the Fire-Head [Samādhi].
After the Great Mind, the Great Jewel Flame arises; it has already attained true detachment, yet it is merely that the initial mind cannot reach it.

If one contemplates through the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without their opposites; as long as there is opposition, there is no supreme enlightenment. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Wind is of the nature of movement. From movement comes stillness; since movement and stillness are relative, they do not constitute perfect penetration and are therefore excluded.
If one observes through the nature of space, it is dark and dull, originally not consciousness. Without consciousness, it differs from Bodhi; how could one attain perfect penetration?

That which preceded it was not awakening; it arose from delusion regarding emptiness. This is ignorance, and thus belongs to the realm of dullness. Compared to the present deluded mind, that which preceded it was not awakening.

If one observes with the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, and realizing that maintaining the mind is merely false and illusory, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Xunwen says: "It is not permanent. If the beginner takes consciousness as their object, then thought after thought will flow on, making it truly difficult to enter the Way. Gushan says: "The mind is originally without mind;

to harbor it is delusion. *Buyi* says: "Does Maitreya’s ‘contemplation of consciousness-only’ not realize the eternally abiding? We know from this that for the beginner who contemplates consciousness, they cannot immediately realize that the aggregates are true."

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now yield such disparate results—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

Regarding the passage "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," etc., it means that for a beginner today who wishes to rely on the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛti-indriya*) to achieve penetration, this is impossible. When a beginner moves their thoughts, they immediately fall within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), which is impermanent.

Since this nature of mindfulness exists at the level of an ordinary being, it is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. How can one use a cause characterized by arising and ceasing to realize the fruit of perfect penetration? Tiaoxi says: "The above two..."

The fourteen sages all relied upon their respective attained roots of perfect penetration; however, as these were not the faculties appropriate for this land, they were excluded. How could it be that Mañjuśrī harbored pride, or that the other sages possessed a sense of shame?
Those whom Mañjuśrī set aside were subsequently superseded by the selection of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as the faculty suited to the capacities of this land.

This must be explained in terms of the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) within the state of deluded aggregates (*skandha*). Among these, the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are excluded—some because they pertain to high stages, others because of long-standing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that prevent entry for beginners. These are what are set aside. Mañjuśrī...

This is because one must first establish the ear-faculty as the appropriate capacity for the sentient beings of this land. Otherwise, all eighteen realms can give rise to the faculties of sentient beings;

since the various sages originally encountered these conditions according to their circumstances, even though [the teaching] resides with Mañjuśrī, it is truly impossible to exclude anyone. Now, this [text] selects based on the characteristics of the six objects, six faculties, six consciousnesses, and the seven elements; how could it ever interfere with the affairs of the various sages?

If one says that one must know the selection of sages, this is entirely a selection of capacities and does not exhaust the principle. One must know that the selection of dharmas is entirely a selection of capacities.

I now address the World-Honored One: Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this direction lies in purity within hearing and sound. If one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through the midst of hearing;
thus one leaves suffering behind and attains liberation.

Changshui said: "In the Sahā world, the faculty of hearing is the most acute; therefore, sound is employed as the means for performing Buddha-work. Shoujian said: "Because the previous question asked, 'By what gate of skillful means can one easily achieve accomplishment?

the present response says: 'In truth, one enters through hearing. This means that for beginners in this land, by relying upon the faculty of hearing, awakening to the Way is swift and samādhi is easily accomplished."

Because their other faculties are dull, they awaken to the Way slowly and their contemplative practice is difficult to accomplish. This is because consciousness is generated from the faculty of hearing by means of sounds, which induces the wisdom of hearing within the sixth consciousness.

Based on names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and sounds (*śabda*), one cultivates the seeds of understanding through hearing; these are accepted as the essence of the teaching (*deśanā*). Once the essence of the teaching is established, one subsequently engages in contemplation and cultivation, entering *samādhi* and attaining great liberation.

The Master of Tiāoxī said: "The essence of the teaching should include sound (*śabda*), name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and letter (*vyañjana*). Now, when it is said that 'sound is heard,' this is because sound is a real dharma (*dravyadharma*), while the other three are provisional (*prajñapti*).

By subsuming the provisional into the real, it is simply called 'sound. Sound is the object that is heard, and hearing is the faculty that hears. By citing the object to reveal the faculty, the nature of hearing itself is directly demonstrated. Therefore, he says: "Desiring..."

"Taking [the sounds] as equal," etc. Furthermore, "sound" refers to all vocal sounds; it is simply the sound of one's original nature. According to the meaning of the *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal) school, "sound" is the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), while the "nature of hearing" is the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).

These constitute the two divisions of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*). Therefore, vocal sounds do not transcend one's own original nature. In the preceding text, it says: "Because I did not contemplate my own ears, I contemplated the observer. This is precisely "returning the hearing.

The subsequent text speaks of the "perfect reality," the "penetrating reality," and the "constant reality"; this reveals that because the nature of sound and hearing is the returning of the hearing, it is empty. When one contemplates emptiness through emptiness, it is pure. Hence, it is called the "Brahma-sound."

By means of the nature of hearing sounds through sound, one hears voices to rescue beings from suffering; thus it is provisional (samvṛti). Therefore, it is called the "Oceanic Tide Sound. When one reverses the direction of hearing, one does not fail to seek out sounds to rescue beings from suffering;

yet when responding to the various capacities of sentient beings, one does not depart from the self-nature through reverse-hearing; thus it is the Middle Way (madhyama). Therefore, it is named "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin).

How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as minute as motes of dust and attains the power of great mastery. He bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings.

With his wondrous voice, O Avalokiteśvara—your Brahma-voice and ocean-tide voice—you bring peace and security to all who seek salvation in the world; by transcending the world, you attain eternal abiding.

Changshui says: "The first line provides a general introduction to the praise; the next two lines praise the thirty-two manifestations; the following two lines praise the fourteen fearlessnesses, as well as the four inconceivabilities;

and the final two lines praise the virtuous titles. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The *Book of Documents* says, 'Excellent indeed are the limbs. 'Excellent' (*liáng*) means good. Guanyin occupies the position of succession in An-yang while assisting in the transformation of beings in Saṃsāra;

both of these carry the meaning of 'limbs. Gushan says: "Because his wisdom is merged with the subtle principle, he is called 'Sublime Sound' (*Miaoyin*); because his compassion transforms all living beings, he is called 'Observer of the World's Sounds' (*Guanshiyin*). This is a praise based on the Dharma. His wisdom is merged with the principle...

Therefore, there is no defilement from either extreme; like the purity of the Brahma-voice, it responds to the capacities and stimuli of beings within the ten realms through compassionate transformation, never overstepping its bounds, much like the tide. This is said in terms of sighing and lamentation.

The World-Savior’s binding of the *chao-yin* (tidal sound) accords with the capacities of beings; the world-transcending binding of the *fan-yin* (Brahma-sound) accords with the profound principle. This is also to cause sentient beings to first attain worldly happiness and subsequently obtain eternal bliss.
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has taught:
"Suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions; they hear them from all ten locations at once. This is the perfect reality."
Changshui says: "This refers to the virtue of liberation. Xunwen says: "'Dwelling' means sitting, as in the *Yili* [Book of Rites], 'dwelling at ease' (*yanju*) or 'dwelling in leisure' (*xianju*).

Regarding the samādhis previously described by Avalokiteśvara, the excellence attained therein ensures that his responses to sentient beings are never mistaken; he universally responds throughout the ten directions and ten realms. "Striking the drum" signifies the activation of the mechanism; "those who hear it at once" signifies that his response does not fail.
That his responsive bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are immeasurable is precisely the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna*).

The eyes do not perceive what lies beyond obstructions; the same is true for the mouth and nose. The body knows only through contact; the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and disordered. Hearing sounds across a wall, one can hear both the near and the far.
That which the five sense organs cannot align is precisely that which penetrates reality.

Changshui says: "This refers to the virtue of *prajñā*. Gushan says: "The mouth, nose, and body are all joined together within the cognition. If one were to place the phrase 'only by joining them does one know' at the beginning, the meaning would be consistent;

it is merely a reversal of the wording. Xunwen says: "'The mental thoughts are chaotic and without end. According to the *Shuowen*, 'end' (*xu*) refers to the tip of a thread. This means that mental thoughts are as disordered as a thread without a beginning. Buyi says:

"The mind’s disordered thoughts frequently result in loss of mindfulness and健忘 (*jiànwàng*, forgetfulness), like a thread losing its end. By this, he clarifies the sense that the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) possesses the quality of obstruction and separation.
Tiaoxi says: This clarifies perfect penetration, temporarily employing the function of the ear to demonstrate that the nature of hearing differs from the five sense organs.

Since its function has time and place, and can be measured by distance and proximity, those who have not yet attained realization might mistake it for being impermanent; therefore, the following section clarifies its true permanence to manifest this distinction.

The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it may be present or absent. When there is no sound, one is said to have no hearing, yet this is not truly the absence of the nature of hearing. Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising.
Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality.

Changshui said: "This refers to the virtue of the Dharmakāya. Zhenji said: "It is like Rāhula striking a bell; within the hearing, the sound naturally has movement and stillness, which are then described as existence and non-existence."

This does not mean that the nature of hearing exists or does not exist. If worldly people were to call it "no-hearing" at the time when sound is not heard, then the nature of hearing would have already ceased; yet, when the object of sound arises again, who is there to hear it?

Thus we know that when sound is present, the nature of hearing is not produced; when sound is absent, the nature of hearing is not extinguished. Since it is entirely free from both arising and ceasing, it is for this reason called the eternally real.
"Even though one is in a dream, it is not absent when there is no thinking. When awakening and observation transcend discursive thought, body and mind cannot reach it.

This is like the previous case where, while in deep sleep and mental activity has ceased, one hears the sound of pounding and yet perceives it as something else. At that time, how could one be mindful of stillness or movement? One should know that the nature of hearing is uninterrupted;

therefore, it is said, "it is not absent when there is no thinking. As for "awakening and observation transcend discursive thought": since this does not correspond with recollection or ideation, it immediately transcends the realm of awakening, observation, and discursive thought. (The translator’s note follows.)

The phrasing is not exhaustive; therefore, the syntax is inverted. *Vitarka* (覺) and *vicāra* (觀) are precisely *vitarka* and *vicāra*. *Cintā* (思惟) is the universal mental factor (*sarvatraga-citta-saṃprayukta*) of volition (*cetanā*). Both are mental concomitants (*caitasika*) and are all dissociated [from the primary mind], which is why they are termed "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Furthermore, *vitarka* is fundamental awareness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*), which is the nature of hearing. *Vicāra* is illumination. This follows the literal text. When one dreams of hearing the sound of pounding, although there is no deliberate reflection (*cintā*), the nature of hearing does not cease.

When *vitarka* and *vicāra* are exhausted and hearing no longer abides, such that the perceiving subject and the perceived object are both empty—how then could body and mind reach it? This is because the preceding phrase was attached to the following one.
Because it is not that there is no thinking, it is said that vitarka and vicāra arise from thought.

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics (*śabda-vidyā*) has been proclaimed and clarified. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; by following sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth. Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts.
Is this not because he follows what he has sunk into? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.
Ānanda, listen attentively. Empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, the inconceivable, illusion-like, true samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.
Gushan said: "Vajra is emptiness; like an illusion, it is provisional; the Buddha-mother is the middle.

You have heard of the myriad Buddhas and all their secret gates, yet you have not first eliminated the outflows of desire. To amass learning while harboring such errors constitutes a transgression. If you intend to maintain the Buddhas through hearing, why do you not hear that which hears?"
The Supplement states: "Accumulation enters from the outside; it is not that which exists within. To linger in verbal expressions is merely to pursue the external. Mount Gu says:

"You take your deluded hearing that follows sounds to uphold the teachings and words of the Buddhas; why do you not instead turn back to contemplate your own nature to seek liberation? Above is the hearing of the wisdom that is able to observe;
below is the hearing of the principle that is observed.
"Know that hearing does not arise spontaneously; names exist because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who can name that which is capable of detachment?

Tiaoxi said: "The preceding section has already cautioned against [relying on] one's own hearing. Now, the characteristics of cultivation are briefly shown. First, it is pointed out that deluded hearing does not arise without conditions; its arising must rely upon causes, and these causes are the teachings of sound.

One should employ the three types of wisdom to turn back this faculty and its objects, causing both to detach from their stickiness. Once what is grasped is dissolved, what name or description could there be for the wisdom capable of detachment? Even the 'capable of detachment' itself vanishes."
Furthermore, who is it that names these things? It is precisely this capacity for naming that constitutes the characteristic of their potential for extinction.
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.

Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataract-roots are removed, sensory dusts vanish and awareness becomes perfectly pure. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, one encompasses the void.

Xunwen says: "Furthermore, returning to that original hearing and breaking through ignorance is therefore called 'removal. 'Awakening to purity' refers to the wisdom of partial truth (*prativedha-satya-jñāna*).

'Purity reaching its ultimate limit and light penetrating through' refers to the culmination of true wisdom. If the mind gives rise to views, there will be the characteristic of non-seeing; since the mind is already free from views, this is the meaning of 'all-pervading illumination. Changshui says:

'Purity reaching its ultimate limit' means full purity, which is the perfection of liberation (*vimukti*). 'Light penetrating through' means full awakening, which is the completeness of prajñā. 'Quiescent illumination' refers to the true principle, the culmination of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since the three virtues are thus perfected, the three...
Obstructions are forever exhausted; it is like awakening from a great dream, like a lotus flower opening. Looking back at the world, who could remain as an obstacle?
Returning to observe the world, it is like matters within a dream. Māraṅgaka is in a dream; who can detain your form?

Just as a skillful worldly illusionist skillfully creates various men and women, and although their sense organs are seen to move, they are all pulled by a single mechanism; when that mechanism ceases, everything returns to stillness, and all illusions become devoid of intrinsic nature.

Zhaoxi said: "The illusionist is a metaphor for True Suchness (Tathatā); the illusions created are a metaphor for following conditions. The union of the true and the false transforms into the six sense organs, like various men and women.

'One mechanism' refers to the ear organ. One should understand that 'withdrawing' means to detach from the revolving hearing-sound. As it says in the *Xunwen*: 'It is like taking away the rotating mechanism of the ear organ from a wooden man; then all the movements of the organs cease simultaneously.

Furthermore, one should know that one must use 'one mechanism' to withdraw. 'Mechanism' (ji) refers to a mechanical device; although it moves like a person, it fundamentally lacks a sovereign controller. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:"

All dharmas taught by the Buddha are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and devoid of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). It is merely through the conjunction of various dharmas that sentient beings are conventionally designated;

they are like wooden mechanical puppets. Although they can move and act, there is no master within them. If one examines the preceding passage which speaks of "illusory men and women," it might seem as though these are not wooden puppets, but rather that illusory magic causes the wooden puppets to move, thereby manifesting the appearance of the movement of their faculties and mechanisms.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Illusion" is a conventional designation; it does not necessarily mean that an illusionist uses magical drugs to transform [substances] into men and women, but simply that wooden [puppets] are fashioned as such.
A person is simply called a magician who conjures illusions.

The six sense faculties are also like this: originally they depend on a single luminous intelligence, which divides into six harmonious combinations. When one faculty comes to rest and returns to its source, the functions of all six cease to operate.

Zhaoxi says: "The 'original reliance on a single lucidity' corresponds to the preceding illusionist; the 'delusory functioning as that which relies' refers to the basis for both the true and the false. This can be seen in the phrasing of the text regarding their division and integration.

Guxiang says: "'Cessation' (xiū) means goodness; it is the restoration of one's nature. Furthermore, it means rest; it is the resting from and detaching from the state of being stuck together, thereby restoring one's nature."

Dust and defilements dissolve at the mere thought [of this], achieving perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity. Remaining minor traces of various studies persist; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata. Tiaoxi says:
"The first two lines refer to ascending to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-chu zhù); the latter two lines refer to progressing from the stages of power (*li*) to the ultimate."

The great assembly and Ānanda, turn back the mechanism of inverted hearing and the self-nature of hearing-hearing; when this nature is perfected, the Unsurpassed Way is realized. Such is the true reality of perfect penetration.

Xunwen says: "Now, as for the term 'faculty' (*jī*), it should also follow the previous metaphor of 'drawing out the faculty.'* The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: 'Reversing the hearing means not following after sensory objects. Regarding 'hearing one's own nature,' one takes the nature of the ear’s hearing as the object of hearing;
