this 'hearing subject' is contemplation (*guān*). As previously stated: 'Why not hear the hearing itself? Here, too, the upper character 'hearing' refers to the contemplating subject, while the lower character 'hearing' refers to the ear-faculty (*karṇendriya*).

The nature of hearing illuminates its own nature, and one silently returns to the True. *Note: The metaphor of "drawing out the faculty" likely refers to the process of withdrawing the mind from external objects to focus on the internal faculty of hearing.*

These are the subtle-dust Buddhas; this is the single path to the gate of nirvana. All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; all Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; I, too, have realized it through this, not only Avalokiteśvara.

Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has inquired of me regarding various skillful means to rescue those of the final age and to enable those seeking the supramundane to achieve the mind of nirvana—Avalokiteśvara is the foremost among them.

All other skillful means are due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; they involve relinquishing worldly toil through immediate circumstances rather than through long-term cultivation and study. These teachings on both the shallow and the profound are spoken by him in common.

Zhaoxi said: "This refers to those in this land who attain enlightenment through various skillful means. By the power of the Buddha, it can be inferred by contrast that in other lands, those with other faculties may be sharp while those with the ear-faculty are dull.

Changshui said: "The first four lines of the verse praise the Buddha’s instruction to select those who have achieved success; the final two lines specifically point to the Perfect Door (the *yuanmen*), which is clearly and appropriately fitting.

As for the remaining five lines, they clarify how the twenty-four sages each accomplished their contemplative practice (*guanxing*) according to their respective causes and circumstances; all were brought about by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and skillful means."

That attainment of the Way is not merely a dharma-gate for those of shallow or deep capacities to enter together through long-term cultivation and study. This sufficiently demonstrates that the Avalokiteśvara [dharma-gate] is precisely a dharma-gate for those of both shallow and deep capacities to be taught and enter together through long-term cultivation and study.
The *Shiyao* states: "To abandon worldly toil through phenomena" means to enter the reality by means of the provisional and small [vehicles].

It also refers to matters such as [encountering] lust, thorns, and water. The *Buyi* states: "Only the remaining five phrases below constitute the text that distinguishes the perfect penetration among the various sages. The meaning is that [all others] are excluded, with the exception of the ear.

Apart from those who have attained perfect penetration through the sense-faculties (*indriya*), as for other practitioners who have attained perfect penetration through the sense-bases (*āyatana*) or sense-objects (*viṣaya*), it is by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that they are able to abandon worldly afflictions even through these secondary matters;

however, this is not the eternal rule. This is because it does not properly accord with the spiritual capacities of those in this land; therefore, it is said that "this is not for long-term cultivation and study.

While the previous examination of the characteristics of the dharmas stated that [the others] were not perfect penetration, this current examination concerns the practitioners who enter [enlightenment]—they too possess perfect penetration, yet they simply cannot serve as the eternal rule for this land. The preceding twenty-four sages recounted what they had realized in the past. In...

If small, it is shallow; if large, it is deep. This "shallow and deep" refers to those who gain entry through other sense organs and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*); it cannot be equated with hearing the preaching of the Dharma through the ear organ.

Therefore, it is said that "the shallow and the deep alike hear the preaching of the Dharma," for the aforementioned [term] is not a two-character compound governing what follows. Furthermore, it may also be understood as "mutually doubling" in terms of slowness and speed, as they do not belong to the same category.

Generally, in this land, those who gain entry through other sense organs and objects must first alike hear the preaching of the Dharma, taking the teaching of sound as the foundation, before they can enter the Path. Therefore, it is said: "All are due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power," and so forth, down to "and the shallow [and deep]."
This is the same as what was stated previously. Therefore, Jingxi said: "Those who enter [the path] in this land do not rely on external sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

Although there are instances such as the physical forms of the sutras after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the fragrant food of Vimalakīrti, and awakening through the contemplation of the Dharma-practice, these all take the oral teachings of the Golden Mouth as their foundation."

Homage to the Tathāgatagarbha, untainted and inconceivable. May you bestow your grace upon those of the future, so that they may have no delusions regarding this gateway. May it be easily accomplished through skillful means, such that it may be taught to Ānanda and to those submerged in the final age of decay.
If one cultivates by means of this faculty alone, its perfect penetration will surpass all others; such is the true nature of the mind.
Changshui said: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the single essence of the Triple Gem, for it is fully endowed with untainted, inherent merits.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly clearly understood in both body and mind, receiving a profound revelation. They contemplated the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far away on business and has not yet returned, yet clearly knows the path by which they must return home.

Mañjuśrī pointed out the mind that had already been selected as the perfect penetration (*avivarta*). The faculties and capacities of the assembly were diverse, with varying degrees of greatness and smallness.

When the preceding section on Avalokiteśvara’s discourse concluded, all the Buddhas immediately responded by emitting light that came together to confer empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) upon one another, while simultaneously conferring it upon the great Bodhisattvas and the Arhats. Those who received this light all at once attained the Vajra Samādhi.

This clearly demonstrates how the various distinct contemplative gates of the twenty-four sages were, in a single moment, perfectly integrated into the cultivation and realization of Avalokiteśvara. Now, after Ānanda and the other beginners heard these verses, they followed [the teaching].

There are differences in the stages of their realization and entry. Ānanda and the others had only just realized that perfect penetration enters through the faculty of hearing; they had not yet attained direct verification. Thus it is said: "They clearly understood the path by which their respective families return. Handian (Handian) says:
The initial statement, from "I do not know the eternally abiding true mind" up to "I do not know the perfect fusion of the seven elements," represents the awakening within understanding.

The subsequent request, "Show me the path of my original aspiration," followed by the statement, "I have not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration," led the Buddha to command the various sages to each speak of their primary gateway. Furthermore, he commanded...

Mañjuśrī selected this because it is easy to enter. He then led [the assembly] by saying, "By practicing within this, one attains freedom from doubt. This is precisely the awakening within the midst of practice.

Thus, both in understanding and in practice, it is straightforward and clear, such that it can be taken up and enacted; hence there is the metaphor of "having found the way back home. Yet, it has not yet been fully realized.

The entire assembly— the eight classes of devas and nāgas, those of the two vehicles still in training, and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands— each attained their original mind,
distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, obtaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Zizhong said: "The 'purification of the Dharma-eye' (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*) in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* refers to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*). If one follows the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it corresponds to the initial mind of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"In the Small Vehicle, the purification of the Dharma-eye refers to the Path of Vision of the First Fruit (*srotāpanna*). Therefore, in the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], it is modeled after the first stage and the first abiding. If we rely on Tiantai’s definition of the purification of the Dharma-eye as the overcoming of the 'dust-like' delusions (*chen-sha-wu-ming*), it should occur from the eighth level of faith (*xin*) and above within the Perfect Family."
Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī of the *xing* [lineage] attained arhatship.

Gu Shan said: "Although the name 'arhat' is small, its realization is perfect. According to the 'Chapter on the Four Reliances' in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the fourth reliance refers to the person named an arhat.

Tiao Xi said: "In the four-fascicle version, it states that Dhanika only attains the third fruit; however, when categorized according to the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*), this corresponds to the stage prior to the seventh level of faith (*shixin*). If one uses the four reliances to judge the stages here, [it would fall within that range].

Fearing that ascending too high would be inappropriate—since the fourth stage relies upon abiding in the tenth ground—one should simply represent her as acting as a śrāvaka, equally eliminating the four *āśraya-vāsanas* and realizing arhatship, similar to the analogy in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding hearing of the eternal and attaining the fruit.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the understanding is perfect while the practice is gradual; through the provisional use of a small fruit for respite, one immediately enters the perfect [stage].

If one were to correlate this with the perfect stages, her prior attainment of the third fruit would correspond to before the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*). Her current status as an arhat corresponds precisely to entering the seventh stage of faith; thus, while the name is partial, the meaning is perfect.
Immeasurable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

According to Zhiyi’s commentary on the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the initial resolution of the bodhicitta marks the entry into the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Thus, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang Prajñāpāramitā) states: "The Bodhisattva of the ten wholesome paths resolves his great mind;

he forever parts from the ocean of suffering in the triple world. The Supplement (*Bùyì*) notes: "One who resolves the mind must equalize that mind through the wondrous principle of *tathatā*; this is indeed the 'peerless' (*asama*)."
Yet, they are equal in their discourse. This is truly because the mind and the Buddha are non-dual; what, then, could be equal in their discourse?

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and with his mind and its traces perfectly luminous, he was moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy. Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha.

The Supplement states: "Mind-trace" (*xīnjì*) is synonymous with "mind-object" (*xīnjìng*). Tiāoxī says: "One grieves that [the truth] was not heard in the past, and rejoices that it has now been attained through awakening.

Furthermore, one grieves because sentient beings of the future have not yet awakened, and rejoices because the great assembly of the present is gaining benefit. "Perfectly luminous" (*yuánmíng*) refers precisely to the path traversed by the mind; hence it is called "mind-trace. Since the realization is profound, it is stated below that there is "no doubt or confusion."
O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now awakened to the Dharma-door of attaining Buddhahood; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion.

I have often heard the Tathāgata speak these words: "The Bodhisattva resolves his mind when he seeks to deliver others before he has himself been delivered; the Tathāgata appears in the world when he has realized his own perfection and is able to awaken others.
Although I have not yet been delivered myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final kalpa.

The four vows of a bodhisattva take the salvation of sentient beings as their priority; the ten titles of a Tathāgata take responding to the world as their foundation. One should know that only when the five abodes are thoroughly exhausted and the two types of death are forever extinguished can one be said to have attained deliverance.
World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha. Teachers of false doctrines are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

If they wish to gather their minds and enter samādhi, how can you cause them to establish themselves at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from the works of Māra, and ensure that their resolve for bodhicitta never regresses?

Changshui said: Although the preceding sections have extensively explained the cultivation and realization of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), for ordinary people beginning their studies, obstacles and difficulties are especially profound.

This is all the more so in the final age, when heterodox schools arise in chaotic competition; their false words delude the orthodox, and demonic sophistry mimics the truth. Since those who are confused by such spurious teachings are numerous and their followers many, if these are not carefully discerned, they will hinder correct practice.

Therefore, one must test them through the precepts, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*); thus, the source of the heterodox will reveal itself. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Even Māra can transform his body into that of a Buddha. How much more so...

One cannot yet be a Bodhisattva of the Four Reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). The *Shiyao* states: "The stage prior to [the first] abiding is called the First Reliance; this refers to the five grades and the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*). From the first abiding to the fifth abiding is called the Second Reliance."

The dwellings of the sixth, seventh, and second [stages] are called the three reliances; the dwellings of the eighth, ninth, and tenth [stages] are called the four reliances. They are collectively termed "reliances" because, possessing the internal dharmas of the Path, they are capable of being relied upon by those in the realms of humans and devas.

This is an assignment according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Fearing it would confuse and delude the world, the Buddha did not speak of it. If one says that the possession of the eight kinds of impure things is permitted—namely:

first, fields and houses; second, planting roots and seeds; third, storing and accumulating rice and grain to seek profit through management; fourth, male and female slaves and people; fifth, raising herds of livestock; sixth, gold, silver, and treasures;

seventh, ivory carvings, various precious items, large couches, and so forth; eighth, copper and iron cauldrons and pots—this is what Māra has said. Since even external objects are not permitted to be possessed, how much less so are sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying!

Fundamentally rooted in greed and anger, there are fools in this world who, deluded by Māra, slander the precepts, claiming they belong to the Hīnayāna while asserting themselves to be Mahāyāna practitioners free from hindrances and possessing sovereign mastery.

The subsequent sutras extensively refute these views, identifying them all as the works of Māra; therefore, the Buddha issued profound warnings. These [teachings] are called the definitive Mahāyāna and the clear, manifest doctrine.

Ānanda, a great master of expedient means, took pity on those of the future who would surely fall into the perils of Māra, and thus earnestly requested [this teaching] to serve as a perpetual and true admonition. Regarding the phrase "the false teacher preaching the Dharma," the *Xunwen* (薰聞) states that it is like Liang Su’s *Zhi guan tong li* (止觀統例).

It is said: Since the Sage departed long ago, no sages have appeared; only the dull and ignorant remain among those who possess consciousness. This has allowed demonic and heterodox delusions to flourish in various factions.

In vain they produce much talk, creating pits and traps. Some are stuck to the literal words and dare not move; some are swept away by turbulent waves and cannot remain still; some find it too distant and willingly do not reach it;

some find it too near, realizing that it is their very own self; some mistake a withered tree for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); some mistake a hollow sound for wisdom (*prajñā*); and some rush headlong along paths that are not the Way.

Regarding what is called "expediency" (*upāya*): there are those who rely on spirits and deities to claim supernatural powers; those who let their minds run wild to claim vastness; those who speak sparingly to claim secrecy; and those who transmit teachings through whispered words from mouth to ear to claim oral instructions.

All such categories establish themselves as patriarchs, succeed their predecessors, and form distinct lineages; they subvert the fundamental principles and deviate from the sages, yet the ignorant do not perceive it.

Now, Ānanda’s intention in making his request was that at such a time, he feared sentient beings might be deluded by them; thus he asked how to cause them to collect their minds and enter meditative concentration, and so forth.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda amidst the great assembly: "Excellent, excellent! Regarding the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as you have asked, which protects and delivers sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
"Ānanda and the great assembly replied, 'So be it,' and respectfully received the instruction.

The Buddha told Ānanda: 'You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three principles of definitive meaning for the practice of cultivation. These are: to take the gathering of the mind as the precept;
from the precept arises concentration; and from concentration issues forth wisdom. These are called the three trainings in the outflow-free state.'"

Changshui says: This section provides a general clarification of the three trainings; the following sections specifically demonstrate the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), because the two gates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have already been explained previously. Thus, upholding the Vinaya while discussing the eternal [Dharma] is identical to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that "the two gates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have been explained previously": from the beginning up to the middle of the fourth fascicle, the sutra as a whole constitutes the opening of understanding, which is the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).

From the passage where Ānanda offers the analogy, "It is like a celestial king bestowing a magnificent mansion," until this point, it clarifies the study of concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*). Therefore, what follows below explains exclusively the study of precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*).

As for the phrase "upholding the *vinaya* while discussing the eternal" (*fú lǜ tán cháng*), the intent is to clarify that this sutra reveals only the Perfect and Sudden (*yuán-dùn*) teaching, and thus should properly explain the Mahāyāna observance of the precepts. Why, then, does it only clarify the four fundamental precepts (*mūla-śīla*)? This is because it accords with the disciplinary regulations of the Hīnayāna as a final exhortation, thereby encompassing [the entire scope].

The mind is the precept; even the nature of cessation does not exist. This is precisely the upholding of the precepts in the Mahāyāna. Therefore, one knows that while the names are the same as in the Hīnayāna, the upholding of the mind is eternally distinct.

Guishan says: *Vinaya* here is translated as "discipline" (*lü*). Guxiang says: by means of this method, the name "discipline" (*lü*) translates the term "*naiye*" from that land. "Discipline" (*lü*) signifies "explanation" (*quan*).

It explains and measures matters such as the gravity [of offenses], whether they are transgressions, and so forth. The *Fengsu tong* states: "Gao Yao advised the Lord of Yu and created the laws (*lü*); 'law' (*lü*) is explained as 'explanation' (*quan*). Furthermore, the *Shangshu datuan* states: "The great law of Heaven," with the commentary noting: "To serve Heaven."

This is the Great Dharma. "Dharma" is also "Vinaya. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "One should know that herein, because it upholds the Minor Vinaya, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first.
As this school belongs to the [Mahāyāna] reality, taking the mind as the basis for the precepts differs from the Hīnayāna, which merely disciplines body and speech."
Ānanda, what is it that I call the precept of restraining the mind?
If the beings of the six realms throughout all worlds do not harbor lustful thoughts, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

Gushan said: "In the Mahāyāna, the precept against killing is placed first because compassion is its foundation. In the Hīnayāna, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first because people frequently violate it. Now, following the Hīnayāna discipline, we take sexual misconduct as the first.

Furthermore, among the four grave offenses (*caturmahāvaśāra*) of the Hīnayāna, only the killing of a human being is proscribed; since such violations were rare, it was placed after stealing. Now, since we prohibit the killing of animals, it must be placed before stealing."

Furthermore, the four grave offenses (pārājika) are prescribed for the monastic community, while the five precepts are prescribed for the laity; thus, they are likewise different. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, although sexual misconduct does not cause distress to sentient beings, it binds the mind from moment to moment, and is therefore considered a great transgression.
For this reason, within the precepts, sexual desire is placed first; for laypeople, the precept against killing comes first because they seek merit.

You, however, cultivate samādhi with the primary aim of transcending worldly toil; if you do not eliminate the mind of lust, you cannot transcend the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and various states of meditative concentration manifest before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of demons.

As for the superior grade, one becomes a demon-king; the middle grade, a demon-subject; and the inferior grade, a demoness. These various demons also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

Xunwen said: "Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall into the path of demons. One should know that this refers specifically to bhikṣus and others who are practicing correct meditative concentration."

Even if one succeeds in entering the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), if one does not sever sexual desire, it is directly inverted into perversion and is identical to the deeds of Māra. The same applies to the precept against killing.

However, according to the power of one's meditative concentration, these may be divided into three grades, allowing for a temporary birth in the heavens; yet once the heavenly retribution is exhausted, one falls back into hell. As stated below: "When the blessings of Māra are exhausted, one falls into the Avīci Hell."

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic followers will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). They will cause all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views, causing them to lose the path to Bodhi.

Regarding those who fall into the pit of craving and views: the meaning of "craving" is as previously understood. As for "views," it refers, for example, to preaching to sentient beings that engaging in sexual desire is not an obstacle to the Path, or alternatively, erroneously teaching that sexual desire is itself the Path, and so forth.

When you teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, they must first sever sexual desire in the mind. This is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.

Although the name "precepts" (śīla) is the same as that used in the Hīnayāna, there is a difference in how they are maintained. Here, one maintains them by internally preventing each thought-moment, whether light or heavy; there, they are accomplished according to external circumstances as they arise.

The gravity [of offenses] follows the precepts; therefore, one first severs sexual desire in the mind. Thus, the Treatise says: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.

For this reason, it is entirely distinct from the observance of precepts in the Hīnayāna. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "This refers to the two types of precepts within the Vinaya—the precept of undertaking (*śīla-samādāna*) and the precept of following (*anuśīla*). First, one vows to undertake them before a teacher; subsequently, one follows and practices them. The *Xūnwén* (Perfuming the Hearing) states:

"I now say that 'first severing sexual desire in the mind' expresses the intent of preventing the sprout and blocking the gradual onset [of evil]. It does not mean that as soon as the thought arises, one incurs an offense identical to the examples in the first fascicle. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:"

Verbal mockery, the sound of bracelets heard outside a wall, and men and women pursuing one another all defile the pure precepts. The *Tiantai Pusa jie shu* (Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts) points to these as defiling the "precepts shared with meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samvara*).

Furthermore, it states that acts such as touching [the body] are all skillful means for the precept against sexual misconduct; they all constitute violations of the light secondary offenses (*āpatti*).

One should know that when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says that a bodhisattva’s observance of prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) is no different from the gravity of natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), it is because one must be cautious regarding minor transgressions just as one guards against the grave offense of violating the *brahmacarya*.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust while practicing meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that they will become rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would still only be called hot sand. Why is this?

This is not the original rice; it is composed of sand and gravel. You seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body; even if you were to attain wondrous enlightenment, it would all be rooted in lust. With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape them.
By what path could you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?
One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, and even the nature of this severance is non-existent. Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken in this manner is the teaching of others.

Changshui says: "The correct term is *Pāpīyaṇ*. This is translated as 'the Evil One' (*èzhě*). Xunwen says: 'Alternatively, it is called "the Killer. Because he cuts off the roots of goodness in people, he is named "Killer";
because he opposes the Buddha and disrupts the Sangha, there is no sin greater than his, hence he is named "Evil. *Pāxún* is a corruption [of the original term]."
Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor a mind of killing, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

You practice samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; if the murderous mind is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.

Those of the highest grade will become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade will become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade will become earth-walking rākṣasas. As for those spirits...
The ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

While practicing dhyāna while maintaining a habit of killing, they are reborn as deities; those whose merit is profound and whose blessings are abundant become powerful ghosts, such as those enshrined in the sacrifices of the Five Peaks and the Four Rivers.

Those whose merit is shallow and whose blessings are inferior are ranked among the middle and lower eight classes of beings, including the rākṣasas dwelling along the shores of the great ocean. Because they have practiced meditative concentration, they all possess karmic supernormal powers that are swift and unimpeded, yet they do not cease from killing.

Therefore, they undergo this miserable rebirth as servants driven by the gods. If one does not cultivate meditative concentration nor cultivate merit, but practices only killing, one enters directly into hell without such gradations of transition.
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one finds the path to Bodhi.

Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced through my supernatural power; they originally possessed no life-force. You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the soil is mostly damp and humid, further compounded by sand and stones, so that grasses and vegetables do not grow.

Through the application of my great compassionate supernatural power, and because you entered into a state of compassion, these were provisionally called 'meat' so that you might obtain their flavor."

Xuanli said: In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa asked the Buddha, "Why did the Tathāgata previously permit bhikṣus three kinds of pure meat? The Buddha replied, "It was for the sake of gradual regulation according to circumstances.

As for the "three kinds," these exclude ten types—human, snake, elephant, horse, donkey, dog, lion, fox, pig, and macaque—and any meat that is not seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for oneself] is called pure.

The present mention of "five kinds" adds two more: meat from animals that died naturally and meat left over from a meal. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of nine kinds of pure meat; this is achieved by further subdividing each of the three aforementioned purities into those that are permissible and those that were previously prohibited.

This refers to the subsequent preparatory action (*paścāt-karman*). Guxiang says: "Within the categories of what is seen, heard, or suspected, three characteristics are explained for each. First, regarding the three within 'what is seen': seeing [the animal] being led away as a beast is called the preparatory action;

seeing it at the moment it is about to be killed by the wielder of the blade is the fundamental primary offense (*maula-āpatti*); seeing it after it has been killed and feeling joy is called the subsequent preparatory action.

Not seeing these three is termed 'pure meat. The same applies to the three cases of 'hearing. Regarding the three cases of 'suspecting': the initial, fleeting arousal of the mind is called the prior preparatory action; the subsequent deliberation and reflection, suspecting [the meat] to be for oneself..."

Killing is termed the fundamental primary offense (*maulāpatti*). To feel joy after having harbored doubt [regarding the act] is termed the subsequent preparatory stage (*prayoga*). Meat that lacks these three types of doubt is called "pure meat.

However, while all Vinayas clarify that fish and meat may be eaten, only the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and this present sutra proclaim the total cessation of eating meat. This is because the teachings are directed toward specific capacities; matters involve both sudden and gradual approaches. As it is with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), so it is with the precepts (*śīla*).

Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* establishes a sudden prohibition, forbidding the consumption of meat for those of the Separate and Perfect capacities (*vyavasthāna-yāna* and *pariniṣpanna-yāna*) from the outset. However, since the Deer Park, the Vinaya has established prohibitions gradually, opening the allowance for the three [types of pure meat] because it was directed toward those of the Tripitaka capacity (*śrāvaka-yāna*).
[The teaching on] purity: as the path of transformation was nearing its end, [the Buddha] shifted from the gradual toward the sudden. Thus, three sutras all proclaimed the cessation of meat-eating;

the *Laṅkāvatāra* restricted this to Bodhisattvas of the *Śrāvaka* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles (*zàng-tōng*), while this sutra (*Nirvāṇa*) further restricts it for all three vehicles. Upon reaching the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, he specifically restricted it for the *śrāvakas*, earnestly instructing them, saying: "O Brahmin, among the four castes in the West, the Brahmin is considered the highest;

therefore, the five regions of India are all called the 'Country of the Brahmins,' and the monastic community is likewise called the 'Brahmin Sangha. This is fully recorded in Xuanzang’s *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*.

How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings call themselves disciples of the Śākya? You should know that such meat-eaters, even if they attain a mental opening that resembles *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*.

When their retribution ends, they will surely sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha. For such people, killing one another, devouring one another, and eating one another will never cease.
How could such people ever escape the three realms?

Changshui said: "This resembles the *samādhi* of ghosts and spirits; it can also cause one to know matters of the past and future. It is similar to wholesome *samādhi*, as described in the *Awakening of Faith*."

When you instruct the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, they must first cease taking life; this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking someone not to hear them;
such people are said to be "the more they wish to conceal, the more they reveal."

Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not even tread upon living grass when walking on a forked path, much less pluck it with their hands. How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?

Xunwen said: "Grass and trees are originally insentient; externalists claim they possess sentience. The Buddha refuted this slander and therefore established the precept against destroying life. Even those who maintain the pure precepts do so with great vigilance—how much more so for those among the class of sentient beings?"
If there are bhikṣus who do not wear silks, cottons, or flosses from the East, nor the boots, leather shoes, furs, or woolens of this land, nor consume milk, curd, or clarified butter;

such bhikṣus are truly liberated in the world. They have repaid their karmic debts from past lives and no longer wander within the three realms. Why is this? Because wearing any part of their bodies [made from these materials] constitutes a causal connection with them. It is like a person eating the various grains of the earth whose feet cannot leave the ground.

You must ensure that, regarding all sentient beings, neither your body nor your mind—through either of these two paths—wears or consumes anything belonging to them. I declare such a person to be one who has attained true liberation.

Zizhong said: "In the Western Regions, this region is referred to as the East. There, they do not even permit the use of wild silkworm cotton to make new bedding; how much less so domestic silkworm silk?

According to the Vinaya, if there is an offense, one must cut and chop it to plaster over the earthen floor, never to wear it again. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "It seems that for those who have committed the offense, the cotton or silk is cut and chopped and used to plaster over the mud floors, demonstrating its uselessness.

This repays past debts in this very lifetime; once this body is cast off, one will be utterly separated from the three realms. The *Shiyao* (Essentials of Explanation) states: "The *Wuli lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Things) says: 'The *liang* is [a measure of] millet...'"

*Ji* (millet) is the general name for all grains. *Dào* (rice) is the general name for both non-glutinous and glutinous varieties. *Shū* (beans) is the general name for all legumes. Each of these three types of grain has twenty varieties, totaling sixty.

When combined with the fruits of vegetables and trees, which total twenty, they constitute the "hundred grains. Master Jing said: "This is taught for the sake of ordinary persons seeking liberation—namely, those who practice the path of the sages while still on the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*).

If it were practiced on the level of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), it would be neither an ordinary person's dharma nor a sage's dharma. Only if [the teaching] can serve as a condition for them is it employed to deliver and liberate them."
As I have spoken this, it is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which is not so spoken is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in the world do not harbor a mind of theft, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

When you cultivate samādhi, its fundamental purpose is to emerge from worldly toil. If the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever this thievery, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths.

You may become possessed by high-grade spirits, mid-grade demons, or low-grade deviants and various malevolent influences. These groups of deviants also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the final dharma, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world. They will secretly harbor deceit while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), each asserting that they have attained the dharmas of a superior person.
They will entice and delude the ignorant, terrifying them so as to cause them to lose their minds; wherever they go, the households they visit will suffer depletion and ruin.
Xunwen said: "To conceal one's deceit and fraud is to harbor the mind of a thief; to claim the title of 'Good Spiritual Friend' (Kalyāṇamitra) is to steal the name of the sages and worthies.

If, according to their respective assertions, they claim to have attained the 'Dharma of the Superior Man,' this already constitutes the offense of a great falsehood. Now, they merely use it as a pretext for acquiring wealth. To prove this, he cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which enumerates six kinds of thieving minds:

taking by means of harshness (meaning begging in a piteous manner); taking with contempt (meaning manifesting an air of authority); taking under another's name (meaning "I am a Good Spiritual Friend"); taking by forceful intrusion (meaning insulting others to make them submit to oneself); taking what has been entrusted (meaning being...); and [the sixth].

Regarding "taking interest from what has been entrusted to others" (meaning to demand interest on money lent to others), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* lists four types: namely, with a deceitful mind, a crooked mind, a hateful mind, and a fearful mind. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* lists ten types:

namely, a dark mind (meaning not knowing cause and effect), a perverse mind (meaning not recognizing correct principles), a crooked and distorted mind (meaning being sycophantic), a fearful mind (meaning fearing only the loss of the object), a constant intention to steal another's property (since it says "constant," it implies one must desire to steal regardless of the amount), taking by determination (meaning taking by force regardless of whether it is permissible or not), taking what was entrusted, and taking through intimidation (meaning using words to frighten them, such as speaking of retribution in other hells or using unsettling matters to extort wealth).

"Taking upon seeing an opportunity" (meaning to spy for a moment when one can be taken and then steal from them); "taking by relying on others" (meaning to falsely rely on power and influence). The Sūtra says, "fearing they might lose their minds," which refers to taking through intimidation; "losing their minds" means causing the person before one to lose their right mindfulness and fall together into false views.

Now, I say that this Sūtra conceals such treachery and deception; though its words are brief, they are sufficient to cover all such cases. As for the fact that it specifically points to those called "good friends" (kalyāṇamitra), could this not be because the Tathāgata, foreseeing the future age, perceived that their followers would indeed be numerous?
Those who uphold this Sūtra should reflect upon themselves accordingly.
I instruct the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to their direction, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves;
they entrust their remaining lives to a transient sojourn within the three realms, demonstrating a single round-trip after which there is no returning.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that to prepare food with one's own hands constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*). The Vinaya texts state it constitutes a downfall (*pāyattika*).

Yet, how is it that these thieves, wearing my robes, engage in trade and commerce under the name of the Tathāgata, performing all manner of deeds while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma? They instead disparage ordained monks who possess the precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path.
Because of this, they mislead and delude immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell.

"Bī" means to attach; it refers to attaching oneself to the Buddha-dharma merely to sustain one's own livelihood. Furthermore, "bī" means to augment, as when a merchant increases the price of his goods.

To lack actual virtue yet augment it for the sake of selling it, seeking thereby to become a teacher, is nothing but the commercialization of the Buddha-dharma. Zizhong said: The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Perversions," states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, Māra Pāpīyas will gradually corrupt and disrupt my True Dharma, even assuming the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and arhats. By means of these outflows..."

This body is called untainted (*anāsrava*). It is even said that there are no four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata* rules, thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, or ninety *pāyattika* offenses.

The four methods of repentance, the numerous rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), and so forth—therein there is no *sthūlātyaya* offense, nor are there the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or even the icchantika;

even if one commits such offenses as these, there is no retribution. Those who speak thus are all speaking the words of Māra, and so on. I have often heard from Lengqie’s *Yeyu* (Night Talks) that once, during the summer months, he encountered a Chan practitioner on the road.

He asked where he was coming from, and the man replied, "I am returning from Min Province after eating my fill of fresh lychees. He asked again, "Where are you going now? The man replied, "I wish to go to Mount Lu to read what I have not yet seen."

It is merely a stone monument. I asked, "Why did you break the summer retreat to leave? He replied, "How could the regulations of the summer retreat have been established for people like us? (Regarding that text: Alas! How can one be so utterly lacking in discernment?

How could anyone, who disregards the Buddha’s regulations while being preoccupied with mouth and belly, still wish to be called [a practitioner]? There have been many such instances where the ignorant follow in his footsteps and treat the Buddha’s regulations lightly;
should we not believe that they will surely fall into hell through their delusions?

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to practice samādhi and is able, before an image of the Tathāgata, to light a lamp from his own body, burn a finger-joint, or burn a single incense stick upon his body—I declare that such a person shall at once repay all karmic debts from beginningless time.
Having taken a long farewell to the world, they shall forever be liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they have not yet clearly illuminated the path to supreme enlightenment, such a person has already attained a resolute mind regarding the Dharma.

Gushan said: "A thief takes another's *niśraya* (supportive conditions) and resources for his own body; now, by damaging one's *vipāka* (fruition body) to provide for the Supreme Sages, one is thus able to overturn the karma of theft accumulated since beginningless time."

Supplement: Master Jing (Ouyang Xiu) of the Tiexi River states in his *Shiyao* (Essentials of Exegesis): "In the 'Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja' chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is said: 'If someone asks whether the Vinaya regulations state that burning one's body incurs a *thullaccaya* offense and burning a finger incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense, how is it that this [sūtra] praises such acts?
Now, I shall answer this. The rules of permission and prohibition differ between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The Hīnayāna establishes prohibitions; the Mahāyāna enjoins burning.

Thus, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it says that if one does not burn oneself, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva. How could it be that [the Mahāyāna] only enjoins laypeople while prohibiting monastics? Therefore, we know that following the Hīnayāna practices is easy; what difficulty is there in not burning oneself?"

From the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it is difficult to burn away [defilements], for it is not easily done. If the world regards non-retention as "great," then both the small and the great will collapse together. To place one's hand upon the chest is called a *yi* (prostration).

When Lü Shiji first met the Lord of Pei, the latter was having two women wash his feet; Lü Shiji performed a long *yi* and did not bow. A long *yi* is said to resemble the gesture of bowing and then departing. Now, when it says "a long *yi* toward the world," it likewise conveys the sense of taking leave and severing ties.

If one does not perform this minor act of self-sacrifice, then even if one attains the unconditioned state, one will inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay past debts, just as it was with my own experience of horse-barley; the two cases are exactly the same and no different.

Zhaoxi said: Regarding the circumstances of the "Horse Barley" (aśvaka), the *Udānavarga-vyākhyāna* (*Xingqi xing jing*) states: In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Buddha was a brāhmaṇa who was extensively learned in the scriptures and taught five hundred youths.

Once, when a king hosted a feast and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, there was one bhikṣu who was ill and unable to attend. After the Buddha and the great assembly had finished eating and were returning, they requested food on behalf of the sick bhikṣu.

As they passed by the mountain of the brāhmaṇas, the brāhmaṇas smelled the fragrance of the delicious food and spoke with jealousy, saying: "These shaven-headed śramaṇas should properly eat horse barley; they should not [eat such fine food]."

Having partaken of this offering of sweet delicacies, he addressed the young boys. The boys said, "These masters should likewise eat horse fodder. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "The brahmin at that time was none other than myself;

the five hundred boys are now these five hundred arhats; and the sick bhikṣu was Maitreya Bodhisattva. Because of these causes and conditions, I and you all underwent countless thousands of years in the hells.
Although I have now attained the Way, due to the lingering karmic conditions of that time, I ate horse fodder for ninety days in the village of Verañjā."

Furthermore, the *Madhyamāgama* (Zhōngběnqǐ jīng) clarifies that in the city of Śrāvastī, within the district of Sūlana, there was a brāhmaṇa named Ajātaśatru who invited the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus to provide them with food for three months.

At that time, the brāhmaṇa was deluded by a celestial Māra; he became addicted to the five desires and withdrew into the inner palace. Since that district was suffering from famine, people did not favor the Way.

The Buddha and the bhikṣus each went out to beg for alms, but after three days they returned empty-handed. Then, a horse trainer offered barley-rice to the Buddha and the bhikṣus, and so forth. Changshui says: "As stated previously..."

"Mātanga appeared in a dream; who could have retained your physical form? Now you say that even if one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one must still repay past debts. This demonstrates that karmic retribution does not perish:

even after attaining the unconditioned, if a conditioned body still exists, one must still return past debts—how much more so for one who has not yet entirely left the conditioned, yet wishes to falsely evade the fruits of karma; how could that be possible?"

"You shall teach the people of the world to practice samādhi first, and only thereafter renounce stealing. This is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past."

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease stealing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup hoping to make it full; even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.
Tugxiang said: A *zhi* is a drinking vessel.

If various bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, and give whatever remains from their begged food to hungry sentient beings; if, at great assemblies, they join their palms and pay homage to the multitude; if someone strikes or reviles them, they regard it as equal to praise;

and if they ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished—sharing their very flesh, bones, and blood with sentient beings—they will not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and turn them back [to serve their own ends].
This interpretation has already misled beginners. Foyin (Buddha-seal) was a person who attained true samādhi. Xunwen says:

The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states that when begging for food, one should divide it into four parts: one part to offer to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), one part to give to the destitute beggars, one part to give to the various benevolent deities, and one part to eat oneself.

The first two lines, beginning with "superiors" (*upari-pudgala*), refer to the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*); the latter two lines, beginning with "one's own body and flesh," refer to the relinquishing of the body. This may also be understood as the relinquishing of the body.

At this juncture, one must eliminate the mind that clings to its own ability to renounce. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is easy to give up the body, but difficult to give up the mind. Tiaoxi remarked:

"Prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, all teachings outside the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) were of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*), for therein the provisional and the real had not yet been integrated. Now that they have been revealed and manifested, they are identical to the perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra*; how could one use what is incomplete to mislead beginners?

If one discards the real to adopt the provisional, merely using it to entice others to follow oneself—is this not a great thief of the Buddha-dharma? Changshui said: "One must not take the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*) and turn them back into one's own mind..."

The doctrine of solitary awakening uses this to delude ignorant beginners, enabling them to obtain "pure meat. It is only upon reaching the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) that all [meat] is prohibited.

Those who do not understand the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) take it to be the ultimate discourse. As the *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "Foolish ordinary beings, bitten by evil views and intoxicated by perversity and delusion, falsely claim that these were spoken by the Omniscient One. Huīguǎng’s commentary says:
"Those without wisdom do not understand that the Tathāgata’s teaching was spoken through skillful means (*upāya*), yet they falsely claim that the Omniscient One made this an ultimate statement."
What I have spoken is the teaching of the Buddha; to speak otherwise is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

Ānanda, although the sentient beings of the six realms in this world may have perfected the three practices of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexuality within their bodies and minds, if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity.
They will become demons of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata.

Gushan said: "If one internally craves fame and profit, desiring that others hold oneself in high regard, this constitutes the demon of attachment (*rāga-māra*). If one internally gives rise to false views, equating oneself with the sages, this constitutes the demon of views (*dṛṣṭi-māra*)."

This refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, and declare they have realized what they have not realized. Or, seeking worldly honor, supremacy, and preeminence, they say to others:

"I have now attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of an *anāgāmin*, the path of an *arhat*, the vehicle of a *pratyekabuddha*, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), or the various levels prior to the stages. Thus they seek the prostrations and repentances of others, coveting their offerings.

Xunwen said: "Not having attained the three fruits, and not having realized the stage of no-more-learning—this resembles the demon of views; or seeking inferior [attainments] is precisely the demon of craving.

Changshui said: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the 'Chapter on Perversions,' states: 'If someone says, "I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," for what reason? Because they possess Buddha-nature.

Since those who possess Buddha-nature will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it should be known that such a person commits a pārājika offense. For what reason? Although they possess Buddha-nature, because they have not yet cultivated the various skillful means of goodness, therefore...'"

They have not seen it. Because they have not seen it, they cannot achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, know that those who do not cultivate the abandonment [of afflictions] even in brief, yet claim for themselves to be Buddhas, are all uttering great falsehoods.
Having committed a *pārājika* offense, one is no longer a disciple of the Buddha.

Such a person is an icchantika who extinguishes the seed of the Buddha; like a man cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword, the Buddha declares that this person’s roots of goodness are forever destroyed and they will have no further knowledge or vision.
They shall sink into the ocean of the three sufferings and fail to achieve samādhi.

Gushan said: "The sin of great falsehood is equal to that of an icchantika. Xunwen said: "The form of the tāla tree is like that of the *zōnglǐ* (caryota); those that are tall reach seventy or eighty feet."
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest bodies within that age of the final dharma (mappō), assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra.

Whether appearing as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, officials, boys, or girls—even as prostitutes, widows, adulterers, thieves, butchers, or merchants—I shall engage in their common activities and praise the Buddha Vehicle, causing them to enter samādhi with body and mind.
Yet, I shall never say of myself, "I am a true bodhisattva" or "I am a true arhat," lest I reveal the Buddha’s secret cause and speak lightly of those who have not yet studied.

Changshui said: "The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) benefit sentient beings by performing various forms of transformation. First, one brings them to accord with the Way; later, one exhorts them toward the Buddha Vehicle. All of this is for the sake of beneficial transformation and not for the greed of self-interest. The *Shiyao* says:

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are as follows: First, giving, which involves both material and Dharma gifts to cause others to draw near to oneself. Second, kind speech, using gentle and compliant words to comfort those who receive the Path.
Third, beneficial conduct, benefiting others through the three karmas to inspire their reverence. Fourth, common purpose, engaging in various activities identical to theirs. The Supplement states:
"Leaking the Buddha’s secret causes" means that whenever a manifested transformation appears identical to ordinary beings, this constitutes a secret cause for becoming a Buddha.
"Except for at the end of life, when the *skandhas* (aggregates) are left behind.

Guishan said: "This was not intended to delude the public; it was merely shown privately to individuals. This refers to the words of Nanyue regarding the "iron wheel," the instruction on the "five grades" by Tiantai, the verse spoken by Guṇakāra, and Master Zhiguan counting on his fingers—these are precisely those instances.
Guyang said: "When Nanyue was approaching death, he said to his disciples: 'In my lifetime, I hoped to enter the copper wheel [stage] and lead followers...'"

It is too early. This would harm oneself while benefiting others; for now, it is merely the Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*). The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* uses ten wheels as metaphors for the stages: iron for the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), copper for the stage of abiding (*sthiti*), silver for the stage of practice (*pratipatti*), gold for the stage of penetration (*prativedha*), and crystal for the ground (*bhūmi*).

Maṇi and others. At Mount Nanyue, the purification of the six sense faculties corresponds to the stage of the ten rounds of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching. When Zhiyi was approaching death, he said to Zhilang: "I shall not lead a community; I must purify my six sense faculties.

Because I benefited others at the expense of myself, I have remained only at the level of the five stages. Guṇavarman—translated as "Armor of Merit"—was the son of the King of Kaśmīra. He arrived in Jiankang during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.

At the time of his death, he spoke a verse in Sanskrit and entrusted it to his disciple Hesaluo to be sent back to the Western Regions. Emperor Wen ordered it to be translated, and it was found to be from the Jambuvana forest.
The monk Zhen-guan of Tianzhu Monastery in Qiantang, during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, upon his death, bent two fingers to signify his attainment of the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin).
[Later], he bent three fingers to signify his realization of the third fruit (anāgāmin).
"How is it that such a person deludes sentient beings and commits a great falsehood?

You must teach the people of the world to practice samādhi and subsequently eliminate all great falsehoods. This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past."
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease this great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood; to seek its fragrance is impossible.

I teach the bhikṣus that in the dojo of the straightforward mind, even amidst all actions within the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense. How then can one claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person? It is like a pauper falsely styling himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution;

how much more so for a Dharma King to thus falsely usurp [the title]? If the ground is not true, the fruit will be crooked. To seek the Bodhi of the Buddha while in such a state is like a man trying to bite his own navel. He wishes—

Who achieves this? It is one who invites the fruit of the three miserable realms through circuitous karmic paths. *Xielin* says: "The metaphor of biting one's own navel illustrates that seeking Bodhi is beyond reach. *Xunwen* says:

In the sixth year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, King Wen of Chu was attacking Shen and passed through Deng. The Marquis of Deng said, "He is my nephew," and detained him to offer him a banquet. Zhai Sheng, Nian Sheng, and Yang Sheng requested that they kill the King of Chu. Deng... [text ends]

The Marquis would not permit it. The three nephews said, "The one who will surely cause the state of Deng to perish is this very man. If you do not plan for his removal early on, later Your Majesty will find yourself biting at your own navel"—a phrase meaning that once the situation has reached such a point, it is impossible to remedy.

If there are bhikṣus whose minds are as straight as a bowstring, who are entirely truthful, and who enter samādhi such that demonic obstacles never arise, I certify these people as having accomplished the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva.
What I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; if it were not spoken thus, it would be the teaching of Pāpīyān.
