Regarding your question on the gathering of the mind: I shall now first explain the sublime gateway for training in the entry into *samādhi*. Those who seek the Bodhisattva path must first maintain these four kinds of restraint with clarity and purity.
Like ice and frost, they cannot produce any branches or leaves themselves. "Three of the mind and four of the mouth" means that birth [in the higher realms] will certainly have no cause.

Zhenji said: "The three of the mind are greed, anger, and false views; the four of the mouth are lying, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. The former refers to "lying" (妄語) as being major, while this "false speech" (妄言) is minor;

or perhaps it merely cites the total number (though the total is said to be four, the specific instances are the latter three). Xunwen said: "The four parājikas are like the roots; the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas and so forth are like the branches and leaves. The former was based on the destruction of the precepts.

Regarding those roots of goodness, it is illustrated by the analogy of a person cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword. Now, in terms of upholding the precepts to extinguish the root of evil, it is therefore illustrated by saying that [the tree] cannot produce any branches or leaves on its own.

The "three of mind and four of body" constitute the essence of karmic actions such as the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (saṅghādisesa) offenses; they also encompass the preliminary and subsequent stages of the four *pārājika* (pārājika) offenses.

However, the delusions that arise simultaneously with greed, anger, and ignorance cannot be suppressed or severed without a concentrated mind (*samādhi*). Here, we speak only in terms of what is common to other chapters, for the purpose of stopping their coarse manifestations. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Precepts are like..."

"Arresting the thief" refers to discipline (*śīla*), which is like binding the thief; "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is like killing the thief. One should know that the three obstacles are all termed "thieves. That which is arrested by the observance of discipline is primarily karmic retribution, though it also includes the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Ānanda, if these four matters are not lost or neglected, the mind will not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; how then could any demonic activities arise?

If there are those whose past habitual tendencies cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct such persons to single-mindedly recite this unsurpassed divine mantra of mine, the Buddha-Usnīṣa-Vijaya-Mahā-sātrapatra.
This is the heart-mantra spoken from the crown of the Tathāgata’s invisible summit, the unconditioned mind-Buddha, who radiates light from his crown while seated upon a precious lotus flower.

Master Xunwen said: "Regarding 'past habituation' (*suxi*): in general terms, this encompasses all afflictions and karmas, such as the four heavy offenses, because they have been perfumed into seeds since beginningless time.

In specific terms, it refers precisely to the habituation to sexual desire, for it is the most difficult for ordinary beings in the realm of desire to guard against. How is this made clear? As the subsequent text specifically points to the habituation to affection between Ānanda and Mātanga;

furthermore, in the ritual chamber, one is instructed to place an image of Acala (Ucchuṣma), because this holy one had much greed in his past lives and attained perfect penetration by contemplating the sensation of warmth."

Furthermore, when Ānanda was previously overcome by lust, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to go and protect him with a mantra. Is there not a specific intention behind the fact that no other mantra was used? Changshui said:

"Although it was previously explained at length that his observance of the precepts was pure and clear as ice or frost, and thus he committed no new transgressions and was already free from demonic affairs, he still possessed the defilements and obstructions of beginningless habitual tendencies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Like a shadow following a form, these hindered the Way; whether it be frequent illness and vexation, excessive lust and anger, the interference of false teachers and demons, or the simultaneous arising of various calamities—all of these stem from the beginningless past."

It is unwholesome. For ordinary persons who have only recently begun their training, the power of the Path is weak and cannot dispel it; therefore, the Buddha possesses a sublime divine mantra that can extinguish the evil habits of past lives so that they no longer cause disturbance.

Through the power of the Way, one quickly achieves success without encountering discouragement. What was previously explained regarding concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is that they destroy the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); furthermore, it was clarified that the study of precepts (*śīla*) merely stops sinful karma.

Now it is taught that divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*) can destroy past calamities while simultaneously eliminating the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). If these three obstacles are truly eliminated, what need is there to wait for realization? The *Śìyào* states: "The observance of precepts merely blocks present karma;

however, if there are calamities from beginningless enmity or past misfortunes that cannot be dispelled, or if they arise within meditative concentration, even the three methods for subduing demons will not provide relief. Only by establishing a ritual site (*maṇḍala*), reciting mantras, and prostrating to the Buddha can one overcome them."
Thus, other powers can provide a remedy.

Furthermore, the karmic causes and conditions of your past lives with Mātanga, as well as the habitual tendencies of your affection over many kalpas, were not formed in a single lifetime or a single kalpa alone. When I proclaimed [the truth], your love was forever severed and you became Arhats.

Even she, a courtesan who had no intention of practicing, was secretly aided by my spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). How much more so for you, the Śrāvakas gathered here, who seek the supreme [enlightenment]?
In the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna), one is certain to attain Buddhahood; it is like scattering dust with the wind at one's back—what difficulty or peril could there be?

Regarding the "Perfuming of Hearing" (Xunwen), the *Nü jing* states that in the past, five hundred years ago, Ānanda was once her husband. That Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) scripture merely refers to what occurred in the recent past.

Zhaoxi said: "The eternal liberation from the heart of craving" refers to her initial hearing of the mantra. "Attaining the stage of Anāgāmin and becoming an Arhat" refers to the passage following Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect means of penetration (*avavāda*).

If this is so, since she only became one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) by virtue of hearing the Dharma, why speak of the "mysterious assistance of spiritual power"? This is because she secretly received the power of the mantra while manifestly relying on the sound of the Dharma; only through the internal support and external cultivation could she realize it so swiftly.

If it were due to the mantra alone and not the Dharma, why did it previously state that the Bhikṣuṇī Śailā became an Arhat upon hearing the verses? [In those verses] "dust" is used as a metaphor for past [afflictions].
Habits are like a divine spell. Just as dust is easily scattered when carried by the wind, so too is it not difficult to cast off habits once the spell has been recited to eliminate them.

If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they must first uphold the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu. They must select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher.

If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, their observance of the precepts will not be perfected. Once the precepts are perfected, they should don new, clean robes, burn incense, dwell in seclusion, and recite this.
Recite the Heart Sūtra’s Divine Mantra one hundred and eight times. According to the subsequent text, it states:

"First uphold the four parājikas and eight sikkhāpadas of the Śrāvaka, and subsequently practice the pure discipline of the Bodhisattva. Thus, the precepts currently upheld should encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

For those who have left the household life, apart from the inherently pure nature of the precept-substance (*śīla-skandha*), they must perform repentance to purify them; if they further receive the Bodhisattva discipline, their goodness will be even more enhanced. As for those remaining in the household, whether they have previously received the *upāsaka* [precepts]...

Regarding the precepts of practice (*pratipatti-śīla*): one may simply receive the Bodhisattva precepts, as there are laypeople (*avadātavasana*) who engage in correct cultivation. *Xunwen* states: "The *Sifen lü yi* says:

'If a disciple knows that the preceptor has violated the precepts, knows that one should not receive the precepts from such a person, and knows that although they receive them, they do not obtain the precepts—if one possesses such full knowledge, the reception is not accomplished; the opposite constitutes its accomplishment. Nanshan says:

'As for the other nine masters, there are no explicit texts in the Vinaya; they may be understood by analogy. As for what is taught in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, one must receive [the precepts] before a Dharma master who already upholds the Bodhisattva precepts.'"

If there is no one capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand *li*, one may receive them through a self-vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, provided that one seeks a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*).

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Now, this initial observance of the pure prohibitory precepts by a *bhikṣu* accords with the twenty-five methods of skillful means in *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. In the degenerate age, one must first maintain the purity of the precepts. Within the section on 'Purity of Precepts' in *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there are four points;

the fourth is named 'Purification through Repentance. The first point states: 'Both transgressions of the phenomenal and the noumenal obstruct *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, such that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do not arise. However, this is discussed in relation to the Hīnayāna."

Offenses have degrees of gravity: those that are light may be expiated, while those that are grave cannot be expiated. If one commits a grave offense, they are as dead within the Buddha-dharma; in the Hīnayāna, there is no method for expiating grave offenses.

However, according to the Mahāyāna, repentance is permitted, as explained in the *Four Kinds of Samādhi*. Regarding the "True Limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is said that reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times symbolizes the removal of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).

According to Xunwen, [the verse] "Suffering contains all [afflictions]" means that while the Truths of Origination and Cessation are free from the three views, the Truth of the Path removes two views. Furthermore, in the higher realms, hatred does not operate; this includes the ten innate [afflictions] along with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

108. Then, having established the boundary and set up the *maṇḍala*, one should pray for the Tathāgatas currently dwelling in the lands of the ten directions to emit the light of great compassion and pour it upon one’s crown.

Ānanda, if such pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors (*dānapati*) in the final age extinguish greed and lust and maintain the pure precepts of the Buddha, they shall give rise to the bodhisattva vows within the *maṇḍala*.

Whether entering or leaving, they bathe and practice the Way during the six periods of the day. Thus, without sleeping for twenty-one days, I manifest my own body before that person, stroke their head to comfort them, and cause them to attain awakening.

Gushan said: "The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent; he exists because the mind is pure. When the water is clear, the moon appears; response and resonance are spontaneous. If one perceives this sign, one should contemplate emptiness and stillness.

Then the Buddha will become manifest, whereas the māra will vanish. Xunwen said: "Regarding the *Zhengzhen* [Treatise], it states that whenever entering a dharma hall, if one does not rely on the Tiantai *Zhi Guan*, there is only fear that the heterodox and the orthodox will be difficult to distinguish.
That treatise is precisely the practice method for cultivating the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already attained awakening. I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

When establishing a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for cultivation during the Dharma-ending age, how should one perform the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) so as to accord with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the final age wish to establish a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa), they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fragrant herbs of those mountains.

This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle. One may take this dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the ox's dung will be foul and unsuitable for smearing the ground.

Otherwise, one should dig into the soil of a plain five feet deep and take the yellow earth, mixing it with sandalwood, aloeswood (agaru), *suhaka*, frankincense (*turuṣka*), saffron, and white [sandalwood]."

Take glue, *qing* (blue vitriol), *mu* (mushroom), *lingling* (calamus), *gansong* (spike-nard), and *jisheliangxiang* (clove); grind these ten ingredients into a fine powder. Mix it with earth to form a paste and smear it upon the ground.
Construct an octagonal altar, sixteen feet square in circumference.

Zhaoxi says: The former [term] refers to a "field" (*cháng*), as it is today; the latter, being called an "altar" (*tán*), must necessarily involve piling up earth to create it. Thus, one first clears the ground to form the field, and subsequently takes yellow earth mixed with incense to make mud.
Upon that field, one coats it with this mud, raising it to form the appearance of an altar. This involves clearing and sweeping. Zheng says: "To mound earth is called an *tán*;

to clear the ground is called a *shàn*. The *Guoyu* states: "The area cleared for an altar is called a *cháng*. "Piling up earth" is the same as "mounding earth," meaning to raise the boundaries of the mound. This is intended for placing offerings within the inner chamber.

The dimensions of the high and low [terraces] may be understood according to one’s own intention. Lord Jing said: "The nature of water is inferior to that of fire; it solidifies into high mountains. Mountains are earth, and earth is faith.

The Snowy Mountains are vast and expansive, where fragrant herbs and clear waters grow; this is a metaphor for the vast and expansive mind of faith. The great-power white ox is pure white and without admixture; although it possesses great power, it remains in accord with sentient beings."

This is an analogy for the Mahāyāna Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The rich, fatty fragrant grass symbolizes sublime goodness; the clear water symbolizes pure wisdom; and the dung symbolizes the residual remains. Just as sandalwood removes the heat and swelling caused by wind, it symbolizes the ability to eliminate suffering and affliction.
The pure and good Mahāyāna Buddha-nature relies upon vast faith and is nurtured and perfected by pure wisdom and sublime goodness; even its residual remains are not coarse or defiled.

It can harmonize and eliminate suffering and affliction. Its pure goodness adorns and completes the ground of the field of *nirvāṇa*. The level plain is a metaphor for the vast and impartial mind of one who has given rise to faith. The five colors above it, with yellow as the primary, are a metaphor for the Middle Way and right faith.

The ten fragrances are a metaphor for the ten *pāramitās*. Being able to reach the bottom of the abyss of wisdom constitutes the *prajñā-pāramitā*. That which sinks down to the very bottom of the water is *agarwood* (*candana*);

this represents the power of strength (*bala-pāramitā*), whether by the power of spiritual transformations, the power of wisdom, or the power of pure conduct, being fully endowed with all of them and able to travel far. *Candana* is either red or...

Whether black or white, the superior sandalwood is that which, at a single *zhū*, its fragrance is said to reach forty *lǐ*. By uniting the essence with the spirit, one obtains the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha; no demonic activities can obstruct or hinder this, serving as the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

*Suhak* (sugandha) kills ghosts and malevolent spirits, removing depravity and enabling communion with the divine; everything it enters becomes non-evil conduct, serving as the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).

*Ketu-candana* (chicken-tongue sandalwood) may be blended with various incenses, causing the body to be fragrant; it preserves refined wisdom and gives rise to clear vision, serving as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). *Jingling* (Zingiber officinale) can arrest the essence and brighten the eyes.

It is that which governs the mind, harmonizes the breath, eliminates toxins, removes malevolent influences, and extinguishes impurities to give rise to purity; it constitutes the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Turmeric (*uragasāra*) removes disturbances of the mind and breath, poisons from *gū* spirits, demonic possession (*jìù*), and foul odors.

To be free from the hindrance of sleep and to remain constantly aware whether awake or asleep constitutes the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). *Aśoka* wood can awaken those who suffer from nightmares and sleep.

To endure all things as if there were no sensation of pain constitutes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). *Bdellium* can alleviate pain. To eliminate bodily unwholesomeness and attain liberation, resulting in a complexion free from sores and blemishes, constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

*White glue* can remove foul odors from the body and eliminate sores and ailments. To harmonize the various perfections, causing all that is unreal within the multitude to be liberated from internal suffering, constitutes the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). *Spikenard* can harmonize various fragrances and eliminate [impurities].

It is for those who suffer from abdominal distension and seek to expel gas. If one cannot proceed as previously described, yet can give rise to right faith in the Middle Way with an impartial and expansive mind, and based upon these various *pāramitās* initiate pure practices, this will serve as a skillful means (*upāya*) for entering Buddha-nature and is sufficient to adorn the site of practice.
To grind fine hemp into powder and mix it with soil to form mud is analogous to using extremely subtle wisdom to combine with right faith in the Middle Way.

Regarding the "Purification of Hearing" (*Xunwen*), it states: "A square or circular area of sixteen feet is made into an eight-cornered altar; one should take a diameter of sixteen feet, which is precisely appropriate. This is like the ritual methods of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras)."
Furthermore, have an altar constructed, one zhang and six chi in length and breadth.

At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood. Upon the flower, set a bowl. Within the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month, and place whatever flowers and leaves are available within the water.

Take eight circular mirrors and place them at each of the cardinal directions surrounding the flower and bowl. Outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotus flowers; arrange sixteen incense burners interspersed among the flowers to adorn the site.
As for the incense burner: burn only aloeswood (agaru) so that the flames are not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels.

From the milk, prepare pancakes, along with various sugar-cane candies, oil cakes, milk porridge, storax (sugandhaka), honey, ginger, pure ghee, and pure honey—each of these in sixteen portions outside the lotus. Surrounding the exterior of the flower, offer these to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
Gu Xiangyun said: "The dew of the eighth month receives the full essence of yin energy. Changshui said: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not eat this food;

they manifest eating it in order to increase merit, so that practitioners may be endowed with both merit and wisdom and quickly attain perfection. It is like the Buddha accepting Cunda’s final offering, thereby enabling him to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā."
This is also done in this manner.
At every mealtime, or at midnight, take half a *śu* of honey and three *liǎng* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Before the altar, set up a small fire hearth separately.

Boil *turuṣka* incense to produce scented water, with which you bathe the charcoal until it blazes fiercely. Cast the clarified butter and honey into the flaming hearth and burn them until the smoke has vanished, thereby making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Xunwen says: "Dhūpa (兜樓婆香) was formerly called 'white mugwort incense' (白茅香). Gushan says: 'To offer' (享) means 'to sacrifice' (祭), or it is written as 'xiang' (饗). 'Xiang' means 'to incline toward' (鄉). Only after one has inclined toward [the deity] can they be offered to;
this means that one's heart is directed toward them. Through sacrifice, one is then received. Jing Gong says: "The altar is in the south, the ground of Perfect Enlightenment (正等覺地).

Five *he* of honey and three *he* of clarified butter (*sarpis*) are blended together in the ratio of three and five. A small brazier is set apart; for the coarse, one uses a large [vessel], but for the subtle, one uses a small. Dhūpa is a red incense, which harmonizes with the pure goodness of awakening."

Boiling it extracts the fragrant water, which corresponds to the awakening of pure wisdom (*jñāna*). Bathing its embers purifies the smoke of afflictions, corresponding to the awakening of the power of compassion (*maitrī*). Then, one causes it to blaze fiercely.

Thus, when one desires the blazing radiance, one offers ghee and honey, burning them until the smoke is exhausted; this signifies the extinguishing of desire and the total eradication of compounded afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).

At the time of eating, one engages with objects; at midnight, one discerns objects. During these two times, one partakes of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), uniting with the pure wisdom of awakening that is utterly purified.

Through the power of compassion free from attachment and views, the blazing radiance extinguishes compounded formations (*saṃskāra*) so that afflictions are brought to an end. This is the internal reason for partaking of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Have banners and flowers hung everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the sanctum of the maṇḍala, arrange images of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas upon the four walls.

Directly facing the entrance, display images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha. To their left and right, place images of the various great transformation-emanations of Avalokiteśvara, as well as Vajragarbha.
On the side of the door to the left, display images of Śakra and Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, Lambodara, the various Cundās, Bhṛkuṭī, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka.
Thus they are installed.

Changshui (Changshui Zongze) said: "Hang banners and arrange images so that each one casts its reflection in the mirror. This is intended to allow the practitioner to become thoroughly familiar with this realm, whereby the principle of the *dharmadhātu* of non-obstruction between phenomena (*śaśva-śaśva-anāvaraṇa-dharmadhātu*) will be easily realized.

At any time and in any place, within a single thought-moment, one traverses the ten directions, universally beholds all Buddhas, universally performs the Buddha-work, and universally receives offerings."

Nurturing. Once it is so for a single thought-moment, it is thus for every atom (*dharmadhātu*). Tiāoxī said: "In the Western Regions and Dangyang, [the orientation] always takes facing east as primary; regarding left and right, the right is honored and the left is inferior.

Ānanda, this is the subtle and wondrous chapter of secret verses from the *Śvetāra-bhadra-rāja-sarva-tathāgata-uṣṇīṣa-śītala-tārā*, from which all Buddhas of the ten directions are born.

By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). The Tathāgatas of the ten directions uphold this mantra-heart to subdue all Māras and to restrain all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Ten...

When the Tathāgatas mount this mantra-heart, they sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-heart, turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.
Changshui says: *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā* means "White Parasol. This refers to the hidden mind (*garbha-citta*). Because it does not correspond with delusive defilements, it is called "white.
Because it universally covers all phenomena, it is called a "parasol. Because the secret divine mantra flows forth from this, it is called the "mantra-heart.

Furthermore, as it is the essential core of all mantras, there is not a single Buddha who does not attain perfect enlightenment by means of this mantra, subdue demons and heretics, respond to various lands, and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. Xiaoxi says: Regarding the general term "mantra-heart," it is...

The preceding text states: "This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Unconditioned Heart-Buddha, who possesses the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown. Xunwen says: "This explains the 'Heart-Mantra' by means of the 'Heart-Mantra' itself. Yuan’s Commentary states:

"Because it flows forth from the Tathāgata-garbha heart, it is called the 'Mantra-Heart. Furthermore, it is said that this is the Dharma-gate of the heart-seal of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;

thus it is called the 'Mantra-Heart. It is also the essential dharma within the Secret Treasury; thus it is called the 'Mantra-Heart. This interpretation takes the essence of the mantra to explain the 'Mantra-Heart,' as stated by the Wise One (Zhiyi)."

There are three kinds of "mind" (*citta*): first, the mind of deliberation and cognition; second, the mind of grasses and trees; and third, the mind that accumulates the essential. Here, the "Secret Treasury" (*Guhyakośa*) carries the meaning of accumulation. The "mantra-mind" is the mind of the essential.

Now, "mantra" refers to incantation (*jūzo*), and it is also called "prayerful invocation" (*jūgan*). By means of these words, the Buddha invokes blessings for sentient beings to give rise to good, eliminate evil, transform from the ordinary to the sagely—just as one uses the "fruit-weak" incantation to transform the larvae of the *mingling*.

This is likewise a secret exposition of the meaning of *Śūraṅgama*, no different from the power and function of the preceding explicit teachings; it merely differs in its application to objects. —Tiantai.

The Fivefold Summary of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā. First, regarding the arousal of the great resolve (*mahācitta*). The term *citta* is a sound from India; in this land [of China], it is translated as "mind" (*xin*), which refers to the mind of deliberation and cognition.

In India, it is also called *haritaka*; in this land, this refers to the "mind" of plants and trees. Furthermore, it is called *yilida*; in this land, this refers to that which accumulates the essential [qualities] as the mind.

Regarding the single character "mind" (*citta*) in this sutra, one must trace it back to its Sanskrit original and translate it according to the specific context of the text; only then can the intimacy between the dharma and the metaphor be determined. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"This refers to the manifestation of the power of the divine mantra by way of the birth within the Buddha-realm. The first two lines provide a general explanation, while the subsequent section beginning with 'the ten directions' provides a detailed explanation. It says that because the Buddhas of the ten directions obtain this mantra, they realize the path through the eight phases of enlightenment.

That they initially rely on this 'Mantra-Mind' constitutes the gateway for entering the Path at the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), encompassing [the stages of] descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, and crossing [the river]."

The "city" and so forth represent the marks of attaining perfect enlightenment and realizing the Way. "Holding this mantra-heart" means that mantras have the meaning of destroying evil; internally, one holds the mind that destroys delusions, and externally, one subdues demons.

"Mounting" refers, at the very least, to the eighth stage of practice and the turning of the wheel of Dharma. The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that all phenomena are empty as the seat; here it is said that the Buddhas take the mantra-heart as the dharma from which they are born, which is likewise.

Thus, externally, they sit upon lotus flowers to respond to sentient beings. "Containing" has the meaning of being fully endowed with the Dharma; the mantra is complete with the thousand dharmas of the hundred realms.
Therefore, externally, it can manifest the great within a minute particle.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart; they can bestow the prediction of enlightenment by touching the crown of the head throughout the ten directions. Even before their own fruition is complete, they likewise receive the prediction of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

Relying on this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to rescue and deliver beings from the various sufferings throughout the ten directions—namely, those of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; the suffering of the blind, the deaf, and the mute; and the suffering of meeting with the hated and being separated from the beloved.

One shall be freed from the suffering of separation, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the blazing intensity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). All manner of calamities, both great and small, shall be simultaneously liberated. Perils from bandits, armies, kings, and prisons, as well as perils from wind, water, and fire, along with hunger, thirst, and poverty, shall be dissolved at the mere thought [of this mantra].

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, enable one to serve spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) throughout the ten directions and to make offerings according to one's wishes during the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*).
Among the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he is promoted as a Great Dharma Prince. "Holding" refers to the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*);

internally possessing the power of mindful retention, he is externally able to bestow predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "one whose own fruit is not yet accomplished":

this means that although the Buddhas of the ten directions have themselves entered the path from ordinary being to sage, they have only just begun to attain the partial fruits and have not yet perfected the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); therefore, they receive the Buddha's prediction. Bestowing predictions upon others while simultaneously receiving them for oneself must necessarily rely upon internal mindfulness.

It means "power" (*bala*). It takes the sense of "relying upon. One relies upon divine mantras for one's own practice, and one also relies upon them to transform others through the Way. It takes the sense of "serving. One serves divine mantras in one's own practice, and externally, one can serve spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth.

The Supplement states: Various texts speak of the "intense suffering of the five aggregates" (*pañcaskandha-duḥkha*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle eleven, asks: "What is called the intense suffering of the five aggregates?

The suffering of birth, up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—this is called the intense suffering of the five aggregates. These are the eight sufferings; the former seven are specific, while the latter one is general. Thus, there are five [categories].
Because the body is the locus where the *skandhas* (aggregates) flourish, there is great suffering. This is also as Laozi said: "I have a great affliction, which is that I have a body.

Thus, one must know that one must directly forget the self; fundamentally, there is no body that undergoes birth and death. It is not that it is absent because of some deliberate act; rather, it is because its original nature is non-existent. Guishan said:

The *Guanding jing* states, "There are nine major calamities and countless minor calamities. Xunwen said: The twelfth fascicle of that sutra says: "First, sudden illness; second, sudden verbal disputes; third, suddenly encountering government officials; fourth, the body..."

1. To be emaciated and lacking merit, yet to maintain the precepts without transgression, only to fall victim to the opportunistic machinations of ghosts and spirits. 2. To be unjustly robbed and stripped by bandits and thieves. 3. To be unjustly swept away or consumed by fire and water. 4.

To be unjustly devoured by various kinds of birds and beasts. 5. To be unjustly subjected to the curses, spells, and sorcery of enemies, or to be led astray by malevolent deities, receiving only calamity without attaining any merit.

6. To be led away by deceased ancestors; this is also called an untimely death. 7. To have an illness that is not treated, nor is merit cultivated, while the administration of decoctions and medicines is improper, and the application of acupuncture and moxibustion is ineffective.

They lose their proper measure and fail to rely on a true physician; thus, being caused by their illness, they perish. Furthermore, they place their faith in worldly sorcerers who cause them agitation through cold and feverish speech, and they recklessly expend their merit.

Their transgressions are many; their minds are naturally unrighteous and they cannot find stability. They resort to divination and seeking omens, slaughtering pigs, dogs, oxen, sheep, and various other animals, offering sacrifices to the spirits and summoning all manner of *māra* and ghosts to beg for blessings.
Yet, though they desire longevity, they ultimately cannot attain it. Foolish and deluded, they believe in heterodox and inverted views, and thus they die.

They enter hell, transmigrating within it without any time of liberation; these are called the nine untimely deaths. The Supplement states that in the phrase "to be struck by enemies and the like," the character *wei* (為) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Originally, those who performed false talismans and incantations to harm enemies instead attracted malevolent spirits; rather than obtaining the merit of avenging their grievances, they instead suffered the consequences thereof.

Those who caused terror, chills, fever, or delirium were led by such heterodox masters to produce deceptive words through the medium of these illnesses to frighten and agitate the patient. Regarding "divining to seek the cause": whenever one is ill, one inevitably seeks the underlying reason.

Regarding "offering petitions to the divine spirits": the character *jie* (解) is pronounced as *guǎi* (古買反); it means to resolve and disperse the illness. "Offering" (*zòu*) is like a Daoist master presenting a ritual petition (*zhāng*). *Nirvāṇa* is also... [text ends]

It is taught that there are nine types of untimely death. The "Chapter on the Noble Virtuous King" (*Nirvāṇa-guṇa-rāja-parivarta*) states: There are nine causes and conditions that can cause one’s life to be cut short prematurely.

First, knowing that food is unwholesome, one eats it nonetheless. Second, eating too much. Third, eating again before the previous meal has been digested. Fourth, not voiding excrement or urine at the proper times. Fifth, not following the instructions of the physician when ill.

Sixth, not following the instructions of the caregiver. Seventh, forcibly suppressing the urge to vomit. Eighth, wandering at night and being struck by malevolent spirits. Ninth, excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse.

Gu Xiangyun said: "In the past, because one's causes were not pure, one now encounters many instances of injustice and untimely death. By relying on the power of cultivating the mind and practicing the Way, and by depending on the merit of the secret mantras' hidden assistance, these injustices and untimely deaths are both eliminated, and each fulfills their natural destiny.

Furthermore, those deluded in the world generally hope for wealth equal to that of Yi Dun and for longevity like that of Rong Chengzi. They perform deeds as small as cicada wings in the morning and look for blessings as vast as hills in the evening;

yet they fail to realize that the power of the Sages provides hidden support, and instead claim that the words of the Buddha lack efficacy. The Dharma says: 'Can life be increased? It replies: 'By virtue. One asks: 'Is it not virtuous to turn back a cow [from a dangerous path]? "

[The interlocutor] said: "It is because of his virtue. [The Master] replied: "If it were someone like Hui or Nuo, who were cruel and treacherous, how could such a thing have happened? The commentary states: This means that the recurrence [of illness] is even more extreme.

Furthermore, even those among the Confucians who have attained eminence know of hidden benefits and do not harbor doubts regarding premature death or illness; how much more so for those who study Buddhism, who realize that the three realms are like flowers in the sky and perceive worldly affairs as dreams—what "wealth" or "longevity" could they possibly possess?
If this is so, then one who is able to uphold this sutra is truly free from shame regarding their virtue.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart; it enables them to gather and sustain their kinsmen and causes those of the Hīnayāna, upon hearing the Secret Treasury, to feel no alarm or fear.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart so that, after their parinirvāṇa, the affairs of the Buddha-dharma may be entrusted to others for ultimate maintenance, and the precepts may be strictly purified until all attain complete purity.

The term "practice and grasping" (*xingqu*) signifies the principle of the superior overcoming the inferior. Internally, one uses divine mantras to subdue one's own delusions and karma; externally, one is able to open the small to reveal the great. "Recitation" (*song*) signifies the meaning of moment-to-moment continuity (*kṣaṇa-anantara*).
Within this secret treasury of the mind, through moment-to-moment continuity, one accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way, sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and enters *nirvāṇa*.

Thus, it is possible to proceed from the cause through to the stage of fruition and reach the state of *nirvāṇa*. In this text, while explaining the meaning of penetration, it also encompasses the aforementioned accomplishment of the Way. The meaning of transmission and maintenance extends even until after [the Buddha’s] extinction, as in the previous chapter.

The nine [aspects] are identical to the characteristics of *nirvāṇa*. They may also constitute *anuttara-bodhi*, referring to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), which differs from the partial fruits (*fen-guo*).

Collectively, they are said to produce these eight aspects of the partial fruits of the First Abode (*prathamā-vihāra*). Guishan says: "However, all of these are esoteric explanations of the eternally abiding true mind (*zheng-chang zhen-xin*) that pervades the Dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*).
Therefore, there are various merits such as cause and effect, self and other, the production of good, the extinction of evil, merit, and wisdom."

If I were to recite this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Pāṭala Dhāraṇī from dawn until dusk, with the sounds linked together and the syllables and phrases never overlapping, it could not be exhausted even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, this dhāraṇī is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata."

For you who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, to resolve with such sincerity as to attain arhatship, yet fail to hold this mantra while seated in the place of practice (bodhimaṇḍa), thereby allowing your body and mind to remain far removed from all demonic activities—
such a thing is impossible.
Ānanda, if in any world, within any land, there are sentient beings who, according to what is produced in that country— whether birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk, or white wool—

write down this dhāraṇī and store it in a fragrant pouch; and if these people, their minds being dull and unable to recite or memorize it, either wear it upon their bodies or inscribe it within their homes, you should know that for as long as they live, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to harm them.

On the palm leaves of India and the paper and silk of this land, those who write and faithfully accept these mantras will not give rise to the three poisons and will remain far removed from all demons.
Ānanda, I shall now further expound this mantra for you; it protects and delivers the world, granting great fearlessness, and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all sentient beings.
The supramundane wisdom and the sublime mind of the Three Vehicles are realized instantaneously and all at once.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age are able to recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such sentient beings who maintain this through recitation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons.
Furthermore, no evil spells—whether from nāgas, devas, ghosts, spirits, terrestrial deities, or malevolent demons—can take hold of them. Their minds will attain...

In right concentration, all curses, spells, bewitchments, poisons—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the poisonous vapors of any object—that enter this person’s mouth shall turn into the taste of nectar.

No evil stars, nor any ghosts, spirits, or those with cruel hearts and poisoned minds, can give rise to malice toward such a person. Nor can the Vināyakas, the various evil kings of ghosts, and their retinues [do so].
All shall receive this profound grace and be constantly protected. Master Jing said:

"Sampatti (correct reception) is also called samādhi (correct concentration). The objective realm experienced within correct concentration is termed sampatti, as it differs from the objects perceived through ignorance. Regarding "samādhi-sampatti" in the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhicitta-uttaratantra-sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng), Xūnwén states:

"'Yà' refers to a ghost; Master Yìngfǎ says it is a name for a demon that brings inauspiciousness during sleep. To 'fù' (subdue) and accord with the human heart is called yà. 'Gǔ' refers to a pestilential spirit."

"Poisonous insects within the belly" (*fùzhōng gǔ*) refers to the practice of *gǔ* (poisonous magic) that administers venom. In the *Shēnglèi* (Classified Sounds), it is transcribed as "yì" (弋) with the tone reversed; this refers to creatures that harm human beings. In the *Zhèngfǎhuá jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), there is mention of "poisonous foxes" (*gǔhú*);
in the old *Wéimó jīng* (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra), there is "demonic *gǔ*" (*yāogǔ*). Master Yìng followed the phonology of the *Shēnglèi* for both. Now, however, we simply follow the reading "gǔ.

The *Bùyí* (Supplement) states that the *Fànwǎng jīng* (Brahmajāla-sūtra) also mentions "producing gold and silver poison," meaning these two substances mixed with poisonous flavors that damage things.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) *koṭis* of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas.

Each of these has a retinue of vajra-beings who attend upon them day and night. If there are sentient beings who, with a distracted mind and not in *samādhi*, merely remember it in their hearts and recite it with their mouths, these Vajra Kings will constantly follow those sons of good family;
how much more so for those whose bodhicitta is resolute! These Vajra Bodhisattva Treasury Kings, with their refined minds, secretly and swiftly manifest [their power].
That divine consciousness enables this person, at that time, to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons; they will thoroughly and universally know them, attaining freedom from doubt.
Xunwen says: "Nayuta" corresponds here to ten thousand *billion*; "Koṭi" corresponds here to ten million. See Master Ying’s *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings). Lord Jing said:

"Nayuta" corresponds here to the number *jing* (ten thousand million); "Koṭi" corresponds here to the number *yi* (hundred million). Regarding Vajragarbha-rāja, Cien translates *Śūraṅgama* as "Vajragarbha.

Thus, these bodhisattvas are named after this because they have realized this samādhi. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "The 'shading' (*yin*) of the mind is subtle and swift," meaning that Vajragarbha-rāja has attained the Tathāgatagarbha-mind; having removed delusions, it is pure essence, subtly hidden.

"Divine swiftness. This refers to the spiritual consciousness of that person who maintains the mantra. Xingfu said: "First, the ghosts and spirits receive grace; subsequently, they withdraw their traces and add their protection secretly.

From the first kalpa until their final existence, in every birth they shall not be born as yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and so forth—nor among any of the hungry ghosts, whether with form or without form, with thought or without thought.
Such evil states [shall not befall them]. If this son of good family reads, recites, copies, transcribes, or wears [this scripture]..."
If one conceals various material offerings, one will not be born into poverty, low status, or undesirable states in every kalpa.
According to the *Xunwen* (薰聞), *Pūtana* is translated as "stench-eater" (*chou'e*). *Kaṭapūtana* is translated as "bitterly strange stench-eater. *Kaṭa* is the same as *Kheṭapūtana*.
These are called the "Pungent-Odored Ghosts.
Even if these sentient beings do not perform meritorious deeds themselves, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall bestow all their merits upon such a person.

By virtue of this, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), unspeakable (*anabhilāpya*), and beyond description—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas. Their immeasurable merits will be like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits, cultivated together in that same place forever.
There is no dispersal;
it is like a cluster of akṣa fruits. This metaphor signifies that there is no dispersal from the Buddhas.

Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of virtue; it enables those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; and it enables those who lack diligence to achieve diligence, as well as those who lack wisdom.
This causes those who lack wisdom to attain it, and those who are not pure to quickly attain purity. Those who do not maintain the fasts and precepts will spontaneously fulfill them.

Tiaoxi says: "Regarding the time before one has received and maintained [the precepts] refers to the period after having committed a violation of the precepts, but before having undergone repentance and receiving them again. This is said with reference to laypeople;
the two groups of the ordained are discussed separately in the following text.

Ānanda, when these sons of good family uphold this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all offenses of breaking the precepts—regardless of whether they are light or heavy—are extinguished at once after upholding the mantra.

Even if they should happen to drink alcohol, eat the five pungent roots, or consume various kinds of impure things, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, and spirits will not regard these as transgressions.

Even if one wears impure, tattered, and worn-out clothing, whether walking or standing, one is entirely equal to those who are pure. Even if one does not construct an altar, enter a *dharma*-hall, or practice the Way, by reciting and upholding this mantra, it is identical in merit to entering an altar and practicing the Way;

there is no difference between them. If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) or the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of monks and nuns, once this mantra has been recited, such heavy karma will be completely eradicated—just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand—leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind.

Xunwen says: The *Jingchao* (Essential Commentary) cites a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*: "In terms of location, excluding only the northern continent; in terms of persons, excluding the Śiśumāra. [The offenses consist of] four bodily actions and one vocal action; three are killings and one is false speech.

One is the preparatory act for killing. Maturation occurs over one *kalpa*. Suffering increases in accordance with the increase of the offense. The eight bhikṣus are divided into two groups to constitute the 'schismatic saṃgha,' and so forth."

The Supplement states: Regarding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), in terms of location, the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) is excluded; in terms of person, the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) is excluded. Four belong to bodily action (*kāya-karman*); the schism of the Saṃgha belongs to vocal action (*vāk-karman*). Three belong to killing;

the schism of the Saṃgha consists merely of false deception, while shedding the blood of a Buddha is merely the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of killing—a crime of preparatory application—and not a completed primary offense, because a Buddha cannot be killed.

One heinous crime results in the retribution of the Avīci Hell for one *kalpa*. "Matured" means being born there. As the offenses increase, the suffering increases; thus, one who commits two heinous crimes should receive two *kalpas*, and so forth. [This applies to] the eight types of monks.

Second: speaking in the absolute minimum, originally there were eight bhikṣus who constituted the entire assembly; they split into two groups and mutually disputed right and wrong. Four or more individuals constitute a formal assembly (saṃgha).

Therefore, it is explained by way of the eight bhikṣus: namely, those who kill their father, kill their mother, kill an arhat, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, shed the blood of a Buddha, Devadatta, and the one who seeks to learn the ways of causing a schism in the Saṃgha and shedding the blood of a Buddha.

Regarding the shedding of the blood of a Buddha: while the Buddha was staying at Lake Anavatapta, he said, "I was walking up and down on Vulture Peak Mountain when Devadatta raised a stone from the high cliff and hurled it at my head.
A mountain deity caught the stone with his hand, but a small fragment splintered off and fell, wounding the Buddha’s toe. Thus it is said.

In the *Karmavarga* of the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is stated that "eunuchs" (*ṣaṇḍha*) refers to those who are impotent. Regarding the inhabitants of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and eunuchs, because their parents have little affection for them as children and thus lack a sense of profound gratitude, these acts do not constitute immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).

Four [offenses] belong to the body and one to vocal action (*vākkarman*). The first four belong to bodily action; the schism of the Saṃgha belongs to vocal action. Three are killings and one is false speech; the schism of the Saṃgha is one instance of false speech. One is the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of killing that results in drawing blood from the body of a Buddha;
because the body of a Tathāgata cannot be harmed, one incurs the offense of the preparatory stage of killing, but not the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*).

It ripens for one *kalpa* in the Avīci hell; as the offenses increase, the suffering increases. One phrase clarifies the time and place; one phrase clarifies the increase in suffering. Depending on how many heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) one has committed, one experiences the Avīci hell for a long duration; this is because of the multiplicity or the completeness [of the offenses]. [The schism] is divided among eight bhikṣus.

Second, regarding the saṃgha that is to be split: there are two types of schism in the saṃgha, namely, the schism of the Wheel-turning Saṃgha (*dharmacakra-saṃgha*) and the schism of the Ritual Saṃgha (*karmasaṃgha*). The Wheel-turning Saṃgha exists only during the lifetime of a Buddha; the Ritual Saṃgha exists both during the lifetime of a Buddha and after his parinirvāṇa.

To split the Wheel-turning Saṃgha requires nine persons because a Buddha is present; to split the Ritual Saṃgha requires eight persons. This is because eight bhikṣus are divided into two groups: four constitute the orthodox assembly and four constitute the heterodox assembly.
Furthermore, there must be those who commit the same type of grave offenses, such as the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).

Ānanda, if there is a leader of a multitude who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas past, has accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstructions that have remained unrepented since previous lives—

if such a person can read, recite, copy, or wear this dhāraṇī upon their body, or place it within their dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then these accumulated karmas will be dissolved like snow melting in boiling water, and before long they shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The *Universal Worthy’s Contemplation Sūtra* says: "All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them. Now, the power of this mantra is likewise so.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who have not yet borne sons or daughters and wish to conceive, if they can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Śītavana-tārā* [mantra] upon their bodies, they will give birth to sons or daughters endowed with merit and wisdom.
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who wish for the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall quickly attain them.

It is perfected. Their physical life, complexion, and strength are likewise so. After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows; they will certainly not be born in border regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.
If at the end of life one can still be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas according to one’s vows, how much more so will one obtain what is sought in this world?

Ānanda, if in various kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages there is famine, pestilence, or the calamities of war, bandits, and strife—indeed, in any place of such misfortune—write down this divine mantra and install it at the four gates of the city, as well as at all *caityas*, or upon the tops of towers.
Cause all sentient beings within that kingdom to welcome this mantra with reverence, prostrating and paying homage to it.

With single-minded devotion, make offerings to it, causing each of the people to wear it upon their person or to place it within their respective dwellings; thus, all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished.

Zhaoxi says: *Cetiya* is translated as "spiritual shrine" (*lingmiao*), or alternatively as "place worthy of offerings. It is further said that if it contains *śarīra*, it is called a *stūpa*; if it does not contain *śarīra*, it is called a *cetiya*.

For example, the *Āgama* mentions four sites of significance (the *zhizheng*—pronounced *zhīyǐ*): namely, the place of the Buddha’s birth, the place where he attained enlightenment, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and the place of his parinirvāṇa. Zizhong [Dao]tuo says: *Jaya* is a Sanskrit term; it is translated as "banner" (*dang*).
Ānanda, wherever in any land there are sentient beings who possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons; the five grains will be abundant;

and the myriad people will be peaceful and happy. Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars; transformations and calamities according to the directions shall not arise; no one shall suffer untimely death; fetters, shackles, stocks, and manacles shall not touch their bodies;
they shall sleep peacefully day and night, and never have evil dreams.

The five grains refer to hemp, foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, wheat, and beans. Ten billion is called a *zhào*. Where the Noble Dharma resides, even evil dreams do not occur, let alone other calamities or misfortunes.

Ānanda, in this Sahā world, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous transformations and malevolent stars; twenty-eight great malevolent stars act as their leaders, and furthermore, eight great malevolent stars serve as their sovereigns.

When they manifest in various forms appearing in the world, they can produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings. Wherever this mantra exists, they shall all be extinguished. Twelve *yojanas*...
The ground of the boundary established for ten days cannot be entered by any evil calamities or portents. Changshui says:

"The eight great malevolent stars refer to Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the comet. Although there may be auspicious constellations, they turn into disasters. Regarding the nine planetary deities (*navagraha*), excluding the sun and moon, one takes Rāhu and Ketu as the eight.
The *Mayūra-vyamsaka-sūtra* states: "The sun, the moon, and Mars; Mercury, Saturn, and Venus; Jupiter, Rāhu, and the comet—these are all called the planetary deities (*graha*). This is because...

"Ten" (*daśa*) is correctly called *yojana*; this is translated here as "should be calculated together," meaning that such a measure should be reckoned as a whole. Alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent for this term;

rather, it refers to a lodging where a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) halts during his tour of inspection, similar to the guesthouses and postal stations (*gongdi*) of this region. However, those *yojanas* vary in size: they may be forty *li* or twenty *li*. Among the various sūtras and śāstras, the smaller figure is generally used. The Supplement states:

according to the classics and histories, an omen that first appears regarding matters of good or ill fortune is called a "portent" (*xiang*). The *Yixun* says: "When Yi Zhi was the minister to Taiwu, there were [omens] at Bo..."
Auspiciously, the mulberry and the oak grew together at the court.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has proclaimed this mantra to protect all beginners and practitioners in future ages, so that they may enter samādhi, their bodies and minds become serene, and they attain great peace and stability.
Furthermore, no devas, māras, ghosts, spirits, or the karmic debts of past offenses and calamities accumulated since beginningless time shall come to cause you harm.

You, along with all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, by relying on my maṇḍala and upholding the precepts according to the Dharma, and receiving the precepts from a pure monk, shall not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart.
If these good sons do not attain mental penetration within this body born of their parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.
Xunwen said: "One obtains its benefits only by fulfilling four conditions: first, relying upon my ritual altar; second, upholding the precepts according to the Dharma;

third, receiving the precepts from a preceptor who is a pure monk; and fourth, harboring no doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart. Those who memorize and maintain this mantra should reflect for themselves whether these four conditions are complete or deficient.

If the first condition is not fulfilled, one will be ignorant of the third; yet if one upholds the precepts without doubt, can one not exert oneself? Every time I read to this point, grief fills my breast. Although I am diligent in oral recitation, furthermore—"

If one’s mind has attained penetration yet does not reach [the goal], how can one know that what follows will not be as described in the scriptures? Tiāoxī says: "Mental penetration consists of no more than three meanings. First is the realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*): this refers to sitting upright for a hundred days;

those with sharp faculties may attain the stage of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats. Second is the development of understanding (*adhimukti*): this means that even if one’s physical body and mind have not yet achieved the holy fruit, one knows with certainty that one will become a Buddha without error.

Third is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajātismaraṇa*): this means that such a person, at that time, is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons, comprehending them all thoroughly."
Having understood that there are no obstacles or delusions,

and having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of vajras in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "In accordance with what the Buddha has taught,
we shall protect with a sincere heart those who thus cultivate bodhi."
At that time, Brahmā-rāja, Śakra-devendra, and the Four Great Kings also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with our whole hearts and utmost sincerity, ensuring that everything they do throughout their lives will accord with their wishes."
Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, and the great ghost kings and ghost commanders of the pinayakas;
these also join their palms before the Buddha and pay him homage. I, too, vow to protect and sustain this person, causing their bodhicitta to quickly reach full perfection.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Sun and Moon Devas, as well as the Masters of Wind, Rain, Clouds, and Thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and others—the officials who cycle through the years and the retinues of all the stars—who also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the Way, establishing them in the site of enlightenment so that they may attain fearlessness."

The Supplement states: "When Yin and Yang interact, they condense to form thunder; lightning is the radiance of thunder. As for what is called the 'Master' (Shi) and the 'Elder' (Bo), there must be divine beings presiding over them."

Furthermore, there were immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, as well as the spiritual essences of all lands, waters, and those that move on land, by water, or through the air, together with the Wind Kings and the gods of the formless realm.

Simultaneously bowing their heads before the Tathāgata, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi and forever remain free from the works of Māra."

Zhaoxi said: "The gods of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) merely lack coarse form (*audārika-rūpa*), but it is not that they lack subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*). Therefore, there are instances of them prostrating and addressing the Buddha. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

'If the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception and so forth were without form, how could they have coming and going, or advancing and halting? Such meanings belong to the realm of the Buddhas and are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

The *Antarābhava Sūtra* also says: 'The gods of the Formless Realm prostrate to the World-Honored One. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'The olfactory faculty of a Bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the Formless Realm. The *Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī Sūtra* says:"

The heavens of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) rain down various fragrant flowers. As stated in the Āgamas, when Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, tears fell from the sky of the Formless Realm like fine spring rain. Thus we know that the Formless is not entirely devoid of form.

The biased calculations of people in the past were not only dark regarding the Mahāyāna, but they were also ignorant of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). When the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that this is "not known by the two vehicles," it does not mean they know nothing at all;

rather, it means they have not yet understood the characteristics of subtle form. The *Supplement* says: "Whether form exists or not in the Formless Realm cannot be calculated one-sidedly; one must investigate the attainment of the three realms."

This name is derived from its relative position above and below. It is designated by focusing on one side; yet, when discussed comprehensively, the absence of desire implies one has already transcended the three realms (*tridhātu*), and the absence of form implies one has already departed from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
If one were to say that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks the aggregate of form, it would be merely following the conventional name of that realm and thus a partial conceptualization.

*Nirvāṇa* is not something known by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for the analytical discernment of form within the formless realm belongs to the wisdom of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). Furthermore, the devas of the formless realm are not listed among the celestial hosts; their inclusion among the miscellaneous assembly is because they lack physical form.

Because they belong to the same category as those mentioned previously, they are discussed here in conjunction with the formless wind-spirits; thus, they are included among the miscellaneous [categories]. If there were subtle forms within the formless realm, then even the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of a Lesser Sage (*hīnayāna-ārya*) should be able to perceive them.

Why, then, is it stated that they are not objects of their knowledge? One should perhaps fear that the divine eye of the Lesser Vehicle perceives only general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). If it concerns the coming and going or the movements [of beings], these cannot be known by the two eyes—the divine eye and the Dharma-eye—of anything other than Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, we, like those of our kind, have long accomplished the meritorious works required for bodhi and shall not enter nirvana; we shall constantly follow this teaching to protect and deliver those in the final age who practice samādhi and cultivate correct cultivation.”

“World-Honored One, if those who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration—whether they are in a place of practice, on their walking path, or even when their minds are distracted as they wander through villages—we, the members of our assembly, shall constantly follow and attend upon such persons.
Even if Māra or Maheśvara seek an opportunity to harm them, they shall ultimately find none.

Lesser spirits and ghosts shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous people, with the sole exception of those who have resolved to joyfully cultivate meditation. World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or their retinues wish to come and harass these virtuous people, I [shall protect them].”
With a precious vajra, he shatters their heads into mere dust, constantly ensuring that whatever this person undertakes accords with their wishes. Gu Shan says:

"The aforementioned multitude of spirits have all attained the fundamentally wondrous mind and abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; they are able to establish great principles and manifest in the forms of bodhisattvas, devas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth."

This is for the purpose of protecting the practitioner; as for the statement that one's head is shattered by a precious vajra, it is because when Great Sages instruct sentient beings, they sometimes employ methods of gathering and receiving, and sometimes employ methods of subjugation.
Thus, the various evil ones are either moved by their kindness or intimidated by their majesty; through these two paths, all are led to liberation.

Now, by employing subjugation, they cause them to fear their majesty—just as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of killing the icchantikas, the *Lotus Sūtra* of destroying all afflictions and disturbances, and the cases of Xianyu’s execution of those of pure conduct and Zangman’s slaughter of sentient beings—all of which arose from abiding in unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*).

Only those on the Stage of the Single Child (Ekaputrabhūmi) can act in this way, for they regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their only child. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that one who dwells in the second stage achieves the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Their compassion does not abide in the joy [of the third stage], but dwells in the Stage of the Single Child; their equanimity (*upekṣā*) dwells in the stage of emptiness and equality. All of these are attained through partial realization (*praticchaka-satya*), yet externally manifest as subduing measures.

Regarding the passage from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* which states: "One incurs sin by killing a single ant, but incurs no sin by killing an icchantika," the commentary explains: Killing an ant is a transgression because it is an innocent being; killing an icchantika is beneficial because such a person deludes the masses. — *The Lotus Sūtra*.

The rākṣasī addressed the Buddha, saying: "If anyone does not comply with my incantation and disturbs or disrupts those who preach the Dharma, their head shall shatter into seven pieces, like the branches of an *ari* tree.

The Supplement states: "The *ari* tree does not exist in this region [of China], and thus it is not translated. This tree resembles the *lǎnxiāng* (lan-xiang) plant; its branches will inevitably break into seven pieces if they fall to the ground. This is recorded in the *Cí'ēn dàcǎo* (Great Drafts of Cí'ēn).
The *Nirvāṇa-saṃyukta-āgama* states: In a past life, the Tathāgata was a king named Śakrāditya. Because five hundred brāhmaṇas did not believe in the Mahāyāna, the king killed them all.

Due to this slander of the Dharma, he fell into hell. Once born there, three thoughts arose in him: he knew it was hell; he knew it was caused by slandering the Dharma; and he knew it was due to the king’s execution of them. He then changed his mind and reproached himself.

Instantly, he left the hell and was reborn in the buddha-field of King Amṛtadundubhi, where he obtained a lifespan of one kalpa. The character *lù* (戮) also means "to kill"; the character is also written as *lù* (僇). This is from the Chinese translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, regarding Sudhana’s arrival at the city of Pūrṇakūṭa.
He fulfilled the king’s command. He saw immeasurable sentient beings who had violated the king’s laws, their bodies bound with the five fetters;

some had their hands and feet cut off, some had their ears and noses sliced off, some had both eyes gouged out, some had their heads severed from their bodies, some were thrown into boiling ash, and some had their bodies wrapped in layers of cloth, doused with oil, and burned with fire. Sudhana asked, "How do you practice the Way? He replied, "I have attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Illusory Transformation.

There are ten-fold evil sentient beings who cannot be transformed through ordinary means; I manifest as suffering to subdue them, causing them to abandon evil, to become endowed with goodness, and to attain happiness, thereby inspiring them to resolve upon enlightenment."
"Possessing all-encompassing wisdom, you should know that I do not give rise to a harmful mind even toward an ant, much less toward a human being.

Ānanda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We were ignorant and simple, fond of mere erudition, and had not yet sought liberation from our defiled minds.

Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained the correct method for renewed cultivation; our bodies and minds are refreshed and delighted, and we have gained great benefit."

“World-Honored One, when one has thus cultivated and realized the Buddha-samādhi, yet has not yet reached nirvāṇa, why is this called the stage of ‘dry wisdom’? From what point among the forty-four minds does one gradually attain the vision of cultivation?

To which place must one go to be said to have entered the stages? And what is meant by an ‘Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva’? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground.
The great assembly, with single-minded devotion, waited for the World-Honored One’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with wide-eyed, fixed attention.

Tiaoxi said: "There are two intentions behind Ānanda’s request. First, since he has received the practice-gate (xingmen), there must necessarily be stages and positions within it; just as one who enters a house through its gate must know the depth and arrangement of the halls and rooms, he therefore makes this request.

Second, at the beginning of the sutra, the Buddha told Ānanda: 'Because the mind and speech are direct, from the beginning to the end of the stages and positions, there will forever be no signs of deviousness.

While the previous explanation—that the resolution of practice and realization is seamless—implies that the mind and speech are direct, the fact that the stages and positions are free of deviousness remains unknown in its specific manifestations. It is for this reason that he requests [further clarification]. This has not yet reached Nirvana."
This refers to the ultimate *nirvāṇa* and the sequence by which one attains the vision of practice. This question concerns the correct practice for entering the stages (*bhūmi*).

According to the three types of gradual sequences explained below, the first consists of eliminating its auxiliary causes, namely the five pungent herbs; this is not yet the primary practice. Upon reaching the second, one excises its primary nature, namely the mind of lust.

For this reason, by practicing *samādhi*, one can attain the third stage, which opposes current karmic activities, leading even to the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, the second gradual sequence is called "True Cultivation," which is precisely the title for the practice. It should be...

One knows *nirvāṇa* as the destination reached; the various stages (*bhūmi*) as the path traversed; and spiritual practice as the steps taken upon it. When these three factors are complete, the task of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* teaching is finally fulfilled.

Changshui said: "Abiding has causes and effects; afflictions have coarseness and subtlety; wisdom has clarity and dullness; severance has shallowness and depth; and realization has partiality and fulfillment."
There are distinctions of superiority and inferiority. If one is ignorant of this principle, it is not true cultivation; one falls into the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

Because within my teaching there are differences in the excellence or deficiency of progress, virtue, and the cultivation of practice, fifty-seven stages are established that enter gradually and deepen progressively. This differs from the external paths and celestial demons (*māra*), which possess no ultimate fruit of *nirvāṇa* whatsoever—that is, no destination reached by these stages. The stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*) is the initial cause.

The stages of "Faith," "Abiding," "Practice," and "Direction," along with the four levels of preparatory application (*prayoga*), are called the forty-four minds; these constitute the stage of faith, understanding, and practice, and are termed "cultivation. First...

From the stage of the path of seeing up to equal enlightenment is termed "entering through realization," which is the partial realization of the fruit. Although one knows the names of the various stages, one has not yet been able to discern the meaning of those names or the characteristics of the practices for cultivation and realization;
therefore, this question is asked. This [passage] demonstrates that [the interlocutor] does not understand.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future末 (mò) ages who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna—from the stage of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) up to Great Nirvāṇa—a suspended demonstration of the unsurpassed path of correct cultivation. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
Zhaoxi said: "To 'excavate' (kū) means to remove. One removes deluded thoughts in order to receive the True Teaching.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'You should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; fundamentally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings.'"
Because of delusion there is birth; because of birth there is extinction. Birth and extinction are termed "delusion. Changshui says:
