when the power of such recollection is perfected, they are able to know those objects—this is merely the worldly supernormal knowledge of others' minds and past lives. Zizhong said: "Those who 'consume and ingest' eat hemp seeds."

These are of that category. As for "metal and stone," it refers to the ability to transform the bones into immortality. The use of "solid metal and stone" is also spoken of in terms of ingesting medicinal elixirs.

This is because those who attain the ten types of transcendence all achieve success through the preservation of mental visualization (*saṃkalpa*) and the fortification of the physical form. Those who practice the "five penetrations" (*pañcābhijñā*) are individuals who have attained the penetration of the divine transcendents (*ṛṣi*). As for those who practice "transcendence by cessation," their transformations are unceasing, such as the class of "corpse-liberation" (*śavotsarga*).

According to the *Zhen'gao* (True Declarations) of the Daoist school, there are two paths: the Yin path and the Yang path. If one refines the form so that the Way is harmonized, and the respiration becomes purely Yang, then the physical body itself will gradually undergo transformation.

It sheds its skin; having shed it, it becomes even more wondrous. The body enters the formless, and the skin shed is exactly like the shell of a cicada. After this transformation, because there are no longer bones or marrow, even if one is buried in a tomb, only the sword, shoes, sandals, and staff remain.

This is the "transcendence by means of the Yang" (yángdù). As for "transcendence by means of the Yin" (yīndù), this refers to the terrestrial immortals (lùxiān). Regarding the phrase "awakening and perfect realization," it means severing the functions of sight and hearing so that one is like withered wood.

Regarding the phrase "the firm and the meeting," it refers to the *I Ching* saying: "When male and female meet their essence, the myriad things are transformed and born. The *Biographies of Divine Immortals* (*Shénxián zhuàn*) says:

This is precisely the kind of thing Zhang Zhi taught regarding the arts of the inner chamber. The *Qiqiu chao* states: "Zhang Ling exhorted people to practice the arts of the inner chamber, yet the *Zhen'gao* repeatedly censures the impurity of the red and white vital energies and such debased matters.

Now, if those who practice the refinement of the essence were of this sort, they should be as described in the following text: only those whose minds do not wander toward sexual misconduct can enter this realm.

Because their practice is inferior, they rank below the heavenly realms. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "As for 'ingestion,' it refers to cinnabar and hemp seeds; therefore, [they belong to] the earth..."

The Practice of Flying: Grasses and trees provide only pine and cypress for sustenance; thus one attains lightness of movement. Refining gold and stone can transform the bones; thus one travels through the human world, drifting as if merely lodging there.

"Movement and stillness" refers to the spirit moving while the body remains still; after a long time, one is able to tread upon emptiness. Firmly retaining the vital essence and keeping the spirit secluded, one does not interact with the realm of desire; this is roughly analogous to the heavens. The Practice of Penetration: Having already spoken of inhaling the pure essence, one thereby penetrates the profound mystery.

The Practice of the Way refers to the way of incantations and arts. The Practice of Illumination refers to knowledge of past lives and the minds of others. The Practice of Refinement employs arts within the chamber. The Practice of Severance is the severing [of worldly ties].

Regarding thoughts and perceptions: however, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are also able to practice dhyāna and attain supernatural powers (abhijñā). For instance, among the ten classes of ṛṣis, those who travel on the earth or fly through the air possess the supernormal power of bodily mastery (kāya-vaśitā-abhijñā). As for the ṛṣis who illuminate their conduct:

Since it is said that "firm and steadfast mindfulness" constitutes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), then within the practice of illumination, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and knowledge of past lives all possess the sense of illumination. Master Jing said:

The Earth-Walking Immortals (*bhūcarāḥ siddhāḥ*) can prolong their lives but cannot fly. The Flying Immortals (*khecarāḥ siddhāḥ*) can fly but cannot travel at will. The Wandering Immortals (*vicarāḥ siddhāḥ*) can transform themselves as they travel.

The Space-Walking Immortals (*ākāśacarāḥ siddhāḥ*) can solidify their vital breath (*prāṇa*) and leave behind their physical forms. The Heaven-Walking Immortals (*divicarāḥ siddhāḥ*) act without lust; they share the same virtue as the heavens. The Universal-Walking Immortals (*sarvacarāḥ siddhāḥ*) are able to harmonize the two essences (*bindu*).

The Way-Walking Immortals (*mārgacarāḥ siddhāḥ*) are able to expound the spontaneity of the Dao through ritual methods. The Illumination-Walking Immortals (*jñānacarāḥ siddhāḥ*) are able to maintain silent illumination through contemplative awareness. The Essence-Walking Immortals (*sāracarāḥ siddhāḥ*) are able to stabilize themselves by gathering and refining their essence.

The "Juexingxian" (Transcendent of Cessation) merges with those among the twelve classes of beings who correspond to his own kind. Xunwen says: According to Liu Xie’s *Miehhuo lun* (Treatise on Extinguishing Delusion), the Daoist establishment of the Dharma comprises three grades:

the highest designates Laozi; the next describes the Transcendents (*shenxian*); and the lowest follows Zhang Ling, taking the Most High (*Taishang*) as its宗 (patriarchal source). Examining the records of the Grand Scribe (*zhushi*) and the excellence of his reclusive seclusion, we find that only the Great Sage composed books to discourse upon the Way.

Its value lies in non-action (*wuwei*); its principle returns to stillness and silence; its transformation is rooted in emptiness and flexibility. Nevertheless, it does not record the three periods of time, nor is the cultivation of wisdom (*huiye*) heard of therein. This is indeed an excellent book for both the secular and the monastic.

[This is] not a sublime scripture of world-transcendence. [Question: The Way of the Immortals contains the principle of longevity and immortality; it ought to rank above Laozi. For what reason did Liu Xie suppress it into the Middle Grade? [Answer:

Where there is name but no reality, the gentleman does not accept it; how could there be any suppression? Thus Mouzi said: "The books on immortals such as Wang Qiao and Chi Song—when one listens to them, they flow profusely and fill the ears;

yet seeking their efficacy is like grasping at the wind or catching a shadow. He further said: "Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius each did not live for a hundred years, yet in this degenerate age, the foolish..."

How deluded! To wish to take elixirs and abstain from grain in order to seek eternal life—how pitiable! Formerly, the eminent monk Tanluan, desiring to seek the methods of the immortals to prolong his lifespan, went to the south to the abode of Tao Yinyun to seek them.
Having obtained ten scrolls of such texts, he was about to arrive at Luoyang when he encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Central Kingdom.

Tanluan asked, "Is there such a method for longevity and immortality within the Buddha-dharma? Bodhiruci spat upon the ground and said, "What kind of talk is this? It is not comparable at all. Where in this land is there such a thing as longevity and immortality?"

[The opponent asks: "If that is so, then when the scriptures of this land state that by 'maintaining mental images one can solidify the body and live for ten million years,' is that also false? [The response: "Although such [practices] do not exist here in this land, they may exist in the Western Heavens (India).

There, non-Buddhist practitioners study the four Vedas and cultivate various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) to attain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). For instance, the Rishi Kanthaka, fearing the death of his body, went to the realm of Maheśvara.

One should know that the great illusionists mentioned in the preceding text, such as the Rishis Kapila and Kātyāyana, cannot be spoken of on the same level as the non-Buddhists of this region; how much less so [can they be compared to those who practice the true Dharma]!"

Now, these ten immortals all achieved the perfection of their Way through the refinement of the mind; for the most part, they attained this longevity by relinquishing one life to enter another. Former scholars have consistently interpreted this as referring to the present life alone.
Often they come to doubt the likes of Shuangqiao and become confused by the teachings of Huang-Lao.

Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening; instead, they attain a mode of existence that grants them a lifespan of millions of years. They dwell in deep mountains or on great ocean islands, far removed from the realm of men.

This, too, is merely the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra. Failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

Zhaoxi said: "The preceding passage describes those with little emotion but much conceptualization who, through their lightness and levity, become flying immortals (fei-xian) without traveling far; this is spoken in terms of taking birth according to one's karma at the end of a life.

The subsequent passage speaks of 'thoroughly investigating the seven destinies,' all of which are the signs of the conditioned states of delusion, where one takes birth through false imagination and follows karma through false imagination. Now, however, it says [the place] is deep mountains and sea islands, cut off from the realm of human beings."

This refers to severing one's karmic retribution. It should be understood that for those who refine their minds while among humans, it does not consist merely of ingesting elixirs to sustain life; only when this is combined with precepts and wholesome deeds can it be called "refining the mind.

As for attaining a distinct principle of longevity, this is precisely due to karma performed while among humans, which separately evokes the retribution of rebirth in the realm of immortals (*ṛṣi*). Even if one were to manifest the principle of long life and far-reaching vision while in the human world, how many such cases would there be?

If one is born into the realm of immortals, then a lifespan of thousands or tens of thousands of years is indeed possible. As the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states: "Mount Kunlun, the wilds of Guangdu, [and] the [palace of] Xuanyuan..."

"Qiu, there is a land of immortality where there is neither cold nor heat, and its people all live for several thousand years. This, too, is merely a shared portion among many; it is not that there is no fixed location [for such a state].

If one merely seeks to solidify the physical form without refining the mind, yet hopes to reach a thousand-year lifespan, this is like seeing the morning light and seeking the hour of night—it is an overestimation. To seek transcendence at the end of one's life is it not delusion? Thus says the *Shoujian*.

Those among humanity who refine their minds do not realize that human life does not pause, passing faster than flowing water; that youthful vigor does not remain, like a galloping horse; and that they thus cling to a substance that is but a dream and an illusion.

[The text] considers [this] to be the principle of firm longevity. Changshui says: "The principle of life" refers to the principle of long life. In the sutra, this specifically points to the methods of the immortals as the principle of life; these are precisely the ten aforementioned methods of refinement.

While the practices of the Three Vehicles are all taught by the Buddha, this sutra even rebukes those of the Two Vehicles for failing to recognize the root of birth and death and practicing in a confused manner—how much more so regarding the cultivation of the immortal path?

To solidify the form and preserve the mind is to focus on long life and immortality, so that this physical frame remains firm and indestructible. The deluded thoughts thus cultivated are, as stated above...

These ten methods of cultivation are all characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*). Advancing, they do not equal the gods; retreating, they surpass ordinary humans. Therefore, dwelling in mountain forests in places inaccessible to common people is called the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*).

However, this destination is not mentioned in other sūtras because its collective retribution is the same as that of human beings. The reason it is opened up in the present sūtra is because it pertains to specific practices, is not subsumed within the two destinations of humans and devas, and is categorized among the types of external paths (*tīrthika*).

Nevertheless, these are prohibitions and restraints that are not the Buddha’s true precepts; they merely prohibit coarse and frivolous behaviors, which constitutes the "clinging to rules and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Such false imaginings are not real, and one will ultimately fall according to one's karma.

Ānanda, there are people in the world who do not seek the eternal, yet are unable to abandon their affection for wives and concubines; nevertheless, they refrain from sexual misconduct so that their minds do not flow toward it, and they polish themselves until clarity arises.
After their lives end, they draw near to the sun and moon. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Gushan says: Because the mind of perverse desire has ceased, it is clarified and polished; because the factors of the precepts (*śīlāṅga*) are pure, luminosity arises. Xunwen quotes Zhizhe as saying:
"It is the primary summit of the ascent, the first heaven of the lower realm, situated halfway up Mount Sumeru," and so forth.

Their sensual desire for their own wives is slight; they do not find complete satisfaction even when dwelling in the Pure Abodes. After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm.
This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When dwelling in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), one cannot obtain the full flavor; this is because during that time in the Pure Abodes, one cannot obtain pure flavors. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three kinds of flavors: first, the flavor of renunciation (*pravrajyā-rasa*).

Second is the flavor of recitation; third is the flavor of seated meditation (*dhyāna*). Now, the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens] still practice seated meditation. "Trāyastriṃśa" is the correct term for the Tuṣita heaven; this is translated as "Thirty-three."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* refers to it as "Wondrously High" (*Sumeru*). Gushan says: "On each of the four sides of the summit there are eight great celestial kings, with Śakra residing in the center;

thus this number [of heavens] arises. Jinggong says: "Trāyastriṃśa means 'Capable Ruler,' for Śakra is taken as the capable ruler. The *Supplement* says: "In the fourth heaven, Tuṣita, one first cultivates the concentration of desire.

Since this Trāyastriṃśa heaven is also called 'Pure Abode' (*Śuddhāvāsa*), we know that while those above Trāyastriṃśa all cultivate the concentration of desire, their perfection is achieved in Tuṣita; therefore, it is said that [the lower heavens] do not obtain the full flavor [of the fruit]. This is why the name 'Flame' (*Jvalana*) must be used."

In the human world, there is more stillness than movement; it is only upon reaching Tuṣita that one speaks of being "always still. This refers to the attainment of the characteristics of the coarse and subtle stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

When encountering desire, they may briefly engage with it, yet afterwards they have no thoughts or recollections of it. Because there is little movement and much stillness in the human realm, after the end of life, they dwell serenely and radiantly in the midst of empty space.

The light of the sun and moon cannot shine upward to reach them; these beings possess their own natural radiance. Such a class of beings is called the Suyāma Heaven (the Heaven of Delightful Splendor).
Xunwen says: "Movement" refers to the scattering of desire; "stillness" refers to tranquility. This is spoken with reference to the *kāmadhātu-samādhi*.

However, since [the beings there] have not yet attained coarse abiding or subtle abiding, this serves as evidence that the inhabitants of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) previously mentioned must be those who have newly begun practicing the meditative concentration of the desire realm. Gushan says: "Suyama" means "time-period" (*velā*); they constantly sing of joy at all times.
Jing Gong says: This is called "Good Time" (*suvakṣa*). One knows the time-period by the opening and closing of the lotus flowers.

It is tranquil at all times. When those who should touch it arrive, they cannot violate its nature. After death, one ascends to this subtle and refined realm, no longer descending to the levels of humans or devas of the lower worlds, until even the three calamities that destroy a kalpa cannot reach it.
This class of beings is called the Tuṣita Heaven.

Changshui says: "Ying" means "correspondence. Even when encountering objects of desire, one still complies with and follows them; therefore, it is said that one has not yet been able to resist or oppose them. According to this, even when being born in Tuṣita, there is still the grasping of hands;

since this occurs while practicing the causes in the human realm, one has not yet escaped desire. Gushan says: "Tuṣita" means "Contentment" (Zizu) in Chinese, because [the beings there] know contentment regarding the five desires.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* names it "Joyful Contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*), meaning that Bodhisattvas in their final birth cultivate joyful contentment extensively therein. This heaven is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, and it is not affected by the three calamities.

Furthermore, this is stated in reference to Maitreya’s dwelling place; other ordinary devas will still be subject to destruction by the three calamities. Changshui says: "There are two meanings for 'one who is to be reborn in the next life' (ekajātipratibaddha)."
First, regarding the aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), there are three types: (1) one birth among humans; (2) one birth among devas; and (3) one descent into a final birth.

Second, regarding the actual retribution (*vipāka*) of one birth, this refers to the fact that among the four kinds of transformational death and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-cyuti-janman*), there is only the very last kind, which is termed "bound to the single stage of non-existence" (*abhava-ekayānika*). As explained in the *Commentary on the Higher Birth* (*Ūrdhva-janma-vyākhyāna*).

I have no desire; I shall comply with your actions. At the time of union, my experience is like chewing wax. After my life ends, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).

The mind has no intention toward the object, yet the object comes of its own accord; the object itself possesses a mind, so what flavor can the self find therein? Thus it is said that the flavor is like chewing wax. Because one enjoys the objects of the five desires through the transformation of pleasure, the *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"While in the causal stage, one cannot yet avoid the horizontal presentation and mutual entanglement; only upon being born there can one face and smile. Yet, at the time of physical union, the flavor is like chewing wax.

Regarding the cause for the sixth heaven, even within physical union there is no slight flavor; therefore, it is said that one "clearly transcends" it. As for the term "horizontal presentation": *(Note: The original text contains a typographical error regarding the character for "smile" [笑], which appears as "face" [面]. The translation corrects this based on the context of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and related commentaries.)*

In the *Fengfu* (Satirical Rhapsody) by Song Yu, it says: "With a heart of trepidation, like a monkey on a bed, I lie stretched out beside my lord. Regarding the character *lè* (joy) being read with a departing tone (*qùshēng*) as "huà" (transformation), the *Xunwen* states:

"One is born in the land of transformation (*huàdì*). The *Hongchao* states: "The various heavens utilize objects of maturation (*vipāka*), but this heaven is not so; although it possesses the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of maturation, one enjoys them through self-transformation.
Thus, because one transcends the lower [realms] and transforms, it is called 'transcending and transforming' (*yuèhuà*)."

They possess no worldly mind, yet they engage in worldly activities. Amidst these interactions with worldly affairs, they clearly transcend them. After their lives end, they are universally able to emerge and transcend both realms of transformation and non-transformation.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Gushan says: Because they joyfully enjoy the five sensory objects manifested by others, and because they possess sovereign power, they cause others to manifest them for their enjoyment.

The fifth heaven consists of manifested realms; the four lower heavens consist of non-manifested realms. The aforementioned four heavens all dwell in the void. Changshui says: "The activities and matters intersect" is also a horizontal presentation [of the same meaning].

Although there was previously no flavor [of desire], the mind still gave rise to longing when encountering objects; now, however, there is no such mind, hence it is said that one "clearly transcends. In the aforementioned six heavens, all are attained because the desire-mind gradually lightens and the resulting retribution gradually improves.
If one’s emotional desires are heavy, one will certainly not be born in these heavens. *Xunwen* says: "To 'clearly transcend' means that there is also no longer the taste of chewing wax. Question:

Even those at the stage of fruition in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) may still experience regression due to sexual matters; how can an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) remain without such a mind when facing sensory objects? Answer: It is indeed as you have asked. I have once investigated this matter: one must...

Approximately one part among those who practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is able to do so because they have firmly suppressed their afflictions (*kleśa*). Alternatively, by relying on the Buddha’s teachings to cultivate the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*)—namely, the wisdom of impurity contemplations such as the nine perceptions—it is only then that such power arises.
In the sutras, this is generally described merely as the characteristic of being free from desire, yet the reason for such liberation is not revealed.

If one lacks both concentration and wisdom, how could it be possible for a distracted ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to act like one who possesses no worldly mind and transcends worldly affairs? It would be like making a hungry and thirsty person find no flavor in food and drink. —Tiaoxi

It is said: According to the teachings of the Master of Tiantai, the karma of the six heavens of the desire realm all has the ten wholesome actions as their basis. If this is combined with a mind that protects the Dharma, it is the karma for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

If it is combined with compassionate transformation of humans, it is the karma for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If it is combined with non-affliction toward sentient beings and the full maturation of skillful means, it is the karma for the Yāma Heaven. If it is combined with the cultivation of dhyāna-concentration, including both coarse abiding and subtle abiding, [it is the karma for the Tuṣita Heaven].

This is the karma of Tuṣita Heaven. The *kāmadhātu-samādhi* (desire-realm concentration) is the karma of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration) is the karma of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Now, as for why this sutra limits the division of the six heavens based solely on the gravity of desire-related matters, there should be two reasons: first, because it serves as the occasion for Ānanda to initiate the teaching; second, because it concerns the fundamental basis for taking birth within the desire realm. The intent is to encourage the observance of the precepts.
This also supports the subtle purport of the Vinaya.
Ānanda, in these six heavens, although their forms are mobile, their minds and traces still intersect; from here downward, they are called the Realm of Desire (kāmadhātu).

Regarding the two realms of humans and devas, they receive the designation of "active" because their sexual conduct still manifests in the form of physical union. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The six [classes] experience desire through union, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.

This means that among the two classes of earth-dwelling devas, there is physical union; in Yāma, there is embracing; in Tuṣita, there is holding hands; in Nirmāṇarati, there is laughing at one another; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, there is mutual gazing.

One must understand that this text speaks according to the specific manner in which each of these six heavens experiences desire. In contrast, the present sutra distinguishes the gravity of sexual acts solely with respect to the human realm, in order to clarify the six [levels of desire].

The retributions experienced by devas differ; therefore, one should analyze this through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, physical union occurs while the mind does not: this refers to the sixth [case] of this sutra, and it also applies to the fifth. Second, mental union occurs while the body does not:

this refers to the latter two [cases] of the *Abhidharmakośa*. Third, both mind and body unite: this refers to the first four [cases] in both this sutra and the *Abhidharmakośa*. Fourth, neither mind nor body unites: as in the stages from the first dhyāna upward.
In contrast to the two destinies of humans and *ṛṣis* below, it is said that they "exit" and "move. "Moving" means to fly up, which humans cannot do; "exiting" means to transcend [the realm]. Thus...

Although the immortals (*ṛṣi*) fly about seeking liberation, as their destination has not yet transcended the human realm, they should perhaps be categorized within the human realm. However, since they are already capable of flying, they are far superior to ordinary humans; thus, it would also be appropriate to categorize them within the celestial realm.

This is similar to how those with few afflictions and many thoughts are included among the Four Heavenly Kings and other such beings. Now, because they alone have not yet been reborn in the heavens, it is said that they have "not yet emerged.

Although they dwell within the human world, they remain separated from ordinary people. Changshui says: "The various classes within the human realm have short lifespans and undergo constant, unstable change, whereas the merit and lifespan of the heavens are ultimately—"

It is difficult to shake. Because one still encounters the signs of the realm of desire, it is said that "the mind and its traces still intersect. If one reaches the stage of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), there will forever be no confrontation with desire.

The *Shoujian* states: The *Loutan jing* says that the various devas of the desire realm possess ten dharmas: first, they can fly here in unlimited numbers; second, they can fly away in unlimited numbers; third, they go without obstruction; fourth, they come without obstruction.

1. The bodies of devas have no skin, sinews, veins, blood, or flesh. 2. The bodies of devas have no impurities, such as feces or urine. 3. The bodies of devas never experience exhaustion. 4. Deva maidens do not give birth.

In the ninth heaven, his eyes do not sleep. In the tenth, his body and mind follow his will: if he desires blue, it becomes blue; if he desires yellow, it becomes yellow; and the same applies to all other colors.

All those in the world who cultivate the mind, if they do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), will lack wisdom. Yet, even if one can merely restrain the body from practicing sexual desire—whether walking or sitting—one should contemplate...

With both thought and reflection absent, and no arising of craving or defilement, they leave no desire realm behind. Such a person should consider themselves a companion of Brahmā; this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya).

Zizhong said: "Without relying on *dhyāna*, there is no wisdom" means that, generally speaking, the cultivation of practice all relies upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*) before wisdom arises; only when concentration and wisdom are equal is it termed *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (静虑). This is the general explanation of the name *dhyāna*.

"Whether walking or sitting, if conceptual thoughts do not arise" refers to the initial exhaustion of desire for sensory objects, where pure signs manifest before one. To take pleasure in this and give rise [to further states] is called the "Assembly of Brahmās" (*brahmakāyika*).

This is precisely the state of subduing afflictions through the six practices cultivated by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The *Shoujian* says: "The six practices are the contemplation of activities," meaning they are the stage of ordinary beings.

This describes the mode of activity for subduing afflictions by means of the mundane path. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "What do the mundane paths take as their objects, and what modes of activity do they employ? The verse states: "The mundane uninterrupted paths and liberated paths..."
They take the lower and upper stages as their objects respectively, performing the three aspects of coarse, suffering, and obstructive, as well as pure, sublime, and detached. The Commentary says:

The mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the lower and upper stages as their objects respectively, performing the three aspects of coarse, suffering, and obstructive, and the three aspects of pure, sublime, and detached. That is to say, the path of uninterrupted transition takes the impure phenomena of its own level and the immediately lower level as its object, performing one of the three aspects among coarse, suffering, and obstructive.
As for the paths of liberation, they take the impure phenomena of the immediately higher level as their object, performing one of the three aspects among pure, sublime, and detached.

Because it is not tranquil, it is coarse; because it is not sublime, it is suffering; because it is not a departure [from saṃsāra], it is an obstacle. One should understand that the pure, sublime, and transcendent are the opposites of these three.

That is to say, if one applies diligence as this path of severing the fetters through these six modes of practice, one suppresses the afflictions of the lower stages and, at the end of life, immediately receives birth in the two higher realms. Furthermore, within these six modes, there are three each for delight and aversion.

As for the essential nature of what is delighted in and what is averse to, they differ according to each respective stage: for example, sensual desires and unwholesome states are what is averse to the first dhyāna; vitarka and vicāra are what is averse to the second dhyāna; and so on, up to the sphere of nothingness.

There are those who dwell in tranquility and are weary of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and there are those who, in successive order, aspire to what is above; these cases may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, the first dhyāna is aspired to by the mind of the lower *anāgamya* stage as being "pure, sublime, and detached," yet it is rejected by the proximate stage (*sāmantaka*) mind of the second dhyāna as being "coarse, painful, and an obstacle. Thus, the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exclusively objects of rejection and not of aspiration, while the phenomena of the Peak of Existence are exclusively objects of aspiration and not of rejection.

The phenomena of the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) are accessible to both rejection and aspiration. Xie Liyun stated: "The term 'not depending' refers merely to not cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path]."

It is said that concentration and wisdom are their defining characteristics; the rest is the same as the six practices. The Supplement states: "They maintain bodily precepts, yet their mindfulness is not fixed during walking or sitting.

Once the habit of desire has been eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests. They take delight in and accord with all forms of discipline (*vinaya*). Such persons are able to practice the virtue of Brahma at the appropriate time. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*)."

Gushan said: "Internal concentration and external precepts are twice as superior as before; thus one is able to practice the virtue of Brahma and serve as a counselor to the king. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"Once the habitual tendencies of desire are eliminated, this is called 'subduing' which is synonymous with 'elimination. When the mind is free from desire, the first dhyāna manifests. Because there are nine grades within the first dhyāna, it manifests sequentially."

With body and mind wondrously perfected and majestic deportment unimpaired, and possessing pure prohibitive precepts augmented by clear awakening, such a person is able, at that time, to preside over the Brahma assembly as a Great Brahma King.
This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven.

The *Shoujian* states: As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says, because it is free from desire and tranquil, it is called "Brahman" (*brahma*). In full, it is *brahmā*; here it is translated as "purity and tranquility. This means that because one has newly departed from the defilement of desire, it is called "purity";

because one attains the fundamental meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "tranquility. His appearance is like that of a youth; his body is the color of white silver, and he wears garments of gold.

He takes the joy of dhyāna as food and is the lord of the Sahā world. Guishan says: Regarding the fact that in the aforementioned three heavens the practice of dhyāna is not explicitly mentioned, but only the observance of precepts is spoken of, this is because this sutra upholds the Vinaya.

This is for the purpose of encouraging future generations. Zizhong says: "The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* explains that Mahābrahmā dwells alone, possessing majestic virtue and radiance; he has no *vitarka* (applied thought) and only *vicāra* (sustained thought), as this is induced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The two lower heavens possess both *vitarka* and *vicāra*. Xunwen says: "The treatise explains that there are three types of *samādhi*: first, with both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, which refers to the First Dhyāna and the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*); second, without *vitarka* and with only *vicāra*, which refers to the Intermediate Dhyāna;

third, without both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, which refers to the threshold of the Second Dhyāna up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and so forth. Now, regarding Mahābrahmā..."

The Heaven of the Intermediate Dhyāna (*madhyama-dhyāna*) is that which is induced by the power of meditative concentration. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Zizhong quotes the *Abhidharmakośa*, saying that Mahābrahmā is 'without vitarka and with only vicāra. This must refer to Mahābrahmā of the First Dhyāna who has advanced to cultivate the Intermediate [Dhyāna]. If one speaks of the First Dhyāna itself, it is simply 'with both vitarka and vicāra. Furthermore, because externalists do not perceive that the kalpa ends later and begins earlier, they cling to [Mahābrahmā] as being eternal. *Xunwen* says: "The *Zhengzhen* states: 'When the kalpa first formed, the Great Brahmā King still remained for one kalpa. It is merely that his lifespan is long; therefore, he is called "Great. It is like calling a person "great" when their wealth is vast. This is why the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "Because his lifespan is long, he is called 'Great'. This is what is meant. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "In the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka, only vicāra. This refers to the intermediate dhyāna within the Second Dhyāna.
