The *Shoujian* (Hand Mirror) states: "Indeed, the calculations of all outsiders do not exceed two heavens: first, Maheśvara; second, Viṣṇu. Maheśvara is translated here as 'Great Sovereign' (*Mahādeva*).

He is the heaven at the summit of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*), possessing three eyes and eight arms. He rides a white ox and holds a white fly-whisk. He possesses great majestic power and is able to..."

It overturns the world; all in the world honor it as the fundamental source of transformation. Viṣṇu is translated here as "Pervasive Victory" (Biànsèng) or "Pervasive Purity" (Biànjìng). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that this is the summit of the third dhyāna.

Some say this is the limit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The god of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*) has four arms; he holds a conch and a wheel, and rides upon a golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*).

He possesses great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) but is prone to anger and harm. At that time, people, fearing his majesty, came to revere him. At the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), he had one thousand heads minus one and twenty-four hands; he was born by transformation (*upapāduka*) upon the waters, with a thousand-petaled lotus flower at his navel."

Within the lotus there was light; the light was like ten thousand suns shining together. Because of this, the Brahmā King descended to be born. He thought to himself, "Why is it empty and devoid of sentient beings?

While he was thinking this, eight deva-sons who were destined to be born in this world from other realms suddenly manifested through transformation. These eight deva-sons are the parents of all sentient beings; the Brahmā King is the parent of these eight deva-sons;

and Viṣṇu is the parent of the Brahmā King. This is a tracing back to the ultimate origin. The *Piyuping jing* (Sutra of Similes) says: "Various outsiders reckon that the Brahmā King gave birth [to all things]."

Regarding the four castes: the Brahmin is born from the mouth, the Kṣatriya from the arms, the Vaiśya from the sides, and the Śūdra from the feet. The *Madhyama-āgama* and *Dīrgha-āgama* also provide further explanations; these all share the same names with slight variations.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also figuratively designates the Brahmā King as the father of all sentient beings, which is likewise a remote inference based on the ultimate origin. Lord Jing said: "Brahma" means "purity.

Indeed, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* has both a "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-parivarta*) and a "Chapter on Brahma-Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*); thus, when one is as pure as heaven, one is called "Brahma."

Ānanda, these three superior practitioners cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction. Although they have not yet attained the true, correct Samādhi, their pure minds remain unmoved by any outflows;
this is called the First Dhyāna.

Zizhong said: "It cannot be oppressed by any suffering" refers to being free from the eight sufferings of the desire realm. Gushan said: "There are four types of dhyāna: first, contaminated dhyāna, which refers to the present four dhyānas;

second, uncontaminated dhyāna, referring to the nine notions, the eight contemplations of repulsiveness, and so forth; third, both contaminated and uncontaminated dhyāna, referring to the six subtle gates, the supernormal powers, and the clear illumination;

fourth, neither contaminated nor uncontaminated dhyāna, which is the samādhi of principle within this King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi. The present statement, "although it is not the true, correct, and ultimate *samādhi*," refers to the first [type].

The "fourth purity of mind" mentioned here specifically refers to the first dhyāna. "The outflows (āsrava) are unmoving" means that the afflictions of the desire realm have already been suppressed. Master Jing said:

"Although 'the outflows are unmoving' does not yet mean the outflows have been fully subdued, it means they can be maintained so as not to move; this heaven possesses the factors of vitarka and vicāra. Master Tiaoxi said: "In the first dhyāna, one cultivates five dharmas and abandons the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa)."

It consists of five factors and possesses the eight contacts and ten meritorious characteristics. According to Xunwen, the five dharmas are desire, intention, diligence, concentration, wisdom, and single-mindedness. As for the five hindrances:

The [five hindrances] are: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The five factors [of the first dhyāna] are: vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and ekāgratā (one-pointedness). The eight tangibles are: movement, itching, coolness, warmth, lightness, heaviness, roughness, and smoothness.

There are another eight tangibles, namely: agitation, pliancy, cold, heat, buoyancy, sinking, hardness, and softness. Although these eight are largely the same as the previous tangibles, if one distinguishes them minutely, there are slight differences.

Taken together, these are called the sixteen contacts (*ṣoḍaśa-sparśa*). As for the ten virtues: first, concentration; second, emptiness; third, clarity and purity; fourth, joy; fifth, bliss; sixth, the arising of a wholesome mind;
seventh, clear knowledge and vision; eighth, liberation from burdens; ninth, the manifestation of the objective sphere; tenth, the mind becoming pliant and supple, and so forth.

Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, where the Brahmās preside over their followers and perfect their Brahma-conduct. With minds clarified and unmoving, they give rise to light from profound stillness. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).

Next, the text cites the preceding Great Brahmā; "purifying the mind" below correctly clarifies the Limited Light Heaven (*Parīttābha*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The Sūtra cites the preceding in sequence to show that one person, by relying on this, practices the stages in succession.

'Governing the Brahmā people' cites what preceded; 'fulfilling the holy life' initiates what follows. Zizhong says: "From the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no speech; one merely emits light through a concentrated mind.
Because the light has degrees of superiority and inferiority, their respective heights and depths are distinguished."

Light illuminates light, shining forth without end; it reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally transforming them into lapis lazuli. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*). Changshui says:

"From the previous Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), they further emit abundant light; as the characteristics of their light increase further, it is called 'light illuminating light'. Zhenji says:

"'Reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions' refers to their meditative light (*samādhi-ābhā*) as it is experienced in various directions such as east and west; it does not mean that [the physical world] pervades the entire realm of the ten directions."
Inhalation and retention constitute the perfected body of the teaching (*śāsana*), while the manifestation of transformation is pure and its application inexhaustible.

This class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*). Guishan says: "The ancient interpretation states that grasping the application of the light of wisdom constitutes the expressed body of the teaching; because it uses speech as the means of expression, it is named 'Light-Sound.

As for 'the manifestation of transformation is pure,' this refers to the fourteen minds of transformation. 'Wisdom and desire' refer to the perfect light. Zhenji says: 'The body of the teaching is precisely verbal expression. Taking light as sound, it signifies infinite comprehension.'"

Therefore, it is said that "the emanated transformation is pure," and so forth. Changshui (Zhangshui) says: "Because the realm and stage of the second dhyāna lack the five consciousnesses, when followers of the external vehicles or ordinary beings are in meditative concentration, they are all unable to give rise to the first five consciousnesses for the apprehension of objects.
They instead employ light as their means of expression; taking light as their sound, they are called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven). Jingong (Jingci) says:

"It is not merely that they inhale and maintain the perfect light, but they can also accomplish the substance of the teaching; therefore, it is named Light-Sound. 'Inhaling' (xi) means not dispersing; 'maintaining' (chi) means not losing. This heaven possesses the factor of internal purity."

Ānanda, these three superior types of practitioners cannot be assailed by any anxieties or apprehensions. Although they have not yet attained the true, correct Samādhi, because coarse outflows have been subdued within their pure minds, this is called the Second Dhyāna.

Zhaoxi says: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* designates the second dhyāna as the "dhyāna accompanied by joy" (*prīti-sahagata*). When this concentration arises, it emerges together with joy; therefore, it is now said that one cannot be oppressed by any anxiety or distress. Question:

Since the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) of the first dhyāna already include joy, why is it only the second dhyāna that is designated as "accompanied by joy"? Answer: In the first dhyāna, there is applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), which still carry a trace of anxiety and distress.

Now, since applied and sustained thought have been exhausted, it receives this specific designation. Xunwen says: This [second dhyāna] has four factors, namely: internal purity (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). When this dhyāna arises...

At that time, it is like a person emerging from a dark room and seeing the light of the sun and moon; their mind becomes suddenly expansive, clear, and bright. The eight contacts and ten merits are the same as in the first dhyāna, with the sole difference that they arise together with internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).

"Hanging" means being bound; because one is detached from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), there is nothing to which one is bound or attached. Lord Jing said: "Those who have already suppressed the coarse outflows possess the factor of internal purity;

however, since the factor of joy (*prīti*) still remains, they are only able to suppress the coarse outflows of the lower stages, while the subtle [outflows] of the higher stages cannot yet be suppressed."

Ānanda, when the celestial beings thus perfect their radiant halos and voices, and by uncovering their voices reveal the sublime, giving rise to refined conduct that penetrates the bliss of quiescent extinction—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha).
Zhaoxi says: "The perfect light forming sound" refers to the essence of the preceding teaching. "Disclosing the sound to reveal the subtle" means the manifestation of pure transformation.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "These two phrases reiterate what preceded. 'Disclosing the sound to reveal the subtle' below correctly clarifies the third dhyāna. 'Disclosing' means casting off the traces of the teaching of the 'light-sound'; it reveals this concentration of the wondrous nature.

This is because the second dhyāna has the defilement of internal joy; since that is removed here, it is called 'pure. By advancing in the cultivation of the third dhyāna, one thus manifests and perfects refined practice, and realizes the attainment of 'limited purity.'"

It penetrates the bliss of cessation (*śānti-sukha*). It is the concentration of pure cultivation that brings about the arousal of diligent practice. Penetrating the bliss of cessation is the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). Master Jing said:

"To 'uncover' (*pī*) and 'reveal' (*lù*) the subtle means that one can uncover and manifest the primordial sound (*dhvani*), thereby knowing the source from which the teachings arise; and one can open up and manifest the wondrous nature, seeing the origin from which the light emerges. This is because this heaven possesses the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*)."

When pure emptiness manifests before them, it induces boundlessness; their bodies and minds become light and tranquil, achieving the bliss of cessation. This class of beings is called the *Apramāṇa-śubha* (Immeasurable Purity) devas. Tiaoxi says:

"Once the sign of limited pure emptiness has manifested, they further employ the power of meditative concentration to induce that limited sign to become boundless. Compared to those above, this is not yet all-pervasive;
compared to those below, it is more extensive. Therefore, it is named 'Immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*)."

The world, body, and mind are all perfectly pure; having accomplished pure virtues, they manifest a supreme reliance and return to the bliss of nirvana. This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (the Heaven of Universal Purity).

The aforementioned physical and mental pliancy refers to the internal; now, "the world and so forth" collectively encompasses the external. As the objects of focus for supreme meditative concentration, all pure signs appear before one.
One returns to the bliss of inner quiescence. Master Jing said: "To bring forth and perfect refined practice so as to penetrate the bliss of quiescence—this is merely to be able to penetrate.

When pure emptiness manifests before one, it induces boundless physical and mental pliancy; only then is bliss perfected. When the supreme reliance manifests, there is a ground upon which to rely; therefore, it is called 'returning to the bliss of quiescence.'"

Ānanda, these three superior types of practitioners possess great conformity. Their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, attaining immeasurable bliss. Although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of correct cultivation, within their peaceful and secure minds, joy is fully present;
this is called the Third Dhyāna.

Zizhong says: "It is fully endowed with great compliance (*anuloma*), because the maturation (*vipāka*) of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) complies with and is sovereign over bliss. Xunwen says: "'Maturation-bliss' refers to that which penetrates the mental ground and brings pervasive physical satisfaction;

it is associated with the five consciousnesses and cannot be conceptually differentiated. Tiaoxi says: "The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* identifies the third dhyāna as 'dhyāna conjoined with bliss. It possesses five factors (*aṅga*), namely:

equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). Because the merits of this concentration arise together with pervasive bodily bliss, although there is bliss in the first two dhyānas [it is not of this specific nature]."

The factor of *prīti* (joy) is obstructed by the factor of *sukha* (pleasure). Now, because joy is extinguished and pure pleasure remains, it receives this name. As for the statement that "delight (*prāmodya*) is fully present," the names are identical but the entities are distinct;

one should not let the literal phrasing damage the intended meaning. Master Jing said: "Within a mind of tranquility, the full presence of delight constitutes the factor of *sukha*; it is not the agitation of *prīti*."

Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose bodies and minds are no longer oppressed; the causes of suffering have been exhausted, yet pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably perish after a long time. They simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the mental states of suffering and pleasure;
their coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and a nature of pure merit arises. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).

Furthermore, the phrase "lower fetters" indicates the virtues of the third dhyāna, while "pleasure is not lower" reveals the faults of the third dhyāna. If "pleasure is lower," it correctly demonstrates the arising of merit. In the third dhyāna, there are no causes for the suffering of the lower realms;

although it is called "pleasure," pleasure that lasts long must eventually perish, and its perishing also becomes suffering. Now, since one has abandoned pleasure, suffering does not arise. The *Bhūmisaṃgraha* names this the "dhyāna accompanied by equanimity" (*upekṣā-sahagata-dhyāna*), which carries the same meaning. The *Supplement* states: "This refers to the preceding three dhyānas.

Because they are free from the agitation of internal joy belonging to the lower realms, it is said that they do not oppress body or mind. Pleasure is not permanent. Regarding "pleasure": [it is impermanent].

This arises from the suffering of decay (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*); it is not that which constitutes merit (*puṇya*). *Xunwen* says: "Pure merit arises from the nature (*dhātu*). "Nature" refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*); this is also explained in terms of the internal.

This dhyāna arises together with subtle and sublime equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and is therefore called "dhyāna accompanied by equanimity. It possesses four factors (*aṅga*): first, the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure; second, equanimity; third, purity; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind. This is "merit-arising."
In other sūtras, this may be called the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*).

The second, the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), is so named because their equanimity is perfectly integrated, their resolute understanding is pure, and they attain a sublime conformity within unobstructed merit that extends to the limits of the future. This class of beings is thus called the Heaven of Merit-Love.

The Supplement states: In the previous Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*), one took the relinquishing of pleasure as merit. Now, because the mind of relinquishment has become even more excellent and one takes delight in this merit, it is called "Merit-Loved" (*Puṇyaprasāda*).

This distinguishes it from the previous Heaven of Merit-Born in terms of depth and intensity. The following three phrases clarify that because of this "merit-loved" state, two branches diverge. The first two phrases correctly define "merit-loved" through the increasingly superior mind of relinquishment;

because this delight does not cease, one is born in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) or the Unconscious (*Āsaṃjñika*) realm. From the Heaven of Vast Fruit, one gives rise to the five types of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) karma that is untainted (*anāsrava*), which persists until the end of the future, drawing from its source.
This is because it arises from a mind of merit, affection, joy, and delight. The reason for speaking of this here is to clarify the efficacy of merit and affection. Tiāoxī says:

"Attaining wondrous compliance" refers to the two divergent paths mentioned in the following text. Because the essential nature of this pure merit is unobstructed, one affectionately delights in practicing the supreme and wondrous Dharma;

thus, the two paths supported by merit do not merely pertain to the present life, which is why it is said they "extend to the limits of the future. Chángshuǐ says: Within merit and affection, two directions are distinguished: first, the direct path, which leads straight to the Vast [Vow].

The fruit. Second, the circuitous and deviant path, which leads directly to the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*). The Supplement states: "Thus, the reason why there are two distinct paths within this region is truly due to the excellence and subtlety of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*)."

If one's merit is pure and substantial, it is capable of serving as the foundation for transcending the world. By adding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one is born into the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*). If one relies on the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) to extinguish and sever biased views, one is therefore born into the Heaven of No-thought (*Asaṃjñisattva*).

Indeed, the Dharma of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has misled many people. For example, when the three types of persons in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) realize emptiness, the two vehicles take this realization as their final attainment, whereas the Bodhisattvas, while within emptiness, are naturally able to transform sentient beings.

Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths. If one dwells in the cultivation and realization of the previously mentioned immeasurable pure light and the perfect brilliance of merit, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).

Zizhong said: "From within the heavens of merit and affection, two heavens are distinguished: first, the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala), and second, the Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva). This Heaven of Vast Results [attains its state] by perfuming meditative concentration with the merit of the four immeasurable minds."

Having detached from the defilements of the lower stages, those who are moved by vast merit are called the Gods of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala). According to Xunwen, they dwell having cultivated and realized the causes for the Vast Fruit;
this is said with reference to their non-arising in the Realm of No-Thought (asaṃjñika). If, however, they grow weary of form and exhaustively reach emptiness, they likewise have no fixed dwelling.

If, from the preceding state of mind, one simultaneously loathes both suffering and pleasure and cultivates a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), continuing it without interruption until the path of equanimity is fully perfected and both body and mind are extinguished;

if the mental faculties remain as still as ash for five hundred kalpas—because such a person takes arising and ceasing as their cause, they cannot manifest the nature that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing; and if they cease during the first half-kalpa and arise again during the second half-kalpa—this class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

Zizhong said: This [state] reckons non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) as *nirvāṇa*. Taking the relinquishing of the mind as the means, one first relinquishes the coarse mind and enters the subtle mind;

from the subtle mind, one further enters the extremely subtle mind. From the extremely subtle mind, one then becomes like ash or ice, practicing this constantly without ceasing. At the end of life, one is born here. After five hundred great eons, one eventually falls back and degenerates.

Such a person does not understand that the nature of the delusive is essentially empty; instead, they grasp at arising and ceasing as a source of toil and anxiety. Loathing this arising and ceasing, they seek that which is non-arising and non-ceasing, yet it is not true non-arising. They merely perceive the sixth consciousness.

They do not act like a pair of tongs grasping a fish in ice; unaware of subtle arising and ceasing, they falsely claim it to be *nirvāṇa*. Consequently, for half an eon (*kalpa*) after taking birth, there is existence, and only after another half eon does cessation occur.

According to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, citing the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, regarding the stages of birth and death therein: having first been born in that heaven, one enters the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) only after half an eon has passed.

When the desire-realm becomes impermanent, one emerges from that maturation; for half an eon thereafter, one possesses mind, and only then does death finally occur. The Supplement states: "One should know that the lifespan in the state of non-conception is five hundred great eons; however, this refers only to the period from the initial birth until reaching that state."

For half an *kalpa*, they still perceive that they possess a mind; only then do they enter the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*). Therefore, it is said that "in the first half-kalpa, they cease. When their lifespan of five hundred *kalpas* has reached its end and the time for retribution is fulfilled, they again experience the perception of mental activity for another half-kalpa before finally undergoing impermanence.
Therefore, it is said that "in the latter half-kalpa, they are born. Because they regenerate the perception of mental activity, it is called "birth. The *Xunwen* (薰聞) states:

"In the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, this is termed the 'retribution of non-conception' (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), which belongs to the category of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Its commentary states: 'Because one cultivates [the path] in the desire realm, one brings about the fruit of that heaven; it is named the retribution of non-conception, also called the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*')."

This has three meanings. First, it ripens through transformation; it is only by means of maturation that one can subsequently attract a fruit. Second, it ripens at a different time; having performed a cause in the past, one obtains the fruit in the present.

Third, maturation occurs across different categories: wholesome and unwholesome causes may induce neutral results. Chengzhen says: "However, regarding these four dhyānas, there are only three grades of collective retribution and individual karma that induce birth in the lower three heavens.

The Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is merely a distinct retribution within the Heaven of Vast Results (*bṛhatphala*). This is the upper limit of the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). As for the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), they are likewise noble ones who have cultivated meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in a mixed manner;

they utilize their karma from the Heaven of Vast Results to produce five distinct superior grades, whereby they are born there to experience bliss. This is not the same as the case of ordinary beings."

Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly states of suffering or pleasure. Although they are not the unconditioned stage of true immovability, because their mental acquisitions have been purified through the maturation of effort, they are called the Four Dhyānas.
Zizhong said: The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the fourth dhyāna is free from the eight calamities, namely: vitarka, vicāra, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, it cannot be moved by the three calamities of water, fire, and wind; thus it is called the "Unshakable Ground" (*aniñjya-bhūmi*).

Ānanda, herein there are furthermore five types of non-returner heavens. Within the lower realm, the nine grades of habitual tendencies are extinguished simultaneously; with both suffering and pleasure vanished, they no longer dwell below.
Therefore, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).

Regarding the five types of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*): those who have attained the third fruit have severed the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm; since both their seeds and their manifest activity are exhausted, they will no longer return to seek rebirth in the lower realms, and are thus called "Non-returners.

Regarding the phrase "the duality of suffering and pleasure has vanished": they are further able to sever the defilements of the third *dhyāna*; having already transcended the lower stages but not yet surpassed the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they establish their dwelling therein.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because there are five distinct grades of mixed cultivation of *dhyāna*, one is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). As for 'mixed cultivation,' it is practiced by alternating between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)."

...is what is meant. In Sanskrit, this is called *anāgāmin*; here it is translated as "Non-returner" (*bùhuán*) and also named "One who does not come back" (*bùlái*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are five types of *anāgāmins* in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). The verse says:

"Among these, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), upon birth (*upapadya*), with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*), or without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*); and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) through mixed cultivation, reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Regarding the five types: first, the "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*), meaning one who, having gone to the realm of form, attains parinirvāṇa while remaining in the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

Second, the "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), meaning one who, having been born in the realm of form, attains parinirvāṇa shortly thereafter. Third, the "one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), meaning one who, having been born in the realm of form, [exerts effort] for a long time...

At that time, their preparatory application does not cease; they attain parinirvāṇa only through great effort. Fourth is the one who attains parinirvāṇa without application (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin). This refers to one who, having been born in the realm of form, after a long period of application becomes indolent and attains parinirvāṇa without much effort.

This is of two types, distinguished by the difference between cause and fruit. As for the difference in cause, there is that with mixed cultivation and that without mixed cultivation. As for the difference in fruit, there is reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven or the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

The former is the practice of insight (vipaśyanā), while the latter is the practice of tranquility (śamatha); this is because they differ in their preference for wisdom or meditative concentration. Among these five non-returners, the first is one who delights in wisdom.
These are the births resulting from that. In the first, second, and third dhyānas, there are nine grades of cultivated afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), all of which are termed "defiled.

The verse says: "By means of five grades of mixed cultivation, there are five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). The commentary says: Because the fourth dhyāna is cultivated through mixed perfuming in five grades, there are only five Pure Abodes.

These five grades of mixed cultivation of dhyāna induce the five Pure Abodes in their respective order. Other masters say: "Because faith and the other [faculties] increase in sequence, they induce the five Pure Abodes," and so forth. The *Shoujian* states: "The five Pure Abodes..."

Regarding this, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The noble ones who have abandoned desire are called 'pure' (*śuddha*) because they wash away the stains of affliction with the water of the Noble Path. Because they dwell in these pure bodies, they are called 'Pure Abodes' (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Alternatively, because they dwell here until the very limit of saṃsāra—like having fully repaid a debt—they are called 'pure. Because they are the dwelling place of those who are pure, they are called 'Pure Abodes.

Alternatively, because there is no mixture with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) here, and they are inhabited solely by noble ones, they are called 'Pure Abodes. As for the "five grades": it means that through karma consisting of a mixture of contaminated and uncontaminated provisions and vast results, one's state becomes preeminent, and one is reborn into the five Pure Abodes.

Regarding the Abodes of the Gods (*devanikāya*), there are thus five categories. Why, however, must they be mixed? It is because the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*) have no separate projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).

By the natural law of all sentient beings, within the Fourth Dhyāna there are only three grades of collective-projecting karma that lead to birth in those three heavens. Since the Noble Ones (*ārya*) are free from afflictions (*kleśa*), they must practice the mixed cultivation of the lower three heavens;

thus, by means of former karma, they are born in the five heavens. However, while the former karma that serves as the support is one, there are five modes of activity due to the supporting causes; therefore, the five heavens are induced. As for the five grades, they are: low, medium, high, higher-high, and highest-high.

"Supreme" (*śreṣṭha*) means "ultimate. The *Shoujian* states: These five [stages] all consist of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the fundamental [attainment], and furthermore, the initial lower grade. First, one gives rise to many moments of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [thought];

then, one gives rise to many moments of outflowing (*sāsrava*) [thought]; finally, one again gives rise to many moments of outflow-free [thought]. When they are thus gradually extinguished until only two moments remain, this is called the preparatory application. Next, one gives rise to one moment each of outflow-free, outflowing, and outflow-free [thought].

This is called the "fundamental" [meditation]. That is to say, the preceding and succeeding moments are untainted (*anāsrava*), while the intermediate moments are tainted (*sāsrava*); because they are practiced in an interspersed manner, it is called "intermixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*).

By means of this, one relies upon former karma; thus, passing away from the Bṛhatphala heaven, one is reborn in the Avṛha heaven. Next is the medium grade, which consists of six moments of mind. One employs the three moments of the aforementioned inferior grade as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), further inducing three moments of mind—consisting of one moment each of the untainted, the tainted, and the untainted—which serve as the fundamental [meditation].

Relying on this former karma, one passes away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and, by leaping over the Avṛha heaven, is reborn in the Atapa heaven. Third is the superior grade, which consists of nine moments of mind.

Using the first six moments of mind as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one further induces three moments of mind to bring it to completion. Supported by previous karma, one transcends one or two stages to arise in the third; this superior grade of the fourth [dhyāna] consists of twelve moments of mind.

Using the first nine moments of mind as the preparatory stage, one further induces three moments of mind as the fundamental stage. Supported by previous karma, one transcends three stages to arise in the fourth; this superior grade of the fifth [dhyāna] consists of fifteen moments of mind.

Using the first twelve moments of mind as the preparatory stage, one further induces three moments of mind as the fundamental stage. Supported by previous karma, one is able to transcend the four [lower] heavens and be born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

"Ultimately, Ānanda, when both suffering and pleasure have ceased and the contentious mind no longer engages, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha). When the mechanism of the senses functions alone and there is no ground for the friction of contact, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).

When the wondrous vision of the ten directions is perfectly clear and serene, with no further images of dust or any lingering defilements, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa). Their refined vision manifests before them."

They mold and cast [beings] without obstruction; such a class is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. They have reached the ultimate limit of all phenomena and exhausted the nature of form, entering into the boundless; such a class is called the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Zhaoxi said: "If there is suffering and pleasure, their forces will inevitably contend with one another; this is like a battle waged within the inner mind. Furthermore, when the mind encounters an object of suffering, it contends with the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); when the mind encounters an object of pleasure, it contends with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Since both have now ceased, it is called 'Free from Affliction' (*Avihā*). Changshui said: "When the mental states of suffering and pleasure cease, their opposition vanishes.

Since the mutual dependence of form has disappeared, it is said they do not contend. When they do not contend, there is no affliction. This explains that the initial cessation of the two forms of suffering and pleasure—the mental states that depend on them—constitutes the first stage of the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*). *Śrāvakabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Explanatory Essentials).

It is said: this refers to the support of the lower grade of mind. That is to say, after the practitioner has first entered the fourth dhyāna, within that concentration, they first give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind;
next, they give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind; and again, they give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of uncontaminated mind.

When one gradually reduces these until there are two moments of uncontaminated mind, two moments of contaminated mind, and two moments of uncontaminated mind, it is called the completion of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of mixed cultivation. Next, they give rise to one moment of uncontaminated mind and one moment of contaminated mind...

One contemplates the untainted (*anāsrava*). Reaching this point is called the fundamental fulfillment. Because one practices by intermingling the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), and it is also termed "interlaced perfuming meditation" (*miśra-vāsanā-dhyāna*).

By using the untainted (*anāsrava*) to interpenetrate and perfuse the tainted (*sāsrava*), the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) becomes increasingly luminous and the karmic retribution (*vipāka*) becomes increasingly superior. Through this support and these karmic causes, one passes away from the Bṛhatphala Heaven and is reborn in the Avṛha Heaven.

Being slightly free from the hindrances to meditative concentration is what is meant by "Avṛha" (Free from Trouble); "vṛha" refers to the hindrance itself. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "If one is below the third dhyāna, suffering and pleasure battle within the breast.

Guishan says: "The 'ji' is the trigger of a crossbow; the 'gua' is the notch of an arrow. Whenever an arrow is released from a crossbow, it must hit the mark; there is a place where they meet and rub together. Now, [the practitioner] abandons the mind..."

Practicing alone, there is neither suffering nor conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). The objects of opposition and conformity are like arrows shot that cross paths. Since there is neither opposition nor conformity, there is no affliction of feverish distress.

"Absence of distress" refers to the severance of external objects; "absence of fever" refers to the severance of the internal mind. Changshui says: "In the superior grade of mixed cultivation, this grade consists of nine moments of mind. The first six moments are used as the preliminary application (*prayoga*)."

Furthermore, three minds arise as the foundation. Because they serve as the resources for past karma, one passes away from the Bṛhatphala Heaven and is born in the Sudarśana Heaven. There, the power of the outflow-free (anāsrava) state is manifest; concentration and wisdom have eliminated all obstructions.

Thus, one is able to perceive the worlds of the ten directions with wondrous clarity and perfect purity; hence it is named the Sudarśana Heaven. "Dusty images" and "sinking defilements" refer precisely to the obstructions of concentration and wisdom. Gushan says:

"It is like a potter making a vessel or a smith casting an image," speaking of the mastery of its function. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The 'refined vision' refers to the aforementioned Sudarśana; 'casting and forging' specifically refers to the present passage. Good.
"Seeing" refers to the essence (*tǐ*); "Subhūti" refers to its function (*yòng*). "Molding" is synonymous with "producing," for it is able to give rise to the fourteen transformations with mastery.

Rāoxī (Zhili) says: it is the meaning of ultimate investigation and inquiry. "Ji" (the potential) is the subtle movement [of thought]. By investigating many thoughts until they reach a single thought, one is said to "ultimately investigate the multitude of *ji*. This is accomplished by practicing the five grades of mixed cultivation."

Initially, many moments of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava*) permeate many moments of tainted consciousness (*sāsrava*); eventually, in the final stage, a single moment of untainted consciousness permeates a single moment of tainted consciousness.

This is called the "supreme grade. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is accomplished by a single moment; this is intermingling. "Exhausting the nature of form" (*se xing*)—here, "exhausting" (*qiong*) means "ultimate" (*jijing*); the wording has merely been altered.

Since the mind’s permeation ranges from many to few, form likewise ranges from the coarse to the subtle. Because their coarseness and subtlety differ, it is called "nature-nature" (*xing xing*). "Entering the boundless limit" refers to the intersection between the two extremes of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Above this, there is no further place of residence; because this location is the highest, it is called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate Form). The *Xunwen* states: "This briefly demonstrates the characteristics of the mixed cultivation of the first and last categories.

For example, after one has first cultivated and attained the fourth dhyāna, one further gives rise to it through a continuous succession of many moments of untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration, from which one subsequently induces many moments of tainted (*sāsrava*) concentration."

Thereafter, one again gives rise to multiple moments of untainted (anāsrava) thought—namely, the three thoughts of the first stage. In this manner, they gradually decrease until only two moments remain, which is called the completion of the preparatory application (prayoga).
When only a single moment remains, it is called the completion of the fundamental [attainment] (maula).

Ānanda, as for these Non-returner devas, even the various Heavenly Kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration but cannot know or see them. It is like the vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the holy path in this world today;

because they are all sustained by Arhats, they cannot be seen by the coarse people of the world. Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without social interaction, yet they have not yet exhausted the burden of the physical form.
From here downward, they are called the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).

Gushan said: "Because he travels alone without companions and is devoid of both emotions and desires; yet, because he has not yet exhausted the burdens of the physical form, he still possesses material substance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within this realm of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the limit of form, there are two further divergent paths.

If one illuminates wisdom through the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) such that the light of wisdom becomes perfectly penetrating, one will then transcend the mundane world to become an Arhat and enter the Bodhisattva vehicle. This class of practitioners is called the "Great Arhats who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]."

Zhaoxi said: In the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, those who have attained the third fruit (anāgāmin) possess faculties that are either sharp or dull; thus, two paths are distinguished. Those with sharp faculties give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and, having exhausted all afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, immediately transcend the triple realm.

Those with dull faculties, moreover, by means of a concentrated mind, rejoice in the higher realms and feel aversion toward the lower, thereby being reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It should be understood that the "perfect penetration of the light of wisdom" is spoken of here in terms of the fulfillment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

That is to say, from the point of having already seen suffering and abandoned it, up until having already cultivated the path, is called the knowledge of exhaustion. [The knowledge of non-arising] is when one no longer further abandons [afflictions], and so forth, up until one no longer further...

"Cultivation" refers to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Entering the Bodhisattva vehicle is specifically explained in terms of the superior progress following the transcendence of the three realms. This is also a clear textual authority from the present sutra for refuting the notion of fixed nature (*niyata-dhātu*).

If, through a mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion and perceives the body as an obstruction, such that obstructions dissolve and one enters emptiness—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Once all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation;
therein remains only the *ālaya-vijñāna* in its entirety and a subtle portion of the *manas*—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind is entirely extinguished, the ten directions are tranquil and utterly devoid of any destination—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The nature of consciousness is immovable; having exhausted investigation through cessation, within this inexhaustibility...

Manifesting and proclaiming the exhaustion of one's nature, it is as if existing yet not existing; if exhausted, it is not truly exhausted. This category is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Changshui says: "There are two ways of relinquishing the mind. First, if at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to sever delusions and enter emptiness, this refers to the *sukha-vihārin* Anāgāmin.

Second, if at the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*), one uses the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) to suppress delusions and enter emptiness, this refers to ordinary beings and non-Buddhists. The untainted path refers to the contemplation of the eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*); the tainted path is...

Regarding the contemplation of the six modes and the contemplation of the eight noble lineages: one contemplates the five aggregates as being like a disease, an abscess, a wound, and a thorn—impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and so forth.

Because these two heavens both abide in a state of equanimity and share the same level [of meditative attainment], Zhenji said: "Once all obstructions have dissolved, one grows weary of form and returns to emptiness. When there is no obstruction and nothing to be extinguished, one grows weary of emptiness and rejoices in consciousness;

yet even this 'non-obstruction' is itself extinguished. Gushan said: "In the sphere of infinite space, form perishes; in the sphere of infinite consciousness, emptiness perishes. Now, since even the sphere of consciousness is extinguished, there is nothing at all."

Zhaoxi said: "In the preceding Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), although it is said that consciousness is extinguished, its essential nature remains unmoving; it merely extinguishes the subtle portion of analytical investigation.

Now, within this inexhaustible nature, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion—that is, establishing inexhaustibility once again from within exhaustion. Therefore, the Chan gate of Tiantai cites the interpretation of the ancient masters, saying:

'In this meditative concentration, one does not perceive any marks or appearances, and thus it is called "Non-ideation" (*asaṃjñin*). If it were entirely without ideation, it would be no different from wood or stone; how then could one know there is no ideation? Thus it is called "Non-non-ideation" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*')."

"That which exists as non-existent is 'neither-perception' (naivasaṃjñā). That which is exhausted as non-exhausted is 'neither-non-perception' (naivāsaṃjñā). Xunwen says: "The preceding contemplation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) is 'having perception' (saṃjñin), while the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) is 'non-perception' (asaṃjñin).

Now, both are discarded. Furthermore, ordinary people and non-Buddhists attain this meditative absorption and claim it is the realization of Nirvana; because they have severed all perceptions, it is called 'neither-perception.

The disciples of the Buddha know according to reality that there is subtle perception remaining, abiding in dependence upon the four aggregates (skandhas); therefore, it is called 'neither-non-perception. This is a designation formed by combining the aspects of attainment and loss."

These individuals exhaustively pursue emptiness but do not fully realize the principle of emptiness. Those who reach the limit of the noble path from the Heaven of No-Return (Anāgāmin) are a class known as "non-retrogressive, dull-witted Arhats.

If they exhaustively pursue emptiness from the heavens of the non-conceptualizers (asaṃjñin) among the various externalist paths and do not return, they become deluded and, lacking the hearing of the Dharma, they fall back into the cycle of rebirth.

Zhaoxi said: "These [passages] that exhaustively investigate emptiness refer generally to both ordinary beings and sages. Because their attachment to joy and aversion has not yet been exhausted, it is said they have not fully realized the principle of emptiness. Even if a sage cultivates the contemplation of the eight noble lineages,"

Furthermore, there are four aggregates (*skandha*) whose subtle afflictions have not yet been extinguished. This is because the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) has not yet been attained; thus, "joy and aversion are not yet exhausted. Here, "joy" refers to the mind that exhausts emptiness, while "aversion" refers to the practice of relinquishing suffering.

Since the arising and ceasing still persist within these four stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), true emptiness is not yet manifest; hence it is said they are "not yet exhausted. As for the phrase "even though they are sages," this refers to those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) practicing the contemplation of the eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

Even at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they cannot avoid arising and ceasing. Regarding the "subtle afflictions of the four aggregates," these comprise ten types of mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), namely: sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)... [and so forth].

[The sūtra speaks of] formations, contact, volition, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth. It descends from the realm of the non-returner (anāgāmin) to clarify that there are noble ones born in this place; these are merely those non-returners of dull faculties.

The term "Arhat" is a designation based on their subsequent state. If one descends from the Realm of No-Thought (asaṃjñika), it clarifies that there are non-Buddhists who do not take birth in this place; that is to say, having exhausted the realm of emptiness, they do not return.

The Supplement states: "These refer to the aforementioned four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). 'Exhausting emptiness' encompasses two categories, namely the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and the Non-conceptualizers (*asaṃjñin*). From the section on the Non-returners below, he explains these two categories."

"Those who exhaust emptiness but do not return" refers to the followers of external paths (*tīrthika*) who are able to exhaust emptiness but fail to reflect back upon their own nature; they do not return to the True Principle. This, then, reveals those who are unable to exhaust emptiness and return to the Truth.

However, various masters are mired in the literalism of the scriptures and treatises, asserting that the State of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) cannot again reach the emptiness of the Fourth Dhyāna, or identifying the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*) as being synonymous with No-Thought, or forcibly interpreting "not returning" as "not coming back.
Only Guishan says: "The faculties of people are not uniform; the various teachings merely speak partially of one aspect. Moreover, it is now clearly stated that from the State of No-Thought..."

The gods of the non-Buddhist paths have come; how could one possibly contravene the sūtra? This is because the Heaven of No-Thought is an abode for non-Buddhists, and for the most part, when their lifespans end, they must fall back down. Furthermore, this is a refutation of heterodoxy.

It is simply impossible for it not to be so. How could there be no exhaustion of retribution such that one returns once more to the Four Formless Heavens (*catur-ārūpya*)? One asks: the lifespan in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) lasts five hundred kalpas, during which one remains entirely in a state of stonelike stillness;

how can it be said that the emptiness is again exhausted there? Now, considering the meaning of this, I fear that "exhausting emptiness" refers to the first half-kalpa of birth, when thought has not yet been extinguished; because of this, one exhausts emptiness and returns to be born in the Four Formless Heavens.

Furthermore, after five hundred kalpas, they again experience half a kalpa of rebirth with perception; since they have not yet fallen away, those of sharp faculties exhaust the realm of emptiness and are subsequently born in the higher heavens.

Ānanda, these various devas among the heavens are each ordinary beings for whom the fruits of their karma have ripened as retribution; when that retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth.
Those celestial kings, however, are bodhisattvas who traverse samādhi, gradually advancing along the path of practice dedicated toward the ranks of the sages.

Zizhong said: "According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these are all Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), yet they also serve as heavenly kings. Thus, it is only those Great Beings of the Dharma-body within the Separate and Perfect Teachings who are capable of such a role. Gushan said:

"'Wandering in samādhi' refers to Bodhisattvas who are skillful in entering, emerging from, and abiding in hundreds of thousands of samādhis; therefore, by dwelling in this concentration, they act as lords of the heavens."

"Skillfully entering and exiting" means skillfully entering the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), skillfully exiting through the "lion's bound" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), and skillfully abiding in the "leap-over" samādhi (*vyutkrāntakasamādhi*). Guishan said:
"If one penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of dhyāna, it is then called 'Lengyan'."

Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished; the nature of stability manifests before them, and there is no form resulting from karmic fruit. From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).

The phrase "no matter-of-fact form resulting from karma" indicates that there is form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This form resulting from concentration issues forth the hundred dharma-wheels; in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), it is termed "form produced by mastery over meditative concentration."

This means that by virtue of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains mastery over all forms (*rūpa*). One then uses this concentration to transform and give rise to the objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "It possesses the quality of resistance (*sapratigha*).

Because the dharmas of concentration sustain the mind and prevent it from becoming distracted, they appear as if possessing resistance; they are also 'conventional form' (*prajñaptirūpa*). According to the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Holy Teachings), the form produced by the mastery of concentration is the function of concentration itself, and is not comparable to the fruits of concentration."

All of these fail to understand the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind. Through the accumulation of delusions, they give rise to the three realms of delusion; within them, they follow their deluded karmas, sinking and drowning among the seven destinies, with each *pudgala* following its own kind.

Gushan says: *Pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes rebirth" (*shuququ*). This refers to sentient beings taking birth according to the various realms of existence (*gati*), because they repeatedly take up these various realms.

Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms there are four classes of asuras. Those who, belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), attain supernatural powers through the power of protecting the Dharma and enter into the void—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts.

Those who, having descended from the heavens due to a loss of merit and are cast down, dwell in proximity to the sun and moon—these asuras are born from the womb and are categorized within the destiny of humans.
There is an asura king who upholds the world; his power penetrates all things and he is fearless, able to contend for authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. This...
Asuras exist by reason of transformation and are included within the realm of the gods (*deva-gati*). Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean;

they sink into the mouths of underwater caverns, roaming through the void at dawn and returning to dwell in the water at dusk. These asuras exist by reason of moisture and are included within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni-gati*).

Tiāoxī says: The verse on the four modes of birth (*yoni*) in the *Abhidharmakośa* merely states that hungry ghosts (*preta*) include both womb-born and transformation-born types. Since the egg-born asuras are now subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts, Vasubandhu’s statement seems to be incomplete. Question:

Are the four kinds of asuras listed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* the same as or different from the four kinds mentioned here? Answer: Those four can only be subsumed within these current four; they cannot be sequentially assigned to their respective categories.
Jingxī says: All four kinds in the *Lotus Sūtra* engage in battle with Śakra. Viewed at first glance, they appear to be the same as those in the present sutra.

Third, the category of the ears. Question: Since these four classes of asuras are subsumed within the four destinies (*gati*), they should have no separate place of rebirth (*nikāya-sabhāga*) for their retribution. Answer: Although they belong to the four destinies, it is not that they lack a separate place of retribution.

What is now described as "residing in proximity to the sun and moon" refers precisely to such a place of common rebirth. Furthermore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "In Jambudvīpa there is a Vajra Mountain;

within it is the palace of the asuras, which measures six thousand *yojanas* in extent, with railings, rows of trees, and so forth. Yet, day and night, three times a day, they suffer, and the instruments of torture come of their own accord to enter [the palace]."

Within the palace [of the gods], it is known that this realm takes only a portion of its wholesome retribution, namely that of humans and devas. However, when discussing the experience of suffering, it actually lies below the human realm;

for this reason, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* subsumes them solely within the two categories of hungry ghosts and animals. It is precisely for this reason that Guishan stated: "If one follows the hierarchy of the seven realms, the asuras would rank below the human realm;

however, because their classification is currently indeterminate, they are placed at the end. Xunwen remarked: "They are able to contend for power with the Brahma King"—this refers to the fighting asuras, as detailed in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*.

As stated in the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*: "If the people of Jambudvīpa practice in accordance with the Dharma—filially serving their parents, making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and revering the elderly and the great assembly—then they are superior.

If worldly people do not follow the teachings of the Dharma, then the asuras are superior. The *Lokotpatti Sūtra* says: "The palaces, city-walls, and utensils of the abodes of the asuras are equal in quality to those of the terrestrial devas.

They also have marriage and the social customs of men and women, which are roughly similar to those of humans, though they are distinct karmic retributions. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "They are born from the heart of the great ocean."

This is a general enumeration of its location; "Sinking Water" (Lǐnshuǐ) is a specific designation. It lies in the heart of the great ocean, or at the bottom of the water; hence it is called "Sinking Water.

Alternatively, it is located at the mouth of a drainage hole, hence it is called "Mouth of the Hole" (Xuékǒu). As the *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "The Tail-Gate (Wěilǚ) drains [the sea]," and the commentary notes: "Tail-Gate is the name of a stream in the Eastern Sea. The sub-commentary (*shū*) states: "Tail-Gate is the place where the waters of the sea drain away.

Ānanda, thus it is with the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras. When one minutely examines these seven realms, they are all merely the signs of the conditioned states of delusion;

they are births resulting from false imagination and followings of karma through false imagination. Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky—originally having no point of attachment, being nothing but a single void delusion without any root or source.

Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of saṃsāra. Having passed through immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity, it is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

By reversing these three, one gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. That which possesses [these] is called the realm of ghosts; that which lacks them is the celestial realm. Through the mutual inclination between existence and non-existence, the nature of saṃsāra arises.

Changshui said: "The realms of ghosts and the paths of devas briefly represent two of the four evil and three good destinies. Jing Gong said: "Where there is opposition, there is dependence; where there is grasping, there is release.

To grasp at existence as pleasure is to oppose it with suffering; when that [existence] is released, suffering takes its place. Therefore, human happiness ultimately ends in ruin. To grasp at non-existence as purity is to oppose it with defilement."

In its interpretation, it is stained by the worldly age; thus, celestial purity ends in falling. To fall means that what was not there becomes more so; to be destroyed means that what was there becomes even more non-existent.

If one attains the wondrous arousal of *samādhi*, then there is wondrous, eternal stillness. Both existence and non-existence are absent; even non-duality is extinguished. When there is as yet no "not killing," "not stealing," or "not committing adultery," how could one further fall into the acts of killing, stealing, or adultery?

Gushan said: "Both existence and non-existence are absent; this is the absence of the mundane world of birth and death. Even 'non-duality' is extinguished; this is the extinction of the truth of nirvana. If one does not even cling to the good, how much less would one follow after evil?
One should also say: 'If even non-duality is absent, why follow duality? In the Middle Way there is no attachment; its purport is solely clarity."

Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [cause], and because of these various privacies, the collective share of these privacies has no fixed location. They arise from one's own delusion; this arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced back to its origin.

This also serves as a response to Ānanda’s previous question. Changshui says: "The three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are each committed individually by a person; this is called 'private' (*pratyeka*). Because what is created is common [to all], it is called 'shared' (*sabhāga*).
Regarding the phrase 'due to private [acts]': if taken as the cause of cause-and-effect, it refers to the private cause of creating karma.

If taken as the cause of circumstance, because of these private karmas, one's various privacies aggregate, and thus there is a place of shared existence. 'Shared' (*sabhāga*) is synonymous with 'of the same kind' (*sajāti*). Master Jing said: "Because it joins with external objects, the karma of sexual misconduct does not..."

It is severed. Because one has a share in things, killing and stealing are not severed. Since there is sharing and combination in order to grasp at a self, once the self is grasped, each possesses private attachments.
The deluded karma of shared portions is not without a fixed locus. If one realizes that it is mind-only, then this grasping and attachment will cease.

You must exhort yourself to cultivate practice if you wish to attain Bodhi. You must eliminate the three delusions; if you do not exhaust these three delusions, even if you should acquire supernormal powers, they will all be mundane functions of conditioned effort.

If habitual tendencies are not extinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you wish to eliminate delusion, you will instead increase your falsehoods. The Tathāgata says such people are to be pitied. Your delusions are created by yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.

The preceding statement said that through sexual misconduct one falls into the path of Māra; the present statement says that one does not necessarily fall into the path of Māra by exhausting all three delusions. Ghosts, spirits, and numinous beings who delight in possessing those of depraved character are all encompassed within the realm of Māra.
To speak in this manner is called speaking correctly; for any other to speak thus would be the speech of Māra.

Since they still cling to these worldly afflictions, how could you cause them to shatter that place?
For this reason, spirits, ghosts, and all the celestial Māras, as well as *māṅliang* and *yīnjīng*, will all come to disturb you during the time of *samādhi*.

Xunwen says: The *Zhiguan* states that all ghosts and spirits are under the jurisdiction of the Six Heavens; because they serve as guards within their respective realms, they come to cause such disturbances. "Qiān" means "all."

However, although those demons may be filled with great rage within their realm of afflictions, within your wondrous awakening they are like wind blowing against light or a knife cutting through water; they do not touch it at all. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice;

as the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will melt away before long. They merely rely on their supernatural powers and are but guests; that they succeed in creating confusion and disorder is due to the master of the five aggregates within your own mind.
If the master is deluded, the guest gains the advantage.

The Supplement states: "When the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is victorious, those Māras are about to be defeated; thus they are like guests. This is why a single phrase in the Sūtra says, 'accomplishing the destruction of confusion. As stated further below:

'Then that host of heterodox ones all receive the qi of the netherworld,' because those who have been defeated belong to the realm of dark yin. Regarding the 'master of the five aggregates' (*pañca-skandha*): only when one contemplates the five aggregates and attains their true nature (*tathatā*) is one called the master.

Since the Sūtra mentions the five aggregates collectively, this applies to both form and formlessness; thus, penetrating form is precisely the mastery of the aggregate of form. Tiaoxi says: "This refers to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*)."

Within this state, the two attachments to person and phenomena are suppressed but not yet severed. If the host—the view of self—arises, one is deluded; if the guest—the views ridden by Māra—enters, they gain the upper hand.

If you remain in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and awaken without delusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you. As the *skandhas* dissolve and enter into clarity, all those malevolent spirits will receive only their own dark vapors.
Since clarity can destroy darkness, they will soon perish on their own; how then would they dare remain to disturb your meditative absorption?
Regarding those who all receive the subtle, dark energy: Māra deludes people through darkness. If people are not deluded, they instead receive his energy.
If you do not attain clear awakening and are bewildered by the shadows, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and accomplish the work of a demonic person.

Changshui said: "He earnestly exhorted and awakened [the assembly] so that they might recognize demonic delusions. When one is deluded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), demons find their opportunity. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

'The five aggregates are a collection and concealment of all unwholesome causes, just as a band of thieves hides in the mountains and occasionally emerges among people to plunder their wealth. Therefore, we know that the five aggregates are the dwelling place of demons;
if one can contemplate and break through them, the demons will naturally dissipate. Tiaoxi said: "This was addressed to Ānanda to serve as a warning to the common multitude."

"Mātanga was extremely lowly and inferior; he merely used incantations against you to destroy the Buddha's code of discipline. Among the eighty thousand practices, you have violated but a single precept. Because your mind remains pure, you have not yet fallen into ruin."

Gushan says: "Comparing a prostitute to a celestial Māra illustrates the insignificance of the person; comparing a single precept to preserving one's entire body illustrates the insignificance of the matter. By citing the inferior to illustrate the superior, he exhorts others to maintain profound vigilance.

Since those who have attained the first fruit possess the power of the 'path-concomitant' precepts (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*) such that they naturally do not transgress, it is said that their minds are pure, and so forth."

This means that your entire precious awakening has fallen into ruin. It is like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering the confiscation of their property; they are left scattered and destitute, with no one to offer pity or rescue.

As the *Book of Han* says: "Deprive them of their registers" (*chu qi shu ji*). Ying Shao stated: "A 'register' (*ji*) consists of bamboo slips two chi long, upon which are recorded one's age, name, and physical appearance."

Ānanda, you should know this: when you sit at the site of enlightenment and eliminate all thoughts, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all that is luminous and alert beyond thought will remain unmoved by motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness will be as one.

Zizhong said: "Grasping at objects through deluded thoughts is collectively termed 'various thoughts. If the mind is clear and still such that coarse thoughts do not arise, this constitutes their dissolution. This is merely a coarse concentration of the desire realm attained for a temporary period. Tiaoxi said:
"'Detachment from thought' refers to the preliminary expedients practiced in the Tiantai *Zhiguan*, such as the condemnation of desires and the removal of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Although what is detached from is superficial, the capacity to detach is profound; it is not the coarse concentration of the desire realm. *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "As the power of contemplation gradually matures, one is no longer altered by agitation or distraction; hence it is called 'unwavering. Upon emerging from concentration..."

Movement is activity; entering meditative concentration is stillness. Recollecting with the mind is memory; not recollecting is forgetfulness. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "To cease all signs of objective realms. The present sutra says: "To cause all thoughts to subside and fall away."

The two conditions of subject and object are each mentioned in the sūtras and śāstras. By relying on this to leave behind discursive thought and enter deeply into right concentration, recollection and forgetfulness naturally become one.

One should abide in this state to enter samādhi; it is like a person with clear vision standing in profound darkness. The essential nature is wondrously pure, yet the mind has not yet emitted light. This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

Changshui says: "The mind entering right concentration is like a person with clear vision. Not yet having broken through the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is like a vast, profound darkness. 'Quyu' refers to the realm of the world;
it is called 'qu' because it is like the various territories governed by a king. That which is covered by a single heaven is called 'yu'."

If one’s vision becomes clear and bright so that the ten directions open up like a cave, with no further darkness, it is said that the aggregate of form and name (*nāmarūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted.

Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Zhenji said: "Emptiness is the root of form; based on emptiness, the realms are established; based on the realms, time is established. Therefore, when the aggregate of form is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of the eon. Changshui said: "Question:

The aggregate of form is coarse and manifest, and thus is broken first during contemplation. The turbidity of the eon is most subtle; how can one transcend it [first]? Answer: Since the arising of time has no sequence of before or after, breaking time simultaneously encompasses both the coarse and the subtle. Thus, the text does not become redundant."

The Scripture says: "Therefore, one sees that arising has a sequence. Furthermore, the manifestation of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). Now, when the aggregate of form is destroyed, its manifestation is destroyed; when its manifestation is destroyed, it agitates the fundamental consciousness.

Is the fundamental consciousness not itself the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*)? Therefore, one is able to transcend it. The *Supplement* states: "One should know that 'kalpa' refers to a temporal division. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is only from the period of the decreasing kalpa down to the time when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years that it is designated as the 'turbidity of the kalpa.

What is clarified here in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—namely, delusion regarding the Truth resulting in emptiness, and establishing the realms based on that emptiness—all falls within the meaning of temporal divisions. It is simply a matter of deluding the Truth..."

The kalpa of emptiness was as yet unpolluted; it was only when delusion arose within that emptiness that the realms were established. It was during the time of the kalpa-pollution (kalpa-kaṣāya) that the colors of both the primary and secondary elements appeared. Therefore, by now breaking through the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), one transcends the kalpa-pollution.
Contemplating its origin, one finds that solidity takes deluded thought as its root.
This "solid deluded thought" refers to the firm grasping of awakened clarity, which constitutes the substance of matter through its obstructive nature; hence it is called "solidity."

Ānanda, you should investigate this subtle clarity within it with diligence. When the four elements no longer entwine, in a brief moment the body will be able to pass through obstructions. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the external realm;
it is merely a temporary effect of spiritual practice and is not a sign of saintly realization.

Xunwen says: "The four great elements do not interweave" means that because one realizes ultimate emptiness and abandons the attachment to solidity, one perceives the four great elements as having no characteristic of mutual interweaving.

*Buyi* says: "The four great elements do not interweave" refers to the simultaneous cultivation and simultaneous manifestation within *zhiguan*; because the understanding of the aggregates (*skandhas*) is empty and harmonious, one attains the state where the four great elements have no characteristic of mutual interweaving.

Regarding "the body is able to pass through obstructions," this is because by investigating the wondrous nature, the internal is luminous and the external is void; thus, the conditioned environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) does not obstruct. The passage below concerning "overflowing the physical form" refers to the emptiness and harmony of the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). *Guyang* says: "Overflowing... [text continues].

"Overflowing the external objects before one" means that there is no obstruction to the colors outside the walls. "The subsequent flow overflowing the physical form" means that there is no obstruction to the colors within the physical body.
Not conceiving of oneself as a sage is called a wholesome state; if one conceives of it as being a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.

Gushan said: "In general, although various objects that arise may be virtuous signs, grasping and attachment toward them turns them into the perverse. Conversely, even if they are perverse signs, if one does not grasp and attach to them, the perverse will become correct.
This is because objects revolve according to the mind."

Ānanda, if one further uses this mind to investigate the subtle brilliance until it penetrates the interior of the body, that person may suddenly pick out roundworms and maggots from within their own body;

yet the physical form remains intact, without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the physical body. This is merely a temporary attainment through refined practice and is not a realization of sainthood.
