To not give rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of being a sage, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.

Furthermore, when this mind investigates the internal and external with refined precision, at that time the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, *zhi*, and *shen*—with the exception of the body it clings to as its own—all enter into mutual interaction.

Whether acting as guest or host, one may suddenly hear the sound of Dharma being preached in the air, or hear the secret meanings being expounded throughout the ten directions. This is called the spirits and souls alternatingly separating and uniting; it is the accomplishment of wholesome seeds that temporarily results in such experiences. It is not [the ultimate realization].

*Sengzheng* (Śramaṇa-attestation). The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: This refers to the preceding [discussion on how] external objects and the internal body are empty and harmonious; now, both are investigated together, hence it says "thoroughly investigating the internal and external. The six—soul (*hun*), spirit (*po*), etc.—are all the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

"Will" and "intellect" describe its substance; "spirit" and "energy" describe its vital breath (*prāṇa*); "soul" and "spirit" describe its functions. The *Zuozhuan* says: "When a person first undergoes transformation, they are called *po*; once the *po* has been generated, that which is Yang is called..."

Regarding the *hún* (soul): the *Gǔxiǎng* says, "The *hún* is like a swirling current (*yúnyún*); it moves incessantly in the external realm and presides over the emotions (*qíng*). Regarding the *pò* (spirit): it is pressing and close; it manifests in man and presides over the nature (*xìng*). The *hún* is "weeding" (*yún*); the emotions serve to clear away impurities.

The *pò* is "white" (*bái*); the nature serves to govern the internal. The *jīng* (essence) is "stillness" (*jìng*); it is the transformative breath of the Great Yang, resembling fire in its capacity for generation. The *shén* (spirit) is "vague and elusive" (*huǎnghū"); it is the breath of the Great Yin.
Now, it is said that the *yì* (intention) is the sovereign of the mind (*xīnwáng*), while the *zhì* (will) is a mental factor (*xīn-suǒ*); this is as the saying goes: "it resides within the mind."

"Each expresses his own aspiration. Their aspirations are all different; this precisely pertains to the realm of *saṃjñā* (perception). Guishan says: "Excluding the body that is grasped, all others interpenetrate.

This means that apart from the physical body (*rūpakāya*), the internal *hún* (soul), *pò* (spirit), and so forth—the six [components]—interpenetrate one another. Regarding "suffering as guest or host": if it is like this, when the other five enter the *hún*, then the *hún* is like the host and the five are like guests;

and so on until they enter the *shén* (spirit), where the *shén* is like the host and the rest are like guests. "Alternately separating and uniting" means that the *jīng* (essence) leaves its original position and unites with the *hún*, or the *hún* [unites with the *jīng*], and so forth.
It departs from its original station and merges with the essence.
Not giving rise to a mind seeking sainthood is called a "wholesome state"; if one forms a conception of sainthood, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.

Furthermore, when this mind is clear, manifest, and translucent, its internal radiance shines forth, causing all ten directions to appear everywhere as the color of Jambūnada gold, and all species of beings to transform into Tathāgatas. At that moment, suddenly—

One sees Vairocana seated upon a terrace of celestial light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas; ten billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the defilement of the awakening of the soul and spirit.
The light of the mind is refined and clarified, illuminating all worlds. To briefly attain such a state does not constitute a holy realization.

Xunwen says: "Vairocana" is translated as "pervading all places. This is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If he appears seated upon the Celestial Light Terrace, this must be the retributive body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of Rocana.

This is because during the Tang dynasty, the translations did not distinguish between the Dharma-body and the retributive body. The Supplement states: The *Wenju ji* (Record of the Textual Phrases) says that in recent translations, the Dharma-body and the retributive body have not been distinguished, such that two or three [bodies] cannot be differentiated.

Since ancient times, the sutras and treatises have permitted the existence of three bodies. If one says that Vairocana and Rocana are not distinct, then the Dharma-body would be identical to the retributive body; this refutes the [erroneous] Dharma...

The characteristics of the names and forms are not to be discriminated. Other schools claim that Vairocana is merely a different name for the same essence, a designation for the left and right [hands].
To harbor no thoughts of holiness is called a "wholesome state"; if one treats it as a realization of holiness, one immediately falls prey to various delusions.

Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates the wondrous clarity with ceaseless observation, suppressing and subduing it, restraining and transcending it. At that time, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures;

they simultaneously fill all space without displacing one another, and blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their pure intensity. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its proper limit.
To temporarily attain such a state is not a holy realization.

Zhaoxi said: "Restraint, suppression, subjugation, and transcendence correspond respectively to the four categories of afflictions; alternatively, they may be understood as the elimination of the natures of the four great elements as discussed below.
These names are abbreviated for the sake of brevity."
To not give rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if you take it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall under the sway of various demons.

Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate until it becomes transparent and its refined radiance is undisturbed, you may suddenly see various objects within a dark room at nightfall as clearly as in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.

This is called the mind becoming subtle and dense, clarifying the faculty of sight so that what is viewed penetrates the profound darkness. To temporarily attain such a state is not a sign of saintly realization.

The Supplement states: When one perceives objects in the dark, it is through the power of the practitioner’s contemplation that they see as clearly as in broad daylight. The objects themselves in the darkness remain subject to obscuration;

it is simply that their dark appearance cannot be extinguished. For example, suppose two people are situated in the dark: if one person perceives through the power of contemplation as if it were broad daylight, would the other, who lacks such power of contemplation, perceive in the same way? Of course not.
Not giving rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if you conceive it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately succumb to various delusions.

Furthermore, when this mind enters perfectly into a state of voidity and fusion, your four limbs may suddenly become like grass and wood; even if burned by fire or cut with a blade, you will feel nothing at all. Moreover, the light of a fire cannot scorch you, and even if your flesh is sliced, it is as if wood were being pared away.

This is called the "dusts" [the sense objects] being cast aside and the nature of the four elements entering entirely into purity. To temporarily attain such a state is not a mark of saintly realization.

Zizhong said: "When the mind merges and thought becomes still, grasping and receiving cease to function. The four elements and five sense objects suddenly disperse and dissolve. Since there is no longer a subject that grasps, even being cut or sliced is like empty space. When mindfulness and thought are purely unified, one may temporarily attain such a state."
Not giving rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if one forms the conception of being a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.

Furthermore, when this mind has achieved purity and the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, one may suddenly see the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, complete with the seven treasures and filled with radiant light.

One also sees countless Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filling the void, their towers and palaces magnificent and splendid. Looking down, one sees the hells; looking up, one observes the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision. This is called...
When joyful and wearying contemplations deepen through daily practice and, after long cultivation, become transformed, this is not yet a sign of saintly realization.
*Xunwen* says: "Joyful and wearying [contemplation] should be divided according to two meanings: the pure and the defiled, and the mundane and the sagely."
Not giving rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of being a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate the profound and distant, you may suddenly see at midnight your distant relatives and kin in the marketplace or on the streets, or hear them speaking.
This is called the mind being so intensely pressured that it flies out, causing you to see things at a distance; it is not a sign of saintly realization.

Gu Xiangyun quotes the *Guanzi*, which says: "A merchant must establish himself at the marketplace. Yin Zhizhang’s commentary notes: "To set up a market, one must have it on all four sides, following the layout of a well;

therefore, it is called 'market-well' (*shijing*). The Supplement states: "Regarding those who force the mind and so forth: this refers to the mind that seeks liberation through contemplation. Because it pushes, investigates, and pursues the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), once form has become empty and fluid and can no longer act as an obstruction, [the consciousness] flies out and is thus able to separate from the visual field."
Not conceiving a mind of holiness is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of holiness, one will immediately succumb to various devils.

Furthermore, if you investigate this mind with extreme refinement and see the physical form of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) undergo transformations—changing in various ways without cause in a short moment—this is known as a perverted mind harboring demons, or being possessed by a celestial Mara entering one’s heart and belly to preach the Dharma and communicate profound and subtle meanings without basis; it is not a sign of saintly realization.

Zizhong said: "This person has previously possessed seeds of a deviant mind, which, meeting with external demonic conditions, have caused them to appear together. This is not a wholesome state; it is purely a demonic affliction. It differs from the preceding nine cases, all of which were termed wholesome states.

Only when one gives rise to a mind seeking personal realization does it become demonic. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "A good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the refuge and reliance of a practitioner.

Now, seeing that [the teacher] has changed, the practitioner wishes to ruin the teacher's mind, thinking that he is no longer fit to be a master. This tenth case is entirely the work of demons, leading up to such things as 'preaching the Dharma without cause.'"

This occurs because the practitioner allows the demon to enter their mind; thus, it is possible for such things to happen. Therefore, *Xingfu* (興福) says that this is the celestial demon borrowing eloquence. *Xunwen* (熏聞) states:
"To preach the Dharma without cause is something the practitioner can do themselves; or, having heard a previous teacher preach the Dharma, it causes the practitioner to penetrate the subtle meaning.

The meaning expounded by the *Zang*, *Tong*, and *Bie* teachings should be termed "subtle" (*miao*). Jingxi says: "Within the provisional teachings of the preceding [three] vehicles, the demon is also able to preach."

If you do not give rise to the thought of being a sage, the demonic activities will subside. If you instead form a holy interpretation of them, you will immediately fall under the sway of various demons.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* are all due to the interaction between the mind and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); therefore, these phenomena appear. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they fail to reflect upon themselves and, encountering these conditions, remain confused and fail to recognize them for what they are.

Claiming to have attained the state of a sage, they commit the great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell. After the Tathāgata has passed away, you all should rely [on this teaching] during the Age of Dharma-Decline (*mofa*).
Proclaim this meaning so that no celestial Māras may find an opportunity to exploit you; maintain and protect it until you achieve the Unsurpassed Way. Tiāoxī says:

"The interaction of the mind" refers to the interaction between the mind of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (dhyāna) and the solid delusions of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); therefore, these phenomena appear. This should be understood by analogy for the other aggregates up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Why?

Because each of the five delusions, within the domain of its respective aggregate, becomes the object of contemplation for *dhyāna*; as they are about to be destroyed but not yet destroyed, it is like a lamp about to go out—its light flickering.

The light blazes forth even more intensely. This is because its efficacy lies in contending with the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, whether one succeeds or fails depends upon this; therein lies the distinction between the path of Māra and the path of the Buddha. Changshui said: Question:

"Since this does not employ the sequential contemplation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how can it fully clarify their sequence and their objects? Answer: "Although the contemplation takes the general characteristics of the five aggregates as its common object, the aggregates possess both coarse and subtle aspects.

The coarse aspects are extinguished first. It is like washing clothes: the coarse stains are removed first. Since these aggregates are formed by the accumulation of delusion, when delusion is exhausted, the aggregates naturally cease. This proceeds from the coarse to the subtle."
This is necessarily so.

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and, within śamatha, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested in a clear mirror.

Zhaoxi said: "The exhaustion of the aggregate of form refers to what has already been severed. To perceive the minds of all Buddhas is a partial realization (*sādṛśa-sākṣātkriyā*). As the preceding text states: 'If the eyes are clear and bright, the ten directions open up like a cave, and there is no longer any darkness.'"

If there is something attained that one is yet unable to employ— like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly intact and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is possessed by an external evil spirit so that they cannot move—
this is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).

The Supplement states: The text consists of two sections. The first is the teaching (dharma); the second is the analogy. Regarding the first: when the practitioner advances in contemplation of sensation and mind, it appears as if they clearly perceive without grasping at external objects, manifesting a state of lucidity.

Yet, because they have not yet been able to break through the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), it is said, "If there is something attained, one has not yet put it to use. In the subsequent passage, when the mind is detached from the body and one turns back to contemplate one's own face, moving and staying with mastery—only then can it be truly used.

This is the mark of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation. Although there is now clarity, one has not yet escaped the aggregate of sensation; this is merely a "territory" (a limited domain). Next, the analogy is raised: "Contacting a guest..."

"Deviations" refers to the mind having a sense of aversion that is like encountering a guest demon. This is illustrated by the fact that although the present *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is clear and manifest, one is still ensnared by this *skandha* of sensation.

*Xunwen* says: "The root of 'affliction' (*yan*) is aversion; later people added 'demon' (*gui*). To suppress and harmonize with the human heart is called 'affliction'. *Tiaoxi* asks: "Why is it that the *skandha* of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is severed first and suppressed later? He answers: "Severing is discussed from the perspective of the preliminary instruction, while suppressing is discussed according to the sequence.

If one does not clarify severing, there is no way to know the signs of leaving behind faults and manifesting virtue. If one does not clarify suppressing, there is no way to know the cause by which demons arise based on the *skandhas*. Below are the three [subsequent sections].
The introductory sections of the *Yinwen* all contain this meaning:

"If the affliction of nightmares ceases, the mind will detach from the body and look back upon its own face; going and staying become free and spontaneous, with no further obstructions. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*)."

Zhengi said: "To 'see' means to have the sense of seeking and grasping. Because one apprehends the preceding object, attachment arises accordingly; therefore, when the mind is detached from its form, one transcends the turbidity of views."

The Supplement states: "If one is released from the cage of the aggregates, it is like waking from a nightmare. As for the mind departing from the body: the mind of an ordinary person necessarily follows the sense-faculties to perceive external objects.

Now, because the mind does not follow the eyes and other faculties to perceive objects, this is what is meant by the mind departing from the body. Not only does it not follow the eyes and other faculties to perceive objects, but it can also turn back to observe the very faculties that see and so forth;

hence it is said, 'turning back to observe one's own face. To rely on the faculties is called 'abiding'; to depart from the faculties is called 'leaving. Since leaving and abiding depend upon oneself, it is called 'freedom. 'Perception' (vedanā) takes the meaning of receiving and discerning external objects. Now..."
One does not accept [them], and discrimination also ceases; thus, one transcends the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Observing its origin, one finds that false and deluded conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) constitutes its root.
Zhenji said: "Because it falsely illuminates and realizes, it is called 'empty clarity' (*xūmíng*)."

Ānanda, that son of good family shall therein attain a great radiance, his mind becoming luminously enlightened. Yet, because he represses [his emotions] excessively within, he suddenly gives rise to inexhaustible compassion at that moment.

Thus, even when beholding mosquitoes or gadflies, he regards them as if they were his own infants; a heart of pity arises and he involuntarily sheds tears. This is called the over-repression of one’s spiritual practice.
Guixiang said: "The 'red infant' refers to one newly born who has no eyebrows or hair and whose complexion is red.

To awaken to this is to be without fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. Once one attains clear understanding and is no longer deluded, [the affliction] will naturally dissipate over time. If you take this to be a sign of saintliness, then the demon of sorrow will enter your heart and viscera.
You will feel pity upon seeing others and weep without limit, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin."

Zhaoxi said: "The phrase 'his mind becomes luminous' refers to what follows below: when the veil of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolves and the veil of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear.

Ānanda, furthermore, among those good men within that state of meditative concentration, when they see the veil of form dissolve and the veil of sensation become clear, a superior sign appears before them. Being moved by this to an excessive degree, they suddenly give rise to boundless courage within themselves;

their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve equals that of the Buddhas, claiming that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called 'the overstepping of effort through rashness.'"

The Supplement states: "Gratitude" refers to the experience where the clarity of the *skandha* of sensation seems as though it were due to the power of the Sage; thus, a heart of gratitude arises. Tiāoxī says: "Impetuous" refers to a courageous mind that is lofty and impulsive.

Awakening brings no fault; it is not itself the realization of sainthood. Once one has attained clear understanding and is no longer deluded, [the afflictions] will naturally dissipate over time. If you mistake this for the attainment of sainthood, then mad demons will enter your heart and viscera.

Upon meeting others, you will boast with peerless arrogance; your mind will reach such a state that you look neither to the Buddhas above nor to humanity below. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear. Having nothing new to realize before them, they lose their former dwelling;

their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of inner desolation, seeing nothing at all. Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within their minds, and at all times they remain submerged in this recollection without dispersal, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind and losing oneself through a lack of wisdom."

The Supplement states: When the practitioner has already attained clarity within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), they desire to discard this and grasp that similar state. However, before the new realization has emerged, the clarity of the aggregate of sensation is lost. This occurs precisely because their power of wisdom has declined.

Since the present aggregate of sensation was attained and then lost, it is called the "ground of mid-level collapse. In comparison to the previous similar state, the subsequent aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) will be empty and translucent;

hence it is called "mid. As for "sinking into recollection without dispersal," it means recollecting one's former dwelling place. Regarding the subsequent clarity of the aggregates, the text further states below: "Morning and evening, gather the mind and suspend it upon one [object]."
This is merely the mind hanging upon what has been lost.

To awaken to this is without fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If you take it as such a realization, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and viscera, causing you to grasp at the mind and hang it in one place morning and evening.
You will lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear. Their power of wisdom exceeds their concentration, yet they lose its sharp intensity;

harboring various superior natures within their minds, they themselves suspect they are Vairocana. Content with this slight attainment, this is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, thereby drowning in intellectual views.

The *śamatha* (calm abiding) is retributive wisdom (*vipākajñāna*), because the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) therein is particularly predominant. Changshui says: "Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is slight, one loses constant discernment;
because the power of wisdom is excessive, one sinks into mere intellectual views. Xunwen says: "Losing constant discernment means losing the ordinary mind of careful and thorough investigation."

Awakening to this brings no fault; it is not yet the realization of a sage. If you mistake this for the realization of a sage, then the demons of inferiority and complacency will enter your heart and mind.
You will see others and say of yourself, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," thereby losing right concentration and falling into ruin.

Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exceeds the power of subtle wisdom (*prajñā*), a sudden resolve (*adhimukti*) arises, which triggers the seeds of the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Thus, one clings to what is inferior as being superior; this is why it manifests here.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear. Having newly realized this but not yet attained [the final goal], their former mind has already perished; as they survey these two boundaries, difficulties arise spontaneously.

Suddenly, within their hearts, an inexhaustible sorrow arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison. They have no desire to live and constantly seek someone to end their lives so that they may quickly attain liberation.
This is called losing one's skillful means (*upāya*) in practice.

The Supplement states: This has a general meaning similar to the previous passage regarding "losing what was gained. If so, why is it that the manifestation of the clarity of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) sometimes appears and sometimes vanishes?

One must understand that the clarity of the *vedanā-skandha* is merely its initial attainment; it is not yet the perfection of contemplation. Because the *vedanā-skandha* is exhausted, when one intends to advance further toward realization, this state is immediately lost.

As the preceding passage by Wuxing says: "Because each of the five deluded thoughts is taken as the object of meditation within the domain of its respective aggregate, they are on the verge of being destroyed but not yet destroyed, like the light of a lamp about to go out."

It flares up again; this is the result of his mind warring against the power of meditative concentration. Now that he has for the first time attained clarity regarding the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate), yet it has not reached a state of firm purity, he already aspires for new realizations.
How could he avoid losing the shallow dharma he has just attained?

To realize this is to be without fault; it does not constitute the realization of a sage. If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then a demon of partiality and constant sorrow will enter your heart and viscera. You will grasp a sword in your hand and cut your own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of your life.

Or, constantly filled with sorrow, you will flee into the mountains and forests, unable to bear the sight of people. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

The seeds of regret and affliction are stirred up and give rise [to such actions]. Because one practices without skillful means, one summons demons and spirits. As recorded in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, various bhikṣus by the side of the Vālukā River practiced the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);
becoming excessively weary of the pure, they sought out blades to cut themselves. It was the work of demons that caused this. Had they attained awakening, there would have been no fault.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright. Once they dwell in purity and their minds are settled in peace, suddenly an infinite joy arises within them;
their hearts are so filled with rapture that they cannot restrain themselves. This is called "light ease" (praśrabdhi), yet it lacks wisdom and self-restraint.

Zhaoxi said: "Among the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), the essential nature of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) belongs to concentration (*samādhi*). Xunwen said: "The seven factors of enlightenment are mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity.

The first [mindfulness] pertains to both concentration and wisdom; the next three belong to wisdom; and the latter three belong to concentration. If concentration were to include wisdom, the Path would be fully realized. Now, since that which has been aroused lacks the self-sustaining power of wisdom, concentration instead turns into distraction.
Mara finds his opportunity, and delight enters therein."

Awakening to this brings no fault; it is not yet the realization of a sage. If you mistake this for the realization of a sage, then a demon of partial attachment to joy and pleasure will enter your heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, you will laugh;
by the side of the road, you will sing and dance alone, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation. You will lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright. Believing they have already attained sufficiency, they suddenly experience groundless and great pride (*māna*).

Thus, pride, excessive pride (*atimāna*), and pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), or overweening pride (*adhimāna*), or the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) all arise simultaneously. In their minds, they even look down upon the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, let alone those of lower rank such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior while lacking the wisdom to save oneself."

Zizhong said: "There are seven types of pride (*māna*). To rely on oneself and look down upon others is called *asmimāna* (pride of self). To weigh oneself against others and compare one's own virtues with theirs is simply called *māna* (pride).

To claim superiority over those who are one's equals is called *adhimāna* (excessive pride). To claim superiority over those who are actually superior is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride). To claim attainment of what has not been attained is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride). To feel self-conceited despite knowing one's own inferiority is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).

To disparage the scriptures and images is precisely *mithyāmāna* (false pride). The *Buryi* (Supplement) states: "The seven prides in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* are identical to those in this sutra. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* [also] contains them."

Great pride constitutes eight types of pride. The first fascicle of the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lùn* states: "Pride (*māna*) refers to the mental state of comparing oneself with others and conceiving 'I am superior,' 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.

Its essence is the inflation of the mind through such reliance. It may be innate (*sahaja*) or conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*). Its function is to obstruct the absence of pride. As the Sūtras describe three categories of pride: the category of pride that 'I am superior,' the category of pride that 'I am equal,' and the category of pride that 'I am inferior.

Alternatively, one might raise the doubt: 'The Sūtras already enumerate seven types of pride; why does it further say "and so forth" (*yāvat*)? One must understand that this is stated according to the Buddha’s intention to explain the characteristics of pride as they manifest among sentient beings."

It does not stop at these seven; hence there is this statement. Thus, the current enumeration of the seven types of conceit (*māna*) is also a brief illustration. "Conceit beyond conceit" (*atimāna*) is the conceit among conceits, for it exceeds the preceding conceit by a further doubling.

To awaken is to be without fault; this is not yet the realization of a sage. If one takes this awakening to be the realization of a sage, then a portion of the great demon of pride will enter their heart and viscera. They will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images.

They will say to donors, "These [images] are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood; these scriptures are but tree leaves or folded flowers. Thinking that the physical body is the true, eternal reality, they fail to show it respect, yet instead venerate clay and wood—this is truly a perversion.

Those with deep faith will follow them in destroying and breaking things, burying them in the earth. By misleading sentient beings, they cause them to fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). This shall... [occur].
Regarding "Falling into Ruin," Gushan said:

"One comes to know the True through its provisional manifestations, and realizes the Way by means of words. Thus, one venerates the images to give rise to reverence, and transcribes the words to awaken the mind.

The principle of maintaining the Three Jewels lies herein. If one gives rise to false views, how can they comprehend the Middle Way? Merely respecting themselves while disparaging the scriptures and images, they are delighted when the winds of heterodoxy begin to blow."

Furthermore, in the past, Wei Yuansong remonstrated with Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, advising him not to construct monasteries based on biased views, but rather to take the four seas as the Yanping Great Monastery, to regard husband and wife as the holy assembly, to identify the Emperor himself as the Tathāgata, to plant meritorious virtues as the guiding pillars, and to honor the elderly as the *sthavira*.
Emperor Wu was deluded by these words and subsequently extinguished the Buddha-dharma.

Could it be that these proponents were not actually celestial Māras or non-Buddhists who had entered the Buddha-dharma to carry out their wicked schemes for the purpose of destroying our teaching? Changshui said: "The ignorant who practice meditation all fall [into error]."

These views are all of the demonic kind; they fail to understand the intent behind the Tathāgata’s teachings through images. Furthermore, in the final age, those who maintain the Dharma rely upon these teachings through images;

it is by means of them that renunciants study the Way and cultivate their practice. Yet the demons destroy the causes of faith, causing people to deface scriptures and icons. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "If the Buddha does not preach the teachings, they will perish.

If the teachings perish, who would there be to practice or attain the Way? Fools do not see this passage and thus flatly slander the Buddha, claiming he taught nothing. Therefore, one must know that if the Dharma were not preached, the twelve divisions of the canon would have perished at this point. It is necessary...
Know that those who disparage the sutras and images have demons and devils entering their hearts; this is a great false view. You must clearly recognize this and not join in such slander.

Furthermore, among those good sons in meditative concentration, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear and bright, they may achieve a perfect realization of the subtle principle within their spiritual clarity and attain great compliance.

Their minds suddenly experience immeasurable lightness and ease, and they claim to have become sages and attained great mastery. This is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom.

Zhaoxi said: "As for 'lightness and tranquility' (praśrabdhi), although the name is the same as before, its meaning is different. This is because it refers to attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom.

Herein, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is free from the delusions of heaviness and turbidity regarding all sensory objects, one speaks of becoming a sage and attaining great mastery."

To awaken is to be without fault; this is not yet the realization of a sage. If you take this awakening to be the realization of a sage, then a degree of the "delusive demon of fondness for lightness and purity" will enter your heart and viscera. You will then consider yourself satisfied and no longer seek further progress.

Such people mostly become "monks who have heard nothing," misleading sentient beings and causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall surely sink into ruin.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear. Within this clarity and awakening, they attain a nature of empty luminosity. Suddenly, however, they turn toward eternal extinction;
they negate cause and effect and enter exclusively into emptiness. As the mind of emptiness manifests before them, they eventually give rise to the view of perpetual annihilation.
Xunwen said: The *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "It is better to give rise to the view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness as small as a mustard seed.

To realize this is not a fault; it is not a mark of saintly realization. If one takes this to be a sign of sainthood, then the demon of emptiness will enter one's heart and entrails. Such a person will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Lesser Vehicle.

Believing that a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness and thus has nothing to observe or violate, they will constantly drink alcohol and eat meat before faithful donors, engaging extensively in sexual misconduct. Due to the power of the demon, they will cause those people before them to fail to develop faith.

They harbor doubt and slander; the demonic mind has long entered them. Some consume excrement and urine, while others indulge in wine and meat; in every respect they are empty of virtue. They violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, lead others into sin, and lose right concentration;
they shall surely fall into ruin.
Zizhong said: "This arises from the seeds of false views; it draws this demon of emptiness (*śūnyatā-māra*) into one's heart and viscera. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"Māras can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in the faction of Māras as if with glue or lacquer, such that they do not consider it difficult to sever their hands or cut off their arms. Gushan said: "Alas! In these degenerate times, people conflate the heterodox with the orthodox, taking them to be the Great Way."

They rank the practice of discipline as the Lesser Vehicle; they cast aside the precepts and ritual protocols as things belonging to others; they consider painting demons and spirits a mark of skill; and they treat the lack of restraint as a prevailing trend.

Furthermore, regarding the prohibitions of yin and yang and the deluded sayings of the vulgar, they accept them all with faith, fearing them as if they were severe punishments. I do not know whether the teachings of the Vinaya are superior to the books of yin and yang, or whether the discourse of the Tathāgata is more excellent than the talk of the vulgar.
To turn one’s back on the right and face the wrong is the height of confusion. May those great men who cherish the Way reflect upon this once; or may the masters of our school take it to heart.

To instruct the masses is to strike the thunderbolt of the Dharma for those slumbering in delusion and to illuminate the lamp of wisdom through the long night. If this is so, then the bequest of Nirvana and the admonitions of this sutra will find their fulfillment in such a person, and the Way will be fully realized;

what further need is there to wait for the appearance of the Four Reliances? As the *Guoce* (Strategies of the State) says: "It is easy to skillfully depict ghosts and spirits, but it is difficult to masterfully portray dogs and horses."
Now, by casting aside the restraints of the Vinaya and speaking recklessly of non-obstruction, one is like painting ghosts and spirits. The Grand Historian said:

"I have observed that the arts of Yin and Yang are often overly detailed, causing people to become obsessed with taboos and full of fear. These reckless claims of the common folk are merely further corruptions of the school of Yin and Yang."

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright. They savor this empty luminosity until it penetrates deep into their very marrow. Suddenly, infinite craving arises in their hearts;

when this craving reaches its peak, it becomes madness, which then turns into lustful desire. This is called the meditative state being peaceful and harmonious as it enters the mind, yet lacking the wisdom of self-maintenance, they mistakenly fall into various desires.

Those who savor its empty clarity become attached to the pure state within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) during meditative concentration, taking it for a superior realm. From this, craving arises;
lacking the discernment of wisdom, they activate the seeds of greed, which then erupt as mad desire.

To realize this is to be without fault; it does not constitute the realization of a sage. If one takes this to be the realization of a sage, then the demon of desire will enter their heart and viscera.

Such a person will invariably claim that desire is the path to Bodhi and will convert laypeople to practice desire with equality. They will declare that those who engage in sexual intercourse are "sons of the Dharma" who uphold the teaching.

By the power of spirits and ghosts, they will gather the ignorant and deluded during the final age, numbering as many as a hundred, or even two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, until they reach ten million. When the demon’s mind becomes weary and leaves its body, the practitioner will lose all majestic virtue and fall into royal peril—this is what is meant by "doubt."
This causes sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), leading inevitably to their downfall.

Tiāoxī says: "This is like the state of the afflictions (*kleśa*) about to arise as described in the Tiantai *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation). Zhìzhě said: 'Since birth, the desires of the realm of form and the desire realm have been suppressed and could be halted;

yet what is now arising is an affliction of such blazing intensity that, upon encountering external objects, the mind becomes frantic and the eyes grow dark, like a sleeping lion that roars when touched. If one does not recognize this, it can lead a person to commit [evil deeds]."**
This is a grave offense. Since the present text states that "Māra enters his mind," it means that both the arising of afflictions and the presence of Māra manifest as two concurrent conditions.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* appearing before you are all due to the interaction of the mind with the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation). Therefore, these phenomena appear. Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not measure themselves and, encountering such conditions, fail to recognize their own confusion.

They claim to have attained the state of a Sage; thus, having committed a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You, too, should take the words of the Tathāgata to heart after my parinirvāṇa.

Transmit this teaching to the age of the Dharma’s decline, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity; maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

Ānanda, when that son of good family has cultivated samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted, although his outflows (āsrava) are not yet extinguished, his mind is detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage; he has already achieved this.

Although the outflows have not yet been exhausted—referring here to the outflow of ignorance beyond the realms—one proceeds from this ordinary body upward through the sixty stages of the Bodhisattvas to attain the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who, while in deep sleep, utters words in a dream;

although that person has no conscious awareness of them, the words possess a distinct rhythm and sequence that cause those who are awake to understand their meaning. This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The sixty stages of the sages are presented as a general overview; specifically, they refer to the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*).孤山 (Gushan) says: "From the initial three gradual steps up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there are both the worthy (*ārya*) and the sage (*ārya*);

these are all the positions traversed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and are therefore collectively termed 'stages of the sages'. Question: Since the fifty-five positions on the true path of Bodhi do not include the meaning of the three gradual steps, why are the sixty stages of the sages now included?

Answer: The former was based on a specific discussion, while the present follows the general explanation. Within this general explanation, the meaning includes the external ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) and the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*).

Regarding the stage of reality (*tattva*): if discussed separately, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana*) onward, one begins to correctly clarify the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*). The *Supplement* states:

"The ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, the ten stages, the preceding stage of Dry Wisdom, and the preceding gradual sequence constitute sixty [stages]. One who attains the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) enters into the stage of semblance-saintliness.

In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asks the Buddha: "What is meant by 'mind-made'? The Buddha replied: "It is like the movement of the mind, which is swift and unimpeded; it is named after this metaphor. Furthermore, that sūtra contains...

The two meanings are explained again. The first states: "Just as when one is a hundred thousand *yojanas* away, by recollecting what was previously seen, one reaches that place through a continuous succession of moments.

The second states: "By the power of the *māyopama-samādhi*, one is born because of recollecting one's original vows. In these two scriptural passages, both cases involve being born through mental recollection. Regarding this, *Xunwen* says: "This differs from the explanation in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

The *Xuanyi* follows the perspective of the cause, whereas the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* focuses on the fruit—meaning that at the time of relinquishing the *pariccheda-bhava* (segmented existence) to be born into the *parināmika-bhava* (transformative existence), it is swift and unimpeded. If this is so, does Zhiyi contradict the scriptural text? Answer: He does not contradict it.

It appears that "mental engagement" (*manasikāra*) refers to the mental state that takes the bliss of *samādhi* as its object; thus, the sutra preserves two meanings, which appear sequentially. In the fourth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, three types of "mind-born bodies" (*manomaya-kāya*) are clarified:

first, the mind-born body entering the bliss of *samādhi*; second, the mind-born body awakening to the self-nature of phenomena; and third, the mind-born body of spontaneous birth according to its kind.

In the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the first is correlated with the Two Vehicles entering emptiness, the second with the Shared Teaching emerging into the provisional, and the third with the Distinct Teaching cultivating the Middle Way. They are collectively termed "mind" because the first involves mental engagement.

The first is the mind of emptiness (*śūnyatā-citta*); the second is the mind of provisional construction (*prajñapti-citta*); and the third is the mind of subsequent construction (*paścāt-kṛta-citta*). It is further stated that the "understanding resembling" [the truth] in the Separate and Complete Teachings, as long as true realization has not yet been produced, is all termed "constructed mind.

One should know that the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*) intended in the present sutra refers specifically to this third category. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "In the various texts of the Tiantai school, the 'mind-born body' is explained with its meaning extending through the four teachings; it refers to those of the three vehicles who have not yet severed ignorance."

In total, there are nine types of persons who practice contemplation. This is because the meaning of "forming" (as in forming images) is universally applicable, and the meaning of the "expedient means for rebirth" is also universally applicable. In the *Fahua Xuanyi*, these are correlated with the three preceding teachings; it does not describe them as being "perfect" (*yuan*) or "semblance-perfect" (*si*).

Regarding their inclusion therein, the *Zhi guan ji* states: "Because contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is predominant, the designation 'mind-born' (*manomaya*) is appropriate for the Path of Teaching. As for the *Weimo jing shu*, it contrasts this with the latter three teachings.

All who say they "fear" do so because they dare not make a definitive judgment. In the *Fahua Xuanyan*, it is stated that the "Peaceful and Blissful" [nature] is intended as empty and is directed toward the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The *Zhiguan Ji* states that this is done to encompass both the general and the specific.

Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā*: it correlates "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) with the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), and by analogy, subsumes the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*). Those who enter emptiness do so solely for the sake of the Shared meaning; therefore, various texts proceed and retreat with ease according to the doctrinal meanings of their respective teachings, speaking with sovereign freedom as they adapt to individuals and doctrines.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* text being restricted to the Distinct Teaching yet connecting to the Shared, the *Zuochan sanmei jing shu* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) states: "Both are called 'stages' (*bhūmi*). This is based on the *Laṅkāvatāra*. However, if one follows the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the "body born of the will" (*vaśavarti-kāya*) is somewhat more inclusive in its meaning.

Furthermore, one must understand that at the beginning of the section on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the conclusion indicates the exhaustion of the aggregates, which corresponds to entering the stage of "conformity to practice" (*sādṛśya-prayoga*). This is based on...

Regarding the initial mutual inclusion of the faculties, it is said: if one realizes and enters into the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), not only is the aggregate of form exhausted, but the remaining four aggregates are also empty; thus, one destroys delusion and enters into the principle (*tattva*).

Therefore it is said that one sees the minds of all Buddhas, appearing like reflections manifested within a clear mirror. If one is of dull faculties, one can only see the dissolution and integration of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), yet has not attained any realization.

Therefore, we proceed to examine the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). At present, we shall explain the sequential cultivation of contemplation through the five aggregates for those of dull faculties. It is not possible to point to a specific person practicing the contemplation of the aggregate of sensation who has not already attained realization regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Now, among those cultivating meditation within the five aggregates, all are engaged in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), aspiring to enter the stage of semblance-realization (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*). As for the statement that they "ascend through the stages of the sages" (*ārya-bhūmi*), this text refers to this very stage; in meaning, it is equivalent to the higher and lower stages.

This is because, just as one attains realization within each individual aggregate, one is likewise able to ascend through the stages of the sages. Otherwise, how could there be Bodhisattvas who have attained the body born of intention (*manomaya-kāya*)?

"Is he possessed by Māra? Changshui says: "The analogy below is as follows: because one has not yet shattered the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it is like the delirious speech of one who is fast asleep.

Because there exists a portion of the stage of sagehood, it is like the orderly sequence of phonemes. It causes those who are not sleeping to all awaken to that speech; just as when one realizes one is a sage, one knows that the other person possesses the potential for the stage of sagehood.

Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: 'The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees this person, and they will be able to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: 'Ensnared by the mind of perception, one is as if in a dream; through contemplative understanding, clarity arises.'"

The sequence of the white [categories] is as previously stated. When the mind of one who sleeps is in a state of *avyākṛta* (neutral), it is said that there is no distinct object of cognition; this serves as a metaphor for the absence of a corresponding proof.

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, then within the awakened and luminous mind, it is like the removal of dust and grime. To have a complete and circular illumination of the beginning and end of the single cycle of birth and death is called the exhaustion of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Gushan said: "Awakened clarity is like a mirror; floating thoughts are like dust. When thoughts are exhausted, the mind is clear, yet one still dwells in a semblance [of enlightenment]. The phrase 'having a tail' refers to the beginning and the end. If one awakens to the true permanence..."
There is no distinction between beginning and end within birth-and-death; therefore, it is called "perfect illumination" (*yuánzhào*). The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "It refers to principle (*lǐ*).

Because one can take birth-and-death as a single principle, it is said that 'the single principle has a beginning and an end,' which refers precisely to the end and beginning of birth-and-death. This is merely a re-explanation of the preceding phrase. People take birth as the beginning and death as the end;

now, through the perfect illumination of the single essence, one exhausts the beginning of birth and investigates the end of death, all without departing from this single principle—hence it is called 'perfect illumination. Zizhong says: 'All afflictions arise from conceptualization (*xiāng*). Therefore, when the aggregate of conceptualization (*xiāngyīn*) is eliminated, [then...]"
Transcending this turbidity, one contemplates its origin: pervasive delusive ideation (*vikalpa*) serves as its root.
Ideation is capable of fusing and transforming, penetrating through material obstructions; it is like the mind’s thought of a sour plum, which causes saliva to flow in the mouth.

Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes luminous.
Within this samādhi, his mind comes to cherish its own perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks after skillful means.

At that time, a celestial demon (māra) awaits an opportunity to seize it. He hovers his essence over a person, who then speaks the Dharma and the sutras with his own mouth. The person does not realize they are possessed by a demon; they claim for themselves that they have attained supreme nirvana.

They come to the dwelling of a seeker of skillful means—a son of good family—and spread their seat to preach the Dharma. For a brief moment, their form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them;

or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a bhikṣuṇī; or they may be in a dark room and yet their body emits radiance. This person, deluded and confused, mistakes them for a bodhisattva and believes their teachings, which agitate their mind and destroy [their right resolve].
This Buddha-discipline practitioner secretly harbors lustful desires. He delights in speaking of portents, auspicious signs, and extraordinary transformations;

he may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending conflagration, or describe the terrors of war and enmity to people, causing their household wealth to dissipate without cause. This is called a "strange ghost" who, having grown old, has become a demon.

Zhaoxi said: "When a flying spirit attaches itself to a person, it must attach to one who is worthy of such attachment; that person is surely one who has cultivated meditative concentration and practiced wisdom. *Buyi* says: "These are the ten demons within the realm of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*)."

As for those who clarify [the matter] by citing oral traditions, it is likely because their thoughts are swift and sharp—the very height of discursive observation (*vitarka-vicāra*)—and they lack the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Consequently, they must express [their views] through speech, which is why these are merely demons arising from the fault of mental projections regarding both the speaker and the listener. As the *Xunwen* (Recorded Sayings on Cultivation) states: "As mentioned previously, celestial demons wait for an opportunity to exploit such conditions."
Now, regarding what is called a "strange ghost": previously its leader was cited; now its followers are mentioned. Furthermore, the former was a general name, while this is a specific designation.
It harasses and disturbs this person until it becomes satiated and leaves that person's body; then both the disciple and the teacher fall together into the king’s calamity.

Zhaoxi said: "The disciple and the master are like a child seeking skill and a teacher expounding the Dharma; all subsequent cases follow this principle. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Expounding the Dharma must necessarily involve skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)."
That is to say, one is able to manifest the one as a hundred, a thousand, and so forth.
You should first awaken to this so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, you will fall into delusion and ignorance and descend into the Avīci Hell.

Ānanda, furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect samādhi will give rise to illumination.
Within *samādhi*, the mind fondly wanders; its refined thoughts fly forth, greedily seeking out experiences.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Because the internal cause is moved by the conceptualizing mind, one externally delights in traveling. Consequently, one takes it as a matter to preach the Dharma and transform others, or travels about to seek teachers."

At that time, a celestial Mara, waiting for an opportunity, sends a flying spirit to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with his mouth. This person is unaware that he is possessed by a Mara, and he also claims to have personally attained supreme Nirvana.

He comes to the place of the seeker of the Way, a son of good family, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma; yet his own form undergoes no change. Those listening to the Dharma suddenly see themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into a mass of purple-gold light.

Each member of the assembly experiences this, attaining what they have never known before. These people are deluded and confused, mistaking him for a Bodhisattva, and their hearts become licentious and dissolute, breaking [the precepts].

The Buddha’s discipline is secretly violated by the practice of lustful desire. Such persons delight in speaking of various Buddhas appearing in the world, claiming that a certain person in a certain place must be the incarnation of a particular Buddha come here, or that a certain person is a particular Bodhisattva who has come to transform the human realm.

Because people see them as such, their hearts give rise to longing and craving; wrong views arise in secret, and the seeds of wisdom are extinguished. These are called *pātra* ghosts who, having grown old, have become demons.
They will harass and disturb this person until they become weary and satisfied; having left that person's body, both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (samādhi) gives rise to illumination.
Within this samādhi, the mind becomes fond of a continuous, lingering state; it clarifies its refined contemplation and greedily seeks to achieve a harmonious resonance with the truth.

Zizhong said: "Now, when the mechanism of the mind has perished and there is tranquil illumination, the principle spontaneously accords in mystery. If one seeks to attain union through longing, the very act of conceptualizing the mind introduces error; thus, the celestial māras find their opportunity."

Guixiang said: "The term 'harmonious integration' (*mianhui*) refers to the subtle merging [of mind and object]. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "To speak of 'conformity' (*qihé*) means to seek a correspondence between one's own words and those of the Buddha.

This must arise from views produced within one's own conceptualization, for it does not accord with the sūtras and śāstras. For instance, to say that the Buddha has [distinctions of] great and small, or true and false—is this not a mistaken interpretation?"

At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to seize it. He dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is truly unaware they are possessed by a demon; they also claim to have personally attained supreme *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place where the seeker of the Way—a son of good family—resides, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. Their physical form and those listening to the teaching undergo no outward change. They cause the listeners, before even hearing the Dharma, to experience a spontaneous awakening, with their thoughts shifting and changing from moment to moment.

Some may gain knowledge of past lives; some may possess the power of knowing others' minds; some may see the hells; or some may know all manner of things regarding the good and evil of the human world. Or...

They recite verses aloud or chant the sutras themselves, each praising and delighting in what they have never experienced before. This person is deluded and confused, mistaking himself for a Bodhisattva. His mind is steeped in attachment, and he violates the Buddha’s precepts while secretly indulging in lustful desires.

He delights in saying that among Buddhas there are great and small; that such-and-such a Buddha was a former Buddha and such-and-such a Buddha was a later Buddha; and that within these ranks there are true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas—the same applies to Bodhisattvas.
Because people see him thus, they cleanse their original minds [of doubt] and easily fall into perverse enlightenment. This is called a "possessing ghost" who, having grown old, has become a demon.

Changshui said: Regarding the "male and female Buddhas," [the proponents] claim it is to show that practitioners may engage in acts of lust without hindering their attainment of Buddhahood. While there are indeed partial and perfect Buddhas according to the teachings—wherein the origin is the same but the manifestations differ—how could there be any distinction of "great" and "small"?
It is only heterodox people who clearly speak of such "great" and "small" [Buddhas]. How easily can one know the original and manifested traces of the Tathāgata?

These heterodox people arbitrarily judge that one was first to achieve Buddhahood and another was later to realize it; they do not merely judge their chronological order, but also recklessly act with insolence, claiming there are "true" and "false" Buddhas. This is what must be cleansed from one's fundamental mind.
In turn, they use false views to eliminate right views, as if washing them away until nothing remains.
They torment and disturb these people, and once their hearts are satisfied, they leave the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal punishment.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by deviant thoughts, your perfect concentration will give rise to illumination.

Within *samādhi*, the mind cherishes the fundamental source. One thoroughly examines the beginning and end of the nature of all things as they undergo transformation, refining the spirit and mind to seek analytical discernment.

Tiaoxi said: "The ocean of nature is perfectly clear and still; therein, the myriad phenomena naturally manifest. If one seeks worldly principles with partiality, it will only further increase the outflowing mind, deviating from original *dhyāna*, and allowing malevolent spirits to enter."

At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends forth his refined essence to possess a person. This person speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth; yet they were previously unaware they were possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvāṇa.

They come to the place of those good men who seek the source, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma. Their bodies possess majestic spiritual power, which subdues those who seek it, causing everyone beneath their seat to submit naturally in their hearts even before hearing the Dharma.

These people declare that the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, Bodhi, and Dharmakāya are none other than the fleshly body present before them, wherein fathers and sons are born one after another in successive generations. Thus...

This Dharma-body is eternally abiding and uninterrupted; it points directly to the present as the Buddha-land, without any separate Pure Abode or golden-hued marks. Such a person, having accepted this with faith, loses their former mind.

They take refuge in their bodies and lives, attaining what they have never had before. These deluded and confused ones mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas; yet when one investigates their minds, they violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires.

They delight in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all Pure Lands, and that the male and female organs are the true abode of Bodhi and Nirvana. Those ignorant people believe these defiled words;
this is known as being possessed by harmful spirits, demons, or evil ghosts who have become demons through old age.

The Supplement states: "Regarding the phrase 'this is the Dharma-body,' the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: 'This body of mine is now the Dharma-body. In principle, there is nothing that exists; it is omnipresent within phenomena. Because phenomena are themselves principle, the Dharma-body is present herein.
Heretics falsely conflate this meaning and perversely apply it to mundane matters; failing to comprehend the nature of the metaphor, they ultimately fall into demonic deviation."
They will harass and disturb this person; once their desire for vengeance is satisfied, they will leave that person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal punishment.
You must be aware of this beforehand to avoid entering the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (samādhi) gives rise to illumination.
Within this samādhi, the mind develops a fondness for distant responses; it circulates and investigates with meticulous scrutiny, greedily seeking a hidden resonance.

Zhaoxi said: "To suspend one's response in expectation of the sacred, and to secretly exert oneself in a spirit of self-exhortation, is to seek signs of efficacy before the principle has yet been realized.

At that time, celestial Māras watch for such an opportunity; they dispatch their essence to possess a person, who then speaks the Dharma and the scriptures with their mouth. That person is originally unaware they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place of the good man who seeks signs, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. They can cause the audience to see their physical form as if for hundreds or thousands of years, causing their hearts to give rise to attachment and lust."

They renounce [their own status] and become servants, providing the four requisites of service without feeling weary. They cause each person in their retinue to recognize that these individuals were originally their own teachers and true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Consequently, a distinct attachment to the Dharma arises, as sticky as glue or lacquer; they experience what has never been known before. These people are deluded by folly and take them for bodhisattvas; they draw near to their hearts, violating the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) of the Buddha and secretly practicing greed and desire.

They are fond of saying in their mouths: "In a previous life, during such-and-such an existence, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, they were my wife, concubine, or brother. Now I have come to deliver you;

follow me and we shall return to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha. Or they may say: "There is another realm of great luminosity where a Buddha dwells, the place where all Tathāgatas take up residence.
Those who lack wisdom believe these false and deceptive words and lose their original mind. These are known as *rākṣasa* spirits (*lìguǐ*) who, having grown old, have become demons (*māra*).

The Supplement states: "To know him as one's former teacher" means causing the listener to falsely recall that this person was their teacher in a previous life, thereby inclining their mind [toward him].
They will harass and disturb this person; once their desire for vengeance is satisfied, they will leave that person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, one is no longer beset by perverse thoughts, and through the illumination of perfect concentration, one enters *samādhi*.

Within this state, the mind develops a fondness for deep penetration; one exerts oneself with diligent effort, delighting in dwelling within the stillness of the aggregates and craving a state of tranquil serenity.

Gushan said: "For one who has forgotten the coming and going of existence, even the marketplace and the court are as the rivers and lakes; for one whose sentiments are attached to birth and death, even the mountain forests are like shackles.

Since one clings to stillness, demons find their opportunity. Changshui said: "When the mind is extinguished, objects are stilled; how could this be restricted by worldly clamor? When thoughts stir, conditions proliferate, regardless of whether one dwells in a valley or hides in seclusion.
Tranquility is what is proclaimed in *dhyāna*; if one makes a deliberate effort to crave it, demons find their opportunity."

At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sent a flying spirit to possess a person, who would then speak the sutras and the Dharma with his own mouth. That person was originally unaware that he was possessed by a demon; he also claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He came to the place where the seeker of the aggregates (the *śrāddha* son) resided, spread out a seat, and preached the Dharma. He caused those listening to him to each recognize their own past karmic actions. Or, at that place, he might say to one person: "Even though you are not yet dead, you have already become an animal.

He then commands another person to step on the first one's tail from behind, causing that person to be instantly unable to stand up. Thereupon, the entire assembly bows their hearts in humble submission. There is...

When people give rise to thoughts, he already knows their inception. Beyond the Buddha’s discipline, he subjects himself to further rigorous asceticism; he slanders bhikṣus, reviles his followers, and exposes the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or reproach.

He is fond of speaking of future blessings; when the time arrives, he does not miss a single detail, even down to the finest hair. This powerful ghost has grown old and become a demon. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says:

"To expose" means to attack another's private secrets. When someone gives rise to a thought, [the ghost] already knows its inception; this is the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

He can know that before a person dies, they have already been an animal, seeing their subsequent retribution; this is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), for with the divine eye one can see the subtle forms of cause and effect. This is truly because...
Māra spirits also possess the five supernatural powers; they too fear that [the practitioner] will falsely achieve [realization].
They cause disturbances for this person until they become weary and satisfied, at which point they depart from the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal peril.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by perverse thoughts, your perfect concentration will give rise to illumination.
Within samādhi, one’s mind cherishes knowledge and views; one diligently and painfully investigates, greedily seeking past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).

Tiaoxi said: "Past-life knowledge is one of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); it is accomplished through cultivation in the Hīnayāna, but attained spontaneously upon the arousal of the resolve in the Mahāyāna. Now, [this practitioner] does not wait for it to arise, nor does he attain it through cultivation;
he seeks it by forming a deliberate thought. Therefore, he invites demonic obstacles."

At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sent a flying spirit to possess a person. This person would speak the Dharma and the sutras with their own mouth, yet the individual remained entirely unaware they were possessed by a Māra;

they even claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They would come to the dwelling of a seeker of the Way—a son of good family—and, having spread out a seat, preach the Dharma. That person, without cause, would obtain a great precious jewel at the place where the Dharma was being preached.

Sometimes the Māra would transform into an animal, its mouth holding the jewel along with various rare treasures, bamboo slips, talismans, documents, and other extraordinary objects, first presenting them to that person and later attaching them to their body. Or else, it would entice the listeners to hide [the jewels].

Beneath the earth, there is a bright moon-jewel that illuminates that place. Those who listen to him experience what they have never known before. They consume many medicinal herbs rather than fine delicacies;

at times they eat only one hemp seed and one grain of wheat per day, yet their bodies remain robust and full because the power of Māra sustains them. They slander bhikṣus and revile the assembly of disciples without avoiding public censure.

They are fond of speaking of treasures in other lands and the hidden abodes of sages throughout the ten directions. Following after them, people often encounter strange and extraordinary individuals. These are called the spirits of mountains, forests, land, city walls, rivers, and peaks.

When spirits grow old, they become demons. Some preach licentiousness and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them; others are diligent yet subsist solely on grasses and trees, their conduct lacking any fixed principle.

The Supplement states: "First bestowing an object upon another and subsequently attaching it to their body" means first giving them a strange or extraordinary thing to see, and then concealing it within the person's body;
this is done to incite greed. Alternatively, "inducing a listener to bury something underground" is intended to deceive them by claiming there is a hidden treasure (*nidhi*).
