Regarding "proclaiming lewdness," the *Zuozhuan* records that Lord Ling of Chen, together with Kong Ning and Fu, had an illicit affair with Xia Ji; they all displayed their inner garments and bared their chests while sporting in the court. Xi Ye remonstrated, saying, "The high officials are proclaiming lewdness."
The people will have no model to follow; this is what is meant by "proclaiming and displaying.
They will vex and disturb these people, and once their hearts are satiated, they will leave the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will often fall into royal punishment.
You shall first awaken so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, being deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration will give rise to illumination.
Within samādhi, they take pleasure in supernatural powers and various transformations; they investigate the source of these manifestations and greedily seek spiritual might.

At that time, a celestial demon seizes the opportunity to fly its essence into a person, who speaks the teachings of the sutras. This person truly does not realize they are possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

They come to the place of the good man who seeks such powers, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma. This person may even hold a flame in their hand, grasping that light and distributing it among the fourfold assembly gathered to listen.

Upon their heads, flames several feet long appeared atop the crowns of all those listeners; yet they possessed no heat and never burned them. Sometimes they walked upon water as if treading on level ground;

sometimes they sat cross-legged in mid-air, motionless; sometimes they entered into jars or stayed within bags; they passed through windows and pierced walls without any hindrance. Only with respect to weapons did they lack mastery.

They claim for themselves to be Buddhas; wearing white robes, they receive the prostrations of bhikṣus. They slander dhyāna and the Vinaya, revile their followers, and expose the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion.
Their mouths constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery. At times they cause people to see Buddha-lands from the side, but this is a delusion caused by demonic power and lacks any reality.

They praise the practice of sexual indulgence and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking various vulgarities as the transmission of the Dharma. These are known as mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, earth spirits, and the accumulated essence-demons of plants and trees over many kalpas. Or...

Furthermore, there are dragon-spirits (*nāga-māyā*). Some are immortals who, upon the end of their lifespans, are revived as spirits; others are immortals whose allotted term has expired and who, according to the reckoning of years, ought to die, yet their forms do not undergo transformation. Possessed by other strange entities, they become demons through old age.
Gushan says: "Věi-bǐ" means vulgar and base. In the *Fāngyán*, it means intimacy and familiarity. Guo Pu says: "To be intimately familiar with one another.
To harass and disturb this person, once the mind of satiation has arisen, they depart from the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal punishment.
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by perverse thoughts, your perfect concentration will give rise to illumination.
In samādhi, the mind’s attachments cease. One investigates the nature of transformation and seeks the profound emptiness. As the *Mahāśāstra* says:

"The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness fundamentally to destroy attachment to existence. If there are those who cling to emptiness, the Buddhas cannot transform them. If one realizes that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual and that the three truths are mutually integrated, then whether there is emptiness or existence, or both emptiness and existence, there will never be any grasping or attachment.
Even if demons and malevolent spirits were to swarm about, what could they do to me?

At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends a flying spirit to possess a person. This person speaks of the sutras and the Dharma, yet the individual remains entirely unaware they are possessed by a demon;

they even claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of a seeker of emptiness—a good son—and arrange seats to preach the Dharma. Within the great assembly, their form suddenly becomes empty and invisible to all, yet they emerge abruptly from the void once more, appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease.

Sometimes they manifest their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; sometimes they extend their hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood; or their excrement and urine become like thick rock honey. Thus they revile...

They destroy the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt. Constantly they speak with their mouths that there is neither cause nor effect, and that upon one death there is eternal extinction, with no further rebirths for either ordinary beings or sages.
Although they attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly practice lustful desires; those who indulge in such desires likewise claim to have attained an empty mind and deny cause and effect.

These are known as the spirits of solar and lunar eclipses, essences, gold and jade, cinnabar grass, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes, which remain immortal for thousands of myriad years and become malevolent spirits when born into this land and grow old.

In the Classics and Histories, "bóshí" (薄蝕) is everywhere written as "shí" (食). The *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "shí. The *Jingfang Yichuan* states: "When the sun and moon appear red or yellow, it is called 'bó' (a partial eclipse). Some say that when an eclipse occurs without the conjunction of the new moon, it is called "bó."
Wei Zhao said: "When the breath goes forth and oppresses [the person], it is called 'thinning' (bó). To cause impairment or destruction is called 'devouring' (shí).
It disturbs and confuses this person, giving rise to a mind of satiety, and then departs from that person's body. Both disciple and teacher often fall into royal calamity."
You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra; otherwise, through delusion and ignorance, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and you are not beset by perverse thoughts, perfect concentration will give rise to illumination.

Within samādhi, they cherish long life; through arduous investigation, they greedily seek eternal years. They abandon birth in the realm of segmented existence and suddenly hope for the permanence of the subtle characteristics of the realm of transformation.

Regarding "transformation" (*pariṇāma*): having severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and exhausted them, one is born in the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). Thus, one undergoes transformation. Now, one suddenly desires to transform this coarse body into a subtle substance and change a short lifespan into a long one.

From this point on, [the text] extends into that land. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Within the land of transformation (*parināmika-bhūmi*), there is subtle arising and ceasing; when the conditions for the appearance of birth are destroyed, if one looks at it from the perspective of the *prādeśika* (segmented) realm, it is also called the eternally abiding Dharma-nature body."

At that time, a celestial demon (*devaputra-māra*) watches for an opportunity to seize his chance. He sends a flying essence to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth. That person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a demon; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place where the seeker of the Way dwells, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma. They love to speak of traveling to and from other lands without obstruction, or of passing ten thousand *li* and returning in an instant, always being able to retrieve objects from those distant places.

Or, while staying in one location within a single house, amidst a space of only a few paces, they cause a person to travel from the eastern wall to the western wall; this person runs with such urgency that...

Not yet reaching that age, he thus developed faith in his heart and doubted whether the Buddha was manifesting before him. He constantly said with his own mouth: "All sentient beings of the ten directions are my children; I give birth to all Buddhas; I bring forth the worlds."
"I am the Primordial Buddha. My appearance in the world is spontaneous and not attained through cultivation. This is called the Sovereign Heavenly Mara dwelling in the world.

It is not well understood that many people fall into royal calamities; they have already withered and died before even encountering their execution. Gushan said:

"The Heaven of Sovereign Mastery (Īśvara) is located above the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm; there is a separate dwelling for the Demon King (Māra-rāja), which is also subsumed under the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). Changshui said:

The *viśa* youth is a *piśāca* ghost; this is translated as "one who consumes vital essence. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "In the preceding text, *Cāmuṇḍā* was identified as belonging to the class of the Lord of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*)."

The mention of the Vaiśyas here serves to include the Four Great Kings. As for the phrase "those who have not yet resolved their minds" (*anutpāditabodhicitta*), it refers to those who, having already resolved their minds, protect the Buddha-dharma themselves.

Regarding the statement that they may "speak alone," this means they transform into beautiful women; it does not mean they possess only physical beauty. Sometimes they speak alone without being questioned, uttering words spontaneously. Listeners are then deluded by these seductive and demonic manifestations.
They will harass and disturb that person until their death.

One must first abandon the *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) death before entering the *pariṇāma-vedanīya* (transformative) death. This largely pertains to the general meaning (*sāmānya-artha*), as it refers to bodhisattvas of the general vehicle (*pṛthagjana-bodhisattva*) who have surpassed the stages of the two vehicles, whether they moisten their birth-bodies or do not pass through them.

"Born, one attains perfect enlightenment. All treatises state that one abandons the *pariccheda-śarīra* (the body of segmented existence) and enters the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (body of transformation). He replied: The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that this is based on the *nirmāṇa-kāya*, not the physical form resulting from karma. It utilizes the past karma performed to sustain the present body, causing it to endure for a long time.

The giving of fruits at that time is uninterrupted; the karma that serves as its basis is successively more subtle, like a transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Because it changes and differs from what was before, it is called "transformation death" (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*).

Jingxi said: "In terms of the general principle, there is the teaching but no person [who attains it]. The Ci'en school names this "transformation" as being "the same in function but different. Thus, those of the three vehicles must abandon the *pariccheda* (segmented) death.

According to the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the Small Vehicle takes the fourth dhyāna as the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*). The Immovable [attainment] is the "limit-attainment" (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna). In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is asked: "What is meant by 'limit'? It is answered: "'Limit' (anta) signifies 'boundary,' and 'extreme' (koṭi) signifies 'culmination. Therefore, it is called the 'limit-extreme' (prāntakoṭika)."

Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras will, during the final age, leave the household life to practice the Way within my Dharma. They praise sexual desire and violate the Buddha’s rules of discipline. These former evil māra-teachers and their disciples transmit their lust from one to another. Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch their hearts and viscera;

Gushan said: "This instruction to Ānanda implies that he need not yet enter extinction. Yet, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fǎzàng zhuàn) states: "He entered the Vāyu-pracala-samādhi and divided his body into four parts to enter parinirvāṇa.

encountering these conditions, they remain confused and do not recognize them for what they are. Claiming to have attained the state of a sage, they commit a great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell.

"You must certainly carry the words of the Tathāgata and transmit them after my parinirvāṇa during the age of the Final Dharma. Cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning; do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity.
Maintain and protect [these teachings] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."

Thus, Mañjuśrī asked: "In the future evil age, how can one uphold this sutra? The Buddha instructed him to abide in the Four Modes of Peaceful Practice and extensively explained the avoidance of conditions such as slander and defamation. Is this not identical to the present case?

That good man, having cultivated *samādhi* until the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) is exhausted, finds that his ordinary dreams have vanished and his waking and sleeping states are always one. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky;

there are no longer any coarse, heavy shadows of external objects. When he observes the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they are like reflections in a clear mirror—coming without anything to adhere to, and passing without leaving a trace.
Responses are received in emptiness, and habitual tendencies are utterly extinguished; there remains only the single, refined truth. Changshui says:

"If the skandha of perception still exists, then upon waking one grasps at images, and in sleep one forms dreams. Once this skandha is exhausted, although there is waking and sleeping, there are no dreams or thoughts;

therefore, it is eternally one. Tiexi says: "According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Arhats have sleep but no dreams. This verifies that when perception is now exhausted, the six sense faculties are purified, as that which is destroyed by perfect contemplation extends [to all]."

This distinguishes it from the two delusions. It is like smelting iron where the coarse dross is removed first; therefore, it says "no longer any coarseness" (*dausthulya*) and so forth. "Vast reception and response" refers to the two aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Sensation takes luminous emptiness as its basis, while perception takes the grasping of images as its function. As the text below states: "The various graspings of images, the mind’s arising of forms and grasps, are called the delusion of pervasive fusion.

Now, within awakened clarity, observing all worlds as a mirror reflects objects is precisely the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). "To realize the absence of old habits" means that both sensation and perception are already devoid of old habits, which are the *vāsanās*.

The *Bùyì* states: According to the *Zhou Lǐ* and the *Lí Zǐ*, there are six conditions for dreams: first, the "dream of equilibrium" (*zhèng mèng*), which occurs spontaneously while in a state of composure; second, the "dream of alarm" (*wò mèng*), occurring when one is startled or shocked; third, the "dream of recollection" (*sī mèng*), occurring through deliberate thought;

fourth, the "dream of waking discourse" (*wù mèng*), occurring when one speaks of something while awake and subsequently dreams of it; fifth, the "dream of joy" (*xǐ mèng*), occurring out of gladness; and sixth, the "dream of fear" (*jù mèng*), occurring out of terror. The *Fǎhuá Wénjù* states:
Only the Buddha does not dream, because he is free from doubt and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Dreams arise from five causes, as the verse says: "By means of a doubting mind..."

[Answer: They are distinct. [Dreams] arise from learning, present circumstances, non-humans coming to speak with one, and these five factors; thus, dreams consist of five matters. Regarding the five matters and six periods, they are all fundamentally the *ālayavijñāna*.

The *Xunwen* (薰聞) states that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 92, says: "There are two kinds of sleep: first, sleeping and dreaming; second, sleeping without dreaming. An Arhat does not sleep for the sake of seeking peace or attachment to pleasure."

Receiving only this body composed of the four great elements, the Dharma-nature necessarily involves eating, breathing, sleeping, and waking. Therefore, a brief period of rest is called sleep; it is not the sleep of dreaming.
From this point, the root-source of arising and ceasing is revealed. One perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.

Although one has not yet penetrated the individual threads of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth as shimmering and flickering like a mirage, serving as the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating sense-faculties and their objects. This is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the source of arising and ceasing, for it involves constant flux and volitional activity. Since formations manifest when perception (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, it is said that they are "revealed. As the subsequent text states: "Only arising and ceasing are the limits of formations.

Now, since only formations remain when perception is exhausted, it is said they are "revealed. The *Supplement* (*Bǔyì*) states: "In all cases, it is because formations manifest when perception is exhausted that they are called 'revealed. I now say:

the previous mention of "perception being exhausted" refers to those of sharp faculties who destroy delusions and enter the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*). For those of dull faculties, however, there is merely the suppression of delusions; the aggregate of perception has not yet been destroyed, and they only attain the clarity and brightness of the mind of perception.

This is all; it cannot yet be said to be exhaustive. Now, based on the appearance of clarity and stillness that have just been subdued, I speak of "disclosure. Each is assigned its own origin (*yóuxù*); the karmic characteristics of sentient beings naturally differ according to their good or evil—this is what is meant by "origin. Only those with the clear Dharma-eye can know this.

At present, my station is at the level of the five grades (*wǔpǐn*), where I merely perceive the general characteristics of arising and ceasing. "Origin" refers to one’s nature and destiny (*xìngmìng*), which is precisely the karmic characteristic.

The arising and ceasing of the sense faculties and their objects both proceed from mental formations (*saṃskāra*); therefore, they are called the "pivot-hole" (*shūxuè*). Shen Cunchong’s *Bǐtán* states: "Zhuangzi spoke of 'wild horses' (*yěmǎ*) and 'dust' (*chén*)."

"Dust" refers to two things: the "wild horses" (yema) are merely floating vapors in the fields that, when viewed from afar, resemble herds of sheep or ripples on water. Buddhist texts describe them as being like the "wild horses" or mirages (*marīci*) seen in the heat;
this is precisely what is meant here. Because they arise and perish unpredictably like a mirage, they are called "wild horses. Gushan’s inclusion of "floating dust" (*feiai*) is also an error.

When Gushan says, "exhausting all their categories," he means seeing that all twelve classes of beings emerge entirely from their karma (*saṃskāra*). This is because karma is that which can summon retribution. Although [the text] has not yet...

It penetrates the origins and continuities of each individual life-force. This means that although one may not yet discern their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one has already been able to see, in their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), that those sentient beings all arise through the activity of formations (*saṃskāra*).

Thus, this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is called the "common basis for the arising of life. Its flickering radiance and shimmering appearance refers to the subtle, shifting, and illusory nature of the aggregate of formations, which is like a mirage (*marīci*).

"Clear agitation" refers to what will be discussed below as "profoundly clear and agitated movement. Changshui says: "As for 'not yet penetrating each individual life-force,' although one has already understood..."

The twelve classes of beings all emerge from their respective karmic formations; yet they do not know that the distinct seeds of sentient beings reside within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

This is precisely the seed of karma and suffering within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which constitutes the primary cause and source of the individual life-essence of each sentient being.

If this turbid flickering of the fundamental nature enters its original clarity, and once clarified, its original habitual tendencies are extinguished—like waves subsiding and transforming into still water—it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Changshui says: "The nature enters the primordial clarity" means that when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted, the nature of flux subsides and returns to the single *ālayavijñāna*; this is called "entering the primordial clarity. As the Sūtra says:

"The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternally abiding. Tiaoxi says: "Nature" refers to the nature of arising and ceasing; one "enters" it by means of its revolving back [to the source]. "Primordial" (*yuan*) refers to the primordial pivot-hole; one takes its essential truth as "clarity" (*cheng*).

"Accumulation" (vāsanā) refers to habitual tendencies; it is simply the pervasive afflictions. This can be understood through the analogy of the subsiding of waves. Regarding "transcending the turbidity of sentient beings": the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) serves as the root of birth and death.
Sentient beings grasp at this birth and death as their very substance. Once that root is exhausted, one also transcends this turbidity.
Observe their origins: subtle, hidden delusions constitute their root.
Zizhong said: "Because they are minute, secret, and difficult to know, they are called 'subtle and hidden' (*youyin*).

Ānanda, you should know that among those good men who have attained right knowledge within *śamatha*, their minds are concentrated, luminous, and upright; thus, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find any opportunity against them.
The Supplement states: This refers to the temporary subsiding of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), wherein one becomes still and lucid.

Only then can one investigate and exhaustively penetrate the fundamental source of all living beings. When the primal element within that fundamental source is revealed, one contemplates its profound clarity and its perfect, agitated movement.
If, within this perfect source, one gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the two theories of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

Changshui said: "In investigating the root of the categories of living beings here, one finds that it is solely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), which is profound, hidden, subtle, and ethereal, serving as the source of all arising and ceasing.

Now that this has been laid bare, one realizes there is no other fundamental basis for sentient beings beyond this. Consequently, one clings to the view that the world arises without cause; this is because one does not know that the seeds of the distinctions between good and evil causes and conditions reside within the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).

Thus, the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) arise from this; having practiced until reaching this point, false wisdom suddenly emerges, which is termed 'manifesting'. Tiaoxi said: "Since the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) has already..."

Prostrate. As the turbid and defiled are temporarily clarified, it is said that "contemplation follows from the profound clarity. As one exhaustively perceives the categories of beings migrating through the dark caverns of the five aggregates, it is said that "the perfect [mind] stirs the source of movement."

First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this? Because this person has attained the full breaking open of the life-faculty and, riding upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-organ, sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas.

They see the winding currents of karma as these beings die here and are born there; they see only the cycle of rebirth of sentient beings within those realms. Beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing can be observed. Thereupon, they form this understanding:
"These sentient beings of the ten directions in the world have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas, without any cause."

Gushan said: "When one develops supernormal powers from within meditative concentration, one employs the eight hundredfold powers inherent in the fundamental faculty of the eye to perceive the death and rebirth of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas.

Beyond this, one cannot see; this is also the limit where the power of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted. One does not know the seeds that cause the arising of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness), nor the distinctions in the ripening of fruits induced by the perfuming of ignorance.

Because these are not seen, one then clings to the view that things exist without an original cause—just as when one sees a flying bird and, because it has gone beyond the range of sight, concludes it no longer exists. This is also the case here, due to the sensory objects of the visual faculty."

Originally, there were only eight hundred [merits]. Worldly supernatural powers do not transcend their original causes; if they are supramundane powers, they are unimpeded beyond this limit. Even if an Arhat attains them, these are still worldly powers.

The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava*) of the Lesser Vehicle does not perceive mundane realms. Tiaoxi said: "When the functioning of the mind is completely shattered, the mind becomes even more agitated—this is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Because it is not covered by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), it is called 'completely shattered.

As for the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, since they are discussed in terms of the three periods of time and the three directions, seeing now what was originally without cause is to ride upon past merits. Looking downward..."

The end is causeless. This immediately relies upon future merit; it arises from the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) within meditative concentration, whereby the faculty of the eye manifests this functional power. "The winding flow of karma" refers to the circulation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

"Darkness with nothing observed" refers to the *māyā-tattva* (the principle of illusion) of the non-Buddhists. Indeed, the conditions of good and evil karma are transformations produced by consciousness alone.

Such a person cannot yet perceive the aggregate of formations beyond eighty thousand kalpas, let alone consciousness itself. Therefore, from this point onward, they give rise to the calculation of causelessness. Zizhong said: "To know well arising and ceasing is precisely the aggregate of formations. Furthermore, one observes the aggregate of formations.

The shimmering clarity and agitation are identical to a mirage and lack substantial reality; when the source of birth is exhausted, there is no further principle remaining—this is called the complete shattering of the mechanism of birth.

The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "This interpretation differs from that of Wuxing; it appears each has its own intended scope. However, Zizhi takes 'shattering' to mean the sense of 'opening and revealing.'"
Due to these speculative calculations, they lose their correct and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.

Second, such a person perceives that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because this person, having observed the root of birth, knows that humans produce humans and realizes that birds produce birds; they see that crows have always been black.

The crane has been white since its origin; humans and devas are fundamentally upright, while animals are fundamentally horizontal. This whiteness was not produced by washing, nor was this blackness created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas past, there has been no further alteration or change;

even now, at the end of this physical form, it remains thus. Since I have never seen bodhi from the very beginning, how could there be any further matter of "attaining" bodhi? You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.

Zizhong said: "This person already knows that all things arise from the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and have no other fundamental cause. From this point onward, all things are eternally fixed and likewise have no other cause;

therefore, he says he 'knows that humans produce humans' and 'awakens to the fact that birds produce birds. He does not realize that newly created distinct karma brings about birth in different species;

thus it is said he clings to the notion that there is no cause for the phenomena of the end. He thinks, 'I originally did not see bodhi, and ultimately there is no one who attains bodhi. Since the beginning has no cause, the end cannot be attained either. The Supplement states: "This person claims that sentient beings all arise from [the *saṃskāra-skandha*]..."

Birth and death arise; one fails to realize that the creation of karma from the mind will inevitably result in divergent retributions, instead claiming that the retribution for humans and animals is fixed. Since there is no difference at the root, they argue that the branches must likewise be so. Tiaoxi said:

"There is no further alteration or shifting" refers to those who observe certain classes of humans and animals whose karmic fruits have not yet transformed over a long period of time, and thus give rise to this calculation. As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: [text omitted].

Śāriputra observed the body of the pigeon; for eighty thousand kalpas past and future, its retribution had never changed. Now, within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), having seen this sign, he clings to the notion that all things occur spontaneously (*svabhāva*).

This is precisely because he does not know the life-origins of each of the twelve classes of beings. His statement that "this physical form will end" and so forth clarifies his view that there is no cause for the future;

he should likewise have seen [the continuity] through eighty thousand kalpas. Because non-Buddhists and Śrāvakas share commonalities, the *Xunwen* (Recorded Sayings on Cultivating Hearing) states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, says that when the Buddha was at Jetavana, Śāriputra followed the Buddha’s discourse.
As he was walking, a hawk pursued a dove and flew toward the Buddha. The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Observe the karmic conditions of this dove from past lives.

Śāriputra entered the *pūrvanivāsajñāna-samādhi* (the samādhi of knowledge of past lives) and perceived that for one, two, three, and up to eighty thousand great eons (*mahākalpa*), this dove had constantly been born in the body of a dove; beyond that point, he could see no further.

Rising from the samādhi, the Buddha further commanded him to observe the future: "When will this dove be liberated? Śāriputra entered the *praṇidhijñāna-samādhi* (the samādhi of knowledge resulting from aspiration) and perceived that for one, two... [and so on].

For three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and even for eighty thousand great kalpas, he was not released from his pigeon body. Even after that time had passed, [the Buddha] still could not know [when it would end]. Rising from samādhi, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I do not know when this pigeon shall be released.

The Buddha said, "He shall continue to take the body of a pigeon for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. Only when his retribution is exhausted will he be released, and then he will transmigrate through the five destinies."
Due to this speculative reckoning, they lose correct and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the first type of external path that establishes the theory of no cause.
Zhaoxi said: Master Zhaolun stated that the non-Buddhist Makkhali Gosāla claimed that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are not obtained through karma, but are entirely spontaneous.

A previous sutra states that Makkhali and others all asserted that after this body dies, there is total extinction; now [Makkhali] calculates it to be without cause. Although he does not explicitly say "extinction upon death," once the kalpa is exhausted, he must likewise fall into that same category.

One should know that all views do not go beyond the four propositions: namely, annihilationism, eternalism, both, and neither. Of these, the first two—being without cause—are the view of annihilationism; the latter four concern the pervasive eternity, as well as the partial impermanence and partial eternity [of the self and the world].
"Permanence," and so on, up to "neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death"—these are the latter three propositions. All other speculative views originate from these.
Ānanda, when these good sons within the samādhi concentrate their luminosity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity to interfere.

To exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, one observes that source which is profound, pure, yet eternally subject to agitation and movement. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations within this perfect and eternal reality fall into the four theories of universal permanence.

Changshui says: Because the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) continues in succession without interruption, it is called "constant. Because the four types [of views] one calculates pervade all phenomena, they are called "universal."

First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects, finding no cause in either of these two locations. Through cultivation, they are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas;
seeing that these all circulate in a cycle and are never lost, they reckon them to be permanent.
Zhenji said: "Although both mind and objects are without cause, their arising and ceasing have continued uninterrupted for twenty thousand kalpas; therefore, they are reckoned as permanent.

Second, this person exhaustively investigates the source of the four great elements and finds that their four natures are eternally abiding. Through cultivation, he is able to know that throughout forty thousand kalpas, all the arising and ceasing of sentient beings in the ten directions are entirely constant in essence and never dispersed or lost;
thus, he reckons them as permanent."
Gushan said: "The birth and death of humans do not depart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because the nature of these great elements is not lost, one calculates it to be permanent.

As for the third [type of person], this individual exhausts the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Within the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), there is the fundamental source;

because its nature is eternally constant, through cultivation they are able to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate without losing [this nature], being fundamentally and permanently abiding. Exhaustively finding that the nature is not lost, they calculate it to be permanent."

Zizhong said: "This [state] exists within the six sense faculties and the seventh consciousness; it is the fundamental source of the mind that maintains its nature without ever losing it. One calculates it to be permanent. By citing the 'faculties' upon which it relies, he reveals the 'consciousness' that relies upon them.

Since it speaks of being 'within mind, intellect, and consciousness,' we know this refers to observing the eight consciousnesses. Tiaoxi said: "According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the ālaya-vijñāna cannot be known by any other than Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*);

all other followers of the Two Vehicles and practitioners of external paths are unable to know it. Judging from this, as long as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted, how could one [possibly know it]?"

One reckons this [state] to be permanent. It should be understood that the terms "mind," "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) collectively refer to the eight consciousnesses. The phrase "the original source and its locus" specifically points to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

This is because, through the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one suddenly exhausts the investigation of the eight consciousnesses and perfectly subdues the five abodes of affliction; yet, at the point where the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) is exhausted, one fails to perceive the subtle arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, falsely taking it to be permanent.

This does not mean that one has already perceived the eighth consciousness within meditative concentration. Master Kuò said: "If one has thoroughly understood the eight consciousnesses, how could one harbor divergent views? These words are excellent. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states: "Initially, one contemplates arising and ceasing with respect to the mind and its objects;

next, one contemplates arising and ceasing with respect to the four great elements—this is not yet exhaustive. Now, from the sixth consciousness through to the eighth consciousness, one contemplates their arising and ceasing.

This is the fundamental source of sentient beings, and only then is it exhaustive. The six faculties are the six consciousnesses; 'grasping and sustaining' refers to the eighth consciousness. The triad of mind, intellect, and consciousness corresponds vertically to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, respectively. This may also be understood in this way.

It lies transversely within the three [aggregates]. Whatever arising and ceasing occurs within these three locations is the very source of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) for sentient beings. To perceive that this [stream] is uninterrupted is to realize its constant nature (*dhruva*). Although one passes through the seventh and eighth stages, one observes only the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

Next, one observes the four great elements; thirdly, one observes the eight consciousnesses. Fourth, one exhausts the mind through the conceptualization of views. Furthermore, it is said: "As for the arising of conceptualization within the *saṃskāra-skandha*, one has not yet known the source of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).

If one understands the fundamental cause of the eight consciousnesses, what need is there to discuss divergent views? If one discusses the understanding of the eight consciousnesses such that habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are entirely extinguished, then one universally realizes perfect knowledge (*parijñā*); why then be restricted?"

The "eighty thousand" [verses] are difficult to explain and resolve; one must not harbor doubts. Let them hang high upon the platform of words, awaiting clarity before a decision is made. That text does not mean that [the practitioner] can exhaustively fathom the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Just as the four great elements previously mentioned belong to the category of form (*rūpa*), how could it be said that they are merely observing spatial directions? Rather, it uses form as a provisional basis to infer the source, seeking its arising and ceasing.

This is truly because those among the practitioners of this Perfect Teaching who have lost their way, though they hear of the eight consciousnesses, have not yet exhausted the source of principle. Thus, these people of *samādhi* are merely coincidentally similar to the non-Buddhists.

Fourth, this person, having exhausted the source of ideation and brought about its natural principle, no longer experiences the movement of flowing or ceasing. The mind of ideation, characterized by arising and ceasing, is now forever extinguished; within this principle, there naturally arises that which is neither born nor extinguished.
Because they measure this through the mind, they reckon it to be permanent.

Changshui says: "Since the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and movement has ceased, the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing is naturally the 'activity' (*saṃskāra*). This [view] takes what is subject to arising and ceasing to be non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, it clings to it as eternal. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states:

"The previous three [views] involve calculating the continuity of arising and ceasing at three locations and taking that as eternal. This [fourth view] calculates the cessation of the subtle marks of the mind of perception, clinging to this as the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing; it is superior to the previous three.

While the previous three calculate the continuity of arising and ceasing as eternal, the fourth calculates the subtle similarity between arising and ceasing as the principle, and thus clings to that principle."

It is considered permanent, like seeing a thin stream and calling it still water. Changshui says: "As for the 'source of the principle of arising' (*shengli*), when the conceptual mind (*xiangxin*) is momentarily suppressed, the fundamental source of the class of arising phenomena manifests.

This refers to the subtle characteristics of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as being the "principle of arising. "There is no further flowing or stopping" means that because the arising and ceasing are so subtle, the characteristics of movement and stillness are not perceived.
"Spontaneous within the principle" refers to the spontaneous characteristic of the arising and ceasing of these subtle forms.

By means of these calculations of permanence, one loses correct universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.

Tiaoxi says: "These four [levels] constitute the objects investigated by the 'universal permanence' [view], arranged in order from the broad to the narrow: first, it pervades the five aggregates (*skandha*); second, it is restricted to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); third, it pertains only to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);

fourth, it refers solely to the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing within the aggregate of formations. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The third [level] then pervades the sixth, seventh, and eighth [stages of cultivation], calculating the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the aggregate of formations."

It is merely the perception of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). As previously calculated, once the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is understood to have dissolved, one realizes that what was reckoned as arising and ceasing upon those four great elements is actually the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Therefore, it is said: "Exhausting the root of the four great elements.
This "root" is precisely arising and ceasing. Although the aggregate of form was already contemplated previously, now its very source is being investigated.
This is called the second heterodox school that establishes the doctrine of pervasive permanence.
Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright; thus, Māras cannot find an opportunity to interfere.

Exhausting the fundamental source of all living beings, one observes that profound, pure, and eternally agitated origin. If, within the context of self and others, one gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the four inverted views, specifically the doctrine that "one part is impermanent and one part is permanent."

First, this person contemplates the wondrous, luminous mind as pervading the ten directions of space. Taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate *ātman*, they then reckon that this self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and immovable.

They hold that all sentient beings are born and die within their own mind; thus, their own mind-nature is called "permanent," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.

Zhaoxi says: "The phrase 'observing the subtle' below again raises the topic of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). The phrase 'tranquil and clear' below correctly clarifies the arising of conceptualization. This is also because one does not understand the arising and ceasing of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and falsely claims that the nature of mind at this stage is tranquil and clear, taking it to be the divine self (*ātman*).

As for the term 'divine self,' it is what non-Buddhists call the 'Lord Truth' (*īśvara-satya*), meaning they claim all phenomena are their own property and that all are governed by this divine self as their master.

Xunwen says: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the divine self of the non-Buddhists is nothing other than the six consciousnesses; there is no separate entity. Now, to give rise to such conceptualization within the *skandha* of formations is likewise [an error]."
The consciousness that discriminates phenomena falsely identifies the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as an unchanging self.

Second, such a person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate these as the nature of ultimate impermanence; seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate them as ultimate permanence.

The lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are seen only within a single great trichiliocosm. Zhaoxi said: "Those from the third dhyāna downward are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities;
this is called the nature of impermanence. Those from the fourth dhyāna upward cannot be destroyed by calamities; this is called ultimate permanence."

Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as subtle, refined, and extremely secret; it is like a minute particle that flows through the ten directions, its nature being immutable. It can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant.
This indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self," while all death and birth flowing forth from it is called the "impermanent nature."

Since my [self] is subtle, its arising and ceasing are likewise so; thus it is said that "it arises and ceases simultaneously. Yet this arising and ceasing proceeds from the subtle to the coarse in an uninterrupted succession;

therefore it is said that "all deaths and births, etc. The Supplement states: Because one reckons the essence of the wondrously luminous mind—which pervades the ten directions—to be the nature of the self, the arising and ceasing of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is like fine dust.

Although it flows through the ten directions, because it is so subtle, one does not perceive its movement. Consequently, one reckons that the nature is immutable and fixed as a single extreme of permanence. Thus, the nature of the self as it is reckoned is immovable.

The essence of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is characterized by arising and ceasing; it causes this body to arise and cease moment by moment. One calculates that the physical body is subject to arising, ceasing, and impermanence, yet fails to perceive the subtle arising and ceasing within the *saṃskāra-skandha*, mistakenly regarding it as immovable.

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). They reckon the constant flow of the aggregate of mental formations to be a permanent nature, while regarding the fact that form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now ceased as impermanence.

Gushan says: "One who knows the extinction of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) attains the 'intention' (yi) and immediately enters the stage of semblance (xiangsi). If the initial mind loses this intention, one gives rise to views based on this. This loss of intention refers to the suppression of life-force being regarded as 'extinction,' rather than true severance and extinction.

The preceding and following cases are to be understood accordingly. The *Buyi* (Supplement) says: "The constant flow of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is verified within the previous four [types of] discourses on permanence. In the first three, one directly calculates that birth and death are uninterrupted and thus permanent;

in the fourth, one calculates that the subtle arising and ceasing of phenomena constitute the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing, clinging to this principle as permanence. Tiaoxi says: "These four are inverted..."

[This section concerns] the inversion. First, one contemplates the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) and all sentient beings; this refers to the "retributive fruit" (*vipāka*). Next, one contemplates the land and the eons; this refers to the "supportive environment" (*niśraya*). These two are explained in contrast to others to clarify what is permanent and what is impermanent.

Third, one contemplates one's own mind and body; fourth, one calculates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. These two are explained in relation to one's own matter and mind to clarify what is permanent and what is impermanent. Furthermore, these proceed from the broad to the narrow.
Because they speculate that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the third heterodox doctrine: the theory of partial permanence.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
If, within this state of analysis, they give rise to conceptual calculations, these people fall into the four theories of the finite existence of the world.

First, this person’s mind calculates the origin of birth; its flowing function never ceases. To calculate the past and future is called "having limits"; to calculate the continuous mind is called "being limitless."

Gushan said: "The 'origin of birth' is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the past and future are not perceived, it is called 'having a limit'; because the present continues in succession, it is called 'being limitless.

As for these two, when such a person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas, they see that prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were silent and beyond hearing or seeing. That place where there is neither hearing nor seeing is called 'limitless,' while the place where sentient beings exist is called 'having a limit.'"
Zhaoxi said: "Even after eighty thousand kalpas, it would likewise be as before.

Third, this person reckons that his self possesses universal knowledge and attains a boundless nature; thus, all those people appear within the scope of his knowing. Yet he himself does not know the nature of their knowing;
this is called 'failing to attain a boundless mind' and possessing instead a limited nature."

Gushan said: "One merely perceives that person appearing within the scope of one's own cognition, yet is unable to know that the person's nature is all-pervasive; therefore, one reckons that nature as having limits."

Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Using the pathways of the mind as they perceive them, they deliberate upon all sentient beings, calculating that within a single body, all things are half-born and half-extinguished.
They clarify that everything existing within the world is such that one half has limits and one half is limitless.

Zizhong said: "This person calculates that the place where the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) ceases is emptiness; because it is empty, it is boundless. Yet, when he uses his mind to deliberate, he again perceives the arising of existence; because there is arising, it is bounded. The same principle applies to all things in the world.

He exhausts the emptiness of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, but this does not mean he can destroy the *saṃskāra-skandha* and perceive emptiness. This person sees arising and ceasing within the *saṃskāra-skandha* and, becoming fixated on the aspect of arising, subsequently calculates that the place of cessation is emptiness.

He takes this emptiness—which is boundless—to be what is realized. That which arises on one side belongs to the realm of the bounded; it is not what has been thoroughly investigated. *Tiaoshan* [commentary].

Xiyun said: "These four [positions] regarding finitude are as follows: the first refers exclusively to oneself; the second refers solely to others; the third encompasses both self and others; and the fourth involves a double reckoning of all that is dependent and primary (the environment and its inhabitants) belonging to others.
Thus, the preceding is narrow and the subsequent is broad, thereby establishing their sequence."
From this, by calculating whether there is a limit or no limit, they fall into the ranks of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fourth external path, which establishes the doctrine of finitude.
Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*, those who stabilize their minds with unwavering rectitude will not be given an opportunity by Māra.

As they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and views, such persons fall into four kinds of perverse, "undying" equivocation and pervasive false theorizing.

Zizhong says: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, non-Buddhists reckon that the heavens are eternally abiding and thus name them "Immortality. They further reckon that by answering questions without confusion, one will be reborn in those heavens;

they fear that if they were to answer abruptly while actually not knowing the truth, it would constitute evasive equivocation (*amarā-vikṣepa*). Therefore, when questioned, they reply, "This is secret terminology and should not be fully disclosed," or they provide indefinite answers.

The Buddha’s Dharma rebukes this, saying, "This is truly evasive equivocation"; hence it is called the "Discourse on Immortal Evasive Equivocation. Xunwen says: The *Jieshu* states that non-Buddhists reckon the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) to be the Heaven of Immortality.

First, this person contemplates the source of transformation. Seeing the place where things shift and flow, they name it "change. Seeing the place where things continue, they name it "permanence. Seeing the place where there is something seen, they name it "arising.

Not seeing the place where seeing occurs, they name it "cessation. Seeing the place where the nature of the cause for continuity is not severed, they name it "increase. Seeing the place within the midst of continuity that is devoid [of something], they name it "decrease.

Seeing each individual place of arising, they name it "existence. Seeing each mutual place of disappearance, they name it "non-existence. They contemplate these through principle as a whole, yet their mental application perceives them individually. When seekers of the Dharma come, [they explain this].

When asked about its meaning, he replied, "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing. At all times, he confused his speech, causing the person before him to lose track of the verses and phrases.

Changshui says: Within the single process of arising and ceasing in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), eight distinct meanings are differentiated, namely: permanence and change, arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, existence and non-existence. In the response, six of these meanings are briefly cited;

because the underlying principle cannot be definitively established, the answer merely hovers between two poles, hence the statement "both arising and ceasing," and so forth. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "Mutually" (*hu*) is equivalent to "individually" (*ge*).
All dharmas exist as they arise in their respective places and do not exist where they have perished; all of these are seen within meditative concentration.

Second, this person contemplates the mind with keen observation and realizes that it has no fixed location; because there is no location, he attains realization through non-existence. When someone comes to question him, he answers with only a single word, saying merely "non-existent.
Apart from this non-existence, he has nothing further to say.

Third, this person carefully observes that the mind each has its own location, and through this, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "It is so" (shì).
Apart from this, they have nothing further to say.

Fourth, there are those who hold views that both existence and non-existence coexist; because their objects are fragmented, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they reply:

"That which is existent is also non-existent, yet within that which is non-existent, it is not the case that it is existent. This is entirely evasive and confused, leaving no room for further inquiry or refutation.

Zhaoxi said: From the second to the fourth [of the four propositions], distinctions are made based on the presence or absence [of existence and non-existence] within the preceding eight phrases. The second and third are single reckonings; the fourth is the "both" [reckoning].

Existence is precisely non-existence, like ice being water; non-existence is not other than existence, like ice within water. Among these four propositions, only three are involved, and the "neither-nor" (double negation) has not yet been seen; thus, this reckoning remains coarse.
Due to these speculative calculations, deceptive evasions, and empty nothingness, they fall into the ranks of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fifth external path: the nature of the four inversions, the deceptive evasion of immortality, and the pervasive false theorizing.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, they engage in conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow. Such persons fall into the error of generating a perverted resolve based on the notion that there is a phenomenal form after death.

Zizhong said: "The 'inexhaustible flow' is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because one perceives this as inexhaustible, one speaks of signs existing after death. Either one clings to the body, saying 'form is the self';

or one perceives the self as being perfectly pervasive throughout the lands, saying 'the self possesses form'; or one perceives that external objects follow and revolve around the self, saying 'form belongs to the self';

or again, one perceives the self as depending on the continuity within formations, saying 'the self is within form. All these are conceptual reckonings that speak of signs existing after death. Thus, in such a cycle, there are sixteen signs."

Zhengji said: "Initially, one calculates four propositions regarding form (*rūpa*): namely, 'form is the self,' 'the self possesses form,' 'form belongs to the self,' and 'the self is within form. By analogy, each of the other four aggregates (*skandha*) is calculated in these four ways, thus forming sixteen. Taoci said:

'Now it is said that for the six categories of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the self is distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been destroyed and consciousness has not yet entered the sphere of direct experience, they simply do not mention it.'"

Question: Since the first three aggregates (*skandha*) have already been refuted, why do you again calculate four alternatives regarding the self? Answer: We merely refute their conceptualization; we do not refute the phenomena themselves. Form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates arise and perish, ceasing without pause from moment to moment; this is precisely the inexhaustible flow.

However, this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) differs from the coarse and subtle categories distinguished in common practice. For instance, according to the masters of the *Śata-śāstra*, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is placed first, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) follows next, and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is third.

These three are all neutral (*avyākṛta*) and have not yet produced karma. It is only upon reaching the aggregate of formations that afflictions arise and various karmas are created. Thus, these four...

Among the aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the coarsest. This is said with reference to the ordinary state before [the aggregates] have been broken down. Now, within the practice of contemplation, one has already broken through sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*);

one must know that the coarse characteristics of the aggregate of formations also come to an end, leaving only their subtle characteristics remaining. Therefore, when combined with the previous three aggregates, all are seen to be subject to flux. The source of this profound and hidden [nature] is in fact difficult to understand. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states:

"One should know that there are two different meanings regarding the coarse and subtle nature of the five aggregates in terms of their sequence. If discussed in relation to the creation of karma, it is only the aggregate of formations that is discussed as creating karma; the preceding three are merely neutral (*avyākṛta*). This is why [the *Bùyì* says] 'formations'..."

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the coarsest; this is the purport of the *Śata-śāstra*. To analyze them according to their conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*): the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) differentiates only by way of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—differentiating the arising, ceasing, and shifting flow—is the most subtle.

Now, regarding the sequence of the [five aggregates] being refuted: the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is subtle because its arising and ceasing occur subsequently; thus it is considered subtle. Furthermore, the *Śata-śāstra* places perception (*saṃjñā*) before feeling (*vedanā*), on the grounds that only when perception exists first does the mind subsequently experience the object.

If this were so, there would be no fixed order between the two mental states of feeling and perception; rather, it is simply that after experiencing an object, the mental state of perception becomes predominant. Therefore, most texts speak of them in this manner.
From this point, some may calculate that afflictions (*kleśa*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are two distinct natures that proceed side by side without ever touching one another.

Tiaoxi says: "The preceding four aggregates (*skandha*) and the self (*ātman*), having already died, possess characteristics; or again, they falsely calculate that the principle of afflictions and awakening is likewise.

This is because afflictions arise from the aggregates, while awakening is realized through the self. To say 'ultimate' (*atyanta*) means that these two natures proceed together into the future limit."
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth heterodox school’s inverted doctrine of mind, which posits the characteristics of existence after death within the five aggregates.

The five aggregates are collectively bound together, yet they reside primarily within the first four. Furthermore, although they reside within the first four, in meaning they are solely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Moreover, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity to intervene.

To exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, one observes that source of profound clarity which is constantly in a state of agitation. If, prior to this, one eliminates form, sensation, and perception and gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person will fall into the inverted resolve of the signless state after death.

Seeing that form (*rūpa*) ceases, one finds no basis for its shape. Contemplating that perception (*saṃjñā*) ceases, one finds the mind has nothing to which it is bound. Knowing that sensation (*vedanā*) ceases, one finds no further continuity. The nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) dissipates;

even if the processes of life persist, being devoid of sensation and perception, they are the same as grass and trees. Since this physical substance cannot be apprehended even while present before one, how could any characteristics exist after death?
Examining it through this analysis, there are no characteristics after death. Thus, in this cycle, there are eight instances of the absence of characteristics.

He observes that the three aggregates of sensation, perception, and mental formations have already ceased beneath [the aggregate of form]. Because he has observed the prior cessation of these three aggregates, he concludes that the fourth aggregate currently present is likewise non-existent.

He clearly enters the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), whereby the aggregate of form presently manifest is exhausted. This "substance" (the physical basis) is used here to illustrate the state after death by means of what is presently manifest.

Since it is thus with the aggregate of form, so it is with sensation, perception, and mental formations. Therefore, it is stated by way of analogy: "In this manner, they circulate," and so forth. The Supplement states: "This is the clear observation that the aggregate of form is empty, harmonious, and unimpeded; one cannot find its obstructive substance."
How much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
From this point on, some may calculate that all causes and effects of nirvāṇa are entirely empty, existing as mere names, and that they ultimately end in annihilation.

Zhaoxi said: "The cause and effect of nirvāṇa are cultivated based on the present aggregates (skandhas) and realized in the subsequent aggregates. Since the aggregates themselves are unobtainable, how can there be cultivation or realization?"
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox doctrine: the inverted view of mind within the five aggregates that asserts non-existence after death.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, contemplating that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Within the persistence of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own essential nature and characteristics contradict one another.
Such a person falls into the nihilistic and non-nihilistic heterodox theory that arises after death.

The Supplement states: "To calculate both existence and non-existence together does not mean merely calculating existence and non-existence. Calculating existence as not non-existent and calculating non-existence as not existent—these two mutually negate one another, thereby establishing 'neither of the two' (ubhayānta-vinirmukta)."

Within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, one observes internally that there is neither existence nor non-existence. Thus, through this cycle, one exhaustively investigates the aggregates, elements, and bases, finding them all to be characterized by neither-both-nor.
Upon encountering any given condition, one speaks of the state after death as being either with marks or without marks.

Tiāoxī said: "The non-existence of the three aggregates is like the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the existence of the aggregate of formations is like the non-existence of the three aggregates. Since each of the four aggregates has these two aspects, they are called the 'eight characteristics of neither-being-nor-non-being.

Take the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as one example: its existence is untenable, and its non-existence is also untenable. When one sees that its existence dissolves away, it is then not existent. Yet, following this principle, the aggregate of formations is not non-existent; thus, it is also not non-existent.

This is truly because the subtle arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations cannot be destroyed, so one reckons it to be existent, which conversely negates the prior non-existence. Furthermore, one takes that prior non-existence to negate the present existence."

The Supplement states: The following section explains the dualistic reckoning of existence and non-existence. Within the contemplation of form and so forth, it has already been refuted by stating they are "non-existent"; this is not the same as the "existence" of the currently manifest *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations).
Furthermore, the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is not the non-existence of the preceding aggregates such as form (*rūpa*).

If, among the four [remaining] aggregates, one observes any single aggregate and gives rise to this conception, speaking of "existence" and "non-existence," this refers to what was previously designated as the "dualistic conception of existence and non-existence," wherein the intrinsic nature and its characteristics mutually negate one another. That is, the characteristic of existence is not non-existence, and the characteristic of non-existence is not existence.
This arises because the practitioner, having already refuted the three preceding aggregates, now dwells within the aggregate of formations and thus gives rise to this conception.

Furthermore, because one calculates that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, the mind gives rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are not [ultimately real].

One loses the sense of whether things are empty or substantial. Tiaoxi said: "This refers to the calculation of 'neither-nor'. Form, sensation, perception, and so forth are all called "conditioned phenomena," and they all possess the quality of change and transformation. As the subsequent text states: "The nails grow and hair sprouts;

the breath fades and the face wrinkles," continuing until it says they do not cease for even a single moment—this is precisely their characteristic. Regarding the first four aggregates (*skandha*), there is a "neither-nor" of both existence and non-existence, and there are also eight meanings of "neither-nor. Since this view is subtle, its...

To speak specifically in terms of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): this distinction is made by calculating that within the aggregate of formations, all phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent]. Phenomena arise and perish, shifting and changing without fixed certainty. Within the mind, one opens up the meaning of "neither of the two":

because one perceives their arising, they are not non-existent; because one perceives their cessation, they are not existent. The *Supplement* states: "Virtue and reality" refer to arising and ceasing.
Since these two—arising as real and ceasing as unreal—mutually negate one another, it is said that they are "without fixed measure."

Based on this deliberation, they maintain that after death there is "neither-existence-nor-non-existence. Because the future limit is obscure and beyond description, they fall into the ranks of externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the eighth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of mind which posits "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" within the five aggregates after death.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding non-arising, such persons fall into the seven theories of annihilationism.

Changshui said: "This person perceives the place where the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) perishes moment by moment; this is called 'non-existence in each subsequent [moment]'. Gushan said:

"'The seven types of annihilationists' refers to those who, having calculated that there is no further rebirth after extinction in seven locations—opening up the realms of humans and devas, opening up the four *dhyānas* of the form realm, and combining the formless realm into one—hold such views."

Some reckon on the extinction of the body; some on the extinction of desire; some on the extinction of suffering; some on the extinction of ultimate bliss; or the extinction of ultimate equanimity. Thus they cycle through these until the seven limits are exhausted, manifesting their dissolution before them;
once extinguished, there is nothing more.

Regarding the "extinction of the body": this refers to humans and devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is the extinction of desire, because the defilements of desire are already exhausted in the first dhyāna; it is the extinction of suffering, because there is no sorrow or anxiety in the extreme joy of the second dhyāna;

it is the extinction of extreme pleasure, because the bliss of the third dhyāna is at its ultimate limit; it is the extinction of extreme equanimity (*upekṣā*), because in the fourth dhyāna one abandons applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*); and it is the extinction of form through the abandonment of the obstruction of form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, the term "extreme equanimity" encompasses both [the fourth dhyāna and the formless realm].
Based on this speculative calculation that there is annihilation after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of mind which posits the annihilation of the five aggregates after death.

Zhaoxi said: "This calculation should have originated from the seventh heterodox school. However, the previous discussion was based on the horizontal (transverse) perspective, while the present one is based on the vertical (longitudinal) perspective.

This refers to the sixth [type of] heretic’s fourfold proposition that "form is the self. On the first level, it pertains only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); on the second level, it may extend through the four dhyānas, for how could non-Buddhist practitioners of the four dhyānas be without such a view?

However, based on their firm assertion regarding the self, it appears as if they refer to the form of the desire realm. The preceding [passage] sets forth the subsequent [analysis]: the former is formulated in terms of the objects perceived to give rise to the view;

the present statement, "manifestly attaining nirvāṇa," is spoken in terms of having realized it within the very body. Nevertheless, this view flows from the sixth type of externalist; since it is not the same as annihilation after death, it seems similar to death.

Thereafter, there is the mark of subsequent attainment. Because one does not perceive the subtle arising and ceasing within the five stations, one falsely claims to have attained the peace of *nirvāṇa* in the present.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded realizations in *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner toward the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); thus, these insights manifest. Beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves;

when they encounter these manifestations, they mistake delusion for realization and claim to have attained the state of a sage. Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must, after my parinirvāṇa, take the Tathāgata’s mind as your own.
