I transmit this for the Dharma-ending age, so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to and understand this meaning. Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamities within themselves; preserve and recover [the true nature], quenching and eliminating false views.

Teach their body and mind to awaken to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter divergent branches on the unsurpassed path. Do not let them pray for the heart’s desires and consider a small attainment sufficient; act as a pure guiding finger for the Great Awakened King.

Zhaoxi says: At the end of the preceding stages of form, sensation, and perception, it was stated that one must not allow the celestial Māras to find an opportunity. Now, at the conclusion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), it speaks of the "mind-māra" (*citta-māra*); at the conclusion of the subsequent *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness), it speaks of the "view-māra" (*dṛṣṭi-māra*).

Mind and view do not go beyond the two delusions of views and craving; these are precisely the *kleśa-māra* (the māra of afflictions). Within the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation), the fifth [type of sensation] is the arising of inexhaustible sorrow and the desire not to live;

this is still the *mṛtyu-māra* (the māra of death). Together with the five aggregates being observed, there is the *skandha-māra*. Thus, the four māras are fully present. Xunwen says: Regarding the preceding [stages of] form, sensation, perception, and so forth, they were provisionally categorized according to their major divisions.

Regarding the celestial Māras (*deva-māra*), there are inevitably signs of affliction (*kleśa*) within them; the mental perceptions do not transcend the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This is discussed in general terms.

One must not, however, divide these two delusions and assign them specifically to the two *skandhas* (the *saṃskāra-skandha* and the *vijñāna-skandha*), because within the *saṃskāra-skandha*—specifically within consciousness (*vijñāna*)—all except those of the two vehicles with fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) possess false views. Since the delusion of views is present, there are spontaneously the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that oppose [enlightenment], which constitute the delusion of reception (*vedanā*).

If one classifies this according to the ten objects of practice (*daśa-viṣaya*) in *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it properly belongs to the object of views (*dṛṣṭi-viṣaya*), while also being associated with the object of dhyāna (*dhyāna-viṣaya*). Changshui said: "As long as the *saṃjñā-skandha* is not yet exhausted, one will still be drawn by external Māras."

Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) becomes clearly manifest. However, regarding the objects of cognition, one gives rise to divergent views and clings to them as being correct; therefore, it is called the "demon of the mind. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states:

Māra arises within the mind; one brings this calamity upon oneself. The *Shangshu* says: "Do not give rise to filth, lest you stink yourself. Although the objects of contemplation regarding form, sensation, and perception are still coarse, external celestial Māras are thereby attracted.

Now, as the practice of consciousness has become subtle, Māra is formed merely by internal mental perversity; this is also a general observation. In principle, both must exist. *Xunwen* says: "One gives rise to deep calamity (*nie*) oneself.

The *Shuowen* states that the strange manifestations of birds, beasts, insects, and locusts are called *nie*. Here, it means that the mental Māra self-inflicts harm like those strange portents. "To extinguish" (*xiaoxi*) means to eliminate or destroy. *Buyi* says: [End of excerpt]

To "not encounter divergent branches" means to avoid the evil paths and heterodox ways; for when one follows such branches, the loss of the sheep is inevitable. Do not allow the mind to harbor cravings or seek through restless haste. The demons within the five aggregates arise solely from such longing and impetuous advancement.

Ānanda, when those sons of good family who practice *samādhi* have exhausted the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the subtle and pure nature of all worldly phenomena, along with the stirring movements of the common lot and the generative impulses of life, suddenly shatter and fall away.

The deep-seated cords and knots that bind the *pudgala* to the profound channels of karmic retribution are severed; the resonance between cause and effect is suspended. They are about to awaken to the great radiance of the heaven of *nirvāṇa*, like a rooster crowing at dawn when it gazes toward the east and already sees the first glimmer of light.
Their six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or scattering.

Changshui said: "The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the very essence of the mundane world. The mundane world has three characteristics: first, it possesses arising and ceasing; second, it is with outflows (*sāsrava*); third, it is subject to destruction. Since it falls within the mundane world,"

They are alike in taking the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* as their nature. Tiāoxī says: "The natures of all worldly beings are precisely the essential nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha* of the twelve classes of living beings; they share the same generative impulse."

This means that the mechanism of arising and ceasing shares the same boundaries as all categories of beings. Suddenly, one perceives the signs of the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Formations (*saṃskāra*) are the nature of karma; they are able to sustain the various aggregates, like the main ropes and knots of a net.

"Pu-te" (補特) below clarifies that there is no dragging of future retribution; "ying" (應) here refers to retribution. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "The 'vessel' (*mai*, 脈) is a curtain (*mo*, 幕); the curtain and the network are of one substance. Karma can pull forth rebirth, just as a curtain-network remains unsevered. Gushan says:
"The Nirvana of the Three Virtues is called the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*). The *Buyi* states: "This refers to the preceding practice."

If the *skandhas* are broken, one immediately enters the stage of semblance (*sābhāsa*) and is about to ascend to the stage of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). This is like the dawn approaching in the heaven of Middle-Way Nirvāṇa, resembling the crowing of a rooster and the subtle radiance of the east just before daybreak—this is the semblance of the Three Truths.

Within the five *skandhas*, if the *rūpa-skandha* is exhausted, then all five *skandhas* are broken; having already entered the stage of semblance, one no longer further cultivates the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) on sensation (*vedanā*) and the others.

This is explained through the sequence of the five *skandhas* for those of dull faculties; it is merely that the former [skandhas] are suppressed while the latter are contemplated. How could there be a case where, upon the exhaustion of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*), one enters the stage of semblance and then proceeds to the *saṃskāra-skandha* to practice?

Contemplation. It is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn, for example. When the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, it is said that one sees the mind of all Buddhas, like an image appearing in a mirror. When the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, it is said that one attains the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*).

When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, it is said that one is like the clear sky, where there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadows of external objects. This is similar to the present state of gazing toward the east and already perceiving a refined radiance;

there is no difference in quality between them. This is because when a single aggregate is shattered, delusion departs and principle is revealed; thus, regarding the signs of entering the stages, there is no further distinction of high or low. Tiaoxi says: Five.

The successive stages of suppression have their order, while the severance [of afflictions] has no before or after. Now, taking up the subsequent breaking of specific delusions as the latter stage, and the initial breaking of pervasive delusions as the former, the suddenness or gradualism of this severance and suppression will be explained below.

Since the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, it is called "empty stillness. Because one no longer undergoes birth-and-death in segmented form, it is said that there is "no further rushing or fleeing."

Internally and externally serene and luminous, one enters that which has no entry. One profoundly penetrates the fundamental source of the twelve classes of sentient beings who receive their life-force throughout the ten directions. By observing the source through its attachments, the various classes cease to summon one;

thus, within the realms of the ten directions, one attains sameness. The refined essence does not sink, but reveals what was hidden and secret. This is called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is laid bare, whereby one attains a state of profound clarity. As the subsequent text states: "Furthermore, that which is your brilliant clarity, profoundly still and unmoving, which does not depart from the body in its functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing"—this is precisely its characteristic.

Consciousness, vitality, and warmth combine in harmony to constitute life; at the moment of taking birth, the aggregate of consciousness is primary. Moreover, this fundamental source is the root from which the two attachments to persons and phenomena arise.

Now, although what is seen within contemplation has not yet been entirely dissolved, there are no longer any karmic actions to attract future retribution; hence it is said that "no categories of beings can summon you. Furthermore, you see all the environments and inhabitants throughout the ten directions.

Because it is a transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), it is said that "its identity has already been attained. That the refined essence does not sink is precisely its profound clarity; that it manifests the obscure and secret is that nothing remains concealed. The primary source of receiving life is the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

Since this is the fundamental source of the seeds for rebirth among the various classes of beings, by not giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) and not creating new karma, one no longer undergoes rebirth as a result of grasping. Therefore, it says "all classes. The *Buyi* (Supplementary Notes) states:

"The refined essence does not sink" and "it manifests the obscure and secret"—these two phrases alone constitute the characteristics of the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*. The preceding aggregates of sensation, perception, and mental formations have already been subdued.

Now, observing that the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is luminous and tranquil, its refined essence does not sink, and thus its profound mysteries are revealed. Among the aggregates of sensation, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra*), the consciousness-mind is the most profound and secret;

it is like a master who remains within the chamber while ordering his servants to dwell outside. Therefore, the substance of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) receives the name "profound mystery. As for the observation that "it proceeds from the root of grasping," one observes the source of the aggregate of consciousness, which further serves as the root of the two types of grasping.
By observing and destroying this root of grasping, all categories [of delusion] are no longer summoned.

If, among the various calls [of the senses], one has already attained the same state within them and has worn away the six gates, such that their union and opening are perfected, and seeing, hearing, and the other faculties interpenetrate and are mutually pure, so that the ten directions, the world, as well as body and mind, are as clear and transparent inside and out as vaidūrya lapis lazuli—this is called the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kāluṣya*).

Zhaoxi said: "Although the various summonings differ, the substance of consciousness is the same. If, within this sameness, one grinds away the delusions of the six faculties regarding views and attachments, then these can merge into a single body that opens up as six functions.

When the six functions are not separated, they all interpenetrate; this is precisely what the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies as the 'purity of the six faculties. Changshui said: 'The world, the body, and the mind are all manifestations of consciousness alone.

Now, with the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one perceives only the luminous and wondrous essence of awareness. Like pure lapis lazuli, there is no obstruction whatsoever; this is called 'internal and external transparency. Body and mind..."

The internal is the external world; since neither can be apprehended, it is called "luminous penetration. As the preceding text states: "The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a precious moon suspended within lapis lazuli.

Body and mind are blissful; wondrous, perfect, and impartial, one attains great peace and stability. All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of all Tathāgatas appear therein. This person immediately attains the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena).

Thus, one knows that the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) constitutes awakening according to one's capacity. Mañjuśrī also said: "When rest and renewal are accomplished in a single place, the six functions all cease to function. Dust..."
The defilements should be eliminated through mindfulness, resulting in perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity.
When one examines their origin, they are found to have as their root illusory, empty, and inverted false thoughts.
Guishan says: "Illusory" (*wangxiang*) also means "resembling"; both describe that which is unreal.

Ānanda, you should know that this son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Having returned to the source within consciousness (*vijñāna*), he has extinguished arising and ceasing.

All preceding and succeeding manifestations of objects now reside within the mind of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-citta*). Now, in order to demonstrate the basis upon which these objects depend, I shall explain them through the successive sequence of the exhaustion of the aggregates (*skandha*).

You should understand that once the aggregates are exhausted, even if [objects] manifest profusely, they only further increase one’s correct understanding. If such movements arise within the mind of contemplative practice, to follow them leads to error, while to restrain them leads to correctness. You should encompass all things with this principle.

As for its text: regarding the stages and positions of practice, one is not confused about their directions. The *Buyi* (Supplementary Notes) states: "Regarding the return of consciousness to its source: the substance of the mind is but one; fundamentally, there is no distinction between the 'king' (the primary mind) and the 'numbers' (the mental factors)."

Because one grasps at objects, sensations (*vedanā*) and other mental factors arise latently. Now, through the power of contemplation, these sensations are temporarily suppressed, and one suddenly perceives the source of the mind; this simply indicates that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the origin.

In the ten types of demons described below, it is repeatedly stated, "If, regarding that to which one returns... This refers to returning to the source now. One departs from those sensations and the like, returning to the essence of the mind (*citta-tattva*) to serve as the basis for perception and observation; it is from this that conceptual calculations arise.

Yet, regarding this subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected. It can cause one's own body to merge with or separate from the sense organs, and it can also enable one to communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions. Through this pervasive awareness, one is able to enter the perfect source.
If, however, one establishes a cause of true permanence within that which is sought as a refuge, [the result will be otherwise].

The Supplement states: Because one employs *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (meditative stillness and insight) at the fundamental source of the cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*), one is able to penetrate and realize its perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Thus, the six sense faculties are no longer obstructed; hence it is said that the "perfect source" (*yuan-yuan*) is precisely the cause of the "true permanence" (*zhen-chang*) as previously conceptualized.

"Universal awakening" (*zhulei tongjue*) refers to realizing the nature of awareness (*jixing*); this is not the same as the "attaining sameness" mentioned in the preceding text, which refers to the state of mere consciousness (*weishi*). Regarding the passage beginning with "awareness and knowledge" (*juexi*), the Tiexi commentary says: [the following].

This reiterates what has been previously set forth, concluding that [the mind] returns to the primordial source of the aggregates (*skandha*). This is merely a temporary attainment of such functioning; because one does not develop superior resolve (*adhimukti*) for non-arising, it is called a "virtuous state.
However, due to the arising of false attachments, one falls into the category of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying conditions. They become companions to those who follow the obscure principle (tattva) as taught by Śābikāra; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

Zhenji says: "Because of the attachment to causes and conditions, one mistakes the perfect luminosity for the true and eternal, and reckons that true eternity to be the root of delusion. Xunwen says: "The 'upper cause' points to the essence, which is precisely the perfect and primordial;

the 'lower cause,' in contrast to its function, takes what is truly eternal as the root of delusion, capable of giving rise to all phenomena. Thus, in relation to the functions of all phenomena, the name 'caused-by' is established. Buyi says: [as above].

The initial consciousness takes its own empty and pervasive nature as a permanent cause. Furthermore, because it reckons that all phenomena arise from this cause, it is said [as follows]. Changshui says: "According to the seven subsequent sections, they all speak of 'the capable' and 'the incapable,' etc.;
why is this alone referred to as 'cause' and 'that which is caused'? Answer: All phenomena are transformations of consciousness; this is precisely "that which is caused.

Because one fails to understand them as false and unreal, yet clings to them as a real cause, one is identical to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The subsequent text directly reveals that their very substance is false and unreal; therefore, it says "not the capable," and so forth.

This is called the first establishment of a mind that attains what is acquired, thereby forming a fruit of refuge that is contrary to perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.
The Supplement states: "From this cause of true permanence, one achieves a fruit of permanence; this is what I take as my refuge."
Ānanda, furthermore, when a son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and brought to an end birth and death,

yet his subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected, he may take that which he returns to as his own self-nature. He will then perceive that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space are but a single class flowing forth from within his own body.

Those who give rise to such convictions fall into the dualistic grasping of "ability" and "inability. Maheśvara manifests boundless bodies to become their companions; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision.

Gushan says: "The 'capable' and 'incapable' grasping refers to [the view] that 'I am the creator' and that 'all those things are created. Zizhong says: "Maheśvara is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who has three eyes and eight arms;
he is the object of veneration for non-Buddhists. As the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes the notion of a creator of the world, what benefit is there [in such a view]?"

This is called the second establishment of the capacity for the mind to accomplish its functional fruit; it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of the "all-pervading self" among the gods of great pride.

The Supplement states: To establish the "capable" as the mind is to reckon one's own mind as the productive agent, intending thereby to evoke the fruit of the Sovereign Heaven (Īśvara) manifesting boundless bodies, because that heaven possesses the capacity to manifest boundless bodies—as it is said, "giving rise to the Greatly Arrogant Heaven.
One reckons that all sentient beings are born from this self, and therefore one's own mind is omnipresent.
Furthermore, because there was previously a slight degree of perfect understanding, this reckoning arose; thus, the name "Perfect" (Yuan) is still retained.
Furthermore, there is the "good son" who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, he has not yet perfected it. If, regarding that which is returned to, he takes something as a refuge, he will suspect that his own body and mind flow forth from that source, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it.

Thus, regarding the ground from which everything flows forth, he conceives the notion of a true, eternal body free from birth and death. While still within the midst of birth and death, he prematurely calculates permanence; thus, he is both deluded about non-arising and confused.
Arising and ceasing, they remain settled in delusion.

Because the practitioner contemplates the essence of the consciousness-mind and realizes its quiescent extinction, they claim that this extinction is the basis upon which the mind relies. Failing to understand that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are themselves the principle, they instead harbor doubts that the body and mind flow forth from that [extinction].

This attachment to the notion that there is a principle external to the mind capable of producing [phenomena] is therefore erroneous. Tiaoxi said: "Flowing forth from that" refers here to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the point of ultimate return.

For their sake, they take the perfected origin of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to be eternal, while regarding their own body, mind, and the empty space of the ten directions as non-eternal. That which is non-eternal is subject to arising and ceasing.

Having perceived that the non-eternal flows forth from the eternal, they then reckon that this arising and ceasing is itself the eternally abiding. The principle of the subsequent passage concerning the attachment to "knowledge" and "non-knowledge" is likewise the same.

Zizhong says: "This 'Lord of Sovereignty' (*Īśvara*) is no different from the previous [deity]. This deity currently manifests arising and ceasing, yet they falsely reckon it to be eternal; therefore it is said that within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "This is a judgment."

They have formed a perverted understanding of quiescence; they are unable to realize that the principle is identical with the aggregates (*skandhas*), yet they still calculate that which is subject to arising and ceasing to be eternally abiding. This is premature reckoning. Because they do not understand that the principle is identical within the aggregates, it is said:
"they are deluded regarding non-arising. Because they discard the aggregates as being outside the principle, it is said: "they are also confused regarding arising and ceasing."

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the dualistic attachments of permanence and impermanence; they reckon Īśvara as their companion, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.

The Supplement states: As for reckoning Īśvara as a companion, it is because one reckons that the emptiness of the ten directions emerges from the principle of quiescence; this is because the flavor of the producer and the produced is similar.

This is called the third [type of] establishing a cause based on the mind to achieve a falsely conceptualized fruit. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of inverted perfection.

"Establishing a cause based on the mind" means desiring to rely upon this to seek the fruit of permanence. As for "the cause being based [on the mind]," it refers to the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) relying on principle. Regarding "giving rise to the seed of inverted perfection":
to seek principle outside the mind—how could this be anything other than inversion?
Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), you have not yet perfected it. If, among objects of knowledge, because your cognition is pervasive and complete, you establish a view based on that cognition such that all grasses and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings and are no different from humans—such that grasses and trees become humans, and when humans die they return to becoming grasses and trees in the ten directions—this is indiscriminate and universalized cognition.

The Supplement states: "From observing within the mind, once understanding has arisen and pervaded all things, one then claims that grasses and trees are identical to sentient beings. Examining the basis of this reckoning, it arises entirely from a biased interpretation of the sūtras and śāstras. Because of this, such a conception is born:

as reckoned above, the self-substance of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) can produce the sentient beings of the ten directions. Is this not due to having heard that the *ālayavijñāna* produces phenomena?"

Furthermore, you calculate that the principle of quiescence gives rise to all dharmas; is this not to say that dharmas arise from hearing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? Now, you calculate that grasses and trees possess [Buddha-]nature;

is this not due to having heard the teaching that even tiles and pebbles possess Buddha-nature? That grasses and trees possess nature is the perfect and sudden correct principle, which exhausts the true source and fundamental substance; in that respect, the principle may be consistent. However, to argue based on these superficial matters is to fall squarely into false views.
How could there be anyone who, upon death, would again become those grasses and trees?

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment of knowing non-knowing. They become companions to those who hold the view that all perceptions are real, such as the followers of Pāṭha and Sāṇi; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

Gushan said: "To know that there is no knowledge and yet cling to it" means that while plants and trees are without consciousness, one forcibly claims they possess it. Now, the eternally abiding true mind is a single essence without duality; it is through the operation of various deluded thoughts that the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants arises.

Therefore, sentient beings and grasses and trees are all like flowers in the sky—they are all transformations of the minds of sentient beings themselves. Because their clinging emotions do not understand this, they claim that each individual blade of grass or tree possesses its own consciousness.

Consequently, they say that when wood dies it becomes a person, and when a person dies it becomes wood. Failing to clarify the single essence, they erroneously calculate a pervasive and perfect reality; this is precisely what causes them to deviate from and distance themselves from perfect penetration.

In this regard, the two non-Buddhist teachers known as Vāṭa and Sainika—whom the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* calls Vāsiṣṭha and Arjuna—asserted that all things possessing consciousness have life, even claiming that grasses and trees possess it.
What has now been discovered is precisely the same as their view.

This is called the fourth calculation: the erroneous result of conceiving that the mind has attained perfection. It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of inverted knowledge.
Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena to find them empty, one has already extinguished birth and death.

Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, they have not yet perfected it. If, within the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused faculties, one has already attained conformity, then all things will arise through perfect transformation.

One may seek the radiance of fire, delight in the purity of water, cherish the circulation of wind, or contemplate the perfection of dust; each venerates and serves these objects, taking these various sensory phenomena as the primary causes for their manifestation.

Zhaoxi said: "Perfect transformation" refers to the realm of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) perceived within contemplation, wherein all things are perfectly interfused and transformed. "The generation of all things" refers to the characteristics of the four great elements.

Observing the accomplishment of the minute particles, they are specifically named the earth element; by extension, these various particles refer to all four great elements. Having seen that these all arise through circular transformation, one then calculates that the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits do not transcend the luminosity of fire or the purity of water, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that these are the fundamental causes of manifestation.

Establishing a view of permanence, such a person falls into the attachment to birth as being non-birth. They become companions to those Kāśyapas and Brahmins who, with diligent minds and laboring bodies, serve fire and venerate water in their quest to transcend birth and death;
thus they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision.

Regarding those who establish the view that the arising of the permanent is itself the non-arising of the permanent: this means that the arising of the four great elements is precisely the non-arising of the permanent. Kāśyapa was also a distinct clan name of the Brahmins.
The items listed below collectively encompass their respective categories.

This is called the fifth attachment: the veneration of external objects. With a deluded mind following after things, one establishes false causes for seeking and falsely hopes for results. Thus, one remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.
Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize their emptiness, you have already extinguished arising and ceasing;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected. If, within this perfect luminosity, you reckon the clarity itself to be empty and thereby deny the transformation of the myriad phenomena, taking this eternal cessation as your ultimate refuge, [you will fall into the error of the Unconceivable Transformation].

"Clarifying that which is empty within" refers to what was previously called "formless and non-existent. It does not mean the extinction of the manifold transformations; "not yet destroyed" means they have not been annihilated. The "manifold transformations" refer to the four great elements and so forth.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment of taking refuge in that which offers no refuge. They become companions to the *śūnyatā* spirits among the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.

Gushan said: "To return to that which has no place of return" is why it is called "returning to the non-attachment of returning. This refers to the extinction of the mind and mental factors in the Heaven of No-Thought (Āsaṃjñisattva), [the realm of] Śūnyatāndhara, the Lord of the Deity of Space.

This is called the sixth: the fruit of emptiness and non-existence achieved through a mind of vacuous nothingness. It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of annihilationism.
The Supplement states: "This calculation of vacuity will inevitably result in the fruit of emptiness of the Non-Thinking (Asaṃjñika) heretics."

Furthermore, son of good family, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected:
if they fixate upon this perfect permanence to maintain the body as eternally abiding, they will become identical to that subtle perfection, remaining forever without decay or passing away.

Zhaoxi said: "The clarity and brilliance of the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha), in its state of profound stillness and immovability, is termed 'permanence. Now, seeing this permanence, one clings to the physical body as being identical to this subtle, perfect essence."

Those who give rise to such convictions fall into the grasping of attachment and non-attachment. They become companions to those Asitas who seek long life; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.

Changshui says: "The body is fundamentally impermanent and truly not to be craved as something enduring. Because one now clings to it with firm attachment, it is called 'craving that is not [mere] craving' and 'clinging.
Asita—here translated as 'Incomparable'—is the Longevity Immortal."

This is called the seventh attachment: clinging to the life-root as a firm cause of delusion, which leads to the fruit of long-lasting toil. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of false fabrication.

The Supplement states: "To 'pursue long labor' likely carries the sense of undergoing toil and hardship. Zhuang Zhou said, 'He toils me with life. Now, seeking longevity and the extension of life is not the Dharma-nature body."
It merely results in the fruit of toil and hardship.
Furthermore, O son of good family, one may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and thereby extinguish birth and death;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), one has not yet perfected it. Observing that life-force is interpenetrating, one might instead retain the defilements of worldly toil, fearing their total exhaustion. Thus, at this juncture, one sits within a Lotus Palace and extensively transforms the seven...
"Rare! There are many precious ladies who indulge their hearts to their full extent.

Zhenji said: "Regarding the passage 'observe that life is mutually interpenetrating' below: this means that although one has already attained equality within the collective invocation, there is no further cause for such invocation; yet, fearing the loss of its fruit, one therefore retains the afflictions of the mundane world."

Zhaoxi said: "This is spoken with reference to those who practice dhyāna while remaining lay and thereby attain supernatural powers (abhijñā). Thus, there are instances of extensively transforming the seven treasures and increasing the number of precious ladies (*ratnastri*). A 'lady' (*yuan*) refers to a beautiful woman."

The Supplement states: "Life is itself nature. When the practitioner contemplates the nature of consciousness, it penetrates both the ultimate (paramārtha) and conventional (saṃvṛti) truths. Since both the ultimate and the conventional possess this same nature, they are said to be mutually penetrating.

Now, when contemplating the nature of emptiness, if one wishes to preserve conventional truth yet fails to realize that their essence is identical, one will claim that eternal quiescence means the cessation of phenomenal appearances. Consequently, one leaves behind the afflictions of worldly toil; by increasing attachment to precious women, one falls into perverse desire.

Guishan’s statement, 'One intends to return to the ultimate but instead clings to the conventional,' is precisely this point. This is because the practitioner’s biased interpretation of the sūtras and śāstras—failing to dismantle conventional truth—has led to such demonic realms."

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment to "true" within the "untrue. They become companions to the *Ṭakkirāja* spirits; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision.
Gushan said: "Those who truly lack true attachment intend to return to the state of truth, yet instead remain attached to the mundane. *Takkirāja* has not yet been seen in a correct translation;
since he is able to transform and enjoy the objects of desire, he belongs to the class of the *Īśvara-devas* of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thought to establish the fruit of blazing afflictions. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the lineage of celestial Māras.

Regarding the cause of perverse thought: since one gives rise to this perverse notion within meditative concentration and fails to examine it skillfully, the resulting blazing intensity gives rise to matters of worldly toil; therefore, it is identical to that of the celestial Māras.
Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize emptiness and have already extinguished the cycle of arising and ceasing;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), you have not yet perfected it. Within the clarity of life, you discriminate between the refined and the coarse, and resolve the true from the false.

You seek only for cause and effect to correspond through mutual response, thereby turning your back on the path of purity—namely, the vision of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path. Having come to rest within this state of cessation, you no longer advance further.

Gushan says: "The 'awakening of life' (*ming-ming*) is precisely consciousness (*vijñāna*). This refers to the sudden emergence of a slight understanding within the perfect clarity of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Because of this, one discriminates that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are coarse and false, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are subtle and true. Furthermore, one knows that the fruit of suffering is the retribution for the cause of the origin, and the fruit of cessation is the retribution for the cause of the path. Thereupon, one perceives suffering and abandons the origin, seeking only the path and cessation through responsive resonance (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Having developed this slight understanding, one turns away from the path of perfect fusion, permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha*). Now, among these four virtues, I shall briefly cite one—namely, 'inferior' (*hīna*)—to explain and substantiate what was stated above."

If one gives rise to such a resolute conviction, that person will fall into the category of a śrāvaka of fixed nature. They will become companions to those arrogant monks who have not heard the Dharma; they will be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.

Those who have not heard the Dharma are those who falsely cling to inferior paths as being ultimate; thus, they are of one kind in their harm with those who, out of overweening pride, claim that the four dhyānas constitute the four fruits of arhatship.

This is called the ninth stage: the perfect clarity that accords with the mind and achieves the fruit of quiescent entry. It is far removed from perfect penetration; it turns its back on the city of Nirvana and gives rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned activities into emptiness, one has already extinguished arising and ceasing.

Yet, regarding this tranquil extinction, the subtle essence has not yet been perfected. If, within this perfectly integrated, pure, and luminous awakening, one investigates its profound subtlety and establishes it as nirvana, one will cease to advance further.

In this contemplation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), although the three truths are perfectly interfused, one becomes biasedly attached to wondrous emptiness and consequently gives rise to a limited understanding. Thus, one immediately establishes the *nirvāṇa* as a "transformed city" (*pariṇāmika-nagara*) and fails to advance toward the precious destination of the Middle Way.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction will fall into the fixed nature of pratyekabuddhas; those of their kind who remain solitary and do not turn back their minds will become their companions. They will be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.

Regarding those who attain enlightenment through conditions alone: these are the pratyekabuddhas and solitary buddhas. Because they appear after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there are two such types.

This is called the tenth stage: the mind of perfect awakening (*yuanjue*) attains the fruit of profound clarity. Yet, it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana; it gives rise to the seed of "untransformed perfection" characterized by the luminous clarity of awareness.

The Supplement states: "The nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is the simultaneous operation of quiescence and illumination. To single-mindedly seek only the side of quiescence is to take a biased view of the three truths within Perfect Enlightenment, thereby achieving the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha’s profound clarity.

'The arising of perfect awakening' refers to the emptiness and stillness of the Pratyekabuddha. Zizhong said: 'To indulge in the fruit of cessation constitutes the obstacle of abandoning sentient beings;

this is called the untransformed seed of the circle. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: 'The Śrāvaka has the obstacle of fearing suffering; the Pratyekabuddha has the obstacle of abandoning sentient beings. Changshui said: 'One realizes the perfect clarity of consciousness-awakening, yet lacks compassion.'"

This refers to the wondrous function of transformation; thus it is said that those of the "untransformed perfect lineage" (buhua yuanzhong) are so called because Pratyekabuddhas are unable to transform sentient beings. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "In this way, it is precisely because Pratyekabuddhas cannot transform others that they are called 'untransformed perfect lineage.'"

Furthermore, it may also be said that the Pratyekabuddhas possess a faculty-nature that awakens spontaneously without a teacher. They appear in worlds where no Buddha exists; even a Buddha cannot transform them, which is why they are said to be "untransformable.
This is why there are accounts of them cremating their own bodies or moving away, as they consider themselves and the Buddha to be incompatible.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through their practice because they rely on delusion; one generates a sense of fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled. All of this arises from the interaction of the mind with the *vijñāna-skandha*, which gives rise to these states.

Sentient beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves; when these states manifest before them, each uses their own cherished, previously practiced deluded mind to find rest, regarding it as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.

They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *bodhi*. Having committed this great falsehood, they are moved by external paths and demonic influences; when their karma is exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell. Śrāvaka...
"Upon hearing the Perfect Enlightenment [Sūtra], they fail to achieve further progress.

Regarding "those who speak great falsehoods," this specifically refers to the preceding eight types. These first eight are collectively termed externalists and demonic obstructors; alternatively, seven may be specified as externalists and the eighth as demonic obstructors.
Since none have severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that they "fall into hell. The Two Vehicles differ from these, and thus it is said that they "do not progress."

"You all must keep this in mind. Uphold the Way of the Tathāgata and transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age after my parinirvāṇa, so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to and understand its meaning.

Do not allow them to encounter demons and create deep calamities for themselves. Protect and comfort them with compassion, extinguish their evil conditions, and cause their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From the very beginning, they shall achieve fulfillment and never stray onto divergent paths."

Zhaoxi said: Regarding the statement "seeing demons," "seeing" is defined by its contravention of principle (*yīlǐ*). Among the first eight [demons], two contravene the principle of the True [Dharmadhātu] and give rise to heterodox views within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

The latter two contravene the principle of the Middle Way and give rise to heterodox views outside the realms (*lokottara*). This is because the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is itself ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, among the first eight, seven consist purely of views, while the eighth possesses both views and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because it retains worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) while generating superior resolve (*adhimukti*). Question:

Since one has already transcended the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) once the preceding aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) was exhausted, why do various views arise again during the aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)? Answer: The previous explanation was based on the stage of abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhūmi*). One attains...

To speak of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*): it currently resides in the stage of subduing [afflictions] and emerges from within the domain of the two aggregates. Regarding this text on the five aggregates, if one is confused about the meaning of severance, manifestation, and subduing, then even if one possesses subtle discernment, how could one possibly resolve it?

Regarding this Dharma gate: in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Tathāgatas as many as motes of dust have, by relying upon this, had their minds opened and attained the Unsurpassed Way.

This Dharma gate specifically points to the characteristics of seeing and perception within the dhyāna of the consciousness-aggregate (vijñānaskandha). There have been no Buddhas of the past who did not awaken to this and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is said that "by relying upon this, the mind is opened."

If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably. From within this mutual functioning, you will be able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vimalā*).
Your perfectly luminous and refined essence of mind will manifest transformation therein, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.

The Supplement states: First is the indication; second is the realization. Regarding "the mutual functioning of the sense organs": when the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is momentarily suppressed, the various faculties temporarily attain the appearance of mutual functioning;

this is the entry into the five grades of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). As for the term "Vajra," it receives this name because of the perfect cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is not the stage of the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), as that would be confused with the name "dry wisdom.

It is specifically distinguished by the "Bodhisattva-Vajra": "Bodhisattva" distinguishes it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), while "Vajra" distinguishes it from the partial teachings.

In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the four minds of application; the Bodhisattva’s practice reaches the ten vajra stages, the equal enlightenment, and perfect luminosity.
Next, the method of transcendent realization is shown. Practitioners of sharp faculties may, by means of this, employ the stages interchangeably;

without passing through the five grades, they leap directly into the ten levels of faith, or enter the stages of abiding and entry, and so forth, entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, perfecting bodhi, and returning to the state of non-attainment.

Gushan says: "The adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*kandhī*) is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) of wondrous enlightenment. Upon entering the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is itself wondrous enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that one 'enters into the Tathāgata,' and so forth."

The ocean of wondrous adornment is the culmination of merit; the perfection of bodhi is the culmination of wisdom; returning to non-attainment is the culmination of principle. Merit is liberation (*vimukti*); wisdom is *prajñā*; principle is the *dharmakāya*.

Neither vertical nor horizontal, the secret treasury of the three virtues is fully revealed herein. Tracing its cause back to its origin, it truly arises from the power of the three types of cessation—*śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—cultivated from the very first thought of the path.
This is the subtle demonic activity analyzed by the luminous awareness of *vipaśyanā* within the *śamatha* of the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of the past.
"Vipaśyanā within śamatha" refers to wisdom within meditative concentration. Tiaoxi says: "Subtle demonic activities" encompass all the objects manifested by the five aggregates (*skandha*).

While the previous conclusion regarding the aggregate of consciousness spoke of "the mind opening through this," the current conclusion regarding the five aggregates speaks of "analysis by luminous awareness. One should know that it is because of this analysis that the mind opens, and thus they manifest one another.
This is the stage of *vyañjana* (the letter).

When demonic realms manifest before you, you are able to recognize them; the defilements of the mind are washed away, and you do not fall into false views. The demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) are extinguished, the celestial demons (*deva-māra*) are shattered, and powerful spirits lose heart and flee.
Malevolent ghosts and goblins no longer arise. Until you reach Bodhi, you shall lack nothing; your inferior state will progress, and your mind will never be confused regarding Great Nirvana.

"Powerful spirits and ghosts," etc., specifically refers to those within the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) who have become demons through old age; it means to startle or terrify them. *Xunwen* says: Zhang Pingzi’s *Tongjing fu* states:

"It robs one of their vital energy and strips away their spirit. The commentary states: "To 'strip' means to startle; it refers to seizing and displacing the divine breath, and startling and dispersing the *p'o* and *huai* spirits.

If there are foolish and dull-witted sentient beings in the final age who do not yet recognize *dhyāna*, do not know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*, and you fear they might fall into heterodoxy, you should single-mindedly urge them to uphold my Buddha-Usnīṣa Dhāraṇī mantra.
If they are unable to recite it, write it down in their meditation hall or carry it upon their person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to move them."

Zhaoxi said: "To turn back from delusion and revolve toward the truth, one cannot succeed without practice. The general outline of such practice consists solely of faith and the Dharma. Entering through hearing the Dharma is called 'practice through faith' (śraddhā-carita);

entering through contemplation is called 'practice through the Dharma' (dharmānusāri-carita). Yet these two practices must necessarily rely upon one another. What is now meant by 'not yet knowing dhyāna' refers to the practitioner of the Dharma not yet knowing the present state of the five aggregates within dhyāna.
Not knowing how to preach the Dharma means not knowing how to use practice through faith to support practice through the Dharma. For this reason, they are termed 'dull and ignorant. If, regarding..."
He delights in the cultivation of samādhi. The Buddha, fearing that such a person might be troubled by Māra, therefore entrusted Ānanda with the exhortation to uphold this divine mantra.

Alas! Among those who study the Mahāyāna in this world, who does not claim for themselves to have attained the fruit of true samādhi? Yet when examined through the two practices of faith and dharma, they are utterly empty and void.

Or perhaps they read this sūtra, yet how can they truly reflect upon their own dullness and stupidity, reciting and transcribing its mantras to ward off the works of Māra? If so, then the Great Light cannot dispel the darkness of the long night, and the compassionate mother cannot save her lost child from suffering—how tragic!
Now, you should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and final instructions left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Gushan said:

"He preached the sutras when summer was full and manifested his parinirvāṇa in the preceding spring. Since his passing occurred before long, it is called his 'final instructions. Guxiang said: "It refers to the spring that had passed."
He replied, "The springtime of the past; it was not a springtime already gone.

Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction and admonition, he prostrated himself in reverence, receiving and memorizing it without loss. In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more.

As the Buddha has said, within the characteristics of the five aggregates, there are five kinds of false delusions that serve as the fundamental source of thought. We have not previously received such subtle instruction from the Tathāgata regarding these matters.
Furthermore, are these five aggregates to be eliminated simultaneously, or are they exhausted sequentially? As for these five types, what constitutes their ultimate realm?

I only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest and proclaim great compassion, to clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, and to serve as the future eye for all sentient beings in the final age.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essence is true and wondrously luminous; original enlightenment is perfectly pure. It does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements.

Tiaoxi said: "The 'essence' is the Middle Way. The 'wondrous luminosity' is tranquil illumination. Because it is tranquil, it is the provisional (the conventional); because it is illuminating, it is emptiness. When the three truths are harmoniously integrated, there is fundamentally no defilement.
This is collectively termed 'original enlightenment, perfectly pure. This refers exclusively to the True Nature."
Even up to empty space, all arise from the production of delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*).
This section discusses exclusively how delusive thoughts give rise to all phenomena.

This is originally the wondrously luminous true essence of fundamental enlightenment; through delusion, it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds (*bhājana-loka*), like Yajñadatta who, in his confusion, mistook his own head for a reflection. Delusion is fundamentally without cause.

This section combines the preceding and following sections to clarify how both the true and the deluded give rise to the world. The reason for doing so is that without the former discussion of the single [delusion], one would not understand the meaning of "separation"; without the latter combined clarification, one would not understand the meaning of "identity.
To mistake the head for its reflection is a matter that cannot be treated as distinct or orderly.

Within conceptual construction, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it spontaneity (*svabhāva*). That nature of space is likewise truly produced from illusion. Both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual reckonings of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

The establishment of the nature of causal conditions refers to the four natures: self-nature, other-nature, common nature, and finally, spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Thus, the four natures are complete. That "nature of space" here refers to the nature of the essential substance (*tattva-svabhāva*).

Since space arises through delusion and the world-system is established based upon that space, and since even space is like a phantom existence, the nature of the world-system can be known accordingly. This is what the *Lotus Sūtra* means when it says: "To know that all phenomena are eternally without nature."

Sentient beings, within the state of non-substantiality, deludedly take [conditions] as causes and conditions, as well as an inherent nature; all of these are the conceptual constructions and calculations of the deluded mind.

Ānanda, if one knows where delusion arises, one speaks of delusive causes and conditions; yet if delusion is fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of delusive causes and conditions is itself fundamentally non-existent. How much more so for those who do not know this, but instead speculate about an inherent nature?

The Supplement states: This means that if one only knows that delusion arises from the True, then there can be said to be causes and conditions for delusive thought. However, if one can realize that delusion is itself the True, then no delusion can arise.
Then the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts would likewise be inexpressible.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has clarified for you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is, in essence, identical to deluded thought.
Zhaoxi said: "This serves to conclude what was previously discussed and to introduce what follows.

Since your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents, if your mind were not thought, it would be unable to come into the midst of thought to transmit life. As I previously stated: when the mind thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth;

when the mind thinks of climbing a high peak, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet. Even though the precipice does not exist and the vinegar has not arrived, your body must not be a false thing common to all things. How could the water in your mouth arise merely from discourse?"
Vinegar is produced. Therefore, you should know that this manifested physical body is called the first solidified false imagination (*vikalpa*).

Your substance is the physical body inherited from your parents. "Imagination" refers here to the thought of desire. When you were in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), if you had not possessed the thought of desire, you would not have been able to come into the midst of the parents' desire-thought to receive conception.

As stated below, he next cites the previous analogy used to refute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) to clarify this false imagination. Regarding the "echo in a valley": that which was previously said to arise due to the parents' thoughts—there are cases in the world where it does not [arise] due to...

Through union, a fetus arises due to thought; thus we know that the physical body is born from thought, which is all the more verifiable. *Xunwen* states: According to the *Qiānbǎo Sōushénjì*, during the end of the Han dynasty, the Governor of Lingling had a daughter who was infatuated with a clerk in the governor’s office.

She would meet him through a window, and the clerk sent a maidservant to fetch some of his consecrated water for her to drink. She subsequently became pregnant and gave birth to a son. When the child was able to walk, the governor saw him.

He had an official carry the boy into the midst of the crowd and tell him to seek out his father. The boy went straight up onto the clerk’s lap and pushed him; [the clerk] transformed into a... (text fragmentary).

The people were greatly astonished. They subsequently appointed her as a scribe for the marriage proposal. This serves to clarify that although there are differences between those who unite through causes and those who do not, all such cases arise from mental conception.

When people hear the account of the child transforming into water, they consider it strange and preposterous; yet they fail to reflect that a hundred years spent in this world are likewise like the life of this child.

To take up a physical body and form that very body is also water. Once it dies and perishes, decaying and rotting away, it returns once more to being water. If the child of Lingling were truly so startling, then all people would be equally startling.
Since that [child] was already strange, how could this not be strange as well? Born of deluded thought—how great is the Buddha’s teaching! Changshui says: "Tonglun" means "of the same kind."

This very aforementioned "mind that contemplates heights" can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness. Because sensation arises from causes, it is able to move the substance of form.
That which you now experience before you—the agitation driven by the two manifest states of the beneficial and the harmful—is called the second delusive thought, "empty clarity."

Zhaoxi said: "One should know that the three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception arise through the mutual dependence of delusive thoughts; they are necessarily inseparable. Therefore, the preceding passage states: 'Your body was originally produced from the perceptions of your parents. And the subsequent passage states:
'The mind gives rise to various grasping images, which take on physical forms. These are all like the perception of sourness upon seeing a hanging object over a precipice.

From this it is clear that the substance of these three delusive thoughts is coarse and manifest, unlike the subtle and difficult-to-perceive nature of the [aggregates of] formations and consciousness. For this reason, the celestial Māras manifested within the first three aggregates are also coarse in appearance, whereas those within the latter two aggregates..."

When the mind is aroused, two māras are perceived; their characteristics are also subtle. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: "One imagines being at a high precipice, causing a genuine sensation of sourness and astringency. This means that sensation arises from mental ideation (*saṃjñā*).

It further states that because sensation arises from its cause, it can move the physical body; this means that color-form (*rūpa*) is moved by sensation. For example, when the mind experiences a desirable object, the bodily karma moves and performs actions. The *Tiaoxi* commentary states: "From 'you now' onwards, this correctly demonstrates the characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*).

That which is favorable and beneficial is pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*); that which is adverse and harmful is painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*); that which is neither adverse nor favorable is neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).

"Regarding pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*): the text is merely abbreviated. The *Buyi* (Supplement) states: 'As for "you now, in the present," etc.,' this is because the preceding passage clarifies the matter by means of an analogy."

It is by your thoughts that you cause your physical body to act; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought? Through various grasping at forms, the mind gives rise to the taking on of shapes, corresponding with thought.

When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams. Thus, your thoughts and perceptions, which stir up deluded sentiments, are called the third false imagination, known as "interfusion."

The first two phrases restate the preceding aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). As the previous text states, "Because of sensation, one moves form," this means that it is your own thoughts and deliberations that drive your physical body.

The passage beginning with "The body is not of the same category as thought" next introduces the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Although it was said that because of the mind [driven by] sensation, one can move form and appearance, yet mind and form are of different natures;

how then can the body follow the mind? That which enables the movement of form lies in the power of perception and thought. Therefore, it is said: "Various images are grasped; the mind gives rise to them, and the form takes them up. Because they correspond to the mental conceptions, sensation moves the form. Various...

The various kinds of grasping at forms must necessarily depend on the shapes of mental conceptions (*citta-vikalpa*). When a form confronts an object, it arises; to grasp the image of that overhanging cliff, one must first have this shape within the mental conception before one can cause the body to experience the sensation of aching bitterness.

The merit lies in the conceiving mind. The phrase "awakening is immediately below" clarifies that the conceiving mind is uninterrupted. As for the term "interfusion," it is because there is no distinction between form and mind during both waking and sleeping. *Xunwen* says:

"The body is not of the same category as thought," and so forth, which correctly clarifies the meaning of the delusive discrimination of interfusion. This means that the body and thought, as well as form and mind, are two distinct things, and furthermore, they are not...

Regarding "categories": for what reason does your body correspond with thought? It is truly due to the interpenetration of deluded thoughts that this occurs. Furthermore, it is not only the physical body that is integrated;

it also extends to all dreams and sleep. Thus it is said: "When awake, the mind of thought is equal [to the dream state]. Tiaoxi says: "The mind gives rise to form and takes on shape. This means that if a mental thought arises, a physical form must be assumed.

That high-pitched, sour [dreaming] arises is the proof of its grasping. As for "awake and asleep being equal," it is because dreams are formed by thought, thereby revealing the nature of deluded念 (nian). One should remain uninterrupted in this realization.

The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and migrates in secret with every passing moment. Nails grow and hair sprouts, while vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night succeed one another, yet there is never any awakening to this process.

Ānanda, if this were not you, how could the body undergo such change? If it were truly you, why would you have no awareness of it? Thus, your various formations (saṃskāras) do not cease for even a single thought-moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought.

If this were not you, then as for the pointing out that the principle of transformation does not abide, etc., how could it be that the substance itself undergoes change? This refers to such things as the growth of nails and hair, and so forth. As stated below:

"If one claims that the changing substance is truly you, why do you not perceive this [new] characteristic replacing that [old] characteristic? Because you do not perceive it, the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is called "subtle and hidden.

The Supplement states: "The preceding passage explained the principle of transformation solely in terms of the *rūpa-skandha* (the aggregate of form); therefore, this passage universally applies the principle of the movement of transformation to all phenomena."

Furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the state of your refined clarity, profound and unmoving—does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body. If this were truly refined and authentic, it could not admit the cultivation of delusions.

For what reason, then, did you once in years past behold a strange object, such that over the passing of years there was neither memory nor forgetting; yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same former anomaly again, the memory was as vivid as ever, without the slightest loss?
Thus, within this refined awareness, profound and unmoving, there is the permeation of every thought-moment. How can this be calculated?

Zhaoxi said: "In the current text, seeing and hearing are taken as the refined clarity (*jīngmíng*), and their active functioning (*dòngyòng*) is taken as the constant essence (*chángtǐ*). Why is this so? Consciousness has no fixed location; it pervades all the sense organs (*indriya*).

When the organs encounter their objects, although they engage in activity, this activity resides within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state before good or evil has arisen. This indeterminate state is what is pointed to and named 'refined clarity,' the place that is profound and unshakable.

If one were to define its boundaries, the five sensory consciousnesses, the five mental consciousnesses, and the sixth mind-king (*citta-rāja*) are all its locations. Fearing that sentient beings might reckon this to be permanent, the Buddha first addressed Ānanda..."

Furthermore, it is stated definitively: "That which is called 'eternal'—if it were truly pure and real, it could not admit the habitual delusion. This refutes its permanence. "Purity" refers to luminous purity; "reality" is synonymous with constancy.

Regarding the phrase "for what reason," below this, the characteristics of deluded habituation are shown. "Moment by moment receiving perfuming" means that because one previously perceived objects deposited as seeds within consciousness, if these were not perfumed, then upon subsequently perceiving a different object, there would necessarily be no phenomenon of memory.

Since there is no loss of memory, we know that in the interim, [the mind] is constantly perfumed moment by moment by ignorance. Perfuming is itself delusion; how, then, can there be any such thing as pure reality?

The Supplement states: "In this section, the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is elucidated. As for the establishment of the term 'refinement' (*jingzhan*), it is because the practitioner has already sequentially observed the five aggregates and exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Since arising and ceasing have temporarily subsided, the consciousness-mind within the contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is likewise refined. This is truly because the afflictions and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have temporarily subsided due to the power of contemplation; it is not yet a case of having destroyed the delusions to manifest the principle.

Therefore, the subsequent judgment that this does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is because it still constitutes the sixth king-number [the mind-king]. The analogy of beholding a singular object and forgetting it over many years is like the subsiding of delusions.
This is its characteristic. That you perceive it as being perfectly clear is because delusion arises and thus its profound clarity is lost.

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not true; it is like a rapid stream that appears tranquil from a distance—the swift current is not seen, yet it is not that there is no flow. If this were not the source of thought, how could it receive the habitual tendencies of delusion?

It is not through the mutual functioning, merging, or opening of your six sense faculties that these false imaginings can ever be extinguished. Therefore, within your present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the degree to which you are habituated to them determines the state of that stillness.

Having realized that the internal is formless, void, and non-existent—namely, the fifth stage of inverted, subtle, and refined conceptualization, such as the mutual functioning of the six sense organs—one begins to destroy the *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions of views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions of thought).

Thus, deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is extinguished; this is precisely when the coarse defilements first fall away. Question: In the preceding passage, it was stated that "receiving perfuming" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, you say that deluded conceptualization is extinguished; why stop at merely [extinguishing] views and thoughts? Answer: That which is perfumed by ignorance also contains the seeds of views and thoughts. Therefore, the previous reference to perceiving objects and having recollection or forgetfulness was precisely the coarse [level].

[The interlocutor asks: "Regarding the characteristics [of the faculties]: although their seeds and manifestations have now been exhausted, the fundamental [nature] still remains. This does not mean that the six faculties have attained true mutual functioning. [The Master] asks:

"This Śūraṅgama Samādhi is perfect in its essence and ultimate in its principle. Why, then, is its power and function so limited when it comes to destroying the *skandhas*? [The Master] answers: "It is not that the power and function do not accord with the essence and principle. It is because, among the fifty stages of demonic states analyzed therein, all arise from the deluded thoughts of the five *skandhas* of the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm.

Since the discussion here concludes at this point regarding their cessation, it only extends to the mutual functioning of the six faculties. If, as in the preceding text, one reverses the flow and returns to the oneness of the whole, then the six functions..."
This is not the case. It immediately destroys fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is distinct from the inverted deluded thoughts (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*) discussed here. *Xunwen* states:

"For the time being, regarding those whose pervasive afflictions have not yet been eliminated, whatever is perfumed constitutes the seeds of the household of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*). This is an example of what Jingxi said: "Prior to the purification of the six sense faculties, all mental factors (*caitta*) are termed the mental factors of the household of view-delusion and thought-delusion.

Since there is both recollection and forgetfulness, they are further called deluded thoughts; how could they be anything other than coarse? Moreover, when one reaches the stage of the purity of the six sense faculties, these characteristics cease, thereby making their coarseness even more evident.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of deluded conceptualization.

If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form; only contact and separation constitute the limit of sensation; only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception;
only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into the merging with the profound constitutes the limit of consciousness.

The Supplement states: Within each of the five aggregates (*skandha*), there are their respective causal realms (*dhātu*). Form (*rūpa*) is superficial while consciousness (*vijñāna*) is profound. Changshui says:

"Only form and emptiness" refers to form as shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) and emptiness as manifest-color (*vyañjana-rūpa*); both are subsumed within the aggregate of form. Because false form and false emptiness mutually manifest one another, [the text] briefly cites form and emptiness to encompass all phenomena.

This is explained by correlating the dependent with the primary. According to the Fourth [Chapter]: "You see empty space pervading the ten directions; space and seeing are not distinguished. There is space but no substance; there is seeing but no awareness. Their mutual interweaving of delusion is named a kalpa."

"Turbidity. Furthermore, the ninth [section] says: "If the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, one can transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Therefore, we now know that when it speaks of "form," it must be shown in contrast to external form as the objective environment (*niśraya-vipāka*).

Zizhong says: "Contact and separation are sensation (*vedanā*). Contact involves suffering and pleasure, while separation results in equanimity (*upekṣā*); both are termed sensation. Zhenjì says: "'Remembering and forgetting' refers to perception (*saṃjñā*).

Remembering and forgetting, grasping at images, and clinging to objects are all the domain of perception. "Remembering and forgetting" may also be said such that remembering is like waking and forgetting is like sleeping. Tiāoxī says: "Arising and ceasing are formations (*saṃskāra*)."

These three characteristics of flux all belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The mention of "arising and ceasing" (*utpāda-nirodha*) here is a brief illustration intended to encompass "alteration" (*anyathātva*).
